# Runtime architecture

This document owns the shape of the runtime: what the Rust core holds, what the shell may do, what the engine keeps for itself, and the decisions that were made when those boundaries were crossed the wrong way.
"The shell" means the web shell (`web/`) drawn by hided's snapshot, whether that page is open in a browser or inside the Electron desktop host (`desktop/`).
Read it in full before changing anything under `hide-core/`, `hided/`, `web/` or `desktop/`.
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) keeps the short form of the ownership split; this is the long form with the reasons.
The code is the executable authority: `hide-core/src/` for the core, `hided/src/` for the daemon that hosts it, `web/src/` for the shell, `desktop/src/main/` for the desktop host, and the tests beside each.

## Product usage statistics

The core owns the persisted `ui_state.product_analytics_enabled` choice, default true; Settings changes it with `product_analytics_set`, and generic UI saves cannot overwrite it.
The web shell emits `product_analytics_connected` once after its first snapshot per page lifetime, without recounting WebSocket reconnects.
`hide_agent_started` counts native agent conversations, not panes, turns or launches: the link worker sends it when `apply_panes` writes `pane_first_at` on a `links.sqlite3` session row that had none, the first time any Hide pane on any device carried that session, whether the operator typed the agent or `hide agent spawn` started it.
It names who started the agent in `source`, read under the runtime lock when the event is sent: `mission` when the live delivery registration on the session's pane is a mission node's worker or one of its checkers, `spawn` when that registration has a parent or is a handoff (`origin` set on a registration that is not a fork), and `operator` otherwise, a fork and a pane with no registration included; `source` is left out when the delivery ledger cannot be read or no pane carries the session any more.
The column outlives the daemon, so a restart, a reboot that restores panes, a released tab attached again, a window reload, a resume or a wake of the same session finds it set and sends nothing; a shell pane carries no session and sends nothing.
The worker applies the pane facts as soon as their set changes and again every 60 seconds, so the event lags the core learning the pane's session by at most one link-worker pass.
Version 11 of the store marks every session row it already held, so an upgrade sends nothing for sessions seen before it.
Two recounts are accepted: a row that retention or an archive delete removes is first again if a pane carries that session later, and a store set aside as corrupt and rebuilt counts the sessions its panes then carry once more.
`hide_mission_started` is sent when `hide mission start` moves a mission from planning to running, with `nodes`, the plan's node count as `1`, `2-3`, `4-7` or `8+`.
`hide_mission_ended` is sent by a running mission's first close (`close_mission_with`), with `outcome` `done`, `merge_wait` or `cancelled`; a mission cancelled while still planning, a reopened mission that closes again, and a waiting mission that later lands as done send nothing, so every end has one start.
`hide_practice` is sent when `practice_progress_set` first writes a chapter (`stage` `started`) and when a chapter's progress first turns finished (`stage` `finished`), with `chapter` one of `mission`, `overview`, `agents`, `find` or `project`; a replay keeps the chapter's progress and finished state, so each stage counts once per installation, and a chapter id that module does not spell sends nothing.
`hide_phone_paired` is sent by the daemon when a phone pairs (`mobile::Mobile::pair`), with `route` `relay` or `tailnet` from Mobile's exposure at that moment; the daemon hands it to the owner thread's worker through `CoreHandle::capture_product_event`, and a refused pairing sends nothing.
`hide_active` is sent the first time in a UTC calendar day that the operator acts from a surface, with `surface` `desktop` or `phone`, so a window left open for days counts each day it is used and a paired phone that keeps being used counts apart from its pairing.
The desktop's actions are the operator's own input reaching the core from a window: an input fact a node reports for keys or a paste a screen typed into a pane (`TerminalReport::Input`, which the engine's own input, a letter, a phone's write and an agent never produce), and a Desk message (`desk_send`, which only the Desk composer sends).
The phone's actions are the messages an operator sends by acting in the phone app (`mobile::phone::operator_action`: `input`, `wake_agent`, `human_turn_done`, `answer_mission`, `ask_mission_material`, `reopen_mission_view`, `merge_pr`, `delegate_pr`, `wake_sleeping_session`, `start_agent`), which the daemon hands to the core through `CoreHandle::note_operator_active`; opening or reading an agent, a ping and a notification registration, which the app sends on its own when it opens or reconnects, are not.
An app that is merely open, a reconnect, a snapshot, a resize the shell makes and the work agents do send nothing.
The core keeps the UTC day each surface last sent in the saved core state (`product_active_days`, days since the Unix epoch, never on the snapshot wire, kept against generic UI saves), so a restart, a reload or a reconnect the same day sends nothing and any other day sends again; the day is recorded only while statistics are on and a transport exists, so turning them back on the same day still counts it.
Until the day turns, an action costs two flag reads and one day comparison under the lock the input fact or event already holds (`Runtime::note_operator_active`).
`hide-core/src/product_analytics.rs` admits only `hide_connected`, `hide_agent_started`, `hide_device_connected`, `hide_mission_started`, `hide_mission_ended`, `hide_practice`, `hide_phone_paired` and `hide_active`, spells every property key and value in `Event::properties`, and accepts no caller-supplied properties; the agent is a `hide_session::Agent`, and a kind the session reader does not name sends nothing.
The daemon's `product_analytics` worker sends those event names, a random installation UUID, an event UUID and timestamp to PostHog US over TLS.
Every event's properties are exactly `distinct_id`, `$process_person_profile: false`, `$geoip_disable: true`, `$ip: null`, `app_version` (the build's `HIDE_BUILD_VERSION`, which `hide --version` reports) and `os` (`macos`, `linux` or `windows`, fixed by the compile target); `hide_agent_started` adds `agent`, one of `codex`, `claude`, `grok`, `pi`, `omp`, `cursor`, `opencode` or `antigravity`, spelled in that module, and `source`; the mission, practice, phone and active events add only the properties named above.
`hide_device_connected` adds only `outcome` (`ready` or `failed`) and `platform` (`linux-x86_64`, `linux-aarch64`, `macos-x86_64`, `macos-aarch64` or `unknown` when establishment has not reported an allowlisted system).
A failed event adds `failed_step` (`install` or `download`) and `failure`, the failure's class, never its text, which carries host names, addresses and paths.
`failure` is `download` for a release kit that could not be acquired, which alone has `failed_step` `download`; every other class has `install`.
An `ssh` that did not connect is `ssh_` and the device row's classification: `ssh_sign_in_needed`, `ssh_browser_timeout`, `ssh_sign_in_refused`, `ssh_policy_refused`, `ssh_host_key_changed`, `ssh_name_not_found`, `ssh_unreachable`, `ssh_proxy_failed`, `ssh_unsupported`, `ssh_missing`, `ssh_openssh_old`, `ssh_hide_updated` or `ssh_unclassified`.
The rest are `machine_stopped` (the machine is off and the attempt could not start it), `connect` (the helper could not be reached on the opened connection), `identity_changed` (another machine answers the address), `unsupported` (this build cannot serve the device's system), `install` and `helper` (the helper could not be installed or did not start), `no_transport` (the registration's SSH config or id gave no connection), `worker_unavailable` (this core could not start the connecting worker), `helper_lost` (the link ended before the kit pass finished), `kit_refused`, `kit_failed` and `machine_name` (the machine id the device reports does not name its registration).
Inbound nodes that dial this core perform no outbound bootstrap and are outside this event.
The runtime admits one token per outbound helper establish or bootstrap Retry, associates it with the host generation, and consumes it before capture at the final bootstrap or Apply result.
Only the first Apply claims a token; status polls, snapshots, duplicate completions and superseded generations cannot recapture it, while reconnects and Retry admit a fresh token.
A Retry after a failed start reconnects the device, so the reconnect's token is the one that Retry settles; a Retry of a refused kit admits its own token for the Apply.
Cancellation, consent withdrawal and removal discard pending tokens; at most 128 attempts are retained, with a content-free diagnostic at the cap.
A settled outcome, its `failure` class included, is sent only when it differs from the outcome last sent for that device in this daemon's life, so a device that stays unreachable sends one failure however often its scheduled retry runs, and a reconnect that is ready again after the device slept sends nothing.
Removing the device forgets that last outcome; at most 128 devices' last outcomes are kept, and a device beyond the cap is sent every time, with a content-free diagnostic.
Capture uses the existing bounded Sink under the short runtime admission, with no network, disk, subprocess or new worker on that path; opt-out drops the outcome without replay.
No prompt, response, conversation, code, path, file name, session id, mission title or plan, pull request, provider, model, project name, token count, account identity, device or phone name or local usage ledger enters that transport.
The private `product-analytics-id` file under the core state directory holds the random UUID; it derives from neither the account nor hardware, and remains stable across restarts and moves with the core's state.
The server necessarily observes the connection's source IP; project-side Discard client IP data complements the event flags, and this design does not assert that the events are legally anonymous or that opt-out is sufficient in every jurisdiction.
The owning operator must disclose the purpose, data fields, US destination and opt-out in the product's privacy notice, and assess prior consent where applicable.
The public privacy notice is `site/public/privacy.html` (withhide.dev/privacy); an event's name or fields change its event table in the same pull request, and `site/tests/legal.test.mjs` fails when the table and `Event::name` differ.
One worker waits on a condition variable, retains at most 128 events in memory, sends one at a time with a five-second global HTTP timeout and no redirects, retries or disk spool, and drops pending events on opt-out or shutdown.
Its owner joins it outside `Mutex<Runtime>`; transport failure, a full queue or an invalid identity produces a content-free diagnostic and cannot block a provider request or turn into a user alert.
An already-started send may finish after opt-out; nothing observed while disabled is retained or replayed on re-enable.
The worker is enabled from persisted state before the core starts its background work; an absent build token, a privileged device fixture HOME or a HOME carrying `~/.hide/product-analytics-disabled` starts no transport.
All browser/desktop and package smoke fixture homes write that disable-only marker on every system; it grants no fixture service-control authority.
See [the build input](BUILD.md#product-analytics-build-input) and [Settings](UI_BEHAVIOR.md#privacy); transport tests use a real loopback HTTP peer and pin each event's exact properties, a core test restarts on the same state to show one session counts once and names each source, core tests show a mission's start and first close and a practice chapter's two stages count once, a core test shows `hide_active` counts each surface's first action of a UTC day once across a restart, again on a new day, never for what the app does on its own and never while statistics are off, and the Settings journey restarts the daemon after an opt-out.

## State placement and publication

The standalone `hide-relay` service owns its room membership, connection routing, admission windows and byte counters in one memory-only state object.
It does not link the core, read a credential store or persist state; protocol endpoints alone own Noise keys and ciphertext authentication.
Its listener owns every connection task, each task owns its registration and bounded output queue, and dropping or stopping the service retires them all.
[RELAY_PROTOCOL.md](RELAY_PROTOCOL.md#server-budgets-and-refusals) owns the refusal, restart and resource bounds, with real socket regressions in `hide-relay/tests/it`.

The front Workspace's Git header is ephemeral core state (`runtime/checkout_git.rs`), projected only into that device/path's `workspace_view.git`, never persisted or inferred from visibility-gated Changes rows.
The existing Changes pump drives two single-flight `BackgroundRead` readers (`checkout_git.rs`): one owning-node `Call::CheckoutGit` for the whole checkout, and one core-node exact-SHA GitHub read using fixed allowlisted arguments.
Changing the target or channel advances a generation; ingests compare that identity and the CI repository and complete ordered SHA list before publishing, while a HEAD change immediately clears the preceding CI result.
The core consumes the node's configured origin URL into a private validated provider repository identity and removes the raw URL before retaining or publishing header facts, so URL userinfo never reaches the renderer.
The node performs one porcelain-v2 no-renames status and one log read of its captured exact HEAD, with no base comparison or inactive checkout scan; status output is capped at 8 MiB, the newest five commits together at 64 KiB, and overflow is unavailable, never clean.
Git reads run off-lock at two-second intervals and a three-second node budget; only changed facts, failure/recovery, target changes or freshness transitions notify, and successful identical reads renew an internal deadline without publishing a frame.
CI reads GitHub's aggregate statusCheckRollup for at most five exact SHAs in one fixed allowlisted GraphQL query, with oid and returned commit URL validated against each request identity; provider errors remain unavailable.
One request every 30 seconds is retained only for the front target, with one node `gh` command bounded at 15 seconds and one link wait at 20 seconds.
The pump joins both admitted readers outside Runtime's mutex on shutdown; a superseded read may finish within that bound and its answer is discarded, with no additional job queued for each intermediate selection.
Five seconds without a successful Git observation marks retained data stale; CI ages at 90 seconds and a disconnected shell also labels retained state stale locally.

The read axis's look has one owner, `hide-core/src/runtime/look.rs`: its three inputs, the focus pane the operator chose, the device in front and the agents phones have open, are written only through its setters, and `Runtime::change_look` is the one boundary a selection completes at.
The look is compared once at the outermost selection's end, under the lock that selection already holds, so a worker that moves the look after its own change has it read in that change, with no thread, timer or list of entries to keep.
`navigator.focused_device_id` is the front's projection on the wire, written with it and never read for a decision; `docs/status-model.md`, Hide owns the read axis, owns the rule and its regression tests.

Choose the authority, publication need and durability of a value separately before adding a field, store or worker.
`Mutex<Runtime>` serializes Hide's accepted domain and UI transitions; it is not the place to perform the reads, writes or analyses that produce them.
An off-lock store remains core-owned and must name its scope, freshness rule, resource bound and shutdown owner; a second copy in the shell cannot become an authority.

| Decision | Placement and allowed work | Existing precedent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A value decides the accepted UI or domain transition | Keep the authoritative in-memory value in `Runtime`; admit one typed event and apply a completed worker result under a short lock. | [Stored primary checkout](#stored-primary-checkout), [Workspaces in the web shell](#workspaces-in-the-web-shell); `runtime/workspace_view.rs`. |
| Producing a value needs filesystem, SQLite, network, a subprocess or substantial analysis | Take owned request data under the lock, perform the work in the existing reader/worker boundary, and validate scope or generation when applying the result. | [Project sessions and Memory](#project-sessions-and-memory), [Agent labels in the core](#agent-labels-in-the-core); `runtime/memory.rs`, `labels/analyzer.rs`, `reader.rs`. |
| A transition changes what the operator can see | Publish the changed state through the existing coalescing notifier; a wake, unchanged read or repeated observation alone is not a reason to publish. | [The core, the shell and Herdr](#the-core-the-shell-and-herdr); `handle.rs::ChangeNotifier`, `session_sync/coordinator.rs::agent_tick_needs_publish`. |
| A value must survive restart but is not a screen transition | Save it without publishing a new frame merely to announce the save. | [Agent sleep](#agent-sleep): the last-look stamp is saved when visited and on its minute pass; `runtime/agent_sleep.rs::tick_agent_sleep`. |
| Time passing can be derived from an accepted value | Publish the reference time once and derive the display in memory. | [Agent labels in the core](#agent-labels-in-the-core): `last_prompt_at_unix_ms` and the shared elapsed clock in `web/src/components/elapsed.tsx`. |
| Accepted UI state needs persistence | Reuse the coalesced save: one active worker and one pending flag per store, copying state under the lock and serializing, writing, syncing and renaming outside it. | [Projects and Overview cost contract](PERFORMANCE_TESTING.md#projects-and-overview-cost-contract); `runtime/agents.rs`, `runtime/workspace_view.rs`, `persistence.rs`, `workspace_views.rs`. |

On a high-frequency path such as keystroke ingress, added observational work is limited to bounded in-memory writes.
It must not introduce lock waiting, disk access, a subprocess or large serialization into that path.
The existing short Runtime admission is not permission to add another contended lock or blocking observer; pass owned data to an existing off-lock owner when work needs those resources.
Snapshot capture takes immutable typed sections under the lock and `handle.rs::snapshot_delta_payload` transfers them out of the core owner thread.
The WebSocket transport encodes the selected sections and its envelope once on a blocking transport worker; internal roots and phone followers use the retained typed state without decoding transport bytes.
Each rest field has its own revision and `Arc`, with navigator selection and lists, terminal metadata fields and status fields stamped independently; an unchanged value keeps its allocation and a changed value alone is copied.
Usage lives in its own top-level snapshot section, revisioned independently of navigation; later deltas carry it only when limits or ledger values change.
An omitted usage section preserves the previous value; an empty `nodes` array clears it, and a future revision cursor resets to a full snapshot.
The shell stores usage separately, so a usage-only delta preserves navigation identity and an unrelated menu or layout change neither serializes nor compares historical day arrays.
Pane input never enters the coalesced persistence queue: it must not be dropped or merged to reduce observer cost.
The save workers' pending flags bound the number of pending saves, not the byte size of the saved state; these stores have no general serialized-byte cap.
`Core::drop` joins the UI and Workspace-view save workers outside the mutex, but forced termination cannot promise a pending save reached disk (`handle.rs`).
Before adding resident work, use the [tick/timer/watcher ledger and cost review](PERFORMANCE_TESTING.md#resident-ticks-timers-and-watchers).

### Sidebar tab names

`TabSnapshot.sidebar` serializes the existing `TabNaming` as a manual name and stable tab number, using the same automatic-number convention as the tabbar.
The automatic task label remains the tabbar's own projection; the shell never guesses a sidebar name from that label.
The shell derives physical agent counts from the snapshot and keeps a root's complete subtree under that root's tab, even for cross-tab or cross-device children.
`CheckoutSnapshot.agent_groups` publishes all named and ungrouped memberships, draft identities and start receipts independently of the one group drawn in `workspace_view.agent_layout`.
The sidebar joins these memberships to real tabs and agents, so a hidden group's tabs, empty groups, drafts and terminal-only tabs remain reachable without a second membership store in the shell.
Group disclosure is page-local presentation; group selection and tab membership are core state, and opening a tab or pane selects its owning group and area in the same navigation transition.
A tab has no disclosure state: the former `sidebar_collapsed_tabs` field and its `sidebar_tab_expanded` event are gone, and a state file that still carries the field loads without error and loses it on the next save.
Deriving sidebar rows adds no event, I/O, timer or subprocess to typing or terminal echo; group mutations save through the existing Workspace-view owner described below.

### View openers and comments

Who opened a View and the operator's comments on Views are core state (PRD view-opener-feedback, `hide-core/src/view_feedback.rs`, `hide-core/src/runtime/view_feedback.rs`).
A View's opener lives on its display in `workspace-views.json`, kept by device, terminal id, native session and provider, never by pane id; the pane is found again from terminal and session each time a snapshot is made, and an opener found nowhere is shown closed.
It is written only by a workspace control open whose pane caller Hide proved and by a terminal-link open that carries the clicked pane, and a navigate the operator types clears it; a caller with no proven pane writes none, which `opener.none` in the diagnostic log records with its reason.
A checkout's comments live beside its Views in the same file under `feedback`, saved by the existing coalesced save: at most 50 per View and 500 per checkout, each note at most 4000 characters, each quoted range at most 20 lines, checked in the core; each add, edit, delete, undo, relocate and Send is one event.
The workspace-view snapshot carries `feedback` only while there are comments or a Send to say: the comments of the Views on screen, the recipient groups, the opened Views per pane, and the last Send's state; each display carries its unsent count.
Finding a comment's lines again after a save is the shell's work on the text it already holds, reported once per change as a `relocate` event, so nothing reads a file for it under the lock or on a keystroke.
A Send runs on one feedback worker off the lock with at most 64 jobs: it reads the screenshots from the node that staged them, places them on the recipient's node, then stores the letter as the operator ([delivery.md](delivery.md#the-operators-view-feedback)); no screenshot byte passes through an event, the lock or a snapshot.
Before the core, hided keeps each operator window's comments and Sends on one queue per window, at most 256 waiting and four of them with a screenshot: it stages a comment's screenshot off the socket loop and hands the events to the core in the order the window made them, so a Send never overtakes the comment before it, and a full queue is refused to that window as an error.
The worker waits on a moving core's effect hold, and the comments, openers and waiting Sends travel with the move like the rest of `workspace-views.json`.

## The core, the shell and Herdr

The core (`hide-core`) owns all state behind one `Mutex<Runtime>`.
The core speaks to the program that runs its panes through one engine boundary, `hide-core/src/engine/` (PRD engine-bundle-1 D-2): the `Engine` trait asks for pane existence, layout, zoom, focus, input, reads, process facts, agent starts and metadata, one call per method, never under the runtime lock, and `EngineError` keeps the kinds a caller branches on (nothing ran, the engine refused, the request or answer did not fit, or the call was sent and its outcome is unknown, `Unanswered`).
Its one implementation is the core's own engine (`engine/own/`), which runs a machine's panes in pane holders and is the engine every daemon builds ([The core's own engine](#the-cores-own-engine)); the Herdr implementation, its wire types and its client were deleted with the rest of Hide's Herdr code (PRD engine-bundle-4-herdr-removal D-2, D-18).
`Core::create` takes the local engine as `own_engine`, a connected device's link becomes its own engine when the device connects, and the runtime holds each as a `SharedEngine`.
hided asks the same engine off the owner thread through `EngineHandle`, which the core handle builds once and shares with the core: a pane's proof before a credential (`pane_auth`), a phone's read of a pane and its input, and the idle probe; a device's handle comes from the core (`Core::device_engine`).
An agent's `hide pane` and `hide agent read` commands, `hide workspace purpose` and a `--force` letter's composer read take the engine of the machine they act on from the runtime, under its lock, and call it on the caller's task ([delivery.md](delivery.md#pane-commands)).
Terminal bytes (`TerminalRoutes`) and a machine's own work (`NodeLink`) are outside the boundary and do not pass through it.
`hide-core/src/engine/contract.rs` holds the engine contract: what a caller observes of an engine (a pane made, read, written and closed; a tab zoomed, resized, swapped, a pane moved out and back, a tab exported and applied again, a layout past the limits refused; a refusal under its code; an outcome left unknown).
The core's own engine runs it over pane holders this node starts from the built holder (`HIDE_TEST_HOLDER_BIN`); the test is ignored by default and the real-shell steps of `pr.yml` run it on Linux and Windows.
The shell dispatches typed JSON events in and receives snapshot and delta frames out over hided's WebSocket (see hided and the WebSocket boundary) when the change notifier announces.
An engine says how its changes reach the coordinator (`Engine::changes`): the core's own engine wakes the coordinator, which reads its whole session again; nothing is replayed, so there is no event stream, replica or subscription to keep in step ([The core's own engine](#the-cores-own-engine)).
The coordinator waits on its existing mailbox until the next operation tick or a deadline active for its connection: reconnect while disconnected, the moment a pending agent start can settle (`ProjectionState::settles_at`), and only the operation tick for a connected engine.
Inactive deadlines may remain in the past; they never shorten the wait, and a message, including Stop, still wakes it immediately.
The coordinator (`session_sync/coordinator.rs`) reads the session with `Engine::session` (`session_sync/pulled.rs`) on connect and on each wake, and publishes it through `publish_session`.
A read equal to the last one published, which an engine wake brought, publishes nothing, so an idle session recomputes no projection; a wake the core asked for (`RepublishWaker::asking`: it drew something ahead of the engine, or took it back) always publishes.
The session-sync thread that applies the engine's changes never blocks on anything else (PRD instant-pane-topology D-13): a socket read that opens its own connection, a subprocess, an HTTP request or an fsync runs on a worker or a save thread; `lsof` and the Codex usage request run on their readers' `BackgroundRead` threads, and the label store writes `labels.json` on its own thread.
Their output and intervals are what they were before the move.
Session-sync requests use a one-second read/write timeout for this machine's engine and three seconds for a remote device, including a node that dials this core (`SessionSyncContext::request_timeout`).
The same target-specific timeout covers the session read.
These waits stay on the existing off-lock readers, with no extra retry, timer or pending-work slot; each remote socket read/write wait can last two seconds longer, sequential batches accumulate those waits, and the existing failure classification is unchanged.
A failed session read is published as the session's failure, and the coordinator reads again on its reconnect schedule: 100 ms after a successful connect, doubling to 5 s (`RECONNECT_INITIAL_DELAY`, `RECONNECT_MAX_DELAY`).
No user mutation is retried by this read recovery.
Agent labels are made by the core itself and shown only for the session they were proven for; see Agent labels in the core under hided and the WebSocket boundary, and [status-model.md](status-model.md#task-identity) for how they reach a row.
Tab names use core focus and the same agent row as the sidebar; each pane's foreground process name arrives with the session read (`ProjectedPane::foreground_process`), so no separate reader runs for it.
`rename_tab` keeps retry intent separate from the committed label; only the engine's success commits it, and a refusal or timeout preserves the prior label and a request-correlated inline retry result.
A worker that changed the engine can read the session itself and hand that read to the core (a project's creation does), and that read can be ahead of the next session the coordinator publishes, which can still describe the engine from before the read.
A pane absent from that later session is not a close: taking that absence as one forgot the pane at its node with the size its view had reported, so keys typed into it waited for a view that would not report again (with-hide/hide-private#464).
So the core keeps the terminal of each pane a read of its own showed (a session without tab moves, such as the creation worker's) until a session the coordinator publishes first lays it out or a later read of its own no longer shows it, at most 5 s and 64 panes (`runtime/read_ahead.rs`), and only then does the pane's absence retire it.
A separate 250 ms coordinator tick advances every bounded asynchronous operation, so an acknowledgement or topology wait reaches its deadline even when the engine reports no change.
Before the coordinator's first path answer, a registered checkout's empty tab list cannot prune its saved Agent area layout, and a saved selection whose pane still exists keeps its restore hint until the path facts settle its checkout.
Only an unknown directory of the saved pane holds that restore choice; another pane's unanswered directory cannot delay a known restore or keep a removed checkout selected.
An answered missing path or a pane the engine no longer holds is still a removal; the absence of an answer alone is not.
A publish whose catalog inputs did not move costs nothing per agent, tab or checkout beyond the projection itself (D-18): the catalog is rebuilt only when the registrations, the session's spaces or the worktrees change or its refresh window passes, the purpose mirror is synced only when that catalog or the unconfirmed created purposes change, and the core compares paths by their names while the node resolves them, repositories and branch notes included, only when the set of paths asked changes or the catalog's refresh passes (`workspace::PathIndex`), so an agent status change repeats none of them and the worktree projection under the lock walks no path.
The node's answer for the paths asked stands until that set changes or the refresh passes, so a path created or relinked inside that window is read as the node last answered for up to `CATALOG_REFRESH_INTERVAL`.
While the answer for a new set is pending, the coordinator builds from its last answers unless they cannot place a registration of this machine that the runtime's answers can: a project's creation installs answers that place it (`ingest_workspace_creation`), and a catalog from older ones would draw the new project at its bare path, without its repository's tabs and under No agents, until the node answered (`paths_to_build_from` in `session_sync/coordinator.rs`).
The Git context refreshes local worktree state when a watched Git HEAD, index or ref changes, or the session's worktree topology changes; content-only working-tree edits wait for the next of those.
Worktree and pull request readers run outside the runtime mutex, and a changed repository reuses the other projects' cached answers.
While the Overview's Projects tab is visible it sends `disk_watch {workspace_ids}` with the projects in the order it shows them, and `[]` when it is hidden (`hide-core/src/runtime/disk_sweep.rs`): the core measures them one at a time on the sweep reader beside the right panel's request, every worktree and the shared Git directory of a project in one measurement that counts each inode once, keeps each answer by path while the daemon runs and treats it as fresh for ten minutes, and never measures a device it dials; each workspace row carries the result as `disk`, absent from the wire until measured, with `measuring`, `queued` and the last size kept beside a failure's reason.
Selecting a checkout re-measures its project for the right panel.
The measurement runs on the checkouts' node and sorts each checkout's blocks into build cache, dependencies, worktree source and other (`hide-host/src/disk_layers.rs`), and the workspace row's `disk` adds the volume's free space and the project's layer totals; folder paths stay in the core and never reach the wire.
The disk cleanup sheet reuses the merged-worktree cleanup events: `cleanup_review {workspace_id}` reviews one Git project of C's or of a node that dials C (an M project's runs on M, see [A core on another machine](#a-core-on-another-machine)), `cleanup_confirm {id, paths, cells}` empties the chosen build cache and dependency cells and removes the chosen worktrees after closing their panes through the delete path's pane close, and the review, progress and result ride the reviewed project's `cleanup` snapshot, one active cleanup per daemon.
Pull requests are read for every registered local Git project from the moment a window attaches (at most 64), asked for again five minutes after the project's last answer (30 seconds, doubling to five minutes, after a read that failed), and refreshed from a project's menu or PR popover; all of these reuse the same background reader, cache and generation coalescing.
A repository whose remotes name nothing `gh` could read is answered "no GitHub remote" with no `gh` call, from the remotes its node reads with the catalog's path facts (`PathFacts::remotes`, from the same config read as the branch notes, the repository each remote names and never its URL), and is asked again only when those remotes change or on a refresh; see [status-model.md](status-model.md#github-status-in-the-workspace-row).
A pull request a local agent's session prints the address of, and that the last answer does not hold, has its project read without waiting for the five-minute re-read: the local label worker's read keeps each such sighting under fifteen minutes old (32 at most between hand-offs), and the coordinator passes them to `Runtime::read_sighted_pull_requests` under the brief lock that hands the worker the pull request times back; see [status-model.md](status-model.md#github-status-in-the-workspace-row) for which project is read and when.
The last successful answer per project is saved to `github-snapshot.json` in the state folder by a store thread of its own (`github_store.rs`: one thread, one pending slot, an atomic replacement through `hide_platform::fs`, joined when the runtime drops) and restored before the first frame as stale, so a restart shows the previous run's pull requests until the first read replaces them; see [status-model.md](status-model.md#github-status-in-the-workspace-row).
The Changes reader is also the only Git-status owner for Explorer decorations: it reads the checkout in front, on this machine or a device, while a renderer is attached and Explorer or Changes is visible or a diff tab or new-tab page needs it, and publishes one root-scoped changed-file set for every surface.
With no renderer attached it reads nothing, and the Explorer watch in hided stamps nothing (`WatchService::set_drawn`, set with the core's `ui_attached`); the selection the operator left is kept, so the first renderer back reads the same checkout again.
The read is `Call::Changes` to that checkout's host (`hide-host/src/git.rs`), which runs Git with its working directory at the opened root, normalizes rename and conflict state, and answers only the registered folder's paths; the reader (`changes.rs`) runs it on a `BackgroundRead` thread every two seconds or on a changed request, driven by its own pump (`ChangesPump`) that the core starts once rather than by a session's coordinator; a device helper that failed is not asked again by the refresh.
The background fetch (PRD git-freshness) is the core's too: `runtime/fetch.rs` decides under the lock which registered repository each node fetches next and keeps what its last fetch said, and `fetch.rs` (`FetchPump`, started once like `ChangesPump`) asks the node that holds the repository with `Call::FetchRemote`, one per node at a time, so a device's repository is fetched on that device with its credentials and nothing runs under the lock or on the session-sync thread; the node's answer only moves remote-tracking refs, and the Git facts watcher's own re-read brings the new counts and incoming commits to the header.
The Explorer tree (`web/src/ExplorerTree.tsx`) derives file and ancestor-folder decorations from that snapshot in memory; it never starts Git from a row, scroll, hover, or paint.
Pane output never enters the runtime; it goes from the pane's node to the screen (see The terminal path).
Everything the shell renders comes from that one snapshot pull.
The shell decodes it strictly: one string value it does not know fails the whole decode, the bridge keeps its last good frame, and every later notification repeats the failure until the two sides agree, so an unknown value is a stalled shell, not a blank field.
The string enums the core serializes into the snapshot are therefore pinned in `contracts/snapshot-wire-enums.json`; `model.rs` tests that each variant emits the listed value and `SnapshotWireEnumTests` that each listed value decodes, so a variant added on one side fails a suite before it can reach a running shell (a `PullRequestTitle` origin once shipped as `pull_request_title` against a shell that read `pr_title`).
The bridge publishes `bridgeError` only on change and names the coding path in it, because a repeated failure republished every notification rebuilt every view observing the bridge at the notification rate.

## Stored primary checkout

A local registered project stores `primary_checkout_id` on its `WorkspaceRegistration` in `core-state.json`.
An absent choice keeps the root default for existing registrations; a stored choice remains stored while its checkout is unavailable.
The single `set_primary_checkout` event carries `{workspace_id, checkout_id}`, sent by a checkout row's `Set as default checkout`, and accepts only an existing checkout of that registered local Git project.
Missing projects or checkouts, plain folders and remote registrations are refused with a diagnostic, without changing the selection or presenting an alert.
The catalog projects `CheckoutSnapshot.is_primary` after assigning registration identities and adding Git worktrees; sorting and inactive folding consume that flag, and the web reads it for the house glyph rather than comparing paths.
A change updates the accepted catalog immediately, so stale worker results cannot restore the old choice, then uses the existing coalesced off-lock UI save.
An unchanged choice publishes and saves nothing; there is no additional worker, subprocess, timer or queue.
Checkout fields remain in the hand-maintained `web/src/snapshot.ts` shape; the WebSocket frame generator does not generate this part of the core snapshot.
SSH catalogs currently read the device's session and the device helper, not another hided core's registrations, so they retain the remote root default and do not synchronize a primary choice stored by another daemon.

## Project sessions and Memory

Moved to a private document: `docs/project-sessions-and-memory.md` in with-hide/hide-private.

## Moving a live pane

`runtime/pane_move.rs` admits one typed intent with captured checkout, device, group, source and destination references, reserving both participating tabs before any native mutation.
It saves its intent in the existing Workspace view journal off the render lock and waits for the durable acknowledgement before using the engine's move and swap primitives.
It never reconstructs a terminal by applying a layout (`Engine::apply_layout`).
A same-tab move uses a bounded temporary tab; intermediate topology stays behind the reservation while the terminal projection remains attached.
Creating a destination tab reserves a slot in the same 64-tab admission count as ordinary tab creation, including an unresolved move after reconnect.
Ambiguous answers and recovered pending journals query native placement instead of resending a possibly completed effect.
The final native snapshot remains the affected tabs' publication baseline until the coordinator starts a newer authoritative bootstrap, so a queued older read cannot undo the committed placement or release its terminal.
That bootstrap is a read, never a replay of the move, and its newer topology can retire a terminal another client subsequently closed.
The move follows terminal identity into the pane's new place, and preserves the xterm instance under the new routing address.
The snapshot exposes that native terminal identity alongside the pane address; it is not itself a caller credential.
`runtime/pane_move_preview.rs` reads bounded text on an off-lock worker for an unattached tab, with one running and one latest pending request; it attaches, focuses and resizes nothing.
The shell otherwise copies its cached terminal into an inert preview.
Moves and hover reads use finite request workers holding a weak runtime owner, with no resident polling loop; their admission, deadlines and retained state are described in [the pane movement cost contract](PERFORMANCE_TESTING.md#pane-movement-cost-contract).

## Drawn ahead of the engine

A tab creation, split, zoom, resize or pane close Hide asked for reaches the screen before the engine's layout confirms it (PRD instant-pane-topology D-07, written when Herdr ran the panes and its answer took tens of milliseconds while its layout event arrived hundreds of milliseconds later).
The prediction is drawn onto the session payload after every confirmation has read the engine's own layout (`runtime/drawn_ahead.rs`), so the operation records, the close pipeline and the focus readback judge the engine's layout and never their own drawing.
A zoom, a resize and a close are drawn at the request; a split and a created tab are drawn at the answer, because only the answer names the new pane, and a created tab waits for its pane's layout as a one-pane tab of the checkout's owner workspace (at most `PROVISIONAL_TAB_LIMIT`, each dropped at the close stage timeout).
Opening an owner can acknowledge the new tab before its workspace is known; the same bounded provisional record holds that creation without inventing a workspace or treating its missing layout as a retired pane.
The engine's layout, the existing timeout or connection loss ends that provisional record.
A fork's pane is drawn at the fork worker's answer through the same two records: its own tab as a created tab in the source's workspace and checkout, and its split right of the source as a split Hide asked for (`Runtime::draw_answered_split`), which holds the tab's line, ends when the engine's layout lists the pane and at the same deadline becomes an unknown result (`pane.operation.unconfirmed`) like any split, whether or not the worker has finished; a fork that fails before the engine lays out its pane takes back what was drawn (`tab.create.taken_back`, `pane.split.taken_back`), because its worker closed that pane.
A pane Hide made is in its checkout and tab from that answer (`Runtime::created_pane_place`: a created tab's own, a drawn split's target's), so a focus that reaches it before the catalog does brings that checkout forward and is the tab move the engine answers, instead of leaving the keyboard in a pane of a checkout not in front: there the projection waited on `pane.projection_unavailable` until another focus arrived, or read the front checkout's own pane as a focus the engine moved and followed it (the agent journey's Grok fork on macOS and Windows, 2026-10-18, when Herdr ran the panes); and with the checkout forward but no tab move recorded, Herdr's step through the source's tab on its way to the fork's took the keyboard to the source for one frame.
Geometry is laid out with the same split arithmetic the core's own engine applies (`engine/own/layout.rs`, used by `pane_prediction.rs`), so the confirmed layout replaces the drawn one without a jump when they agree; when they do not, the engine's wins and `pane.prediction_mismatch` records both shapes.
The core's own engine holds a split or a new tab in its layout before it answers, so the first publish after the answer both draws and confirms it, with nothing for a prediction to draw ahead of (a split's answer reached the screen in a median 13.9 ms on it against 10.3 ms for Herdr's drawn prediction, the same one full session update, and the own engine answers about 3 ms sooner); `pane.prediction_mismatch` therefore compares the confirmed layout with the prediction folded over the layout last drawn, which already carries it when a publish drew it, never with the screen from before the operation.
A created tab's session can therefore reach the core before its answer, and then no later session is left to project the visible tab: the answer that moves the keyboard to the new pane projects it in the same step (`settle_selection_projection`), as every other writer of the visible tab does, because a navigator that still names the old tab leaves the selected pane outside the visible tab and a split sent from it finds no focused pane there (with-hide/hide-private#476).
A close is drawn on the canvas only: the closing pane keeps its sidebar row, session and read state until the engine confirms the close.
Whether a close waits in its tab's line is the engine's layout's answer, not the drawing's: once a close draws its sibling gone, a ⌘W on the pane left drawn alone still closes one of two panes in the engine's tab, so it waits behind the close ahead instead of meeting it in progress, stays drawn until it runs, and leaves with its tab.
A waiting close starts only after a settling close ahead has left the tab's records (one that failed or whose result is unknown stays for the operator, so the waiting close starts and meets its refusal, which drops the line) and after the session update in progress has been applied, because it reads the tab's panes from the navigator, which shows the previous session until then; a close started from it would see its tab change before its effect and cancel itself.
A drawn change republishes through `RepublishWaker`, which wakes the coordinator once per burst, so the drawing costs one publish and nothing per frame.

A terminal's grid follows the drawn rectangle the moment it is drawn (PRD grid-ahead-of-herdr D-03, which replaces instant-pane-topology D-08): the shell fits each terminal when its host rectangle changes and sends the changed grid as `terminal_resize`, and the core sends it to the pane's node at once, confirmed layout or not.
That is safe because the PTY is the size the controller client attached with and last sent as `terminal.resize`, never one the engine's layout implies, through a split, a sibling's close and a zoom alike (D-02, measured on a private Herdr 0.9.3 server, whose rule the core's own engine keeps).
So a grid sent on a prediction is right whenever the prediction is, the engine confirming the same layout moves nothing, and a layout the engine draws differently moves the host once more, so the view reports and the PTY takes one more size (`pane.prediction_mismatch` records the shapes); a refusal draws the confirmed layout and the grid returns with it.
The grid hold this replaced waited for Herdr's layout before sending a size, which put Herdr's close answer (0.7 to 4.3 s measured) and its layout event between a pane close or zoom and the terminal's reflow; the "tug of war" that once motivated it (9570a2a) was Hide itself sending two sizes as the optimistic and confirmed layouts alternated, which drawing the prediction over every publish until it settles does not do.
A `pane_op.timing` record's `first_frame` for a resized pane is the first frame after that pane's resize went out, so it may precede `applied` (D-06); the stage names and fields are unchanged.

Keys typed before the pane that should take them exists, or while its terminal session is opening, are held rather than dropped (D-11), by the pane's node (`hide-node/src/terminal/input.rs`), since keys reach it without the core (see The terminal path).
After a new tab or split the shell sends keys against the request; they wait until the engine's answer names the pane and its shell reads keys (below), and are then written to it in order, and a refused creation discards them.
A new tab's or split's pane runs a shell, and until its line editor reads, its terminal is in canonical mode on macOS and Linux: the kernel echoes the keys on a line the first prompt then starts after, and its erase removes one byte, so a Backspace over a Hangul syllable left a broken character that zsh drew as `<ffffffff>` and read together with the next key.
The engine's answer therefore holds the request for the new pane (`held_for`, as a fork's start does) and a worker reads, every 50 ms off the lock, whether the shell reads keys itself: the engine's process facts (`Engine::pane_processes`) name the shell and the node of its machine answers `Call::LineInput`, which is `Keys` while the shell alone holds the terminal, or `Console` for a Windows console, which keeps keys as input events, so there the first read that names the shell ends the wait (`runtime/terminal_input.rs`, `ShellWait`).
The wait ends at most 2 s after the request opened, about when its first key reached the node, with every read cut to what is left of it, so the second left inside the 3 s a held key is still written at covers the core's own lag and a local socket's connect, which has its own bound: a shell with no line editor or still in its startup files then gets the keys as before, and a read that fails (a shell the engine has only just started) is read again until then and named in the end's diagnostic.
A creation the engine answers after that bound (a split queued behind another operation of its tab, a Task's tab after its worktree) gets no wait, since its oldest keys would be too old to be written by the time the shell reads, and a repeated answer for the same pane starts no second wait.
Each end leaves one `terminal.input_shell_wait` diagnostic with its outcome (`reading`, `timeout`, `unreadable` or `late`) and how long the wait took.
Before the pane takes focus the shell's mark sends keys against the request (`web/src/keyTarget.ts`).
Once the pane exists, `RequestHold` binds it to the request on its node, so bare pane keys from every NodeLink client join the same queue without taking `Mutex<Runtime>`; the shell has no duplicate hold rule.
A pane a pending request is held for counts as the request's pane for its layout and close rules below, so keys waiting for a pane that closes or leaves are discarded too.
The core keeps each request's row and tells the node what became of it (`runtime/terminal_input.rs`: `RequestOpen`, `RequestHold`, `RequestResolve`, `RequestDiscard`); keys for a request the core has not named yet are held as pending for up to ten seconds, because they can reach the node before the core's word does.
Each holder keeps at most `INPUT_HOLD_LIMIT_BYTES` (64 KiB) and at most `INPUT_REQUEST_LIMIT` known requests are held at once, with the same bound for requests whose keys arrived before their control.
A pending fork cannot be evicted or have its request id reused by another creation; when all known holders are pending forks, a new fork is refused before it starts with `pane.fork_input_unavailable`, leaving every existing pane protected.
Crossing the byte cap reports `RequestDiscarded`; fork holders also report it at their 30 s deadline on the existing node clock.
The core publishes `terminal.input_hold_failed`, which the shell retains as a dismissible notice asking the operator to type again once the pane is ready (design principle 13).
A failed fork queue refuses subsequent keys until completion, so a lost command never leaves its tail in the launch shell.
Held keys are discarded, never written elsewhere, and each discard leaves one `terminal.input_discarded` diagnostic naming its reason.
The creation made no pane for them: `refused`, `failed`, `not_sent`, `no_pane`, `unknown` (the engine's answer was ambiguous), `unchanged` (the engine answered that the split changed nothing), the reason of the operation ahead when a refusal drops the line behind it, or the agent phase for an agent tab that never started.
The pane was made but will not take them: `not_shown` (created in the background, so keyboard focus never goes there), `pane_gone` (the pane is closing, or left the layouts after it was laid out), `released` (its attach was released) and `session_failed` (its terminal ran out of retries and waits for a manual reconnect).
A cap was crossed: `limit` (64 KiB), `evicted` (a waiting request pushed out by a newer one) and `reused` (a request id taken by another creation).
Outside a fork holder, the keys are too old: `stale`, for each key the pane could take only more than `HELD_INPUT_MAX_AGE` (3 s) after it was typed, because keys typed that long ago are no longer what the operator means to run; the diagnostic names the pane and the byte count, never the content.
Outside a fork holder, each key keeps the time the node received it from the request into the pane's hold, and its age is checked when the core resolves the request to its pane, when the pane's hold takes a newer key (so stale keys never push fresh ones over the cap) and when the session opens; keys arrive in order, so what is discarded is the oldest part and the rest goes in, in order.
The rule is per key, as D-11 states it, so the fresh part can act without the stale part: an Enter typed a second ago runs whatever the prompt holds after the command typed four seconds ago was discarded, and the shell sends each key, a whole escape sequence or a whole paste, as one chunk, so no sequence is split by the discard.
Only the engine's own layout marks a request's pane laid out, never a pane Hide drew ahead, so a provisional tab that expires before the engine lays its pane out keeps its keys; the cost is that a pane the engine names and then removes before any layout lists it keeps its request and held bytes until a newer request evicts it or Hide closes the pane, bounded by `INPUT_REQUEST_LIMIT` rows and 64 KiB each; the bytes reach another pane only if the engine gives that pane the same id within `HELD_INPUT_MAX_AGE` of their being typed.

Every tab creation and pane operation Hide starts leaves one `pane_op.timing` line in the diagnostic log with each stage's milliseconds after the request: the first drawn snapshot, the confirmed layout ingested, its snapshot sent, and the pane's first frame (D-14, `runtime/op_timing.rs`).
The engine's own layout already holds a created pane when it answers, so `drawn` is the first snapshot sent whose layout holds the pane, and for a new tab shows that tab.
The record carries ids and times only, and at most `OP_TIMING_LIMIT` are open at once.

The notifier announces once per burst rather than once per change.
`Core::snapshot_delta` (`hide-core/src/handle.rs`) clears the announcement flag **before** it takes the lock; clearing it after the read would swallow a change that landed during the read.
Launch creates the core once, after the runtime resolution has finished, and never replaces it.
The first attach uses the size the view reported, or the size persisted from the last launch, and never a placeholder; a pane with no known size is held back and says it is waiting.
An attach asks for the grid the view itself reports whenever one is known, because that grid is the one the frame guard accepts: starting at a settled size the view had already left held every frame until a resize, and a pane that is not drawn cannot send one through the display tick, so the shell samples a settled size once its layout is ready.
A frame at a foreign grid is diagnosed once per grid, not once per frame; the held frames themselves are the ordinary signal that the resize has not landed.

A clicked path is one event, not a sequence.
The shell resolves the token on the filesystem and decides which registered checkout owns it by the longest symlink-resolved prefix.
A file of a checkout other than the one in front opens where the operator is and moves no checkout: an HTML file is one `browser_open` naming the front Workspace, and another file or Open source is one `file_open` naming the file's own checkout and the front Workspace as `view`.
The core accepts that `view` only for the Workspace in front and a checkout of its device (`file.invalid_context` otherwise); the file stays its own checkout's editor tab, so hided checks its path against that checkout's root, the read and the save use that root, and the checkout's own Workspace binds the same tab, while the display belongs to the front Workspace.
A display therefore reads from the checkout whose root holds its path, its Workspace's own when it does (`display_source`): a restart's restore, a Retry and the binding of a restored display use it, a checkout adds no display of its own for a tab another Workspace shows, and closing a display keeps its document while any Workspace still shows it.
The Explorer selection follows only a file of the checkout in front, since its tree holds no other.
A file of the checkout in front, an HTML file of another checkout while the Overview is on screen, and a folder go through its checkout as before.
An HTML file opens with one `browser_open` event naming that checkout and `reveal: true`; after the page is admitted, the core uses the existing Workspace reveal operation to bring its checkout and Browser View forward together.
The checkout's View layout selects that page before the checkout comes forward; Agent tabs carry no separate View selection.
Another file, a folder or the terminal menu's Open source sends `reveal_path`; the core then decides the focused checkout, the tree's expanded set and selection, the editor tab and the lane together: a file shows the documents, and a folder, which no tab shows, turns the tool column to the Explorer (PRD lane-two-columns B6, B8).
A window on a node resolves the path against its own machine's checkouts, which the core lists in that node's session rather than its navigator, so the `file_open` or `reveal_path` names the node in `device_id`: hided then leaves the path to the node's helper instead of the core's machine's roots, and the core finds the checkout in its catalog (`catalog_checkout`).
A checkout of a device's session is that device's engine's to bring forward, so the core moves no focus of its own for it: one in front there is revealed at once, and one behind, as a path clicked on the Overview names, is asked of the device's engine with the device brought forward (`Runtime::reveal_when_in_front`), held on the Workspace choice that waits for the device's front (`PendingChoice::reveal`), and revealed once the sync sees the front land there; nothing is read before, and the reveal dies with the request: a refusal or a lost answer, a later choice, the device leaving, the device's front moving to a third checkout, or its deadline passing, `CLOSE_STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS` (5 s) for the answer and, once the device accepts, `CHOICE_LANDING_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) for the landing, which waits on the device's engine and then its session's publish over the link (`Runtime::expire_pending_choice`), drops the choice and all it carries, a Memory visit as a reveal, so a later visit of the operator's own to that checkout opens nothing for the old click; the expiry reaches only the log (`workspace.choice_expired`), since the operator has nothing to act on.
Dispatch is fire-and-forget, so four separate events would arrive as four frames and a refusal partway would leave the screen half moved.
A path outside every checkout never reaches the core.
In the desktop app's window on the core's machine a plain click on such a file opens it in Hide read-only (PRD outside-path-in-hide): the host decides the route in its main process (`desktop/src/main/externalFiles.ts`, `externalRoute`), grants the physical file and its folder to that window in memory, at most 32 grants, and answers the shell a 32-hex grant id, the file's name and its viewer (`text`, `image`, `pdf`, `video`, `html`); the shell sends one `external_open {grant, name, kind, workspace | pane_id + reveal, request_id}` and the core places a display of kind `external` holding those three values alone, focusing the one display a grant already has and stamping its `load` so the shell reads the file again.
The bytes come from the host by grant (`hideHost.external.read`), which reads the path again as its physical spelling with no link followed, so neither hided nor the core ever holds the path, and the core's log for it names the grant, the kind and the outcome only.
An agent's `hide file open` or `hide browser open` of a file outside every checkout takes the same grant (`hided/src/outside_open.rs`): for a caller on the core's machine whose path is written under no registered root (`Boundary::written_under_root`, after the roots are brought current), hided hands the path in its wire spelling to the core machine's window over the browser control gateway (`POST /external-open`, the control token alone), never stores or logs it, and the host judges it as a click with links resolved first (`agentOpen`), refusing rather than handing to the system what no viewer shows (`file_missing`, `file_unavailable`, `unsupported_kind`, `not_html`, `outside_files_full`); with no desktop window hided refuses `outside_file_no_window`.
hided then sends the core `open_external {grant, name, kind}` (`workspace_control::Action::OpenExternal`, which no caller's wire decodes) from the same caller through the same prepare and commit as any open, so the display lands in the caller's checkout's active area, its retry is the request's receipt, and its opener and unseen stamp are an agent open's (`stamp_control_opener`).
A device's agent, and an agent on a node whose core runs elsewhere, has no window on its own machine that grants files, so its outside path still reaches the core as a checkout path does and is refused `outside_file_on_device` with the advice to copy the file into its checkout ([INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md#what-each-system-supports)).
An `external` display is never written to `workspace-views.json` (`workspace_views::save` strips it, and a load drops one with a repair), so a restarted hided shows none; `external_grants {live}` from an attaching window closes every outside display whose grant its host no longer holds, and the snapshot's `external_grants` lists every grant the core's displays stand on, which each browser sync repeats to the host so a closed tab ends its grant.
Any other window, the phone, a browser tab or a window on another machine, has no host that holds a grant: it shows the display by name, dimmed, and a click there takes the operating system route below.
Otherwise the shell hands the path to macOS, opening a file in its default application and a folder as a Finder window, and revealing rather than opening anything whose default application is the operating system running it - an executable file, an application bundle, an installer package - because link detection is a guess over arbitrary agent output and one wrong click must not start a program.
In the web shell the desktop host is that filesystem: `hideHost.probePaths` answers each path's physical path in the wire spelling (The platform layer, `path`) and its kind, taking at most 64 absolute or `~/` paths per call, and `hideHost.openPath` takes a path outside every checkout, or any path on a ⌘-click, and decides open or reveal in the main process (`desktop/src/main/localPath.ts`), so the page never chooses to run anything.
What a type's default application does differs from Mac to Mac, so the host opens only an allowlisted document type or a folder without an extension, reveals everything else and any document with an execute bit or a program's header, and refuses a path that is not its own physical spelling when it is judged or opened, so a symbolic link swapped in after the hover is never followed.
The line a link names travels page-local (`web/src/editor/lineRequest.ts`) to the editor that opens the file, because the core's file events carry no position.
A page without the desktop host, and a pane on an SSH device, resolve no paths and link URLs only ([UI_BEHAVIOR.md: Terminal links](UI_BEHAVIOR.md#terminal-links)).

A spawned child does not split the operator's pane; an agent opened with `hide agent spawn --beside` is the operator's root and never a child ([delivery.md](delivery.md#agent-registration-and-spawning)).
The engine owns split geometry and the PTY size is the controller client's, so a delegated child pane is really moved out - `Engine::move_pane_to_new_tab` to a new tab in the workspace it is already in - rather than left undrawn; a tab holding nothing but delegated children then stays out of the tab strip while remaining in the checkout.
A move stays in flight until the published layout shows the child in its own tab, not only until the engine acknowledges it: the published layout can trail the answer, and asking again before it showed the move moved the pane out of the tab the first move had made, so no layout ever landed and the moves repeated; `RELOCATION_RETRY_INTERVAL_MS` bounds a move whose layout never comes.
Detection is the same on every pass, so a child that arrives while Hide is running and one already split when Hide started take the same path, and a refusal is retried on a fixed interval rather than assumed to have worked.
A child whose spawn record says `beside`, which only a build before `beside_with_parent` made, is left where it is: the exemption is keyed by the spawn's child registration, not by a pane or terminal id, so a restarted Hide that binds the child to its pane again keeps it beside its caller, and a pane the operator moved by hand follows the operator as every manually placed pane does (`Runtime::beside_spawned_panes`).
The engine reports a refusal as an unchanged move with a reason rather than as an error, so the decision reads `changed` instead of trusting a successful request.
Machine-qualified lineage is resolved before tab ownership is projected; local snapshots, remote snapshots and machine identity changes all update the tab strip and Agent area membership in the same transition.
A disconnected parent restores its unresolved local child to normal placement, and reconnecting removes it from the bar while preserving sidebar selection as a delegated canvas.
If normal placement is full, the unresolved child waits and the core moves its keyboard and visible-tab identity to a shown tab in that same transition; a local catalog rebuild preserves known delegation until canonical lineage resolves it.

Ownership is the fifth derived status axis and it is read off the lineage, never stored.
Ordinary delegated rows can only be Working or Seen; their changes turn ancestors unread without changing the ancestors' own groups.
The eight core-owned escalation causes in `docs/status-model.md` are the explicit exception: the child's lineage root enters Needs You and Sessions carrying the child's ask, and the root's pane band opens the child.
The lineage is therefore built before the read axis is applied on every ingest, and there is no clock, timer or second store for it.
Before the lineage, each pane's saved completion is laid back on a pane a restored engine session no longer reports finished (`agent_state::apply_completions`), so an ancestor sees the descendant completion it saw before the restart; [status-model.md](status-model.md#across-an-engine-restart) owns the rule.
The single state owner is `hide-core/src/agent_state/`: `axes.rs` derives lifecycle, completion, ownership and read state, `turn.rs` derives groups, request verbs and runtime action gates, `sessions.rs` derives the Sessions tool's groups and task tags, `escalation.rs` derives the six raise causes from delivery facts, `header.rs` derives each pane's notice and band, `work.rs` associates PRs and issues and assigns each duty, and `tally.rs` owns marks, representative ranks and scope counts.
Its scope projection also carries list sections and checkout trees; the web resolves their pane IDs and physical occurrence indexes and applies locale-aware typography and alphabetical placement without choosing status priority, membership or counts.
The `agent_scope` projection carries physical totals, Overview membership and request membership as separate values because their existing screen rules differ.
Device scopes also carry connected row listings and pane places, and the PR projection carries the tile's turn breakdown, so the shell does not reconstruct ownership or sum attention groups.
`agent_state/tally/scope.rs` owns their calculation and one bounded cache of the current input and output, refreshed on agent or catalog reconciliation, with no worker, timer, subprocess, I/O or serialization.
Existing close targets also carry `tally/close.rs` consequences: confirmation priority, stop-work rows, and outside-descendant rows and counts.
`tally/tasks.rs` derives the Overview's tasks (PRD overview-device-tasks D-04, D-05, D-18): a task is a lineage root and every descendant it has on any device, with this project's checkouts they work in, the pull requests the link record joined to their sessions and the four-step stage `작업 → PR → 검토 → 머지` (absent for a task that is only a conversation).
Each project's `agent_scope.tasks` carries its cards in the section's order (needs you, blocked, working, waiting, done, then resting and cleanup, which the shell folds), each card's members root first, the devices and other projects it delegated into, and its Needs You count.
A device a root's child was started on carries that work as an `incoming` entry naming the root's device and project, which the shell draws dashed and never counts; a child whose parent's machine the core cannot resolve is a root of its own (B15).
A pane is placed once, at its first placement across the local and last-known remote catalogs, so the same task is never counted on two devices.
The tasks are derived, never stored, and rebuilt only with the scope cache's compared input; the shell draws titles, rows and PR marks from the agent rows it already holds and resolves the projected project and device IDs for navigation without regrouping or recounting.
`work.rs` also publishes the request row’s selected PR and ordered issue keys, including folded-chip recency, while `tally.rs` owns local and remote device and removal totals.
`tally/relations.rs` supplies command-palette lineage groups and their issue keys, and `tally/cleanup.rs` supplies checkout-use counts, preserving last-known disconnected descendants separately from live close targets.
Text search and pixel geometry stay in the web; filters select from the core's priority order without deriving a new status.
The cache includes pane close flags and labels so a pane-only change refreshes an open sheet; it adds no close action or runtime enforcement path.
Catalog rebuilding restores cached scope fields before equality checks so an unchanged source does not create a publication merely by constructing new project objects.
`sidebar.rs` retains payload and snapshot assembly, and `request_view.rs` retains request block assembly and timestamp persistence.
The request block also carries the turn card's later half ([UI_BEHAVIOR.md](UI_BEHAVIOR.md), the turn card): `answer`, the label's line for the shown request's turn and the head of the agent's last message in it (`labels::facts::Reply`, at most two lines and keyed by the request's offset, so a new request never shows an old answer), laid once that turn is over; `letters`, the row's slice of the letter index from the request's time (`delivery::correspondence`), folded into a line per agent (at most six) beside the newest eight lines in time order; and `asked`, the question turns after the request (`PaneRecord::asked`).
Laying them is two binary searches and at most eight cloned lines per row, and a row with no letter since its request carries none, so the block grows by at most eight lines of at most 80 characters per row; a phone row carries none of it (`hided/src/mobile/projection.rs`).
The whole message behind `전체 보기` never rides a row: `turn_answer_read` names the pane and the request's offset, and `runtime/turn_answer.rs` reads that one turn where the session runs, the link record giving its file and folder and the node answering `Call::SessionWorkTurn` checked against the witness the turn's judged end kept (`RecentTurn::witness`), on a worker thread with one read running and only the newest waiting, into the `turn_answer` section for one card at a time.
These functions operate on the facts already projected by the core, including remote rows; they introduce no reader, timer, worker or I/O under the runtime lock.
The existing `sidebar::tests`, `request_view::tests` and `runtime::tests::lineage` exercise these shared rules through their original projection callers.
`runtime/session_state.rs` owns durable live resolution: a successful UI-state save acknowledgement publishes the saved resolution, an activity fingerprint rejects stale acknowledgements, and new input, delivery or working activity restores a row.
The same coalesced writer acknowledges dormant conversation and live resolution records from the exact saved frame, applying both results before announcing a change outside the runtime lock.
The owner-thread clock checks the end of the 24-hour Resolved window through the existing tick; it does not create a timer or per-frame publication.
Closed-session PR links are read outside the runtime lock, and Sessions deduplicates them against live PR ownership.
An unchanged remote raw session reuses its complete published projection, including resolution and machine-qualified lineage; applying read fields to a freshly built copy is not itself a runtime transition.
Pane notices and bands travel in `terminal.headers` through the terminal metadata wire and the rest-section stamp.
The stamp compares the core-owned header map, so an unchanged header publishes no rest delta; header changes are copied with the changed owned snapshot and serialized outside the runtime lock.
`docs/status-model.md` owns both rules.
The Agents `My Work` view filters only the core-final Delegated answer and leaves visible orphans in operator-owned groups; `All` changes only the shell's session-local visibility projection.
`agent_start_in_checkout` starts through the task-operation slot that `create_worktree` already uses, creating a tab in the checkout's owner workspace or adding a pane to an explicitly named live tab (see Checkout owner workspace below).
Global start navigation is superseded by an accepted visit, using the existing control serial and explicit visit invalidation; restoring a previously empty checkout's catalog is not a visit.
A fresh external tab or pane focus in the engine that Hide follows is also a visit and invalidates the pending start.
A local pane focus converges without notification only when its tab is the engine's globally focused tab or its latest successful control is awaiting that tab's move, not merely active in a background workspace.
That control confirmation is held in the existing bounded tab-request record, never changes the baseline the tab moves are counted from and is invalidated by a new connection; an unknown answer cannot confirm a retry.
The shell's existing `opening` state presents a correlated start only when the core selects its listed pane, without issuing another focus mutation; its answer bound is the same 90 seconds as the start panel's.
It is the one start path for every surface (⌘N's start panel, New worktree, an issue's Start, a pull request's hand-off, the phone; PRD home-device-rail D-20): it names a checkout by path (a start naming none is refused as `agent_start.invalid_target`, since Hide keeps no Home: see Retiring Home below), and a `device_id` for a device's checkout, which opens its tab on that device's engine through the checkout's owner there (`worktree_control::TabTarget::device`; a tab needs no file helper, so a device whose helper is not ready still takes one).
A start may name a `model` only for an agent whose start declares one, the one rule of the shared adapter (`LaunchDialect::options()`): Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Pi, omp and agy take `--model <id>`, and OpenCode, whose CLI lists no model option, takes none, so a model for it is refused with that reason rather than dropped.
The id must pass `hide_agent_adapter::valid_model` (`[A-Za-z0-9._:/\[\]-]`, at most 80, never starting with `-`), the one check every start and restart uses; the CLI judges whether it knows the model, and a refusal stays on its pane, never replaced by another model.
A start types each argument into the pane's shell single-quoted (`engine/own/shell_line.rs`), so an id such as `opus[1m]` reaches the CLI as written (measured on Herdr 0.9.5, whose line the engine types, with a stand-in agent that recorded its argv, 2026-10-18).
The model and effort an agent was started with are kept for every restart Hide makes of it, as fields and never as a replayed argument list: `ui_state.pane_launches` (`runtime/agent_choice.rs`, saved in `core-state.json`) holds, per pane, the kind, the name Hide started the agent under, the `LaunchChoice { model, effort }` and the conversation it describes, written by the task start, by `hide agent spawn --model --effort` (`Command::Spawn`'s `launch`, kept once the start is typed and before the agent shows its session, which Codex CLI reports only at its first turn), and by every restart below.
