A record describes only the agent Hide started under that name: it follows the conversation that agent reports (a `/clear` moves it along), describes an agent that came back from a restart without its name only while it reports that conversation, and is dropped when the pane shows another name, another known kind or an unnamed agent on another conversation, or leaves its machine's topology, so an agent started by hand in a reused pane id never inherits it.
A removed device's records leave with it, and the map holds at most `PANE_LAUNCH_LIMIT` (1024) records; a start past that is logged as `pane_launch.limit` and its restarts run on the CLI's defaults.
The record covers only agents Hide itself started: an agent the operator typed in a pane (`claude --model opus --effort high`) restarts on the CLI's defaults, and ⌘N, New worktree and an issue's Start carry a model but no effort, so a Claude Code agent keeps its effort across a restart only when it was started with `hide agent spawn --effort`.
A restart names the recorded choice explicitly, so a model the operator switched to inside the conversation (`/model`) gives way to the one the agent was started with.
The record keeps the profile the agent runs with beside its choice, so every restart below runs it with that profile again ([Starting an agent with a profile](#starting-an-agent-with-a-profile)).
A wake (in its pane or dormant), a fork, a pane's Reopen and a closed tab's or pane's reopen each copy the choice into their own record (`SleepRecord`, `DormantRecord`, `ForkRequest`, `ReopenRequest`, `ClosedAgent`) and add it after the resume arguments, because a bare resume leaves it to the CLI's configured default: Claude Code 2.1.302 resumed and forked with the configured effort, and Codex CLI 0.163.0 forked with the configured model and effort (measured 2026-10-18).
The words come from the same declaration (`LaunchDialect::choice_arguments`): the model as the agent declares it and the effort in the kind's declared spelling, `--effort <e>` for Claude Code and `-c model_reasoning_effort=<e>` for Codex; a saved choice the kind does not take fails the restart with that reason, a fork before any pane is made for it, rather than starting it on another model.
A pane with no record (an agent started on the CLI's defaults, or by a build before the record existed) restarts on its resume arguments alone, as before.
Every start and restart Hide makes also carries the agent's permission choice on the machine it starts on (Settings › Agents, `권한`; `agent_permission.rs`), and unlike the model it is read when the start is made, never kept with the pane, so a change applies at the next wake, fork or reopen, and an agent the operator first typed by hand gets it once Hide restarts it.
The core keeps it in `ui_state.agent_permissions` for its own machine and `device_agent_permissions` by device id (saved in `core-state.json`, swapped on a core move as `expanded_paths` is, `node_migration::reown::OWN_PATHS`), and changes it on one `agent_permission_set` event (`device_id`, `agent`, `mode` `full`, `ask` or `custom` with `text`).
A missing entry is `full`, the default for every operator; `ask` adds nothing; `custom` keeps the typed text and its words as `hide_shell::shell_line` reads them, refusing anything but a list of words (at most 512 bytes and 32 words); an entry a build cannot read loads as `ask`, never as full access, and a machine's whole value that cannot be read (or the device map itself) loads as `ask` for every agent Hide starts on that machine (or on every registered device).
`full` adds the options the start dialect declares as `LaunchOptions::full_access` (`FullAccess::Options`, each option's words with its name first, or `FullAccess::NotAsked` for Pi, which asks nothing), each read from the CLI's `--help` on 2026-11-01: `--dangerously-skip-permissions` for Claude Code and agy, `-c approval_policy=never -c sandbox_mode=danger-full-access` for Codex, `--always-approve` for Grok, `--auto` for OpenCode and `--auto-approve` for omp; the `agent CLIs` lane finds each option's name in the pinned CLI's help on Linux, macOS and Windows (`scripts/install-agent-clis.py`), and for Codex, which accepts any `-c` key and starts with its defaults on a misspelled one, runs the pinned Codex with those words in an empty HOME and requires `Approval policy is currently never` and `danger-full-access` in the prompt input `codex debug prompt-input` renders (`FULL_ACCESS_PROOF`).
Each option is one its CLI accepts twice, because a start types the agent's program into the operator's shell, so a shell alias of that program can run and may add the same option again (`alias codex="codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox"` stopped every Codex start Hide made with `the argument ... cannot be used multiple times`, 2026-11-01); Hide leaves the operator's shell, its aliases and functions as they are.
Measured in an empty HOME with the option given twice on 2026-11-01: Claude Code 2.1.316 (both its options twice), agy 1.4.12, OpenCode 2.0.29 and omp 18.7.0 start; Codex 0.166.0 refuses `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` twice and `-a never -s danger-full-access` twice or beside that flag, so its full access is the two configuration overrides that flag sets, which it accepts repeated and beside the flag, the later one winning; its `/status` shows `Full Access` and `codex debug prompt-input` renders the same prompt input as with the flag.
`-c` does not change how Codex runs for Hide: a Codex with the shared app-server daemon starts in its own pane's process with any `-c`, as every start Hide makes already did with `--no-daemon` (`codex_launch.rs`), so Ctrl+C in an empty composer ends the session in that pane and a resume picks it up.
Grok 1.0.70 refuses `--always-approve` twice and `--permission-mode` twice and has no option that does the same and may be repeated, so an alias that adds `--always-approve` stops a Grok start Hide makes (`docs/INSTALL.md`, What each system supports); an alias that adds `--permission-mode bypassPermissions` does not.
Claude Code 2.1.316 stops a start with its flag at a one-time `Bypass Permissions mode` warning whose preselected answer is `No, exit`, so a brief typed at the start would end the agent; its full access therefore also carries `--settings '{"skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt":true}'`, which skips only that warning, writes nothing to Claude's own files and is given again on every start (seen in an empty HOME on 2026-11-01). Codex asks nothing more with its overrides: in a folder its configuration trusts it goes straight to its prompt in `YOLO mode`, as with its bypass flag, and in any other folder it first asks `Trust this folder?` with either form, so Hide records that trust for each worktree it makes before it starts Codex there ([agent-hooks.md](agent-hooks.md#folder-trust-for-the-worktrees-hide-makes)); a checkout Hide did not make and Codex has not trusted stops at that question (Codex 0.166.0 with `--no-daemon`, measured 2026-11-01; a start of the operator's own checkout that Codex has never trusted is unmeasured through Hide).
The words go where the model goes, after a resume or fork selector and before the model, the native arguments and a first prompt (`agent_choice::agent_arguments` for a new start, `launch_arguments` for a restart): `codex resume <id>` and `codex fork <id>` take the same option as a new start (Codex 0.166.0's help).
The task start and an archived session's resume read it under the lock for the machine they start on; a wake and a dormant wake read it for the sleeping agent's machine; a fork, a pane's Reopen and a closed item's reopen carry it in `ForkRequest`, `ReopenRequest` and the closed-item `ReopenRequest` as the core built them; `hide agent spawn` reads the child's machine's from its `CoordinationContext` and puts it before the choice and the native arguments, leaving out, with its value, a full-access option those native arguments already name, since a CLI may refuse an option given twice, except Codex's `-c` overrides, which go first so that the spawn's own `-c` (an effort, or its own approval policy) comes later and wins. A spawn that names its own `--settings` for Claude Code therefore starts without Hide's warning setting and stops at the bypass warning: Claude Code 2.1.316 keeps only the last of two `--settings` (with Hide's first, the spawn's status line showed and the warning came back; the other way round, the warning stayed away and the spawn's status line was gone, measured 2026-11-01), so giving both would drop one of them either way, and the spawn's own settings are the ones its author asked for.
The engine's own restore after a daemon restart resumes an agent's conversation (`engine/own/restore.rs`) with the recorded model and effort when the pane's record still describes that agent (`launch_describes`).
Every start supported by the shared adapter writes that kind and the kind's model into `ui_state.agent_start`, which every start surface preselects next; `terminal` is never remembered, and a store written before this choice existed seeds the kind once from the retired `issue_settings.default_agent`, which the next save drops.
A start carries the surface's `request_id`, stamped on the task receipt and on a refusal's `last_error`, so each surface reads only its own answer.
Retry refusals retain that request identity, including when the original pane is gone or its device is offline.
A group start additionally names `target { group_id, area_id, tab_id, add_pane }`; the checkout and device qualify that target, because different groups can each have an area named `a1`.
Without an explicit target the start reserves a new draft in the checkout's selected group, preserving the independent meaning of the global start panel.
`runtime/group_starts.rs` keeps the stable request's receipt in `WorkspaceView.agent_starts`: its group, area, draft/live tab, pane, recovery marker, provider kind and completion phase, with no instruction text or agent launch arguments.
There are at most 64 receipts per checkout; the oldest settled receipt can leave, while 64 unresolved receipts refuse another start instead of dropping an uncertain effect.
The existing Workspace-view save worker must acknowledge the exact claim before its worker creates a tab or pane, and acknowledge the agent-start phase before the worker starts the agent.
Filesystem work and both save waits stay outside Runtime's mutex.
`checkout_start.rs` saves the exact owning workspace, optional fresh owner seed tab, original target pane incarnation and normal shell command, environment and readiness before `Engine::apply_layout` creates a terminal carrying the opaque `start_claim` label in that same mutation.
The claim is a reserved creation descriptor, never a human title or an exported environment variable; pane and terminal titles, sidebar labels, closed-item capture and reopen discard it while preserving human names.
First start replaces the draft's slot with the confirmed live tab; Add agent creates the claimed terminal separately, durably binds its pane, terminal id, shell pid and kernel start time, then joins it to the exact existing tab with `Engine::move_pane_beside` in the same workspace.
The engine reads those from the pane's record (`Engine::inspect_pane`, the proof `pane_identity` gives).
A pane that cannot be proved (a refused record) can never confirm the claimed terminal, so the start fails for certain (`agent_start.terminal_unchecked`) and closes the tab it created in the same call, before any agent ran in it, leaving no tab, pane or holder that no checkout lists.
Joining holds that tab's existing geometry FIFO through confirmation, including the existing automatic zoom-off behavior, and never reapplies or recreates the target's existing terminals.
A lost creation or move answer receives a bounded inspection of at most 128 physical tabs in that owner, accounting for at most 64 admitted logical tabs and 64 retained starts, never another creation merely because the call timed out.
An exact claim must be unique and its learned incarnation must remain identical; before the first incarnation is saved, two identical owning-node process inspections bracket a fresh claim and normal-shell-command lookup, including when creation was acknowledged.
The recorded launch command must be nonempty and unchanged, because a saved pane whose holder ended gets a new shell on restore, not the recorded command, while a creation answer alone identifies the pane rather than its current shell.
After creation, the existing agent-start admission callback rereads that durable incarnation through the owning node outside Runtime's mutex, then rechecks the task, receipt, connection and node before each dependent launch, including after save and shell-readiness waits.
Only a start whose launch dialect uses the Codex kit capability includes that capability in its admitted intent; a concurrent inspection of Codex cannot cancel a different agent's start.
A default-shell start without that command or a changed, missing or duplicated proof remains unknown with an actionable status check; no cwd, human name or newly observed id substitutes for proof.
The catalog excludes a pending start's exactly claimed staging tab from display and admission, while retaining its draft reservation; a staging tab that contains unrelated panes stays visible.
Pending receipts, including those loaded after restart, recover by inspection only; `confirm_only` loads the receipt's original provider and ignores replacement prompt/model choices.
A failed recovery-worker admission and a refused unzoom after creation retain the pending receipt and its staging reservation rather than permitting another creation.
A definite failure may retry its stable intent, and a definite agent failure retries the existing pane; an unknown launch is not blindly repeated.
The answer fills its original group even when hidden, but a late answer does not take focus from a group the operator has since selected.
When the selected draft becomes a live tab before a newly opened owner's catalog arrives, its selected slot remains authoritative even beside other live tabs; the engine's old tab cannot replace it while the first layout is pending.
No workspace or pane is invented to fill that gap, and an explicit later selection still wins.
The inline form keeps prompt and picker edits in page memory across navigation and failures, while the durable receipt lets a new page inspect the original effect without recovering or replaying the prompt.
Tab-bound input uses the stable tab identity rather than group membership; only a definite failed receipt can be retired after its authoritative target changes, allowing a new decision at the current target.
Pending or unknown starts retain their original intent and target for read-only recovery.
A start may also carry `stay_behind` (the phone's, see The mobile companion): its tab is made without moving the desktop's visible tab or keyboard focus.
A first prompt is typed once the agent's screen takes input, and goes as the CLI's own argument, in the form its start dialect declares (`LaunchDialect::prompt_form`), only in the cells the one standard of [delivery.md](delivery.md#the-input-ladder) proves, read from each agent's declared `input`.
Start support grants no session reader, resume, fork, sleep, letter or bell capability.
A start passes every argument to the shell verbatim, one argv entry each, and a line break or a tab in one cannot be typed safely, so `start_prompt::prompt_argument` writes each line break as U+2028 (LINE SEPARATOR), which the model reads as a line break, and a tab as four spaces, and refuses any other control character and a prompt over 64 KB, since the engine types the command into the pane's shell and macOS bash took 27 s for 76 KB and did not finish 300 KB in 60 s (zsh: 5 s), against the 120 s start wait.
Each start event checks its prompt with that encoder before anything opens, so such a prompt is refused as `agent_start.invalid_prompt` (`worktree.create_invalid_prompt`) with no tab or worktree left behind; a refusal from the engine fails the agent start with its reason, and in both cases the surface that sent the prompt keeps the text.
The engine types the command into the pane's shell, so a first prompt that rides the start can stay in that shell's history and shows in the process list on the machine that runs the agent (D-26); no Hide log carries it.
The provider catalog the model menus list is read while a start surface shows one, or a mission map is drawn, which names each worker's model by that list (`ai_settings.start_observing`, a second hided demand beside the Settings tab's `observing`), without the Settings-only hook diagnosis.
The worker that created the pane then starts the chosen provider in that exact pane with `Engine::start_agent` (`worktree_control::start_task_agent`), after the creation is published, so every request shares one executor and no client starts an agent itself.
The agent is named after its pane (`hide-<provider>-<pane>`), because the engine refuses a name another agent already holds and two tasks often run the same provider.
Every start Hide sends to the engine, a task's, a fork's, a restored tab's and a wake's, goes through `agent_start` (`start_at_shell_checked`, or `start_at_shell_reusing_name` for a Reopen and a wake): the engine types the command only while the pane's shell is available, refuses with `agent_pane_busy` otherwise, and does not wait.
On macOS and Linux the shell is available while it alone holds the terminal (its foreground process group is the shell's own and has no other member, `available_pane_shell_from_job`); on Windows, which keeps no process group, the same rule reads the foreground the platform layer names for a console, from the shell down (`hide_platform::process::console_foreground`).
A pane just made is still running its shell's startup files, so the worker reads the pane's process facts (`Engine::pane_processes`) until that holds and only then sends the start; a busy refusal after a good read (a prompt hook took the terminal in between) goes back to waiting, since the engine typed nothing.
Before that first read the start waits, inside the same 30 s, for the engine's restore (`Engine::wait_restored`), the wait a call that makes a pane already takes: right after this daemon or a device's link starts, a pane is drawn from the saved session before its node has said which holders still run, and until then the node refuses every question about the pane (`pane_owner_unavailable`), which failed a sleeping agent's wake on the first visit after a restart.
The shell holding the terminal does not say its startup files are done: a startup file that asks a question (oh-my-zsh's `[Y/n]` update prompt reads one key with `read -k 1`) leaves the shell alone in the foreground too, and a start typed then answers the question with the command's first letter and runs the rest (`laude: command not found`).
A tab Hide makes for an agent, a spawn's tab, a fork's own tab and the new-agent tab in an existing checkout, therefore runs the account's shell from Hide's own command, the way VS Code starts its terminals: the node of the machine that runs the pane answers that command and its environment (`Call::ShellIntegration`, `hide_host::shell_integration`, a `ShellLaunch`), and the tab is made with `Engine::apply_layout`, whose pane runs the given command (`checkout_owner::open::create_tab_in`, `agent_start::shell_launch`).
zsh starts with `ZDOTDIR` naming Hide's files, which read the user's own in zsh's order with `ZDOTDIR` as the user has it (the user's own value comes in `HIDE_SHELL_ZDOTDIR`) and give it back, unset included; bash starts with `--init-file` naming a file that reads the user's files in bash's own order; fish runs a `-C` command after its configuration; on Windows, Windows PowerShell runs a `-Command` after the user's profile that carries a prompt wrapper reporting the folder as OSC 9;9 (Herdr 0.9.3's own, kept) inline, since a script file would need an execution policy that allows scripts.
Each writes the mark on the screen once the user's files are done (OSC 133;A, with the shell's own `printf` or PowerShell's `[Console]::Write`, so no prompt starts a process); the pane's holder counts it, and a start in such a tab (`ShellStart::Integrated`) waits for it inside the same wait ([Agents on the core's own engine](#agents-on-the-cores-own-engine)).
There zsh, bash and fish also say their folder on the screen (OSC 7, a `file://` URI with `%` spelled `%25`, and none for a folder whose name holds a control character), zsh at each change of folder (`chpwd`), bash at each prompt (`PROMPT_COMMAND`, after the user's, keeping the last status) and fish at each change (`--on-variable PWD`), each once as it starts, because the holder reads the folder a shell reports on the screen; Windows PowerShell's prompt wrapper already says it at each prompt (OSC 9;9).
A spawn records the launched shell with its pane, so a later ask of the same intent waits for the mark too; a shell in the foreground that is not the one launched (a `.zshrc` that runs `exec fish`) marks nothing, so its start is not held for a mark and is confirmed after typing (`shell_wait.other_shell`).
The screen line a refusal carries is the operator's terminal output: it is cut to 120 characters, stripped of control, zero-width and bidirectional characters, passed through `hide_memory::redact`, and never written to the diagnostic log.
The shell starts as a login shell on macOS and not on Linux; bash cannot read an init file as a login shell, so its login file reads `/etc/profile` and the first of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login` and `~/.profile` itself, and `shopt login_shell` stays off.
The owning node returns an explicit command, environment and readiness (`ShellLaunch.readiness`: `integrated` or `plain`) for every normal shell it can confirm, including sh and nu and a shell whose integration could not be installed.
A Plain recipe waits under the existing foreground-shell and line-input policy, without waiting for a prompt token that cannot arrive.
On Linux a Plain recipe directly executes the account's absolute executable shell; on macOS it invokes that node's exact running `hided` path with `shell-exec --shell <absolute shell> --login`, an internal entry point that calls `hide_platform::process::exec_login_shell` before daemon initialization.
That Unix boundary uses `execv` with argv0 `-<shell basename>`, preserving the same PID, kernel start time, cwd, environment and terminal descriptors, with no child or resident wrapper and no PATH or ENOEXEC shell fallback.
Windows keeps the existing PowerShell recipe and integrated readiness.
An absent, relative or unavailable Unix account shell, or an unavailable macOS hided path, fails group starts before any terminal is created, with an action to check that device's shell configuration and reconnect.
The creation receipt saves the exact owning-node recipe and readiness before its effect; recovery never substitutes the local machine's recipe or a new helper path.
A helper update can retire that saved executable before creation, in which case execution fails visibly; a terminal already execed into its shell no longer needs hided's path, and an uncertain creation is inspected rather than replayed.
Older receipts without an explicit command remain unproven after a lost response or restart and cannot be adopted from a retained label alone.
Hide-made agent tabs therefore run the account's shell (Windows PowerShell on Windows).
The zsh and bash files live under `~/.hide/shell-integration/<digest of the files>/`, and the node removes another build's folder (only a digest name or a staging folder) once no pane has been started with it for an hour, since a shell reads its later files only after a question in an earlier one is answered.
Every shell Hide starts runs those files, so the folder is synced to disk before its rename into place, a root another account can change gives no integration, and a version folder whose files differ from the build's text, or that another account could change, is written again before any shell is pointed at it.
`Engine::create_worktree`, `open_worktree` and `create_workspace` take no command, so a newly opened workspace's first tab is replaced, by `Engine::apply_layout` with the tab's id, by one that runs it (`checkout_owner::open::replace_tab`), the web's new-worktree start with an agent included; a new worktree with no agent keeps the engine's first tab.
`Engine::split_pane` takes no command either, so a fork into a split starts plain, as do panes whose shell is another (sh, nu, cmd), and a spawn there confirms its start after typing it instead (`docs/delivery.md`).
Holding the terminal is not yet reading it: until the shell's line editor (ZLE, readline, fish) starts, the terminal is in canonical mode, where the kernel keeps a typed line itself and drops every byte past its limit, the Enter included (1,024 bytes on macOS, 4,096 on Linux).
An agent start may pass a prompt of several KB as the CLI's argument, so typed into a pane whose `.zshrc` was still running it arrived cut at about 1,022 bytes and the agent never started.
A start line that can pass the shortest limit (`PreparedStart::line`, the quoted arguments and the executable) therefore also waits, within the same wait, until the node that runs the pane says the shell's terminal takes keys (`Call::LineInput`, read off the lock by `hide_platform::process::line_input` from the shell's controlling terminal); a terminal still in canonical mode whose limit fits the line, and a Windows console, which has no line discipline, start at once.
A shorter line keeps the shell-holds-the-terminal rule alone and asks no node, so a shell without a line editor still runs it; a long line whose terminal cannot be read is refused with that reason rather than typed on a guess.
A start the engine typed whose agent never showed (a cut line before this wait, a program that exited before the engine saw it) keeps its name held (`launch_pending` with no agent) until that start's own deadline, the 120 s Hide passes (`AGENT_START_DEADLINE`), and a start under the name before then is refused as `agent_name_taken`.
On that refusal a start reads the name once (`Shell::settle_name`) and sends the start again only when the answer is `agent_not_found`; a name still held is an agent's or a start that may still show one, and the refusal is the answer.
A spawn asked again for the same intent waits while the engine holds the name, types the start once more only after it let go and the shell is alone, and otherwise answers `agent_not_started` (`docs/delivery.md`); a new attempt closes the earlier pane while it still runs the terminal that spawn recorded, which frees the name with it.
The wait is capped at 30 s (`SHELL_WAIT`); past it nothing was typed (a terminal still in canonical mode is named, with its limit and the line's length, in the failure's detail and in the diagnostic), the start is a failure the task banner offers to retry, and the diagnostic `agent_start` / `shell_wait.timeout` records the pane's last process state.
A shell that held the terminal but never marked its first prompt stopped at a question: its start fails as `shell_starting` with the screen's last line and nothing else of the terminal, which the spawn's answer, the task banner and a Memory card's failed status name.
`agent_reason` is a code, never a sentence (`agent_start.not_installed`, `agent_start.shell_starting`, `agent_start.refused_by_engine`, `agent_start.unconfirmed`, a session check's own code such as `session_route_unconfirmed`, and the others `worktree_control::AgentFailure` is built with), which every start surface words in the window's language (`web/src/coreError.ts`), a code it does not know as the plain "the agent did not start"; the sentence with the engine's answer or a link error goes to the `task_operation` / `agent.failed` or `agent.unknown` diagnostic, and `agent_line` carries the screen's last line of a `shell_starting` failure, which the screen quotes and no log keeps.
The answer lands on the task receipt's own axis (`agent_phase`: `starting`, `started`, `failed` or `unknown`, with `agent_reason` and `agent_line`): a failure keeps the worktree and the pane, a provider missing from the PATH of the node that would run it fails before the engine is asked (the `agent_installed` call; a device's own node answers for its PATH), a transport failure is `unknown` because the agent may be running, and only a definite failure is offered again (`task_agent_retry`, which reuses the recorded pane and refuses when it is gone).
The receipt cannot be acknowledged while the agent is still `starting`.
The delete dialog's `remove_worktree` event and an agent's `hide workspace remove` start the one removal (`Runtime::start_git_worktree_removal`): the command answers the dialog's checkboxes from its `--force` and `--delete-branch`, refuses an agent still at work in the worktree and the caller's own checkout, and returns its refusal to the caller instead of the screen; the daemon then reads the removal's record until it ends (`hide_core::worktree_command`, [delivery.md](delivery.md#removing-a-worktree-hide-workspace-remove)).
Worktree deletion first asks the checkout's host for a non-mutating authoritative recheck (`Call::WorktreeRemovalCheck`, `hide_host::worktrees::check_removal`) on the action worker, before any chosen descendant or checkout pane closes.
The check refuses a locked worktree with its name, Git lock reason and manual `git worktree unlock` action; no Discard choice unlocks it.
It also rechecks registration, HEAD, branch, protected base, nested worktrees, dirt and the exact ignored-repository names confirmed by the operator.
Only success admits the existing close sequence, whose worker rechecks the same contract before `git worktree remove` and the chosen branch removal (`Call::WorktreeRemove`, `hide_host::worktrees::remove_confirmed`).
That close sequence (`close_checkout_panes`) reads each pane's shell and foreground pids with the engine's process facts (`Engine::pane_processes`), and every process under the shell from the process table of the node that runs the panes (`process_descendants`), before it closes any pane, and after the engine's session confirms the panes gone it waits, within the same `CONFIRM_TIMEOUT`, until those processes have ended, identified by pid and start time and named by their program, all read on that node (`process_starts`).
The engine's confirmation that a pane is closed is not taken as proof that its shell or agent has exited, and on Windows a pane's `cmd.exe` runs the agent through `powershell.exe`, which can outlive both; a running process holds its working folder there, so the folder cannot be moved aside or deleted until it is gone; the wait therefore runs only for a folder on this Windows machine (`ProcessWait::for_folder_removal`), and a device's panes, whose pids belong to the device, and a project removal, which touches no folder, skip it.
A descendant with a console of its own (a new or hidden window) or none (detached) can outlive the close, and the deletion waits for it like any other.
A process still running at the timeout fails the close with its program name and pid, which the delete dialog shows so the operator can end it and delete again, and the worktree is not touched; a refused move into `hide-removed` is logged as `set_aside_refused`, and the removal goes on to Git's own removal at once; on Windows a second line, `set_aside_holders` with the same `attempt`, lists the open handles on the folder or inside it (the owning process, the path, the access, and this process's own id beside them), because the error (32 or 5) names no one. The scan reads the system handle table on its own thread, one at a time (a scan still running makes the next record `scan_busy`), duplicating only handles of the file type, because a handle of some kinds can block the questions asked of it and the removal never waits for the scan.
The phases are `checking`, `closing`, `removing`, `finished` and `failed`; a failed preflight keeps every pane and file.
While the panes close, the core fails the removal if the worktree catalog shows the checkout moved (another HEAD or branch, a deletion gate, or a missing row) only while the reader still answers for its repository: closing a checkout's last pane can end the only workspace that asked for that repository, the next answer then has no project for it, which says nothing about the worktree, and the host checks the registration, HEAD and branch again before it removes anything.
Git is not left to delete the folder: when Git would remove it (registered, not the main worktree, not locked, clean unless forced), `hide_host::worktrees::remove_worktree` renames it into `hide-removed/` under the repository's shared Git directory, so `git worktree remove` finds it missing and drops only the registration, and a background thread deletes the files; a refusal moves the folder back, and a folder that cannot be renamed (another volume) is removed by Git in place within its own 60-second `REMOVE_DEADLINE` rather than the 15-second read bound.
A trash entry is deleted only once Git no longer registers it, and every removal sweeps its repository's trash, so an entry a stopped process left behind goes with the next removal, including a retry of its own.
A finished local removal takes its row out of the worktree catalog in the same frame and counts itself in `WorktreeRequest::removals`: the coordinator rebuilds the rows on its next wake, a read that started before the removal cannot bring the row back, and the reader re-reads only the removed worktree's repository, because Git changed that repository's own directory; a failed removal re-reads every project, since what stopped it is news.
The deletion gate (`worktrees::deletion_gate`) refuses the main worktree, a locked worktree and an unavailable ignored-repository scan.
Other risks are warnings, and a loss the folder would take (dirt, a nested worktree, an unreadable status or named ignored repositories) is a `discard` the operator must accept, which the core rechecks against its current row when the event arrives.
The host reads lock reasons from NUL-delimited Git porcelain and measures each ignored repository boundary, including `.git` directory, gitfile and bare forms, with 2,000,000 scan steps, 30 seconds and 1,024 names as hard caps.
It does not follow directory links or traverse Git metadata; unreadable, invalid or over-budget scans report why review cannot proceed instead of claiming an empty list.
An accepted discard allows nested-worktree and dirt checks through and removes with one `--force`; it never skips the lock or ignored-repository scan.
The event and `ConfirmedRemoval` carry the exact measured repository names the confirmation showed; a changed set requires a fresh review and Discard choice.
A branch the gate warned is unmerged goes with `git branch -D`.
An unsupported host check refuses before closing panes, with no fallback to unchecked deletion.
Git and the engine have no shared atomic reservation: a change after preflight can still stop the final removal after panes closed.
No shell reports a removal's completion, so there is no event a client could send to claim one.
Only a pane outside the set the engine confirmed closed counts as one that appeared during the confirmation, because the navigator still lists the closed pane until the session without it is applied.

## Checkout owner workspace

Every checkout has one owner workspace, read from the engine's session and never inferred from where its tabs sit (`checkout_owner.rs`, PRD checkout-workspace-binding).
A Git checkout's owner is the workspace the engine binds to its path (`WorkspaceInfo.worktree.checkout_path`, which only `Engine::open_worktree` and `create_worktree` set).
A plain folder cannot be bound, so its owner is the live workspace carrying Hide's `hide_owner` workspace token, whose value is a digest of the device and the folder; the engine saves workspace tokens with its session, so the mark survives a restart.
The owner is decided from the session Hide already receives (`CheckoutSnapshot::owner_workspace_id`, never sent to the shell), so a snapshot costs no engine call.
Every tab Hide creates in a checkout goes to its owner: Add Tab, New agent, agent start (including a pull request handed to an agent), Reopen Closed Tab, registering a project the engine has no workspace in (`checkout_owner::open::registered_owner`), and opening a registered project that has no workspace, on this machine and on a device alike (`TabHost`).
A reopened tab takes back its old place in the strip only when it lands in the workspace it was closed from; one closed outside the owner, or in a plain folder whose owner closed with its last tab, keeps the place the engine gives it.
A checkout with no owner open gets one first, on the control worker with the runtime lock released (`checkout_owner::open::open_owner_tab`): `Engine::open_worktree` on its path from the repository's main worktree, which answers with the workspace the engine already binds there (`already_open`), so a repeated or racing request converges on one owner; a plain folder takes a process-wide lock, lists the workspaces, reuses the marked one, and otherwise runs `Engine::create_workspace` at the folder and writes the mark.
A newly opened owner's first tab is the new tab; an owner already open gets `Engine::create_tab`.
A workspace the engine newly opened is renamed as the sidebar names the checkout (a linked worktree by its branch, the primary checkout and a plain folder by the project) with `Engine::rename_workspace`; `Engine::open_worktree` carries no label, and an operator's workspace is never renamed.
A refusal fails the request through the existing tab-creation failure and Retry, with the checkout and reason in the diagnostic log (`tab.control.failed`, `owner.mark_failed`), and nothing is created in any other workspace.
A tab Hide created belongs to the checkout it was created for, never to the checkout its pane cwd names: a new pane reports the cwd it was born with until its shell has entered the start folder, so a pane-cwd read put a new tab under another checkout until an unrelated publish (#400).
The core keeps the checkout from the creation's answer, `CreateTab` and `OpenOwner` acknowledgments and the task slot's agent start (`WorktreeTaskOutcome::created_tab_id`), for at most 64 tabs with the crossing reported to the diagnostic log.
A record lives until the session has carried its tab and then lost it, or until the session becomes unreachable; when the session placed the tab before the answer arrived, the runtime wakes the coordinator to republish at once (`RepublishWaker`).
The record is runtime only, so after hided restarts a tab Hide created is placed like any other; a recorded checkout no longer in the catalog is reported once (`created_tab.checkout_missing`) and its tab falls back to that rule.
A plain folder holds the folders below it for the workspace that carries its mark, as a repository holds its subfolders: a pane of that workspace whose cwd is in no repository is placed under the marked folder when the folder is its cwd or above it (`checkout_owner::marked_folder`, read in the catalog's `inspect_space`), so no project row is made for the subfolder; the folders above a cwd are read from its spelling (`hide_platform::path::wire_parent`), so a Windows device's drive root `C:/` stays a root on a macOS or Linux core.
The mark is the record that survives a restart where the created-tab record does not: the core's own engine saves workspace tokens with its session, so a tab Hide made in a plain folder, whose pane has since moved to a plain folder below it, comes back under that folder.
A pane whose cwd is outside the marked folder, and a pane of a workspace carrying no mark, is placed by its cwd as before.
A new worktree's first tab is recorded from the worktree creation's own tab (`Engine::create_worktree`, `created_tab_id`), under the worktree's path, on this machine and on a device alike.
A new branch, from New worktree, a start or `hide agent spawn`, starts from the commit `origin/<base>` names when the local base holds nothing it lacks, so a worktree never starts from a base that was fetched but not pulled, and a base only origin has starts from origin's commit; a local base with commits of its own, or one with no fetched copy, is started from as before (`worktree_control::new_branch_start`, read on the repository's machine from what the background fetch last brought).
The commit, not `origin/<base>`, is what `Engine::create_worktree` receives, so the new branch takes no upstream from it; a spawn on a device whose helper is not connected leaves the start to the engine, the folder's own HEAD.
Until a pane of a recorded tab reports a cwd inside its checkout, the core reads that pane's cwd, and its agent's, as the checkout's own path, before any reader of the session sees it (`clamp_created_tab_cwds`; the coordinator applies the same clamp before it builds the catalog off the lock).
Every reader then agrees: the project and checkout rows and the purpose mirror (`session_spaces`), the pane's `cwd` and the listeners attributed by prefix (`project_layout_panes`), and the tab's own placement.
Without it a birth cwd in a parent folder made a project row for that folder with no tabs, claimed the listeners of its sibling projects, and could give another checkout's purpose to the worktree's workspace.
Once a pane has reported a cwd inside the checkout the record is `settled` and the cwd is read as reported, so a later `cd` out of the checkout is not hidden.
A folder in another worktree of the checkout's own repository, listed below the checkout (`CreatedTabClamp`), is that worktree's, not the outer checkout's: a pane born there is still on its birth value and stays read as the outer checkout until it reports a cwd in the checkout proper.
A repository that merely sits below the checkout is not one of its worktrees, so a folder in it is the checkout's, as before.
The checkout is read once, when the tab is recorded, and the catalog's worktree paths once, when the catalog arrives, both as the file system names them (`PathRules::Local`); a session then costs one read of each pane cwd and compares the nested worktrees by names, so their number adds no lookup under the lock.
Known limit: the nested worktrees are the catalog's, so a tab whose pane is born in a nested worktree before the catalog has listed it settles at once and its cwd is read as reported from then on, and the settle is not undone when the list arrives.
The reason is that a settled record is a latch (a later `cd` out of the checkout must not be hidden), and a worktree is listed within seconds of the `worktree.create` that makes it, a window a tab created for the outer checkout rarely lands in.
A tab is recorded once: a second acknowledgment of the same tab keeps the first record, its window and its settled state.
A tab that reports no such cwd for 30 seconds (`CREATED_TAB_BIRTH_WINDOW_MS`; the birth value lasted about 20 on a loaded runner) is settled too and reported once as `created_tab.cwd_unsettled`: the clamp is bounded, never a permanent override of the shell's own folder.
The window is measured on the runtime's monotonic `birth_clock`, so a wall-clock step cannot end it early, and a test moves that clock instead of waiting.
Measured against a private Herdr 0.9.1 server, the engine in use then, `workspace.create` and `tab.create` given a link or a trailing `/` answered the pane's cwd resolved through the link and without the separator, and the schema only typed `cwd` as a string.
On this machine the comparison reads both sides as the folder they name (`normalized_for_comparison`), so a checkout recorded in one spelling settles from a cwd reported in another.
The coordinator clones the payload for the catalog only when a recorded tab is in the session.
A tab Hide created on a device is kept the same way, by target and the device engine's own tab id (`created_device_tabs`, at most 64): the device's helper groups a tab by its first pane's cwd, so before the device's projects are grouped the core reads a recorded tab's panes as in the folder it was created for until one reports a cwd there.
A device folder is compared with the device's own strings unchanged (`PathRules::Device`, `hide_platform::path::wire_relative`), never on this machine's files or spellings, where the same name may be a link or another folder; the cost is that a device checkout recorded through a link the device resolves does not settle by path and is believed when the window ends, reported as `created_tab.cwd_unsettled`.
The worktrees nested below the checkout are those of the repository the device helper's worktree answer lists the checkout in, so before that answer arrives a folder in one reads as the checkout's, the same limit as above.
A device tab with no pane in the session is never settled by the window, as on this machine.
An acknowledgment that arrives after the device's session already carried the tab clamps that tab in the stored session and regroups it at once, rather than at the device's next publish; the stored session already shows the other recorded tabs as their folder, so only the new record reads it.
Its records leave with the tab, when the device's session fails, or when the device is removed.
Readers of the cwd that need no clamp: the agent row's fallback name (`project_agent`) runs only when the engine's workspace label is blank, which the projection never leaves blank, and the label worker (`labels/worker.rs`) uses the cwd only as the first directory to look in for a session it already has an identity for.
Any other tab, one made outside Hide by a shell or another tool, belongs to the checkout its first pane's cwd names.
A tab already in a workspace that is not the owner stays in that workspace and is never moved; a delegated child's own tab stays in its workspace.
Tools outside Hide, such as sasu dispatch, choose their own workspace; `hide agent spawn` uses the core's checkout and device start paths.

What an agent has spawned in-process is not in the engine's session at all.
The hook helper reports it, with the session's turn, to the core through hided's hook request (`HookCommand::Status`, `hided/src/hook_request.rs`), which passes the same pane proof as every hook request; a device's node forwards it with the pane's proof (PRD engine-bundle-1 D-7).
The core records it in `hide-core/src/agent_hooks/facts.rs`, a store with its own small lock that the runtime takes under its mutex only to record a report (no I/O) and that a device's coordinator takes alone to lay the facts on the session it is about to project; `Runtime::apply_session_update` lays them on this Mac's session.
A report that changes what a projection would lay wakes the pane's coordinator to publish again; one that changes nothing wakes nothing.
What a restart must keep is saved to `hook-facts.json` on a save thread of its own (`LatestFile`), so nothing of it is the engine's and a restart of the engine loses none of it (D-8).
A count Hide cannot read is reported as unknown, never as zero.

A pane's parent travels the same channel, and it is the only lineage there is: the engine records none.
hided is the sole writer of `parent_pane`, optional `parent_machine`, `child_session` and `parent_session` through `Engine::report_pane_tokens`; the unchanged value and lifetime contract is described in [status-model.md](status-model.md#where-a-parent-comes-from).
A fork is the operator's root, so its pane carries no parent token: hided writes `fork_pane`, `fork_session` and `fork_source_session` instead, which name where it came from without making it anyone's child ([status-model.md](status-model.md#where-a-parent-comes-from)).
Those tokens die with the pane, not with the agent, so a relationship holds only while both panes still report the sessions it was written for: `engine/tokens.rs` compares the child's, `agent_state::apply_lineage` the parent's, and an agent that took over a pane is a root.
A spawn without `--parent` is an operator handoff: `AgentRecord.parent` is empty and its separate optional `origin` records the spawner.
Delegated origin is derived from parent, and all CLI agent answers include nullable origin.
Origin never feeds lineage tokens, sidebar ownership, ancestor unread state, descendant badges, subtree close or the links worker's parent edges; a handed-off session remains linked to its own branch without a delegation line.
The one thing the screen reads from it is whether Hide itself started the agent: a handoff whose origin is Hide's code-owned identity (`docs/delivery.md`).
That is a third ownership value, `HideAi { operator_turn }`, beside the operator's own and a delegate's: such a row is a member of no operator list (checkout trees, Working, Done, Idle, badges, rail counts, Overview, the phone's list, notifications), and it is listed only while the operator has something to do, which `agent_state/turn.rs` derives as an ask of its own or a home turn (`PR #n 리뷰` while the attempt's pull request awaits the operator, `CI 실패` once checks failed and the agent stopped), never from the screen ([status-model.md](status-model.md#work-hide-ai-does-for-a-home)).
The core derives that from the ledger alone (`coordination::started`) and lays it on each live agent row as `hide_ai` (with the task Hide gave the spawn) and on the snapshot as `navigator.hide_ai_checkouts`, the checkouts Hide made, keyed by device and path.
The checkouts are a list beside the catalog and not a field on a checkout row because a row is rebuilt from Git and the session at several places and would lose a value laid on it, and a checkout stays listed after its agent ends.
The derivation runs inside `publish_delivery` and is compared by value with the last one, so a letter, a watch or another agent's registration stamps no new revision; only an agent or checkout Hide started appearing or ending does (`runtime/tests/lineage.rs`).
The home turn is computed from the attempt's pull request the Memory tracker already reads (`runtime/memory_promotion.rs`, `PromotionTracking.homes`), keyed by agent, and applied to the rows only when that table or the agent set changed, so a pass whose facts did not move adds no work to the snapshot path and `lay_hide_ai` touches no operator row.
When the tracker finds the attempt's pull request merged or closed it retires the attempt, off the runtime lock and capped at 16 attempts per check: the pane of the agent the promotion recorded (its coordination id, resolved to a pane through the ledger when the check is planned; an attempt with no recorded agent ends none, and no agent is chosen by its name) closes, and the worktree is removed with its branch kept when its tree is clean and no other agent or running program is in it, otherwise it stays with a `promotion.worktree_retired` diagnostic (the decision is `runtime/worktree_retire.rs`, which a mission's merged nodes share); a retire that could not be completed stays in the table and is tried again on the next check, and the same attempt retires once, so a repeat has no second effect.
The spawn receipt's `parent` continues to name the caller that authorizes every creation phase in both modes, with an explicit `SpawnMode` distinguishing responsibility and watch behavior.
Only delegation installs an automatic watch; handoff retains normal mail and explicit watches.
Version-1 receipts lacking mode default to delegation, and legacy `no_watch` fields are ignored while completed receipts and existing watches survive unchanged.
Caller plus intent is still the receipt key, and a mode change is an `intent_conflict` before side effects.
Both paths create a separate tab without focus, including a tab in an already-open checkout; interactive product tab creation retains its existing focus behavior.
Hide's fork and delegated `hide agent spawn --parent here|<self id>` register the relationship only after the engine produces the real pane, agent and session; a registration failure preserves that pane and records a diagnostic instead of inventing an edge.
A registration whose agent has not shown its session yet (Codex reports it at its first turn) waits in the ledger, and the lineage writer finishes or ends it from the agent lists the session sync already reads (`coordination::identity_wait`, [delivery.md](delivery.md#a-registration-that-waits-for-its-agents-session)).
Hide's fork registers the fork with no parent and the source as `origin`, which only the source's own live registration may ask for: `coordination::link_fork` registers the source and records the wait, and the wait registers the fork.
A fork runs on a worker (`fork::worker::run_agent_fork_with_registration`): it makes the pane where the operator asked, a tab in the source's workspace whose pane runs the shell integration's launch, as any agent tab does (`checkout_owner::open::create_tab_in`: `Engine::apply_layout`, or `Engine::create_tab` when the node has no launch), or a split right of the source (`Engine::split_pane`, which takes no command), both without focus, and hands the pane to the core under the lock (`Runtime::ingest_fork_pane`) before it starts the agent with the fork's resume arguments and the launch choice the source was started with (Agent start above), which the fork's pane then keeps.
The core then puts a fork tab right of the source's tab in the source's Agent area, through the same `agent_placements` queue a restored tab uses when the engine's session has not carried the tab yet, draws the fork's pane ahead of the engine's layout (Drawn ahead of the engine above; a device's pane is its device's to draw), and, for the operator's own press only (the event's `origin`; a fork another caller asks for waits where it was put, as an agent's spawn does), moves the keyboard to the fork with an ordinary operator pane focus, which brings the source's checkout forward when another is in front, unless a view was chosen on the control lane after the press (`last_view_intent_serial` above the serial at the press), the rule a new tab follows, or the Agent area has no room to show the tab (`agent_can_show_created`).
The core's own move for one fork is not a view the operator chose: it records it (`ForkFocus`), so of two forks starting at once the later press keeps the keyboard, and a pane made before the engine's session was replaced by a reconnect is neither placed nor focused by the fork (`PendingFork::generation`); a pane focus already queued on the control lane when the session is replaced is the lane's, as any queued focus is.
Keys typed from the press until the agent starts wait in a fork input request (`InputOrigin::Fork`).
The start acknowledgment only says its command was typed: the fork worker reads the agent for the reserved name until the expected agent kind in the created pane accepts input, using the same `Readiness::accepts_input` predicate as delivery (`Ready` alone, never launching or not ready).
This wait decides only input release, never fork success: an expired deadline, changed identity or lost daemon owner discards held keys and preserves the successful fork's pane; a transient read failure keeps waiting within the same bound and is recorded if that bound expires.
Only discarded bytes produce the existing input-loss notice, once; with no held keys there is no loss notice.
Released keys wait in the pane's one replay queue (`input::Replay`, `Inner::replay`), in the order typed, with the operator's keys typed after the release behind them and a letter's held keys, typed before the fork held the pane, ahead of them; nothing leaves it while a letter is being typed.
Once the fork's terminal takes keys the whole queue goes to its holder at once, each operator Enter with the plain keys typed right before it as one submission (`ClientMessage::Submit`, `input::submissions`): the holder writes those keys, waits 300 ms (`input::REPLAYED_SUBMIT_GAP`), writes the Enter, and writes the input sent after it only then, because held keys reach the program together and Codex reads an Enter inside keys that arrive together as a newline of a paste, so a fork's held prompt stayed in its composer.
The queue is held at most 3 s after the release (`Replay::ends`); a queue whose submission would end its gap past that is dropped rather than started, and a submission handed over always gets its Enter, so no text is left without it; the queue keeps 64 KiB, past which the latest typed keys are dropped and reported once (`limit`); a dropped queue, or one for a holder built before submissions, produces the input-loss notice.
The existing worker polls every 100 ms, with each socket read bounded by five seconds and the remaining time, until 115 seconds from worker entry, including pane creation and the start acknowledgment, so it never extends the engine's 120-second start reservation and makes at most 1,150 reads.
Each read checks the named fork's pane and kind and the weak daemon owner for every agent kind, including Claude and Codex; it does not read the parent's changing status or lock Runtime during polling.
It adds no work per key or worker, and a timer only while a held Enter waits.
Every fork opens a request, including a non-shell caller that supplies no request id.
`RequestHold` binds its pane on the node, where bare pane and request keys share one ordered queue, capped at 64 KiB and 30 s from request opening; keys older than 3 s remain valid while the fork starts.
At readiness the node releases the guard and hands valid queued keys to the pane; if its terminal is still attaching, that separate holder gets its ordinary 3 s window, while input facts retain the original wall time.
Crossing the hold bound clears its queue and refuses later keys until readiness or the input deadline releases the guard; late readiness never replays discarded keys.
A fork that yields focus discards the press's keys and opens a pane-only holder, so later bare keys into that pane still wait for its agent.
A failed fork discards its input, closes its pane, drops its placement and gives the keyboard back to the source.
A start worker panic settles the fork as failed, an input-confirmation panic discards input while preserving the successful pane, and runtime teardown discards every pending input request even when a worker can no longer upgrade its weak owner.
Phone input reserves bytes in this same node holder before its existing engine write; it needs no terminal attachment, and acknowledges only the engine's accepted write.
The node scans a collection capped at eight known and eight early request rows per key, publishes only failures or existing input facts, and reuses its clock for deadlines; no additional thread, I/O or Runtime lock is on the key path.
`engine/tokens.rs` names the tokens and their checks.
The consented helper supplies `hide_platform::host::machine_id` once in its connection greeting; the device worker applies it only to the established connection generation, outside `Mutex<Runtime>`, before resolving machine-qualified lineage.
A failed identity read logs a lineage diagnostic and leaves the parent unresolved while the helper stays usable; there is no SSH-alias fallback or extra identity SSH command.

Every shown Agent tab stays attached; recently shown tabs fill the remaining retention window.
The total is `max(ATTACHED_TAB_LIMIT, shown_count)`, at most six tabs, so an unseen attach never displaces a shown tab.
The core releases tabs outside that bounded set through the ordinary session drop.
A released pane keeps its projection entry carrying `released`; the shell disposes its terminal and redraws from the pane's frame on the next visit.
A device's pane in a tab not shown, or of a device not in front, is released the same way (`reconcile_remote_terminal_panes`), and only a pane its device no longer lists is forgotten at its node: a forgotten pane left its node nothing to type a bell, a sleep's quit key or a wake's resume line into (with-hide/hide-private#677, with-hide/hide-private#660).
Terminal metadata belongs to each session pane, independently of which pane is selected.
A selection that moves, including a switch to another checkout, an acknowledged new tab awaiting its layout, or a selected pane that retired clears only the selected pane's presentation and cannot erase other retained tabs' metadata; each authoritative layout still prunes panes that actually closed.
The shell disposes a parked terminal whose entry is missing, so a single list without a retained pane throws its renderer away even when the next list brings the pane back.
The attach window continues to release its oldest tab normally, and returning to an evicted tab restores its PTY content with a new renderer.
The idle tick attaches every shown tab's panes, while focus, read and sleep-visit state follow only the active area's tab.
All shown tabs count as on screen for sleep prevention.

Hide owns local Agent area membership and tab order.
Moving, reordering or splitting a tab changes the persisted Agent tree without `tab.move`, workspace creation or pane movement, preserving pane identity and lineage.
The engine remains authoritative for tab existence; its reorder does not rearrange the saved tree.
Device strips retain engine-confirmed reorder (`place_checkout_strip`, `place_device_strips`): a move of a tab within its owning workspace sends `Engine::move_tab` to that device's engine, and an offline device refuses it.
The legacy host without `workspace_views_path` retains its mixed file/engine strip compatibility path; the web host refuses its obsolete local `reorder_tab` event.

A pane that is going away ends its attach quietly.
The engine ends the pane's PTY before its session stops listing the pane, so the attach child ends while the pane is still drawn; projecting that as `ended` is what flashed "terminal attach ended" over a pane the operator had just closed.
A close Hide asked for, or a pane the engine has already stopped listing, projects `closing` with no notice chunk and keeps the pane's last frame until it is removed.
Every other reason still reports `ended` with its message.

## Local agent delivery and inactivity watches

Receipt-proven spawn names use the existing lineage worker and delivery writer.
An append-only receipt count and placement revision guard naming admission, so unrelated letters and unchanged native observations build no naming plan.
Each batch admits at most 32 receipts, with one active and one pending batch and at most 4,096 attempted receipt ids per connection.
Each receipt needs at most four one-second engine calls and a five-second durable checkpoint wait, all outside Runtime and the session-sync thread.
The worker checks shutdown between receipts; stopping can wait for the current receipt's bounded calls.
Workspace and tab outcomes are persisted separately from spawn completion, and completed replay does no naming I/O.

The core's delivery worker owns a separate private ledger and returns mutation success only after atomic persistence outside `Mutex<Runtime>`.
Runtime holds an immutable ledger projection; one bounded writer queue and separately owned doorbell/watch producers stop and join with Core outside the lock.
Beside it Runtime holds the letter index the turn card reads (`delivery::correspondence::Correspondence`): each pane's letters and started agents by time, interim reports apart, each line keyed by the agent on its other side, built by the delivery worker from the ledger it just saved, before it takes the lock, so the lock compares one digest and lays the rows again (`sync_request_rows`) only when the digest moved; a delivery step that changes no card line, such as a bell or a receipt, lays nothing.
The existing pane input path adds only timestamp assignments (the last input, from a key, paste, phone write or agent-find key; a submission is stamped only by a phone reply or a prompt hook of the pane's own session); the observation adds the time the pane entered `working`; watch snapshots publish start, warning and end transitions.
The daemon exposes typed `hide request`, `inbox` and `watch` commands through the existing caller-bound Workspace boundary without requiring a renderer.
The doorbell decides from hide-owned facts only (`doorbell::judge` over the pane's observation, never a screen read) and writes at rest or after the existing mid-turn patience, and prompt-hook stdout flush precedes durable intake confirmation.
The observation carries what the pane's session read says it waits for in the engine's current state (`doorbell::Turn`), taken from the label overlay the coordinator computes before it observes the payload; an agent whose read reports turns is held while a native question or plan waits (`awaiting_operator`) or while no read settled the current state (`session_unread`).
The doorbell's pass also decides which panes show letters waiting on a possible draft (`doorbell::letters_waiting`), in memory under the short lock it already takes to publish its holds and bounded by the open letters, and publishes only when a mark appears or goes; the shell's Deliver now is one event that releases the draft and leaves the ringing to the next pass ([delivery.md](delivery.md#delivering-a-held-letter-now)).
The doorbell also reads the composer of a pane it holds on a possible draft, once per observed draft and state generation, after input is quiet at rest or working, and only for an agent version whose composer check passed: the pane read (`Engine::read_screen`) runs on the doorbell's thread off the lock, within its eight work attempts per pass, is judged by the adapter's composer declaration (`hide_agent_adapter::composer`), and a positive `empty` releases the draft as Deliver now does, so the verdict itself still reads no screen ([delivery.md](delivery.md#reading-the-composer)).
Before an eligible typed bell, an agent with a composer declaration must also read empty through the same guard as a forced letter, even when the draft record is clear, because a delayed status update may cover a key; this read is off-lock, within the existing per-pass budget and retry backoff, and the native and input-generation checks still run before the write.

An agent's readiness is three-valued at the engine boundary (`engine::answers::Readiness`): only a launch in progress or an explicit not-ready refuses, and the unreported readiness of an agent started by hand is decided by those facts; a refusal after the verdict is retried on a capped backoff off the lock ([delivery.md](delivery.md#safe-intake-and-manual-fallback)).
Pending delivery becomes undelivered after 60 minutes; watch warnings use 20-minute inactivity, one tick for a target its own row shows stopped on a question or held at a blocked prompt, and first-warning time plus 60 minutes, with persistent counts and activity reset.
The helper's metadata-only session activity uses the same native ownership proof as the local reader.
A confirmed report to its parent ends the sender's watch immediately; unanswered parent warnings and overdue undelivered letters use the existing human notification paths once per cause.
Each letter keeps a durable `hook_confirmed` receipt separate from cancellation.
Acknowledgement can come only from the recipient's own pane and session, so it is that receipt; it still counts as checking a watch warning and does not schedule another doorbell.
A letter an earlier build acknowledged with `hook_confirmed: false` stays in the bell turn's batch after the pending letters and counts as open until its delivery deadline, when `Ledger::expire` ends that wait.
Automatic doorbells remain limited to pending letters; the delivery deadline ends the intake wait of a pending letter (it becomes undelivered) and of such an acknowledged one.
The first receipt ends a matching report watch; an actual post-flush confirmation still does when cancellation or the delivery deadline arrived between pull and confirmation.
Cancellation and the undelivered state prevent a new pull; an already-printed in-flight confirmation remains valid, preserving cancellation while changing undelivered to delivered.
Replayed confirmation after restart preserves a watch explicitly started after that first receipt; a report whose acknowledgement left no receipt does not suppress spawn's initial watch.
Legacy letters with an absent or null field prove confirmation only in `delivered` state; an older `acknowledged` record cannot distinguish manual acknowledgement from confirmed intake.
Older acknowledged records remain excluded from pull and keep their existing closed-state retention rules unless they still await a reply; the missing receipt never becomes delivery proof.
The same core owns registration, spawning, lineage, the mailbox and inactivity watches; no external coordinator or conflict probe remains.
A registration ends when its host's published session stops listing its pane: each publish hands the published pane set to `Runtime::observe_delivery`, which compares it with the previous one only when it moved (`coordination::gone_registrations`), and the delivery store ends what it found in its next transaction; a connect forgets the host's panes and notes the ledger's next id before asking for the snapshot, so a snapshot judges only registrations made before it.
[delivery.md](delivery.md) owns the CLI, capacities, privacy, completion reports, remote delivery, manual fallback and the residual external-input race.

## Explicit terminal attachments

The browser cannot name a dropped file's or a pasted image's path, so hided's own staging (`hided/src/attachments.rs`, see hided and the WebSocket boundary) is the only source of a `terminal_attachment` intent: it writes the uploaded bytes to disk and sends the event carrying the original pane ID, bracketed-paste mode, a generated request UUID and the staged paths.
hided reports `terminal_attachment_ready` itself once a clipboard image's bytes are staged at the exact path the core reads it from.
No clipboard image bytes enter the JSON event or the render mutex.

`runtime/attachments.rs` owns admission, captured terminal and remote connection generations, one active worker, retry, cancellation and an ordered 64 KiB input reservation.
Subsequent input to the originating pane is held by the pane's node until file preparation and transfer succeed, then the complete quoted path payload and held bytes enter the node's terminal writer together (`TerminalControl::AttachmentHold`, `AttachmentDeliver`).
No Enter is synthesized, and an upload failure never forwards held input, because it may contain an Enter that would submit an incomplete prompt.
Retry keeps immutable prepared bytes; cancel discards held input explicitly.
Missing, closed, released or reconnected targets retire the intent and cannot forward its data to a replacement session or fall back to the local host.
A local pane with no terminal session yet is still a target: the web shows a pane once its layout arrives, before its session attaches, so a drop can reach the core first (issue 735).
That intent waits for the pane's session, taking the first session the pane starts as its own, with the paste and typed input held under the same 64 KiB reservation, and both are written when the session attaches.
The wait is bounded by `COMMIT_GRACE` from admission (`hide-node-link/src/attachments.rs`, how long hided keeps a committed file from eviction, so the pasted path still names a file); the coordinator's operation tick checks the deadline with no event needed and fails the intent as unavailable, with a `terminal.attachment.terminal_wait_expired` diagnostic.
Only admission, completion and actionable failure transitions publish a notice through `status.async_operations`; terminal-specific actions render in the originating pane.

The node that holds the picked files reads them (`hide-host/src/attachments.rs`, the `read_attachments` call, asking the core before each file whether to go on, so a cancel stops the read between files): only explicitly selected regular files, refusing final-component symlinks, special files, control-character paths and files that change while read; `terminal_attachments.rs` keeps the limits' admission and constructs ordered quoted terminal input.
The bounds are eight files, 20 MiB per file and 40 MiB per intent; clipboard decoding additionally allows at most 16 megapixels.
A device stages the immutable bytes through its node's link, the same way over every device link (`Call::StageAttachment`, one file per call so each stays under the link's line cap, answered by `hide-host/src/attachments.rs`, `Staging`), not a shell command, a subprocess or an SSH-only channel, and answers only device paths.
Device staging lives in the node's private `<state>/terminal-attachments` folder, with generated exclusive filenames, 0700 folder and 0600 file permissions, ownership checks and same-byte verification before adopting a completed file on retry; the folder an earlier build staged into, `~/.hide-terminal-attachments`, is swept of expired files and removed once empty.
The node tracks each request until its last file arrives: a link that ends with a request part way removes that request's files, and `Call::RemoveAttachments` removes a request's files when the core cancels, retires or finishes it.
A file still being written when either happens is removed by its own write as it finishes, so neither can leave a file that appears after it, and a write whose worker unwinds drops its request the same way (`hide-host/src/attachments.rs`, `Staging` and its `Writing` guard).
Each file's call is bounded at 60 seconds, a cancel stops the request between files and removes what it staged, and a device whose link is down refuses the request without waking it.
Neither filesystem nor network I/O runs under `Mutex<Runtime>`.

Both staging locations admit at most 128 files and 256 MiB.
Cleanup scans only their immediate generated entries on the next explicit attachment intent and expires entries older than 24 hours; there is no background janitor and successful paths may therefore survive longer while idle.
Local clipboard PNGs remain available after a successful local paste, while remote success releases the local PNG after upload; the core's own node removes it (`Call::RemoveClipboard`, refused for any path that is not a clipboard image), so the core touches no file.
Cancellation, retirement and destruction attempt to remove only that intent's exact generated files; failed remote cleanup is diagnostic and remains bounded by the next-intent expiry policy.
Original user-selected files are never deleted.
This boundary has no provider-specific draft, composer or attachment shelf.

## Reopening locally closed work

The core owns one session-local, twenty-item LIFO stack for file tabs and local pane or tab closes initiated through Hide.
Remote closes and topology changes made by another client never enter it.
Every item names its device: a file tab closed on a device is that device's, a pane or tab close is this machine's.
Reopen restores the newest item of the device in front and `recent_closed` counts only that device's items, so a reopen on one device never restores work on another and never takes another device's newer close off the stack; a device's file reopens through that device's host.
A device's pane and tab closes are not recorded, so a device has nothing of that kind to reopen (PRD S5.5 D-21 exception).
Recording them needs the capture and marker-adoption protocol below run against the device's own engine and its agents' resume on that machine; that stays open until the device control path carries the layout export and the `HIDE_REOPEN_INTENT` adoption, and until then a closed device pane is reopened by making a new one there.
Before sending a close to the engine, a background worker exports immutable layout facts and the core records the close intent in its target scope; it enters `closing` immediately and starts the external effect after capture succeeds.
A close that removes a whole tab (its tab close, or its only pane's) takes that tab out of the Agent areas at once: `shown_agent_layout` publishes and attaches the stored layout less every tab whose close is preparing, transmitting or awaiting topology (`PendingClose::leaving_tab`), and the stored layout keeps the tab, so a refusal, failure or unknown result puts it back where it stood with no layout write to undo.
It is a projection over a close that still waits for the engine like any other; no surviving pane's size depends on the closed tab, which is why it alone does not have to stay drawn.
When the closing item holds the keyboard, the operator moves to what that projection now shows, through the same tab focus a click sends: the engine makes active the tab that takes the closed tab's place, or the last tab when the closed one was last, and with Hide's focus pending, that move is read as its answer rather than followed; a refusal or failure focuses the original tab again when nothing has moved since.
When the projection shows nothing because every tab of the checkout in front is leaving, the operator's close (`retain_for_reopen`, which a sleep's own close is not; a close that leaves a shell in its tab keeps that tab, so its checkout is never empty) brings back the most recent other checkout of this machine in `ui_state.recent_checkouts` that still holds a tab no close is taking, through `focus_checkout`, marks it the Workspace a reload opens on, and records the move in the close's selection restore, so a refusal or failure brings the operator back as it does the tab (`move_from_closing_target`, `leave_emptied_checkout`).
A checkout whose worktree or project is being removed (`worktree_removal` checking, closing or removing, or `workspace_removals_in_flight`) is passed over too, because its tabs can still be open while the removal closes the agents outside it first.
The move is part of the close event, not a second event the shell sends, so a refusal cannot leave the screen half moved; with no such checkout or another device in front, the front stays and the shell draws the empty Agent area.
A primary checkout's last tab closes like any other, linked worktrees or not: the core's own engine has no refusal to close a workspace that has linked worktree workspaces, so no shell is made first.
A named tab's last agent pane gets a shell inside the same tab, which keeps the tab and its place while the agent pane closes (`ClosedContext::replacement_in_tab`, decided by `Runtime::keeps_named_tab`; named means the operator's Rename gave the tab its current label, which the core records by tab id in `UiStateSnapshot::operator_tab_names` because the engine keeps no author for a label, so a spawn's name or a store from before the record never counts): the close worker splits it from the closing pane with `Engine::split_pane`, unfocused, at the checkout and stamped with the close's `HIDE_REOPEN_INTENT` marker, and the pane joins the close's approved pane set before the agent pane's `Engine::close_pane`, so the precondition that refuses a changed tab still holds for every other pane; a retry adopts only the pane carrying that marker and makes a new one only when it is gone, and a failure after the split (a lost answer, a snapshot that does not show it yet) names the marked pane (`ReplacementFailure::shell_in_tab`) so `Runtime::note_shell_in_tab` adds it to the approved set and the retry is not refused as a changed tab.
