Its state on the map (`NodeView.gate`: ahead, open, passed, the waiting time and when it has waited 24 hours) is derived from the line and the decision, never stored apart, and the shell compares the long wait with its own clock, so no timer of the core's runs for it.
Every answer reaches `settle_gate`, the one entry, whether from the decision card, the phone (`MissionAnswerPayload.phone`) or the Conductor's pane (`hide mission gate --said`, `relay_gate`, the Conductor alone and only with the operator's words): a pass records the line as the operator's with where it came from and the words; a fix keeps the gate open, adds the words as a defect line with the same `via`, sets the node working, and wakes the Conductor and the node's worker with them (`WakeEvent::GatePassed`, `GateFix`).
The Conductor's `record`, `skip` and `decide --clear` on it are refused (`mission_gate_operator_only`); the operator's own `끝으로` on a raise, which goes past every line left open as their decision, passes the gate through `settle_gate` too (`GateAnswer::Past`, from the card with the words `운영자 판단`), never around it.
A replan that changes a gate's words or takes it away takes, in the same change (`missions::apply_plan`), the question that gate asked and its raise, so the gate behind it, or the changed one, asks next; a question of the Conductor's own stays.
A known limit: the 24 hours of a gate's long wait count from when it was asked, or raised with no Conductor, so a gate that reached its node while another gate held the decision counts from when its own question stands, not from when it was reached.

## Session plans

A session's own plan (PRD hide-plan) is a core-owned record keyed by the native session, `hide-core/src/plans.rs` for the model and its rules and `runtime/plans.rs` for the commands, the published view, the review question and the hook's summary ([delivery.md: Plans](delivery.md#plans)).
Missions and plans check their graphs with one module, `hide-core/src/dag.rs`: the key rule, unknown dependencies, cycles, the 64-node cap, the walk upstream and the topmost node by depth; a mission's checks moved there unchanged, and a plan adds only its session key, its review, its change reasons and its update time.
Each `hide task` command is one typed event applied under `Mutex<Runtime>`; the plan is saved through the link worker (`LedgerUpdate::Plan`) into `ledger_plans` beside the session's record in `links.sqlite3`, schema 9, and read back once with `LedgerCall::Plans` when the worker starts, so no file of its own exists; the table is deleted with the session's other rows (`remove_sessions`), and the runtime drops a deleted or pruned session's plan and its 보기 slot item in the same transition.
The book holds at most 128 plans, evicting the one updated longest ago whose session runs in no pane.
It is published as its own revisioned rest section, `plans`, one `PlanView` per pane whose session has a plan, made again on the snapshot read only when the book's change count or the panes' sessions moved (`refresh_plans`); a mission node's view carries its worker's `PlanView` (`worker_plan`), and the session record carries the same view, so the map, the chip and the node read one value.
A proposed plan is laid on its agent's row as a question in the local and device pipelines before the read axis and the lineage run (`lay_plan_reviews`), so it rides the ask's band, second line and notification paths with no new state ([status-model.md](status-model.md#a-plan-waiting-for-review-is-a-question)).
The hook's summary (`PlanContext`, `hide_agent_hooks::plan_record`) is made under the lock from the book, the ledger's registrations and the missions, and rides the answer of the prompt hook's letter pull (`hook_request.rs`) and of every `hide task` command; the pre-tool hook reads only the record those wrote, so no tool call reaches the daemon ([agent-hooks.md](agent-hooks.md#the-panes-plan-record)).
The map is a 보기 slot item, `DetailItem::Plan { session }`, which draws the published section and starts no read; a build that does not know the item reads a saved slot holding one as unrecognized and starts with an empty slot.

Handing steps to children (PRD hide-plan-delegate) keeps the same owner and adds no worker.
Every status change, `node` and `set` alike, goes through `plans::judge` under the lock: the order, the evidence each output asks for and a handed step's report; evidence new to a step is not read there.
The command instead answers `PlanTurn::Prove` with what it still owes and the session's node link (`node_link`, the local node or the device's helper), hided runs `PlanProof::run` on its request thread (`gh pr view` through the node's allowlisted `gh`, `GitCommand::HasLocalBranch` for a head that is neither the current branch nor a child's, and `Call::PathFacts`, the same read the catalog uses, 20 s each), and dispatches the command again with the answers; the core judges the plan again as it is then, so nothing read off the lock is applied to a plan that moved, and three rounds bound it.
The spawn's admission (`plan_spawn_admission`) runs in `prepare_delivery` under the lock and hands the ledger the step's link and the main's sleeping children; the ledger counts the cap in its reserve under its own lock, as a mission's cap, so two spawns at once cannot both take the third place.
The B6 wake check reads the same count in `prepare_delivery`, so a spawn and a waking letter that land in the same instant may let a fourth child run until one ends; the cap is counted again at every spawn.
The step's delegation is folded from the published ledger (`fold_delegations`, on `publish_delivery` and when the plans are read back) and saved with the plan, each delegation keeping the last letter id it read, because letters are pruned and the step must say what its child did after they are gone.
`refresh_plans` keys its view on the book's change count, the panes' sessions and the panes and sessions of the children the shown plans handed steps to, so a child that opens, moves or ends remakes the view and a quiet burst does not; a shown plan brings its children's plans with it.

## Session threads

A session thread (PRD session-docs-and-assistant B25-B29) is one agent pane's session drawn as a conversation, and its input box types into that pane.
`hide-core/src/runtime/session_thread.rs` owns it: one thread is open at a time, as one session record is, opened by `session_thread_open {pane_id}` and closed by `session_thread_close`.
The pane's session is the one the engine reports for its agent, kept on its delivery observation for every agent with a thread reader, OpenCode's database included (`ThreadReference`); a pane whose agent reported none, or whose runtime has no reader, opens as `failed` with `no_record`, and a session it reports later in the same terminal is read then.
The record is read where the session runs, by that machine's node (`Call::SessionThread`, protocol 66, the `thread` reader feature), on a worker outside the lock, and the answer comes back under a short lock with the open thread's generation, so an answer for a thread that closed is dropped.
The newest page is read once and kept; what the session writes after it is read forward from where that page ended (`ThreadRead::From`), again when an engine read shows the agent's state or state sequence moved and, while it works, when a once-a-second `Call::SessionActivity` (file size and time, no records) says it wrote.
One live read is out at a time, with one more owed when the record moves during it; a forward read that fills past 512 KiB becomes a kept page and the next starts where it ended, and the thread keeps four whole pages, an older one read on request (`session_thread_older`) refused past them as `capacity`.
A node that cannot be asked leaves the thread as it was with `connected` false and is asked again 5 s later; a busy file is asked again after 500 ms; a cursor whose file was replaced starts the thread over from the newest page; a refusal after the thread drew keeps what it drew and goes to the diagnostic log.
Two snapshot sections carry it, each on its own revision and replaced whole: `session_thread`, the state, the pane check, the live page and the input's state, and `session_thread_history`, the kept pages, which change only when a page is read or the live page fills, so a working session re-sends its live page only.
Each page carries the ACP updates as `hide-session` wrote them and its `parts`: a shell call whose command is a `hide` command that makes a Hide part (`hide task set|node|approve|drop`, `hide agent spawn`, `hide request send`, `hide browser|file|diff open`, `hide mission ...`) is named by what it made, by its tool call id (`hide_session::thread::hide_call`), and a spawn takes its agent id from the call's output when that arrives, on the same page or a later one (B26); the screen looks each part up in Hide's own state by those names.
A page's `sessions` places each session a letter, a spawn or a received letter's sender names (a registration id or name, as written) at the pane and machine of the live registration that answers to it, as a letter's target is found (`coordination::registered_record`), so a chip draws that session's row; an ended or unknown name is left out and its chip draws the name alone.
The read's worker turns the answer into the page the snapshot holds (its JSON updates, parts and sessions) before it takes the lock, from the ledger and the earlier pages' parts it was handed when the read started.

The input box's words reach the pane as a phone's reply does (`hided/src/mobile/pane.rs`): the screen stages its files as a terminal attachment's (`attachment_stage`) and sends `thread_input`; hided commits the stages and sends the core `session_thread_input`, an event only hided makes.
The core sends only to the pane the thread was opened for while that pane still runs the session it was opened for: the same pane, terminal and session reference, else `pane_changed` or `pane_gone`, and one input at a time.
An input for a thread that closed, or for a pane whose thread another window replaced, types nothing and is answered `closed` by its request id on the thread section the core holds, so the screen that sent it gets its words back.
A worker stages a device pane's files on that device (`terminal_attachments::read_sources`, `stage`), puts their quoted paths before the words as a terminal attachment pastes them, waits on the pane node's input permit and the sleep gate, takes the runtime lock once more to check that the thread is still open on the same pane and session, and outside the lock sends the words and Enter through the engine's `submit_text`, which types the words as they are, with no bracketed-paste wrapper, and then Enter, not as keys typed into the terminal ([UI_BEHAVIOR.md](UI_BEHAVIOR.md)).
The send marks a key before it and a key and a submit after it (`note_delivery_reply`), so the doorbell neither types over the words nor takes them for a draft, and reads the thread on.
A screen that reaches its core through a node's daemon stages its files on that node, which a thread's input does not hand on: its files are refused as `unknown_stage` and its words go through.

## The link record

The link record (PRD link-graph) keeps which sessions made or worked on which pull request, which issues each pull request is linked to and from where, and which worktrees each branch had, after the panes, the branches and the provider files that said so are gone.
Owners: `hide-core/src/links/` (`store.rs` the SQLite store, `worker.rs` the one writer, `query.rs` the `hide links` answer, `session_command.rs` the `hide session` answer), `hide-core/src/runtime/links.rs` (the facts handed in and the panel applied), `hide-session` (the shared line parser the link facts come from), and `hide-host/src/serve.rs` (`link_files`, `link_read`).

It lives in its own file, `links.sqlite3` beside `session-search.sqlite3` (`hide_kit::layout::links_store`), so the two have separate failure, write-lock and size boundaries; it reads each project's retention from the old search file's `policy` table through a read-only `ATTACH` (`LinkStore::policies`), and nothing writes that file any more (see [Project sessions and Memory](#project-sessions-and-memory)).
One worker thread, `hide-links`, spawned in `Core::create` and joined in `Drop for Core`, owns the only write connection; the core hands it owned facts (each GitHub project's pull requests with their issue links and sources, the navigator's worktrees, live panes' session ids and branches, and the core's resolved parent relationships) when they change, and it applies them as idempotent upserts.
The schema moves by `PRAGMA user_version` (15 stops reading the retired `direct_observations` table, which an upgrade keeps with its rows; 13 adds `session_reviews`, below; 10 since named pull requests, below; 9 added [Session plans](#session-plans)); a newer version than this build knows is refused (`links_store_newer`), and a file that fails `quick_check` is set aside once as `links.sqlite3.corrupt` and rebuilt from the session files still there, with a diagnostic for what could not be rebuilt.
The file is private, `secure_delete` is on and `max_page_count` caps it at 64 MiB; crossing the cap refuses the write (`links_store_full`) and the panel says so.

Session files are read only through the worker's own cursor, one bounded read per turn (20 ms of work, then a 30 ms rest), `hide-session`'s shared line parser, and never under `Mutex<Runtime>`; the core's own node lists and reads them (`link_files`, `link_read` with one file), so the worker opens no session file itself, and a call that fails ends the listing as failed, to be listed again from its start; the first start backfills the last 90 days once (meta `backfill_done`), then lists files changed since the last list every 15 s, every 3 s while a panel is open (B29), with a 60 s overlap.
A listing is read page by page: a page is the newest 2,000 files, a full page is followed by the next older one (a `listing.capped` diagnostic says so), and the listing's time is recorded (meta `listed_at`, and `backfill_done` the first time) only once its last page has drained with every write kept, so a failed write is listed and read again rather than skipped.
Only a file that is not there marks a line's file gone (`session_file_missing`); a file the system refuses to open is `session_unreadable`, recorded against its stamp and retried when the file changes.
A line keeps the request text (500 characters at most), the branch spans, the pull request addresses it printed (20 per session), the pull requests its tool calls named (200 per session) and its continuation and parent links; no conversation body is copied.
A session is linked to a pull request when it printed the address within -2 s to +30 s of GitHub's `createdAt`, or within -10 s to +30 s when its successful creating call gave the address back (`created`; `PrMark::made`, `links::made_by_print`), when a branch span inside the project's folders overlaps the pull request's life, from the previous pull request on that branch closing to this one closing (`worked`), or when one of its tool calls named the pull request (`worked`); a non-interactive run (Claude `entrypoint` of SDK or print, Codex `exec`) makes no line.
A session a pull request card's `에이전트로 미리 점검` started is linked as `reviewed` (PRD pr-review-status D-11, D-17): `pr_delegate` with `intent: review` makes the runtime follow the start's request to its pane once the start holds the task-operation slot (`runtime/links.rs`, `follow_pre_check`; at most 8 followed, each given up when its start fails, its pane closes after the session list showed it, or 10 minutes pass, every drop a `pre_check.dropped` diagnostic); the pane is taken from the slot before the window's acknowledgement or a next start clears it, and the session is looked for on each local and device session update, and once the pane's agent names its session the worker writes it to `session_reviews` (schema 13, added with nothing dropped or rewritten); the role outranks `worked` and yields to `created`, and survives a restart because it is the record's.
An address a tool only printed at any other time links nothing: a listing, a browser's open tabs or a log prints pull requests the session never touched, and a review session that only listed tabs once sat on every pull request whose page was open.
A call names a pull request when it acts on that one (`hide-session/src/named_prs.rs`): a `gh pr` command given its number or address (`view`, `diff`, `checkout`, `review`, `comment`, `merge` and the other verbs on one pull request; never `list`, `status` or `create`), a `gh api` path under `repos/<owner>/<name>/pulls/<number>` or `issues/<number>`, `open`, `curl`, `wget` or `hide browser open` given its address, a tool whose argument is the address itself, or a GitHub tool given its owner, name and number; every format Hide reads records its calls, so each agent's reader passes them in (Claude Code's `tool_use`, Codex's `function_call` and `local_shell_call`, Grok's `tool_call`, Pi's and omp's `toolCall`, agy's `tool_calls`, OpenCode's tool parts).
The shell text is read by `hide-shell`, the reader the hooks use before a call runs, in the syntax of the shell that ran it ([agent-hooks.md: Which shell reads a call](agent-hooks.md#which-shell-reads-a-call)), so a PowerShell `cd .\app` moves to `app`, a heredoc body, a quoted message, a comment and a letter's body name nothing, and a command one layer deeper (`bash -c`, a script, an alias) is not looked for.
A number named without its repository (`-R`, `GH_REPO` or an address) belongs to the project whose registered folder holding the call's folder is the deepest: the folder a `cd` before the command or the tool's own working folder names, else the folder the record gives for the call, else the session's; a `cd` the reading cannot follow (home, `-`, a variable) names nothing, and a connected device's node converts that folder to the wire spelling as it does the session's cwd.
A record from before version 10 reads every file it had read again from its start once, and lists the last 90 days again on this machine and each device, so the sessions already recorded find what their calls named; the first fill stays done, so no spinner turns for it.
A link is closed by an end time, never deleted, and only when its source says it ended: a closing reference GitHub no longer lists, a Hide branch link that was cleared on a branch a checkout here holds; a failed GitHub read closes nothing.
Retention follows each Project's Copied history: Off keeps a line only while its file exists, which the own node answers for all of them in one `real_paths` call (a call that fails removes nothing; an OpenCode session, which lives in OpenCode's database, until its read finds it gone), otherwise a line stays while it ended within the period, or within a year while its pull request is still open; the prune runs every 30 minutes on the worker.
An archived session (Session archive, above) follows the same rule while it has a line; the core hands the worker the archived sessions it holds, the prune answers the sessions it removed (`pruned`), and the core drops those members, so an archive never outlives the record behind its row.
An archived session with no line expires by its project's period counted from the archive time (`expired_archived`), Off keeping it.
A repository is keyed by GitHub's repository id when `gh repo view` gives it, so a rename keeps its rows.

A connected device's sessions come through its helper: `link_files` lists the device's changed session files and `link_read` reads up to 8 of them, each answer only link facts (helper protocol 32 and later include bounded request and issue facts); the worker asks each ready device at most once a minute, a device whose call failed is left alone for a minute before it is asked again, and a device that is gone keeps every row it gave.
The owning node converts the native cwd in each `LinkRead` answer to the platform layer's wire spelling before sending it, so Windows agent paths relate to catalog paths with the same separators without the core interpreting another device's native path.
The panel's read is one request at a time, the latest only, answered as `link_panel` on its own delta revision beside `rest`; `links_open` names the pull request or issue, a generation fence drops an answer for one no longer shown, and a failure keeps the lines read before.
A store that cannot open is tried again every 15 s, and while it is closed, or while the worker's writes keep failing, the panel's answer is that failure rather than a record that stopped growing.
The worker re-reads an open panel after it writes, and publishes the small per-Project summary (`link_summaries`: session counts by pull request and issue, each session's pull request chips, and whether the first fill of this machine or of a device is running; a later listing turns no spinner) at most every 2 s and only when it changed.
A pass recomputes only the Projects a change since the last one can move (`links/summary_scope.rs`, with-hide/hide-private#571): a session file's read, a ledger update and a pane fact mark their session, and the pass places each marked session with `LinkStore::session_reach` (its folder and the folders it named a pull request from by number, the repositories of what it printed, named, reviewed or sighted, the sessions it continues, its ancestors and its children) against what each Project's last pass read (its places, its repository and every session id its summary names); every other change (Project facts, lineage, a review, a delete, a prune, a ledger call, a write failure, the store opening) recomputes them all, as do more than 512 marked sessions or a reach past 256 sessions.
A Project the change does not reach keeps the summary its last pass made, which a pass over it would make again, and a Project whose last pass held an older part after a failed read, or whose chips reached their limit, is recomputed on every pass; `a_pass_over_the_changed_projects_publishes_what_a_full_pass_publishes` compares the two passes after each write of a mix.
A Project the pass does recompute reads again only the pull requests the marked sessions can reach (`links/pr_cache.rs`): the session lines of each candidate pull request are held between passes and dropped when the pull request's row, the Project's places, fences or repository names changed (found by comparing them), when a marked session's id is one a held line names (what the write took out), when the session printed, named or reviewed its number or worked on its branch (what the write put in), or when the change reaches no one session, a read failed or the Project left; the candidate pull requests are one read of each kind of evidence as a set, not a probe per pull request, and a Project holds at most 8,192 of them, reading the rest on every pass.
`a_pass_reads_again_only_the_pull_requests_a_change_reaches` puts each of those rules to work against a pass that reads every pull request and counts the pull requests read.
The summary also names, in the core only and never on the wire, the checkouts whose work landed: each session line that made its pull request or worked on its branch (a pull request it only named, as a review does, is not work that landed here) is given to the deepest of the Project's current worktrees that holds its folder on its own device, counted only if it started there since that worktree was added (`WorktreeSnapshot.created_at_unix_ms`, so a worktree made again at a used path inherits nothing, even through a resumed or still-running session, and one whose age is unread has nothing); a checkout on a branch weighs only that branch's pull requests, so a branch switched in place starts clean, and a checkout landed when those include a merged one and no open one.
The runtime stamps that onto `CheckoutSnapshot.landed` (`runtime/links.rs`, `associate_landed`) when a summary arrives and on every catalog or GitHub change, only while Git also counts the checkout's HEAD in its base; with no summary nothing is landed, so a checkout with no record of its work, which Git ancestry alone reads as merged, is neither drawn merged nor folded as settled.
`hide links pr <number> | issue <number> | branch <name> | session <id> [--all-projects]` is read-only and answers the panel's record as one JSON line (the target, the repository, each pull request with its state, issue links and sources, worktrees and whether each was removed, and each session with its ids, device, role, times, request, file path, whether the file is there, and parent).
It answers through hided's own core without a renderer, scoped by default to the Project of the calling checkout, which may be a device's (a pane on a device reads that device's Projects, and `--all-projects` reads this machine's and every connected device's, the same catalog the link worker records): a target in another Project fails with `other_project` and a hint to pass `--all-projects`, a missing one with `not_found`, an unreadable record with `links_unavailable`, each with a non-zero exit.

`hide session list | record <id> | read <id> --request <n> | --from <n>` (PRD agent-session-read; `hide-core/src/links/session_command.rs`, drawn by `hided/src/session_cli.rs`) is an agent's read of past sessions in three steps, read-only, through hided's own core without a renderer and with the caller credential `hide links` takes.
Its scope is the calling checkout's Project and every connected device's Project of the same repository (`[HOST/]OWNER/NAME`, case ignored), each Project's repository being the one the operator connected it to, else the one its own checkout's `origin` names as its node read it from Git (`Runtime::project_repository`), never GitHub's answer, so a device's clone GitHub was never read for still joins; the caller's alone when its repository is unknown; a session belongs to one of them when its cwd, or its original project's root, is inside the Project's root or one of its recorded worktrees on the Project's own device and no registered Project nested deeper holds it (the fence a pull request's sessions take, `deepest_owner`), and every descendant of such a session on any device belongs too (`LinkStore::scope_members`, `links/session_store.rs`).
A session is named by its registration id (`agent-N`) or its native id; one the record holds only outside the scope is refused with `other_project`, and one it does not hold with `not_found`.
A connected device whose checkouts Hide has not all read yet (its engine shows a Git workspace `device_worktrees` holds no answer for, as just after Hide or the link starts) is `reading`: its Projects' repositories may be unknown, so `list` names it in `reading_devices` (the text adds a line saying its sessions may be missing) and a session only it holds is refused with `device_reading`, retried once the read lands, rather than `other_project`.
The core takes its part in owned copies under the lock, each bounded by what was asked (`runtime/session_command.rs`: the scope with this machine's node and every ready device's, each listed session's registration id, live state and archive time, at most 512 at once), and the store reads run on hided's blocking task on a read-only connection; nothing writes, and the screen's one record slot is never set, since every runtime call the command makes takes `&self`.
`list` answers the scope's sessions active in the period (7 days unless `--since`), newest first, at most `--limit` (50, at most 200; past it `invalid_request`), with the count left out (`more`) and an empty list, not a failure, for a quiet period; its request count and the flow it names a session after are the record's own (`LinkStore::ledger_flows`, `ledger_store::main_flow`: repeats merged, letters left out), so `list`, `record` and `read --request` count the same requests; a session's activity is its latest request or judged turn, its start only when it has neither, because a live pane stamps every open session's end with the same time.
`record` is the screen's own `LinkStore::ledger_record`, its `PR` sections laid by the runtime with the screen's `family::Sources::lay_groups` (`Runtime::laid_record_pulls`), with its requests numbered from 1 in time order (letters are not counted), each line marked `ai_summary` or `raw` and a request with no summary shown as its first 120 characters; every free text `list` and `record` answer (titles, requests, the live pane's words, summaries, what a reply answers, the `PR` sections' names and holders) passes the same mask as `read` before it is cut, since the reader is another agent, possibly on another device; the CLI folds its oldest past flows, then the oldest requests of the current flow, until the text fits 64 KiB, and both forms carry the counts (`folded_flows`, `folded_requests`).
`read` asks the node that holds the session's file through the raw window Hide AI's investigation reads with (`hide-core/src/session_excerpt.rs`, one implementation for both): 16 events around the request's time or from event `--from` (at most 40), each masked by the Memory redactor (`session_excerpt::mask`, `hide_memory::redact`, which also takes a secret named like an environment variable, an address's password and the common token prefixes) before it is cut to 2,000 characters and every line to 400, and only the events it shows are masked, with `events a-b of n` and the next `--from`; it counts the events to the session's end within the reader's byte bound and its 60 s deadline, and answers `total: null` (`of more`) when it could not; a window the byte bound stops before is `out_of_range` naming the events it could read, never the events it did reach.
A session file whose path names a credential file, a secrets folder or `.git` is refused before anything is read (`credential_path_refused`), as no investigation read reads one; a number past the session, or 0, is `out_of_range` with the valid range in its next action; a record past one of its caps says a retry gives the same answer; a device with no ready node is `device_unavailable`, an agent with no conversation reader `session_unreadable`, a gone file `session_file_missing` and a node that does not answer within 60 s `read_timeout`.
Every refusal logs `session_cli` `session.refused` with the verb, the session id (by its length alone when the id itself was refused), the device and the code, and never a word of the conversation.
Each `list` line names the session's agent by its product (`agent_name`), and the text form of `list` and `record` turns every line break and control character inside a value into a space, so a title cannot draw a line of its own.


### Session work records

The link store's version 2 adds the session work ledger, keyed by device, agent kind and native session id.
Version 3 retains one immutable nullable original project and repository for each retained session, including descendants.
An observed connection can identify only a session that started after that connection was known; first discoveries of older history and records migrated from versions 1 or 2 keep unknown repository identity.
The original project is the deepest connected project root or recorded worktree on the session's own device whose folder holds its cwd, chosen by one SQLite query (`capture_session_origin`).
The record keeps every worktree a project has had, so their number never bounds that choice: loading them all to choose in Rust, behind a 512-row refusal (`ledger_project_capacity`), stopped recording every new session on a machine that had made 572 task worktrees, and each record opened then read as failed.
The writer resets its connection observation window on restart, and an accepted repository edit advances that project's window even when changes return to the same repository before the worker observes them.
The save acknowledgement posts the new connection epoch to the writer for both local and device Projects, with an unknown repository until its new provider read answers.
A retained cursor's same session identity cannot certify a new birth when the native file is replaced or truncated.
Both local and device intake certify only a birth strictly before the node read began, with no newer project facts pending when its answer returns; otherwise ordinary reader data is kept with an immutable unknown origin.
A device clock ahead of the writer may therefore leave its original repository unknown rather than assign a current connection without a valid observation window.
These rows share the store's size cap, device conversion and Copied history pruning; no later catalog lookup fills an unknown original repository or rewrites a known one.
Version 4 adds the backlog's durable add attempts and its missed table (below); a version 3 store keeps its session origins when it arrives.
`links/ledger.rs` owns its values and bounds, `links/ledger_store.rs` its transactions, `runtime/backlog.rs` the backlog's events, and `web/src/SessionRecord.tsx` its read surface.
Only `hide-links` writes it; record reads are latest-only mailbox requests, with separate delta revisions and generation fences.
A backlog GitHub create records the project's `github_place` target and connection epoch when it starts, and a missed line's create first compares the session's original repository with the one resolved now.
An unknown original repository or a confirmed connection to another repository refuses creation with `repository_changed`; a connection edit cancels the creates in flight for that project (`invalidate_backlog_repository`), which check before reading the repository, before reserving and right before `gh issue create`, and a late answer whose target or epoch moved is not published.
Every external create remains pinned to the original reserved repository, and a retry reconciles that durable attempt before another effect; a retry the ledger refuses because the repository changed fails with `repository_changed` rather than make an issue in the new one.
The helper's version 32 supplies canonical request senders and letter kinds from every supported native reader; an older helper keeps its existing raw requests and PR facts until updated.

Version 8 adds each goal chapter's `closed_result`, the line the label gave as the flow closed ([status-model.md](status-model.md#task-identity)); it adds a column and changes no stored row.
Version 9 adds `ledger_plans`, each session's own plan ([Session plans](#session-plans)); it adds a table and changes no stored row.
The record retains requests of at most 500 characters with their summaries, goal chapters (the flows) with their closing lines, END judgments with their lines and artifacts, created outputs and missed work, including asks.
A Claude Code command record (`<command-name>`) is a request only when what Claude Code wrote after it shows the command went to the model: a command it answers itself, such as `/model` with its `<local-command-stdout>` or a `local_command` system record, is neither a request nor a Sessions last request, a search hit or label context.
The incremental reader holds a command record that has no reply in the bytes it read, rereads it with the next poll and so neither loses nor repeats it; a reader of a whole page or file with no reply after the command counts it as a request.
Requests already stored from before this rule are not filtered on read.
It bounds requests and turns at 2,000 per session (`REQUEST_LIMIT`; the record counts the requests it dropped as `omitted_requests`), chapters at 200 (`FLOW_LIMIT`), missed work at 200, new missed items at three per END and 80 characters each, artifacts at three per turn and 80 characters each, request summaries at eight per analysis (`SUMMARY_BATCH`) from at most 16 unsummarized requests in its context (`OWED_IN_CONTEXT`), and a record's artifact list at 24 (`links/ledger.rs`).
Oldest entries beyond a retention cap are removed with a diagnostic, and the existing 64 MiB file and Copied history policy govern the whole ledger.
A record tree has a 2,000-node, 32-depth and 2,000-request/output budget; an overflow is a failed read, rather than a larger snapshot.
The update queue and label context cache each hold 512 entries, worker calls have 16 pending slots, and the context reader handles at most 16 misses per pass outside the runtime lock.
A cold label context requests a worker read and postpones END until authority and open work are known; it never substitutes a root author for unknown lineage.
The postponement is bounded: after thirty seconds of waiting from the turn's first miss (`CONTEXT_WAIT_LIMIT` in `labels/worker.rs`; the turn working again, Agent summaries going off and on, or the generator role changing hands starts the wait over), the turn is recorded unjudged like any failed analysis, its line and end cleared, and `analysis.context_unavailable` logs the pane and session once; it spends no call and holds no other pane.
The record calls a session what its reader calls it, the id in the session's own records, and a lineage edge is keyed the same way.
The engine reports a Pi or omp session as its file, so a registration names such a session by a path; the store names it by the reader's id for that file, which the file's cursor holds once the reader has read it (`session_name` in `links/store.rs`).
Before that read the edge stays under the file, and the read that first names the file moves it to the reader's id in the same transaction, as it would have been recorded had the read come first; Pi 1.0.4 writes its file only at the first message, so a just-spawned Pi child has no file and no record yet (`a_pi_or_omp_child_spawned_by_its_file_is_in_its_parents_record`).
Edges an earlier build left under a file the reader had read move once at open, recorded in `meta` as `session_names` rather than a schema version, since the tables keep their shape and an older build still opens the file (`edges_left_under_read_files_move_to_the_readers_names_once`).
A lineage edge or a file's cursor can still name a session the ledger holds no row for: a spawn known before its file is read, a session retention removed while its file's cursor stays.
Such a session has no record of its own: a tree lists only the children the ledger records, and its label context carries its parent's name and no work, never a failed write (`a_session_the_ledger_never_recorded_fails_no_write_and_stops_no_context`).

START keeps the operator ownership and nullable-goal behavior; both boundaries use `context_label.v26` and return a one-line summary, with the question it answers, for each request the ledger owes one (PRD session-record-goal-flow D-06), and with a `replace` how the flow it closes ended (`closed_result`, PRD session-record-fact-status D-02), and END adds new missed items and asks, resolutions, the pull requests the session made, up to three other artifacts and up to three improvements for Hide AI 제안, read with Hide's count of the turn's tool calls and a long turn's head ([AI_PROVIDERS.md](AI_PROVIDERS.md)), in the existing call.
A flow is a goal chapter; the record places each request in the chapter open when it was sent, by its time, so no judgment assigns work and late lineage moves no request (D-05).
A chapter opens on a `replace` goal and is renamed on `refine`, in every agent; a turn whose request begins with `/goal` in Claude Code or Codex opens one whatever the answer says and marks that request (`goal_command`, read by `hide-session` from the agent's own record) (D-09).
A request is owed a summary when it has none and was recorded after record version 7 came in (`meta.summaries_owed_since`), oldest first; the turn's own request is always among them, and a summary that names an id the context did not list is dropped (`LinkStore::ledger_context`, `labels/context_label.rs`).
The pane draws a `limited` end as `blocked` (`labels/overlay.rs`); the record keeps `limited` and computes its top status past it (D-10).
No chip and no `link_summaries.progress` are derived from the record, and the summary pass reads no record trees.
The one per-pane fact the record feeds is a session's pull request list (with-hide/hide-private `docs/task-identity.md`, One list per session): the summary read carries each recorded session's parent edge (`SessionWorkSummary.parent`, core only) and the pull requests it made with their last-read state (`OutputCreator`, core only), read in the same grouped queries off the lock.
`ingest_link_summaries` rebuilds the recorded index (`agent_state::work::family::Recorded`) only from a summary that moved it, and the cross-row pass lays every row's list from that index, the rows' own pull requests and the GitHub reads in memory, publishing a row only when its list changed; the open record's `pr_groups` are laid from the same function, with the record's own tree as the recorded side, and copied only when they changed.
An unassigned session has no goal chapter; an accepted goal creates its first chapter without inventing a title for a greeting.
A Hide letter is stored as a request with its sender in `letter_from`, drawn dim and never counted, summarized or made the last request; a delegated record's initial prompt and its named parent's work requests are its requests (D-18).
Learned lineage comes from the core's proven parent pane relationship across local and connected-device snapshots, keyed with the owning device's native session identity; retained coordination registrations take precedence and keep ended parents available.
Project, pane and lineage facts use the same combined snapshot set, and a project's GitHub answers are selected by device as well as path.
The borrowed lineage fingerprint costs one pass over current local and device panes, agents and registrations; only a change allocates parent facts or posts them to the existing worker mailbox.
Past requests from summaries Off, failed analysis or a pre-ledger session stay raw and unjudged, without background reclassification when summaries return.
Completion requires the last assigned END to be Done and every assigned PR to be merged; no assigned PR makes the latter condition true.
Only a tool-printed address within -2 s to +30 s of GitHub creation, or one a successful creating call gave back within -10 s to +30 s, makes an output, and descendant outputs are attributed once to the parent's spawn-turn task with their originating session retained.
A call makes a pull request when it runs `gh pr create`, sends a `gh api` POST to `repos/<owner>/<name>/pulls` or is a `create_pull_request` tool, and holds no `||`, whose next command runs because one failed (`named_prs::creates_pull_request`, reading `hide_shell::ShellLine::fallback`); a call its record marks failed (Claude Code's `is_error`, Codex's exit code, Pi's `isError` or a nonzero `exitCode`, Grok's `failed`, OpenCode's status and exit) claims nothing, since a failed `gh pr create` prints the pull request already on its branch; its output's address alone on a line, or the `html_url` of GitHub's answer, is the one it made (`named_prs::created_addresses`), so a body the answer echoes names nothing.
Each format pairs a call with its output by its own id (Claude Code's `tool_use_id`, Codex's `call_id`, Pi's and Grok's `toolCallId`; an OpenCode tool part and a Pi `bashExecution` hold both), and a reader that reads in polls keeps the ids of calls still waiting for output in its checkpoint, at most 16; agy's results name no call, so its prints are judged by time alone.
The early edge stays at 2 s for any print, because a print reads before `createdAt` by the two clocks alone and a listing another session printed then proves nothing; a creating call's print reaches back 10 s (`links::MADE_BEFORE_MS`), since this Mac's record held 234 prints, the earliest 3.4 s before GitHub's time, and mission-13's #1810 to #1813 were each made by one compound call (`cd … && B=…; cat > $B <<EOF … EOF` then `gh pr create … | tail -1`) 2.6 s to 3.2 s before it.
The 10 s bound keeps out a pull request made long ago that the same call also printed (`gh pr create && gh pr view 42`); the risk left is a call that prints, within those 10 s, a pull request another session made.
Version 12 of the record adds `session_prs.made` and reads every file of the last 90 days again, as version 10 did, so a pull request made before the upgrade is found.

The backlog's one add (`runtime/backlog.rs`) is `backlog_add {intent, workspace_id, title, destination?, repository?, missed?}`: the shell names each add with an intent key and an explicit Local or GitHub destination; an omitted destination is always Local.
The shared quick add initially chooses Local; an explicit GitHub choice names the canonical repository and visibility before the external effect.
An add with no valid intent key is refused with an error and no row; every other add ends in a row of `issue_work.backlog`, made, on its way, or failed with why.
A memo is written to `local-issues.json` at once; a GitHub item is a title-only `gh issue create` on a worker, one at a time per device with at most eight waiting (`WAITING_LIMIT`), and an add past them fails at once as `queue_full`.
When one waiting item fails before its worker starts, the next one in line starts, and a worker that panics still answers as `unconfirmed`, so a device's queue never stalls behind a failure.
A GitHub item is pinned at its add to the repository target and connection epoch its project names then; when either differs as it starts or is tried again, it fails as `repository_changed` and nothing is made, in the old repository or the new one.
A GitHub add is a durable attempt in the link ledger, recorded before the external effect, so `backlog_retry {intent}` (even after a restart) first looks for the issue that attempt made and names it instead of making a second one; that search never names an issue number another unfinished attempt in the same repository already claims; that search adopts only an issue the signed-in account wrote (`viewerDidAuthor`), so a same-titled issue someone else filed is never taken for Hide's, and the create itself names the reserved repository outright (`GH_REPO`), so a remote changed after the reserve cannot move it.
The ledger keeps the newest 256 finished typed items and never evicts an unconfirmed one, since its row may still retry it; it holds at most 32 unconfirmed at once (`PENDING_BACKLOG_LIMIT`), all of which a restart offers back, and a new create past them fails as `queue_full` until one is confirmed or put away.
No request, answer or body leaves the device: the issue carries the title alone, and the missed line it came from is kept only in the ledger's missed table (`backlog_key`), which also marks the item's row (`issue_work.missed_keys`).
Each missed flag carries `{task_key, device_id}`: a Local key includes its path and number and requires its actual device, while a GitHub repository/number has a null device and stays shared across projects and devices; each list still holds at most 1024 entries.
One missed line is one item: a second add for the same session and line makes no row while the first is shown, and a memo whose line the ledger no longer has open (another view put it away) is deleted again and its row fails as `refused`.
Each row carries its phase (waiting, creating, created, failed with one of the fixed failure codes) and `retry`, true only on a failed row `backlog_retry` can act on: one whose job is kept, a GitHub create or a memo that could not be saved, which the retry makes again.
An add refused before anything was made (an invalid title, an unknown project, summaries off, a missed line of another device, no link record, a full queue) is a failed row with `retry: false`, `queue_full` for a full queue and `refused` otherwise; at most eight such rows are kept (`REFUSED_LIMIT`), the oldest leaving with a `backlog.refused_evicted` diagnostic.
At most 32 retryable failed items are kept, past which a new add is refused as `queue_full`; `backlog_dismiss` forgets a failed one, and the intents of the last 64 made items no longer shown are remembered, so a late resend of one makes nothing; on a missed line's row it also puts the line away in the same event, and a retry of a missed line's row is refused while summaries are off, as its first press is.
`backlog_undo {workspace_id, task_key}` deletes a memo or closes the GitHub issue (`gh issue close`, on the allowlist) only when Hide made that issue and its repository is the one the project names now, and the missed line it came from opens again; an undo answered after a later one still takes its item out and opens its line, and only the `issue_work.undo` slot follows the newest undo.
A Local undo resolves its device from the admitted workspace and releases only that device's path/number in the ledger, pending rows and origin slots, so another device's same-path memo keeps its origin, missed status and flag; the undo slot carries workspace, device and item identity as well.
Hide made an issue when a typed item's or a missed line's create in the link ledger completed with its number (`MadeIssue`); the worker asks the ledger before anything reaches `gh`, an issue the ledger does not name fails as `refused` with a `backlog.undo_not_made` diagnostic, and without a ledger the undo is refused outright, so Hide never closes an issue someone else made, across restarts and a core move, since the record travels with the ledger.
An undone typed item's create is marked `undone`, so it names the issue no more, and `issue_work.made_keys` lists the issues the ledger names (newest first, at most 1024), which is all the panel reads to offer `되돌리기` on a GitHub issue.
`backlog_origin {workspace_id, device_id, task_key}` first admits the workspace's actual device and task membership, including the Local key's path, then reads where the item came from through the node that holds the session (`session_work_turn`), asking only links that are up and starting no reconnect.
Local ledger reads require that device and path/number; GitHub reads retain repository/number identity.
Starting an item from missed work puts that turn's request and answer in the agent's first prompt on this device only.
Each workspace/device/item has its own slot in `issue_work.origins` (at most 32), and a slot carries that turn's request and answer only while some window shows that owner's panel or Start dialog: a window sends `backlog_origin_close {workspace_id, device_id, task_key}` when the last of its own holders closes, the daemon (`OriginHolds` in `hided/src/demand.rs`, at most 8 items per connection) passes it on only when no other connection holds that owner, and drops a closed connection's holds the same way.
The close uses the exact owner even after its project disappears; a result must match that owner, its newest read generation and current task admission before entering a slot, so a late result or a same-key item's close cannot replace another device's origin.
The daemon sends that close while its holds are still locked, so another window's hold and read of the same owner reach the core after it, and refuses empty identity fields, a workspace or task key longer than 256 bytes, or a device id longer than 64 bytes; a window reads its items again whenever its connection becomes live, since a reconnect is a new connection whose old holds were let go.
A read for an item whose slot is reading or ready leaves it as it is, only a failed slot is read again, and a read past the 32 open items is logged (`backlog.origin_capacity`) and shows no origin rather than an error.
Whether a GitHub repository is public is read with its other GitHub facts and carried as the source's `public`, unknown until GitHub answers.
The removed missed-issue draft (`session_issue_draft`, its templates and form) and the path that always made a GitHub issue whatever the project's source (`issue_create` and the `issue_work.create` slot) are gone.

## Historical usage accounting

`Call::UsageFiles` lists native candidates and `Call::UsageRead` returns one bounded, content-free usage step through the node boundary.
Candidate and read paths use `hide_platform::path` wire spelling, converted to native paths only by the node that reads them.
Both require the live link's independently advertised `ReaderFeature::Usage`; the node repeats that check before dispatch.
This optional reader adds no protocol-version requirement: an older peer grants no usage reader and is refused before a call is sent.
Cursor grants none, and protocol 24's frozen reader facts remain unchanged.

The usage worker owns one writer and reads only its supplied own-node link, alternating agents so a large history cannot starve another.
Each turn performs one bounded read and transaction, then rests for 20 ms; native JSONL parsing itself yields at 10 ms and never exceeds one MiB including its checkpoint witnesses.
That MiB holds the witnesses, Grok's `summary.json` and always room for one whole record at the 256 KiB line cap, so every step reads a record or starts passing one over; a `summary.json` too large to leave that room (over 785,407 bytes) is refused as `usage_read_Capacity`, never read past.
OpenCode's usage read sizes each row from its record header (`octet_length`) before loading it, so a message or part past the 64 KiB row bound is skipped as `record_capacity` and the cursor moves past it; measuring with `length(CAST(data AS BLOB))` loaded the value, and one row past SQLite's 1 MiB value limit failed every read and held the cursor on it.
OpenCode 2.x writes one assistant message per step and sets its tokens and cost once, when the step ends, so a completed assistant message is one usage event, keyed by its message id and placed in its session's checkout; a step still running, or one that failed without usage, is read again or passed, and a completed step with no usage is skipped as `usage_missing`.
The row holds its whole content, which a step that ran a long tool can make several MiB, so SQLite's JSON functions read the step's few fields in place and only those come back, each text cut where it is taken.
A row is scanned up to 8 MiB, and one read scans at most 8 MiB of rows in all: a row that would pass that total waits, the cursor still before it, and the next read takes it, while the first row of a read is always scanned so a read moves on.
A row over 8 MiB is skipped as `record_capacity`, which the worker logs as `usage_records_skipped`, so its step is reported as unread and never vanishes.
A database 2.x migrated from a 1.x one holds both sets of tables, with every migrated message in `session_message` under the id `message` still holds, so one cursor walks the messages of both in time order and the table that holds a message decides how it is counted.
A message the 1.x `message` table holds is counted from its step-finish parts, keyed by part id exactly as before the upgrade, so a ledger filled by an earlier read gets the same keys again and counts nothing twice.
A message only `session_message` holds was written after the upgrade and is counted the 2.x way, keyed by its message id.
A 2.x database with only one of `message` and `part`, or either without a column Hide reads, is no state 2.x makes and is refused as `usage_read_Schema`.
A database of neither OpenCode schema is refused as `usage_read_Schema`.
A failed listing or read is logged as `usage_list_failed` or `usage_read_failed` with the node's `reason` (its refusal code, such as `usage_read_Database`, or how the link failed), and the agent is listed again 30 seconds later.
Two replaceable visibility flags control its work: without a window it rests; candidate discovery runs every 30 seconds, or 3 while usage is open, and changed reports publish every 30 or 5 seconds respectively.
Its owner signals the condition variable and joins it on shutdown, including startup failure and an idle wait.
Complete uncapped listings retire deleted file checkpoints without deleting their totals or recent dedup authority.

`usage_ledger::store` owns `usage.sqlite3`, named by `hide_kit::layout::usage_store` under the core state directory.
Normalized usage events contain native call identity, model, time, session, working folder, provider, tokens and recorded cost, with no conversation fields.
A stored call holds each of those once, in the columns its readers use (the calls format, with-hide/hide-private#672): its key as 32 bytes, its node by the number of a `nodes` row, its tokens and cost as numbers, and its session and working folder by the number of a `places` row, one per (node, agent, session, folder), where a call that named no folder keeps an empty one, which no folder can be.
Nothing reads a call but the dedup lookup, a Claude call's later view, the projects' costs and the pruning, and none of them needs the whole event, so a call is about a fifth of the whole-event JSON version 3 kept beside a hexadecimal key: the operator's 638,000-call store of 512 MiB was 96 MiB converted and compacted (19%), under the 512 MiB bound with five machines of that history.
Whether a later view bills the same call is read from the stored values (time, model, tokens, cost, provider, incomplete), the same values version 3 hashed into a fingerprint column it no longer needs.
An ingestion transaction adds a new call and its daily `(native node, agent, local day, model)` totals together with the file checkpoint; repeated calls add nothing, and changed completed calls keep the first accounting value and report a count-only conflict.
Claude streaming records retain each token field's maximum for that native call, replacing its daily contribution and whole-call pricing band in the same transaction without another call; a later view that raises no maximum writes nothing and counts as a repeat.
A persisted checkpoint distinguishes a yielded read from EOF, so a restart cannot freeze an unread suffix.
Discarded capacity-overflow events leave a durable per-agent limited marker; a future timestamp is counted as skipped without poisoning its valid batch neighbours.
The day is assigned in the core's time zone at first ingestion and stays assigned after the time zone changes or the core moves.
New calls use the current core time zone.

Each agent's first backfill may fill older days within the 400-day retention window, and its event keys stay until that backfill's durable completion marker is written.
After completion, whole days before the 45-day event horizon are frozen: replayed or late calls before that boundary are counted as skipped and never change those totals.
The boundary is retained as a monotonic instant so a clock rollback or time-zone change cannot admit a call whose dedup key already expired.
Maintenance removes at most 512 expired calls, 512 places and 512 expired daily rows per turn; the call bound is one million per native node, the candidate bound 10,000 per agent, the daily-row bound 100,000, the native-node bound 32 and the database bound 512 MiB, with each refusal reported rather than silently growing storage.
A place keeps its newest call's time and is pruned once that call and every other expired call of its agent are gone, so a place outlives no call of its own and a node's places never outnumber its calls.
The store uses SQLite WAL and full synchronous commits, refuses a damaged or newer store without rebuilding it, and travels with `MOVES_WITH_CORE` through the existing consistent SQLite copy.
The `calls_node_at` index on `(node, at DESC)` serves the projects' costs below and the pruning; beside a table without rowids it carries the primary key `(node, agent, key)` too, ascending after the newest-first time, so a read of a node's newest calls ordered by time, agent and key sorts nothing.

A version 3 store is converted in place, never rebuilt, and never all at once.
Its first open by a build of the calls format adds the new tables and a node for each device in one transaction and leaves `events` and its indexes as they were; a store an older build filled to its 512 MiB has no free page for those tables, so there the open makes them in the first step's transaction, after it deletes that step's calls from `events` (`a_version_3_store_at_its_page_limit_opens_and_converts`); the device's count in `devices` stays the one count of its calls in both tables, which a move leaves alone; from then on the worker moves at most 4,096 calls a step, each step one transaction that deletes them from `events` and writes them as calls (`Store::convert`), until `events` is empty.
Until `events` is empty the worker reads, counts and prunes no call and the projects' costs stay pending, since a call still waiting in `events` would not be found as already counted; the daily totals and Hide AI's tables stay readable throughout.
A step that fails or is ended changes nothing, and the next step, in the same process or after a restart or a core move, takes the same calls again; a damaged call fails its step with its cause, logged and on the usage page, and is tried again a minute later rather than skipped.
The operator's 638,000 calls took 156 steps, 92 seconds in all and 2.1 seconds the slowest, on a Mac running other builds at the same time.
Moving leaves the old calls' pages free, and SQLite reuses free pages but never returns them, so whenever more than half the file is free pages, after a conversion or at any open, the worker compacts it once with `VACUUM` and empties the write-ahead log (`Store::compact`, its own two-minute budget, four seconds for the operator's store on that Mac); a compaction that fails is logged and the store stays as it was, larger, until the next open tries again.

Going back to a build from before the calls format, at any point and halfway through a conversion too, keeps every record this build wrote and every count true, and coming back within 45 days counts each call made in between once; outside that rule are a longer stay and a session file its agent removed in the meantime (Claude Code removes a session 30 days after its last activity unless `cleanupPeriodDays` says otherwise), whose calls are not counted.
A device at its limit of a million calls is outside it too: the older build skips the stay's calls past the limit as it always has, marks the agent limited and logs `usage_event_capacity`, and this build does not count them again.
The store's version stays 3, the oldest layout a build reads and writes it correctly in, and every table a version 3 build uses stays as it made it, `events` empty, so such a build opens the store as its own and records Hide AI's calls into `ai_daily`, which the calls format did not change.
A native call it would count goes into `events`, which it reads to find a call already counted and which no longer holds one, so it could count a call this build already counted; the store refuses that write (the trigger `events_closed`), and the refusal rolls back the older build's whole ingest, checkpoint included, so it counts no native call while it runs and its usage page says the ledger failed.
It still finds, merges a later view into and prunes the calls a halfway conversion left in `events` as it always did, taking each it prunes off the device's count in `devices`, which counts the device's calls in both tables, so the count stays the number of calls there are and the limit of a million calls a device is one value for both formats (`an_older_build_pruning_a_halfway_conversion_keeps_one_true_count`).
Back on this build the conversion goes on, and the stay's calls are read from their native files after the checkpoints this build left and counted once, a later view of a call already counted merged as ever (`an_older_build_counts_no_call_into_a_converted_store_and_the_return_counts_each_once`).
A change that keeps an older build able to open the store adds its tables, indexes and refusals beside the ones it uses without raising the version, as Hide AI's tables and the calls format do; one an older build would misread raises it, and that build then refuses the store (`usage_store_newer`) and loses Hide AI's calls of that time when it exits.
Native physical node identities and their qualified source paths stay unchanged when the core's owner changes.

The same store retains the public price cache and the last network-attempt time; that state moves with the ledger so a core move cannot bypass the daily fetch bound.
Daily totals hold four fixed token-only context bands, not another table of call identities, preserving tier-aware repricing across event expiry within the existing row and database caps.
The separately owned price-fetch thread asks the own node for `Call::UsagePriceFetch`, refused for devices.
The node owns the bounded public HTTP read; the core parses the returned body and the ledger's sole writer persists the table before publishing it.
Shutdown closes the own-node link before joining the ledger and price threads, so those joins do not wait for an in-flight HTTP answer.
Closing also releases the node's label-generator locks, even while unfinished calls retain node references; a lock acquisition completing after close releases its file instead of retaining the role.
The teardown-only `AiRelease` and `LabelUnlock` requests remain callable after close under the existing call cap and timeout, because their owners may drop later; closing does not wake or replace their cleanup answers.
The node's unfinished HTTP work retains its capacity slot and five-second deadline until it ends.

`usage_ledger::ai_usage` is the other writer's input: routers tell its bounded `AiUsageQueue` after each attempt, and the same ledger worker drains it at most once a second into `ai_daily`/`ai_state` of `usage.sqlite3` (`store/ai.rs`).
It reloads those rows and publishes only when a usage page is visible, so a hidden window costs the queue push and the batched write only; `docs/AI_PROVIDERS.md`, Counting Hide AI's own usage, owns what counts and the caps.

### Project status and cost

The Project tool's counts and 흘린 것 (PRD project-panel-results D-04, D-05, B1-B17) are derived, never stored, and reach the shell as `agent_scope.status`.
`agent_state/tally/project_status.rs` builds them inside the scope cache (`agent_state/tally/scope.rs`) from what that cache already compares: the PRs list's board rows, each checkout's Git facts (`GitInput`), the facts a 흘린 것 row reads (`StrayInput`: branch, base branch, changed file count, head, last commit and pull request checks), the last session the record says ran in each worktree with something left (`recorded_runs`, looked up for those worktrees only) and the 놔두기 in `ui_state.stray_dismissals`.
So a publish whose inputs did not move rebuilds nothing, and nothing on that path reads a file, runs a process or takes another lock.
`stray` makes a row for a worktree off the default branch with changes, unpushed commits (the rule the worktree's mark reads) or an open, non-draft pull request whose checks failed, unless a live row in its panes works or waits on the operator (`AgentUse`); its name, pane and agent come from the newest live row there, else the recorded run, and its head binds a 놔두기.
`strays` keeps at most `STRAY_LIMIT` (64) rows, newest first, `strays_total` counts all and is the rail's number, and the first crossing logs one `project_status`/`stray_capacity` diagnostic per project.
`runtime/strays.rs` owns the three events: `stray_dismiss` stamps the row's head and failing pull request into `ui_state.stray_dismissals` (persisted, keyed by checkout id and moved with the checkout by `node_migration`), keeping at most `MAX_STRAY_DISMISSALS` (256), the oldest dropped with a `stray.dismissal_capacity` diagnostic; `stray_restore` removes the stamp; `stray_hand_off` takes a request id, refuses one it already holds, and writes the fixed words through its `spawn_stray_prompt` (the engine's `prompt_agent` on a worker, admitted by the input gate) or starts an agent in the checkout through `agent_start_in_checkout`; `status.stray_hand_offs` keeps the last 16 receipts (`sending`, `sent`, `failed`) and every settle logs `stray.hand_off`.
A local agent that stops working has its project's worktrees read again (`read_worktrees_after_turns`), since Git's watch does not see an edit left unstaged (B17).
`git.dots` keeps at most `DOT_LIMIT` (96) marks; the counts stay exact, and each checkout's own scope carries its mark uncapped (`git_mark`, the one rule `checkout_mark`), which the worktree table lists.
The detail item `remains` names a worktree; while it is the shown top of the 보기 slot and no Changes surface is visible, `changes_target` reads that worktree's changes, in front or not.

A project's cost (`usage_ledger/project_cost.rs`) is prepared on the ledger worker, never under `Mutex<Runtime>`.
The runtime tells the worker each local project's checkout paths (`feed_usage_projects`, on a catalog replacement, notifying only on a change); the worker reads the last eight days of its own node's `calls` (`store::recent_calls`, newest first by `calls_node_at` and calls of one time by agent and key, a total order since `(node, agent, key)` is the primary key, so a capped read keeps the same calls under any plan; at most `EVENT_LIMIT` 200,000 calls with a two-second progress budget, `limited` past it), keeps the seven days ending today, gives a call to the project whose deepest checkout holds its session's folder (`files::path_inside_root`, decided once per folder), and prices each (agent, day, model) and (agent, session, model) group with `prices::cost` as a day is priced.
Each call is decoded, added to its groups by `project_cost::Preparation` and dropped, so a build holds the groups and the folder owners, not the calls.
It rebuilds when the projects or the day change, and when ingestion added or rewrote a call of those eight days or a new price table dirtied it, at most once per `COST_REBUILD` (30 s); a backfill of older history and pruning, which removes only calls past the 45-day horizon, leave it as built; a failed build keeps the last value, stays due, is tried again after the same wait and logs each new cause once.
The result rides the usage frame as `nodes[].projects`, absent until a build succeeded so a tile tells a cost not read yet from a read that found nothing (B33), with `projects_failed` while the latest build failed or the usage store did not open; a project that ran no call is not listed, and an agent with an unpriced call is named in `unpriced_agents` with its priced calls still summed and the total marked `partial`; the daily totals, the Overview's Usage and the calendars below are unchanged, and a project on a connected device has no cost here.
The build also keeps each session's spend in a project (`SessionSpend`, core only: its priced amount, new tokens, first and last call and working time, the gaps between its calls up to `WORK_GAP_MS`, five minutes, added up), and Hide AI's own seven days from the `ai_daily` rows (`hide_ai_week_micro_usd` on the frame), which belong to no project.
The runtime keeps the worker's spends (`ledger_spends`) and makes each project's `tasks`, `tasks_total` and `week` in `runtime/project_tasks.rs` with `usage_ledger::tasks::build`, a pure function over the spends, the record's summaries (each session's parent, the pull requests it made or worked on, its folder, the line of its last judged turn and when it last ran `git commit`), the missions, the live rows (who works or waits, the first line of what each last said), the catalog's pull requests and each checkout's left changes and whether its commits are in the default branch.
The session reader marks a tool call that runs `git commit` (`named_prs::runs_git_commit`, past git's own options, in every agent's shell call) and the store keeps one `ledger_sightings` row of kind `commit` per session with the last call's time.
A link store from before version 14 is read again from each file's start, as versions 10 and 12 were, so the sessions already read get their `git commit` calls too.
The Project tool's `남은 것` has a read of its own beside the checkout in front (`Runtime::remains_request`, `ingest_remains`, a second `ChangesReader` on the changes pump): the shown worktree's changes and committed group by its path, with no row and no diff, published as the rest section `remains` with the workspace and checkout it was read for, since a nested worktree's folder lies inside its primary's, while the viewing column shows it and emptied when it closes.
A worktree whose folder this daemon did not open is published as unreadable (`host.root_not_opened`) rather than left waiting, and a failed read keeps the list already shown, marked stale.
A session counts in one task: the mission its Conductor leads, else the nearest forebear that made a pull request or has no parent, so the tasks never sum past the total (D-09, B28); at most `TASK_LIMIT` (200) are sent, costliest first.
It runs when the worker reports, when the record's summaries change and when the agent scopes' compared input moves (it holds the agents, pull requests and Git facts a result reads, and the minute; `Cache::input_generation`), and does no I/O beyond reading the time zone once.
Each call gathers every project's facts (`tasks::Facts`, plain data) and builds a project again only when its facts or the worker's spends differ from its last build (`TasksBuilt`), so an agent's state change rebuilds nothing whose facts it did not move; a build resolves each session's checkout once, a frame whose result is unchanged is not sent, and a project whose tasks cross a cap logs `project_tasks_capacity` once.

`usage_ledger::query` prepares both the 20-week and 53-week calendars on the worker, including every agent selection; the shell formats and draws their prepared values.
The same pricing pass prepares one shared model list keyed by recorded civil date, agent, model and session-or-Hide-AI source.
It retains at most 4,096 keys in deterministic newest-first order within the retained-year calendar, with `models_limited` when older keys are omitted; the complete daily sums are independent of this detail cap.
Each model amount uses the actual reported tokens and the same price resolution as its daily amount, and an unnamed native model remains null rather than being inferred from an agent.
Hide AI model rows count per-model reports; its existing headline and feature rows continue to count backend attempts, including separate unknown-call counts that create no model amount.
The shell filters and sums these prepared records for seven, thirty, ninety or retained-year dates and a selected agent or day, without native reads, repricing or additional polling.
Each range sends inclusive `calendar_start` and `calendar_end` civil dates and only days with recorded calls, including calls with zero new tokens.
The mounted calendar fills omitted dates as level-zero cells, pending while that range is reading; it does not recalculate totals, prices, quartiles, streaks or recorded-day contributions.
This keeps empty history from repeating hundreds of empty amount records on every attach or reconnect.
Only the core's own native-node rows enter these calendars.
New tokens include input, output and cache writes, never cache reads; reasoning is already part of output.
Nonzero closed days determine nearest-rank quartiles, or quarter-of-maximum thresholds below seven active closed days, so today's unfinished spike cannot recolor history.
The calendar starts on the first record's week, capped to the surface's week count, and stays anchored 45 days back during first backfill; agent selection preserves the calendar and the other agents' shares.
Empty days during backfill remain pending, zero-call ranges remain no data, and cost reasons carry at most eight distinct unpriced model names plus the omitted count, together with price-loading, stale-price and incomplete-usage facts.
Agent hover costs cover retained history even when its first days precede the displayed calendar.
Provider provenance is bounded to 32 distinct native ids, and crossing that bound refuses the projection rather than omitting an id silently.
Calendar arithmetic uses civil dates across daylight-saving transitions, and a current streak may include yesterday while today is still empty.

## Agent adapters

`hide-agent-adapter` is the data-only leaf shared by the hook helper, session readers, kit, core, daemon and device helper.
One static row per supported agent declares its canonical id and aliases, labels and programs (read from its [definition file](#agent-definition-files)), skill location, installation and hook dialects, session format, launch/find/usage selectors, links and logo id.
Prompt intake, spawn refusal, subagent counts, Memory, bell eligibility and passive tool-result observation are independent fields: gaining a prompt hook does not make an agent a bell target or make its session readable.
Every row must choose a native or plugin observation dialect, or explicitly declare observation unsupported with a reason.
Guidance, automatic Memory injection and native titles also require an explicit supported route or reader, or an absence with its reason, repository evidence and closure condition, using the same `Support` sum type as usage.
Automatic Memory injection is distinct from the shared Memory store, extraction and search; an installed hook alone does not prove its output reaches the model.
Context routes distinguish native hooks, guidance hooks and plugin prompt delivery, with independent support and installed-host contracts checking the declaration against the implementation.
The hook helper dispatches observations from that declaration; the shared hook contract checks installed native Post events against native fixtures and expected neutral metadata, and exercises every supported route through the built helper on Unix.
Installed plugin rows run their existing host suites independently of observation support, preserving the other plugin contracts.
The common lookup trims borrowed input and compares ids and aliases without case, allocation, I/O, a lock or a cache.
Every start normalizes a known kind to its canonical name at the engine boundary; captured unknown kinds retain their original bytes and gain no capability.
Lifecycle identity checks normalize known kinds while keeping their existing unknown-kind comparisons, and bell identity keeps unknown spellings exact along with pane, name, native session, readiness and sequence checks.
Delegated and handed-off starts use the same known-kind identity for live detection, native readiness, child binding and same-intent replay, preserving captured spellings and every other ownership and receipt check.
Canonical kind names are the agent definition files' ids (`hide-agent-adapter/agents/*.toml`), never a second protocol vocabulary.

The leaf selects dialects but does not implement them.
`hide-agent-hooks` still owns installed hook bytes and command arguments, input/output formats and the only writes to operator hook files.
`hide-session` owns session location and parsing, including whether a format reports user turns; the delivery gate conservatively holds a letter when such a reader cannot establish the current turn.
`hide-session::thread` reads a session as the ACP session updates an editor would receive (PRD session-thread-acp): message and thought chunks, tool calls with their kind, input, diffs and output, and plans, in the official `agent-client-protocol-schema` types it re-exports.
It reads the agent's own records and never an ACP server's `session/load`, which writes to the session it loads ([agent-hooks.md: ACP servers](agent-hooks.md#acp-servers)), and it writes nothing.
