A hook's session-start report carries the account variables its agent runs with (`HookStatusReport::account`, `hide_agent_hooks::account::reported_variables`; an empty list is the default account), and the node lists the variables each profile's start sets (`ListedProfile::account_variables`), both exactly as set, so the core compares the two strings and never looks at a path, which may be a device's (`runtime/account_reports.rs`, D-03).
An account is its values as set (D-15): Claude Code keys its login by the string, so `/a` and `/a/` are two accounts, and an alias that spells a profile's folder another way (a link, a final separator) runs in an account Hide keeps nothing of and reads as before.
Claude Code drops its variables from a hook's environment under `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1`; its hook then reads the folder above the session's `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE`, which Claude Code keeps at `<folder>/session-env/`.
A pane whose report matches one profile's account is read in that account, its conversation reads included (`Runtime::account_launches` hands the reported accounts to the label reads beside the launch records, taken again when either moves), and its row names that profile (B24); an account several profiles share is read there and the row names the agent alone; the default account, and variables no profile sets (an unregistered folder, the node's own default), read as before.
A pane the core started with a profile whose hook reports another of the machine's accounts is read where it runs, its sleep and reopen records take that account's profile, and the profile it started with is marked `wrapper_folder` until a later start of it reports its own account (D-35, B25): each reported start keeps its place among the machine's starts (`account_start` in the hook facts), the high water mark is retained when a pane closes, and the core owns each profile's last sequence and warning together, so an older surviving pane cannot overwrite it.
A repeated session/account report keeps its sequence; the counter refuses overflow.
The mark is laid again on each list the node sends and removed with the profile on an authoritative list or when its device is removed.
The report is kept with the hook facts across a restart, and the answer per pane is worked out again only when a report, a list or the saved facts come in, so a projection reads one map entry a row.

## The platform layer

`hide-platform` is the one place code that depends on the operating system is written, so that macOS, Linux and Windows differ in one small crate rather than in every crate that touches a socket, a process or a file.
It is a leaf: no hide dependencies, no state beyond what an open endpoint holds (a Windows listener's accept thread and its backlog) and the one cache `programs` keeps (below), nothing under the runtime mutex, and no policy; a caller decides what a save or a request means, and the crate only answers the operating-system question under it.
Each function answers the same way on all three systems or says `ErrorKind::Unsupported`; none guesses a default.
`hide-platform/tests/` states each module's contract as what a caller observes (bytes both ways, a timeout that fires after the time and not before, a shutdown that frees a blocked read, a live bind refused and a dead one replaced, an endpoint only the account can reach) and runs unchanged on every system in the `os contract` lane (`.github/workflows/os-contract.yml`, with its macOS leg planned for a change to `hide-platform` and run by the nightly).
The crate is small on purpose, so that lane builds in minutes on a runner with no workspace.
The install policy stays in `hide-kit`: on Windows its ASCII `hide.cmd` forwards arguments and the exit code to a `hide.exe` named relative to the shim's own folder (`%~dp0`, which cmd expands without its code page, so a Unicode path never sits in the batch file).
Every installation's shim names the folder of its `hide.exe` by a plain ASCII relative path and makes no link: the desktop app's its runtime copy (`..\..\.hide\runtime\<build>`), a helper root's the root's `current` folder (`..\..\.hide\host-helper\current` for the default folders), because an ssh session's redirection guard refuses a junction no administrator made ([The install kit](#the-install-kit)); a way between the two folders that is not plain ASCII, or another drive, leaves the command part blocked with that reason.
The `.hide-kit` junction an earlier desktop app made beside its shim goes with the next pass of the installation that made it (with-hide/hide-private#596).
The kit replaces only a shim of its exact form and an owned junction, and leaves competing commands and foreign entries with a reported failure.
The kit record keeps its last installed CLI destination, so a removed old package can be replaced without treating every `resources/hide[.exe]` path as owned.
PATH and registry edits remain the operator's decision.
`memory::return_freed` asks the allocator to give the pages of its free blocks back to the system (`malloc_zone_pressure_relief` on macOS, glibc's `malloc_trim` on Linux, `HeapCompact` on Windows, `Unsupported` for a C library without such a call); it walks the heap, so a caller makes it once its work has gone quiet, never per input ([The pane holder](#the-pane-holder)).
Windows is a host for the app (hided, the pane holders, the desktop window), a core that dials devices, and a device of any core ([A device's ssh](#a-devices-ssh)); this crate serves all three the same way: every function takes a path or an open handle and keeps no state of its own, except the login shell's `PATH` and environment that `programs` remembers, and answers for the machine it runs on; what it reads from the process is the account it runs as, which `private` and `lock` compare against, and the variables `host` lists in `host::VARIABLES`, each of which a caller with its own registry can hand in through a `_from` form instead.

`ipc` is the first module: a Unix domain socket on macOS and Linux and a named pipe on Windows behind `LocalStream` and `LocalListener`, built on `interprocess`.
Its read-only `is_endpoint` tests the entry itself without following a link, using the same platform-specific socket or marker predicate as stale-endpoint removal; callers need no operating-system branch to distinguish an absent endpoint from an unsafe entry.
`remove_leftover` removes what a listener killed outright left at its path, the socket and its lock file on Unix and the marker on Windows, and refuses one whose listener still lives with `AddrInUse`; an entry that is no endpoint is kept (`what_a_killed_listener_left_behind_is_removed_and_a_live_one_is_refused`).
A Unix socket path must be shorter than the address holds (`sun_path`, 104 bytes on macOS and 108 on Linux, with its NUL), and `bind` and both connects refuse a longer one first, before any folder, lock or socket is made, with `InvalidInput` and a reason that names the path, its length and the limit (`a_path_one_byte_under_the_address_limit_binds_and_a_path_at_it_names_itself`); the system's own refusal names none of them.
Nothing moves a path that does not fit to another place: the caller that owns the folder shortens it, and a pane holder that cannot bind records the refusal, with its socket path, in `holder.start_failed`.
A named pipe has no such limit, so the check is Unix's and Windows keeps the pipe name as it is.
A caller that knows the listener's process has ended gives it a wait for the lock: Windows releases a dead process's file locks a moment after the process ends, so a removal at once would still find the lock held.
The address is a path everywhere; on Windows the path is also the pipe's name (`\\.\pipe\<path>`) and a marker file stays at the path while the listener lives, so "the path exists" means the same on every system.
A Windows pipe has no read or write timeout of its own, so a read with a timeout looks at the pipe before it reads, and the Unix side waits for readiness with `poll` instead of `SO_RCVTIMEO`, which macOS refuses to set once the peer has closed even though its bytes are still waiting; the contract tests pin both.
A write with a timeout is the overlapped `WriteFile` the stream makes anyway, waited for with `GetOverlappedResultEx` and waited for again while the deadline has not passed, since a wait can end a timer tick early; one still pending then is cancelled with `CancelIoEx`, retried until the operation has ended because a refused cancel would leave an unbounded wait, and the write lets its buffer go only after that, so the kernel never writes from memory that has moved on; a wait that fails with the operation still running is ended the same way.
A Windows write that finishes in time makes the one wait call a write without a timeout makes, and the cancel and its wait come only for a write the peer holds past its time.
On Unix the write timeout is the socket's `SO_SNDTIMEO`, set only when the timeout a write needs differs from the one the socket carries, so a stream without a deadline sets it once; a send the system ends before the deadline is sent again for the time left, and macOS's refusal to set it once the peer has closed is passed over because the send that follows fails at once; a send that never blocks is not an option, since macOS ignores `MSG_DONTWAIT` on a local socket.
On both, a write that runs out of time answers `TimedOut`, or the count of the bytes it moved, never before its time (`a_write_timeout_ends_a_write_a_silent_peer_holds_after_the_time`), and every later write on the stream, through any handle, answers `TimedOut`, because the peer may hold part of a message (`after_a_write_runs_out_of_time_the_stream_takes_no_more_writes`).
The pipe used to say `Unsupported` there and leave each caller to decide what that meant: `hide-herdr-client` took it for no timeout, on the claim that a request is one line that fits the pipe's buffer, which is a 512-byte hint a 16 KiB hook request passes, and a hook's request took it for a failure, so no Windows hook reached its daemon.
A request with a time bound opens its stream with `LocalStream::connect_until(path, deadline)`, or sets `set_deadline` on a stream it connected another way: the connect, and each later read and write, waits no later than the deadline, where a Windows connect to a busy pipe would wait its full two seconds and a Linux connect to a full backlog would wait until `accept`, and past it each answers `TimedOut` at once (`an_exchange_deadline_ends_its_reads_and_writes_once_it_has_passed`, `a_connect_to_a_listener_that_takes_nothing_more_ends_by_its_deadline`); a Linux connect with a deadline blocks on a socket whose send timeout is the time left, which Linux's connect waits for room in a full backlog by; macOS refuses a full backlog at once, so its connect sets no socket option at all, since macOS refuses every one once the peer has closed and a listener that answers and closes at once, as a pane holder past its opening bound does, can close before the connect is back (`a_connect_the_listener_answers_and_closes_at_once_reads_the_answer_and_the_end`, with-hide/hide-private#616). It is not a nonblocking connect: on Linux a full backlog answers that one `EAGAIN` with no connect under way, and waiting for the socket to be writable then hands back a stream that never connected.
A stream with no deadline makes no call it did not make before, so the Unix side of every other caller is unchanged; the pane bootstrap, a device bridge's bootstrap and a hook's request (`hide_agent_hooks::hook_request`) are the callers with one.
A writer another thread has to free runs on a thread of its own, and a `ShutdownHandle` ends its held write (the contract tests pin that a shutdown frees a blocked write); a node's link streams (`hide-host/src/link_bridge.rs`) give each chunk 5 s and then end the stream, so an end that stops reading never holds a worker of the link's control lane.
A Windows connect waits at most two seconds for a pipe whose instances are all busy (`TimedOut`; the default would wait for ever), and `bind` reads that answer as a live listener; `bind` also removes only a socket (Unix) or the marker file (Windows) and refuses anything else at the path.
A refused connect cannot say whether a listener lives, because macOS answers `ConnectionRefused` for a dead socket and for a live listener whose 128-connection queue is full alike (#403), so `bind` decides by a lock and uses the connect only as a fallback.
A listener holds an exclusive lock on `<path>.lock` (`fs::lock`) from before it binds until it drops, and `bind` takes that lock first: a held lock is `AddrInUse`, a free one means no listener of this build lives, and only then is a leftover socket or marker removed.
The lock file is opened as the account's own private regular file (`private::open_own_file`): a link at its name, a file of another account or one with a second name is refused with the file's name in the error, never followed or locked.
The kernel ends the lock with its holder however the holder ends, so a killed listener never blocks the next bind, and the drop removes the lock file while still holding the lock, but only while the file at the path is still the one it locked, so a lock file a cleaner replaced is left to whoever holds the new one; `bind` checks the same identity after it locks, so a file opened just before a removal is opened again, and any answer but "not there" is a failure of the bind.
The connect that follows the lock is a transition path for a listener of a build that took no lock, to be removed once no supported build binds without it; `a_listener_with_a_full_backlog_is_still_live_to_a_second_bind` pins the full-queue case.
A client that connects and leaves never holds up the next one (#315): a Unix socket queues it until `accept`, while a pipe instance stays taken by a client that came and went until the server clears it, and `interprocess`'s listener keeps one instance and clears it only inside `accept`, so the 33rd of 50 quick connects timed out.
The Windows listener therefore keeps four instances listening with an overlapped `ConnectNamedPipe` each, served by a thread of its own that clears an instance its client left, puts a fresh instance in the place of a connected one before queueing it, and queues at most 64 connections for `accept`, like a socket's backlog; the contract tests connect and leave 40 times with nobody accepting and 200 times against a running accept loop, never more than 32 ahead of it.
Past the backlog the systems differ, and the contract names each answer rather than one: macOS refuses a connect at once with `ConnectionRefused` once 128 (`SOMAXCONN`) wait for `accept`, Windows says `TimedOut` after its two-second wait, and Linux's connect waits for room, or with a deadline answers `TimedOut` at once; the listener serves on once `accept` catches up.
A burst that outruns a starved accept thread is therefore a load past the contract, not a lost listener (#396: a macOS runner refused the 129th connect while the accept loop was still alive), and `a_connect_past_the_backlog_is_refused_and_the_listener_serves_on` pins the overflow answer apart from the burst.
A Windows end is the crate's own `Pipe` (overlapped `ReadFile` and `WriteFile` on the handle it was given) rather than `interprocess`'s stream, because `interprocess` wraps a handle only by reopening it, and a reopen relative to a pipe handle is a new client connect: with one instance listening it fails and the original is kept, with several it takes another instance and the original end closes, so the peer's next write fails with "the pipe is being closed" (the contract test `one_connect_is_one_accepted_connection` pins it).
Closing a pipe end throws away what it wrote and the peer has not read yet, so an end that wrote is flushed on a thread of its own before its handle closes, as `interprocess` does; the pane bootstrap writes its answer and drops the stream at once (`an_answer_written_just_before_the_end_is_dropped_arrives_whole`).
A blocked read is freed by `ShutdownHandle` from any thread on every system: `shutdown(2)` on Unix, `CancelIoEx` on Windows, and a blocked `accept` by `ListenerCloser`: a wake socket polled beside the listener on Unix, an event the accept thread waits on with its instances on Windows.
On macOS every read, with a timeout or without, waits for its socket in `poll` before it reads: a `recv` blocked on a local socket sometimes sleeps through its peer's shutdown, and once it has, through its own end's shutdown too, while `poll` wakes for both (with-hide/hide-private#351, measured at about one end in five thousand at load 30; `a_shutdown_ends_the_peers_blocked_read_every_time` holds it).
That costs one `poll` call per read on macOS, under a microsecond for a small read in a local measurement, and nothing on Linux or Windows, whose reads are unchanged.
The `hide` CLI's connect to the pane bootstrap and the bootstrap's own listener in `hide-node/src/pane_proof.rs` use it, and so do a pane holder's socket and its node's connection to it (`hide-node/src/terminal/holder.rs`), a device node's pane service (`hide-host/src/panes.rs`) and the device `hide`'s connect to it; the opener supervisor's channel is a Unix socket pair because only Unix needs that supervisor (Windows owns the helper through its job object).
The bootstrap accepts on a thread of its own and hands each connection to the async runtime, because `accept` blocks, and closes the listener through its `ListenerCloser` on shutdown.

`process` is the second module and the one place a child is started or a pid is asked about.
`OwnedChild::spawn` starts a child that leads its own group (Unix) or lives in its own job object (Windows, started suspended so it cannot start a process before it is inside the job); `kill_tree` and the owner's `Drop` end the child and everything it started, and the Windows job also ends the tree when the owner dies without a destructor.
No Unix system offers that for a group, so an owner that must outlive its own crash keeps a channel the child watches (the codex app-server's stdin is one; the opener supervisor's socket is another), which is why `OwnedChild` promises the drop and not the crash.
`OwnedChild::spawn_tied` is that channel for a child that watches nothing of the owner's (a device's `ssh`).
On Unix the owned process is the owner's own program started again as the child's supervisor: a constructor in `hide-platform` (the `ctor` crate) runs before `main`, finds `HIDE_TIED_SUPERVISOR`, takes it out of the environment so neither the child nor what it starts sees it, and supervises, so `main` (hided's, a test harness's) never runs; a program started without the variable pays one `getenv`.
Linux runs `/proc/self/exe`, the file the owner runs even once an update replaced or deleted it at its path; macOS runs the file at the owner's path and refuses, as a spawn error, a file put there since (an app update replaces the bundle), which it tells by comparing that file's identity with the one the owner was started from.
`process::program_replaced` names that error, and a device's `ssh` attempt reads it as the typed problem `SshProblem::HideUpdated` (`hide_updated` on the wire), whose action is `reopen_hide`: the device row, a node's stopped core link and the move dialog's connection check say Hide was updated after it started, to quit and open it again, and offer no Retry, and nothing dials again on its own, because every attempt of the running program meets the same refusal; the update's restart relaunches the app, whose bundled `hide connect` replaces a daemon of another build, so only a hided left running from the old bundle meets it.
The variable carries a protocol version, and a supervisor of another version says so on the watch; a program without the constructor says nothing and the spawn fails at its 10 s bound; each is a spawn error the caller sees, never a fallback to another supervisor.
The supervisor starts the child itself, held before it runs until it has read the child's and its own unique ids (macOS), says `spawned <pid>` on the watch, a socket from the owner, while it still holds it, and waits for the owner to answer `go`; only then does it let the child go, and it says `started <pid>` once the child runs its program, or `failed <errno>` and `confirmed 0` once it reaped a child that could not; it lets go of its standard streams so they are the child's alone, then waits for the child to exit, for the owner to write `end`, or for the watch to close, which is the owner's death.
The owner answers `go` only while it is still inside its 10 s start bound (`TIED_START_LIMIT`), so an owner that gave up never lets a child run that it no longer tracks: a supervisor that hears no `go` within the same bound, or reads the watch closed or anything else, ends the held child before it runs, reaps it, says `failed` with `ETIMEDOUT` and `confirmed 0`, and exits.
Before `go` nothing of the child runs, so an error or silence ends the supervisor's group and fails the spawn; once the owner has written `go` the child may run and start processes of its own, so anything but `failed`, silence and the supervisor's end included, hands the child to its owner, whose end of it ends the tree as every end does.
Each way it runs the one end, `end_tree`, says `confirmed` or `unconfirmed <left>` on the watch, and exits with the child's status (a signal that would leave a core dump of the supervisor is passed on by its number, as a shell does).
From before it starts the child it ignores the hangup, interrupt, quit, terminate and broken-pipe signals, which the tree's own `kill 0` would send it, so it ends only by its own decision or `SIGKILL`; the child gets them back as the supervisor was given them before it runs its program.
The child's tree is the child and everything it started, at any depth, `setsid` ones included, named without watching the process table over time: on Linux the supervisor is a child subreaper, so a process whose parent ends comes back under it, and the tree is what is under it; macOS has no subreaper but keeps each process's starter by unique id, also once launchd takes it, so the tree is the child and what chains by those ids to the supervisor or the child, with the gaps [INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md#what-each-system-supports) records.
The end kills every running member and looks again until a look proves that none runs; a look that finds nothing proves nothing by itself.
On Linux the proof is the kernel's: each look reaps what exited, keeping the child's status, and the tree has ended only once waiting answers `ECHILD`, no child of the supervisor left, exited or running, so a process the `/proc` pass missed (one started after it) or could not pin is still counted.
On macOS a look is quiet when it read the whole process table and the ids of every process in it that still existed, and found no member at all, running or not, so a member that ended between the table and the look that filters it makes the look not quiet; the proof is two quiet looks in a row, since a member could have started another process before it ended and one look cannot tell, and anything else looks again within the bound; the ids each look finds are kept for the next, so a process whose starter one look saw still chains once that starter is gone.
Running is decided by `is_alive`, so a Linux process whose first thread has ended, listed `Z` while another thread runs, is a member.
It names each member so that a pid another process took since is never signalled: a pidfd on Linux, checked to be still under the supervisor once open, and on macOS the unique id, read again right before the signal.
The untied `kill_tree` walk pins its members the same way before its first signal.
Past its bound, 5 s (`TIED_END_LIMIT`), which only a process the kill cannot end or a tree that keeps starting processes reaches, the end is unconfirmed: the supervisor writes `process.tied_tree_outlived_its_end` to the owner's standard error, which it was given at start: a file where hided's standard error is one (a core move's start), and `/dev/null` for the daemon `hide connect` starts, where the line is lost, since `hide-platform` has no way into hided's diagnostic log; its lines on the watch never block either.
Every diagnostic of a tied child, the supervisor's and the owner's own drop and reaper lines, goes through a description of its own that no write blocks on (`diagnostics_of_its_own`): a regular file is shared as it is, since a file write never blocks, any other stream is opened again by its name as a new nonblocking description (Linux names every stream but a socket, macOS only a terminal), so the owner's own standard error stays blocking as it was, and anything else gets `/dev/null`; each line is one write, dropped when it does not fit at once, so a pipe nobody empties never keeps a supervisor from exiting or a drop from returning.
`wait`, `try_wait` and `kill_tree` then answer an error, never a status, as they do when the supervisor exits without a report or has not answered `end` within the bound and 2 s, after which the owner kills its group; a device attempt whose `ssh` end is unconfirmed is never counted ended (`host.child_end_unconfirmed`, `Held::outlived`).
Dropping a tied child never waits on it without a bound: it asks for the end if nothing did, waits up to 2 s (`TIED_REAP_LIMIT`) for the process it owns to exit, kills it and waits as long again, and leaves one that still has not exited to the process's one reaper thread, started with the first, which asks each child it holds without waiting every 100 ms and logs `process.tied_child_left_to_reaper`; it holds at most 64 (`REAPER_CAP`), and one past that, or one it has no thread for, is refused and logged (`process.tied_reaper_full`, `process.tied_reaper_unstarted`) and stays unreaped until the process exits.
So once `kill_tree` and `wait` return, nothing of the tree is still on its way out (`a_killed_tied_tree_has_ended_when_its_child_is_reaped`), a child that leaves a detached process and exits at once has taken it with it when its status comes (`a_tied_child_that_exits_at_once_leaves_no_detached_descendant`, `a_tied_child_that_exits_once_its_setsid_process_runs_leaves_none`, `a_tied_childs_process_whose_first_thread_ended_still_ends_with_it`, `a_tied_childs_orphan_ends_with_its_owners_death`), a tree that keeps starting processes faster than a look finds them has ended only once none is left (`a_tied_tree_that_keeps_starting_processes_ends_only_once_none_is_left`), a supervisor that ends before its child, an end past its bound or a process that cannot be pinned never lets the child read as ended (`a_tied_child_that_outlives_its_supervisor_never_reads_as_ended`, `a_tied_end_past_its_bound_is_an_error_not_a_status`, `a_tied_process_that_cannot_be_pinned_leaves_the_end_unconfirmed`), an unconfirmed end blocks neither `wait` nor the drop (`an_unconfirmed_tied_end_blocks_neither_wait_nor_drop`), repeated drops of children whose end stays unconfirmed, with the owner's standard error full, add no thread and leave no child unreaped (`unconfirmed_tied_drops_leave_no_thread_or_child_behind`), the child runs only once its owner answers within its start bound (`a_tied_supervisor_lets_its_child_go_only_once_its_owner_answers`), a macOS member that ends between the table and the look leaves no proof (`a_member_that_ends_between_the_table_and_the_look_leaves_no_proof`), the tree's own group signals at the start leave its end whole while the child keeps its own signals (`a_group_signal_as_a_tied_child_starts_leaves_its_end_whole`, `a_tied_child_runs_with_the_signals_its_owner_gave_it`), and a replaced program file is refused on macOS only (`a_tied_child_after_this_programs_file_was_replaced`).
On Windows it is `spawn` with its end confirmed: the job allows no breakaway and ends the tree with its owner (`abrupt_owner_death_ends_a_tied_child_that_watches_nothing`), and `wait`, `try_wait` and `kill_tree` end what the child left in its job and answer only once its tree has ended as `run_to_end`'s does (below), within the same bound; its drop waits for the child within the same reap bound.
`detach` starts a daemon that no signal to its parent's group reaches and that holds none of the parent's standard streams, nor any descriptor or handle a supervisor lent the parent beyond them (a debugging pipe, a readiness pipe): the child marks every descriptor above the standard three close-on-exec on Unix and the parent clears the inherit flag of its other handles on Windows, because a daemon that kept a lent pipe would keep a supervisor waiting for it as long as the daemon lives (`a_detached_child_holds_none_of_its_parents_extra_descriptors`).
Linux marks the range in one `close_range` call and macOS marks only the descriptors the kernel lists for the child (`proc_pidinfo`, into a buffer sized before the fork), since probing every number up to the open-file limit cost each start, a pane holder's among them, about 7 ms there; either falls back to that probe when its call fails or its list may be cut short.
The opt-in `OwnedChild::spawn_guarded` uses that same ownership helper and waits within an absolute deadline for a cooperative Unix child's `OwnerWatch::from_launch`, which retains an independent socket until all work finishes and ends its still-owned tree on owner loss, and whose reader polls that socket beside a wake channel, so closing the watch wakes the reader by data and end of stream rather than by a socket shutdown or a receive timeout (#446); the runtime descriptor is restored close-on-exec before acknowledgement, and downstream starts remove its metadata.
It admits one watch per process, preserves stdin for the caller's payload, and uses the existing kill-on-close job on Windows; detached daemons and arbitrary uncooperative Unix executables retain the legacy launch contract.
On Windows guarded launch names its job and the child checks both its membership in that exact job and the kill-on-close limit before returning startup proof; its query handle closes before return, leaving the parent the sole persistent job-handle owner, and missing metadata reports a standalone invocation.
`LOGIN_CHILD_VARIABLES` and `restrict_to_login_environment` are the one rule for a child that must find the account's login but must not inherit the rest of the environment (the weekly `/usage` read, the login shell's `PATH`, the SSH host read, and every child the install kit starts for an agent CLI: the Codex capability read, turn-off and trust): `HOME`, `PATH`, `USER`, `LOGNAME` and `TMPDIR` on Unix, and `PATH`, `PATHEXT`, `SystemRoot`, `USERPROFILE`, `USERNAME`, `TEMP`, `TMP`, `APPDATA`, `LOCALAPPDATA`, `ComSpec`, `windir`, `SystemDrive`, `ProgramFiles`, `ProgramFiles(x86)`, `ProgramData`, `HOMEDRIVE`, `HOMEPATH` and `CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH` on Windows, where Node takes its home from `USERPROFILE` and its start-up needs `SystemRoot`; a caller such as `hide-ai` names no variable itself, and a hook or nested-session marker stays out by not being listed.
A caller adds what it targets on top (`HOME`, `CODEX_HOME`, the `PATH` a CLI was found on), never builds the environment from nothing: Codex 0.163.0 from npm on Windows is `codex.cmd`, which runs Node, and with only `HOME`, `CODEX_HOME` and `PATH` Node aborted at start-up (exit 134), so the capability read failed and every Codex start Hide makes was refused.
`clippy.toml` therefore refuses `Command::env_clear` everywhere but this helper; launchd's `launchctl` and `pmset` (macOS system tools that need nothing but the home) and the tests whose subject is an environment built from nothing (an SSH exec's, a login item's, a throwaway agent home's) say why in an allow, and the `windows check` lane runs the Codex read and the kit's child through Node on Windows (`a_windows_codex_that_runs_node_answers_its_features`, `a_windows_program_that_runs_node_starts_in_the_kits_environment`).
`capture_until` drains only currently available stdout/stderr bytes without reader threads or joins, under the same absolute deadline and a caller-selected combined byte limit capped at 1 MiB, and ends at the child's exit by the same rule as `run_to_end`.
Failure retains bounded partial output and reports cleanup uncertainty separately; a failed guarded launch retains its unconfirmed child in `GuardedSpawnError` for explicit recovery, and no timeout asserts that an unobserved exit occurred.
Kernel calls have no universal cancellation guarantee, and Unix ancestry cannot identify a helper that has both escaped its group and been reparented before cleanup observes it.
`run_to_end` observes exit without reaping its leader (a stopped leader has not exited, though macOS's `waitid` answers for it with `WEXITED` alone, so only an exit, a kill or a core dump counts), ends the owned tree while its identity is retained, waits until nothing of the tree is left running, then reads both pipes until they are empty and answers; it does not wait for every write end to close.
A write end can be held outside the tree for as long as its holder lives: a helper that left the group and was reparented before the walk, or a child another thread of the same process started while the run's pipes were being made.
The second is a macOS fact: Rust's standard library makes a pipe there with `pipe` and then marks each end close-on-exec, where Linux has `pipe2(O_CLOEXEC)`, and a child `posix_spawn` starts in between inherits both ends (#729: a hide-kit test's long-lived lock holder kept a `launchctl print` run's pipes open past its 5 s deadline, so a login agent that was never loaded failed retirement).
Windows has neither: the standard library makes a child's inheritable pipe ends and calls `CreateProcess` under one process-wide lock, and a job has no breakaway, so there the pipes reach their end with the tree; the rule is the same code on all three.
Nothing of the tree is left running when every member of the leader's group is ended by `is_alive`'s answer on Unix, and on Windows when the job counts no active process and every process it ever ran has its object signalled.
Signal 0 to the group cannot say it on Unix, because macOS refuses it with `EPERM` both when only zombies are left and while a killed member is still exiting, and a member that left its group is signalled but not awaited.
On Windows the system counts a process out of its job, and sets its exit code, before it closes the handles the process held, and signals the object after, so a count of zero can come while a process that ended on its own, or one started while the tree was being ended, still holds a pipe, a file or a folder (with-hide/hide-private#327).
So each child's job announces every process that joins it on one completion port of this process, set on the job before the child starts, and one thread reads that port for the life of the process.
Each notice costs that thread the same: it checks the next two held processes in turn for their signal, lets go of those signalled and puts the rest behind the others, so a process slow to end holds up no other and one whose exit notice never came is let go on its turn (`an_ended_process_is_let_go_behind_one_slow_to_end_without_its_exit_notice`); the owner lets go of every ended one when it asks about the end.
The port's queue is the system's and Windows offers no limit on it, so notices wait there for as long as processes start and end faster than the one thread reads them; the operator accepted that as a known limit (2026-10-30) rather than a cap Hide could set.
Hide caps what it owns: each notice costs the thread the same, at most 1,024 jobs are followed at once and at most 4,096 processes held per job, and crossing either is a failure the caller sees: a child past the job cap is refused at its start, and a job past the held cap answers every question about its end with that reason.
A pid that no longer opens, or opens as a process outside the job, had its object deleted, after its handles closed.
Microsoft does not guarantee a job's notices arrive, so they are counted against the job's own count of the processes it ever ran, and the end is not confirmed while one is owed; a process that could not be followed (refused, past the cap, or a failed wait) is kept as the reason, logged once as `process.job_follow_lost`, and every later question about that end answers with it.
The port no longer being read is kept the same way for every job, under the same lock jobs join by, so a job never joins a port that is no longer read: it is refused at its start, every job followed already is told, and every later end answers with why (`process.job_notices_down`).
Each job followed then has its notices taken off the port, and one the system refuses to take off is only logged (`process.job_notices_left_set`): its notices keep reaching the port, which no thread reads.
While the end is confirmed, a member still running gets the end again, the group on Unix and the job on Windows: a parent the first signal had not stopped yet can start a process while it is sent, and macOS does not hold that start back.
On Unix the leader stays unreaped until then, because its id is the group's, so neither the members counted nor the second signal can be another group's; it is reaped once the tree has ended.
It reads only available bytes, keeps at most 64 KiB from each stream, and observes the original deadline and stop flag through draining without reader threads or blocking joins.
After ending the tree, the end is confirmed by the leader's observed exit (on Windows a wait on its process handle), because Windows ends a job's processes after `TerminateJobObject` returns and a busy machine can take longer than one poll interval; a stopped run is confirmed the same way, since a process the kill reached is seen ending at once, so only a pathological end delays a quitting owner. A leader still running 10 s after the kill counts as one the kernel could not end and is logged as `process.end_unconfirmed`; that unconfirmed cleanup returns `RunCleanupFailure` inside `RunFailure::Wait`, retaining the original outcome and child owner for recovery without a blocking destructor.
An escaped helper reparented before the process walk cannot be attributed by Unix ancestry, so it is not ended, and its open pipe no longer holds the answer; a kernel call has no universal cancellation guarantee.
`kill_tree(pid)`, `terminate`, `is_alive`, `parent_of`, `descends_from`, `start_time`, `cpu_time`, `cwd_of` and `measure_tree` answer for a pid from the kernel's tables (libproc on macOS, `/proc` on Linux, Toolhelp and job accounting on Windows) and fork nothing, which is what lets the git path and the process cap use them; a start time is an opaque number that only tells a pid from a later process that reused it.
`is_alive` asks whether the process has not yet ended, and every system answers it the same way: a Unix zombie still answers signal 0 until its parent, or init once it is orphaned, reaps it, so the answer also reads the process state (`Z` in `/proc/<pid>/stat`, `SZOMB` from the `KERN_PROC_PID` sysctl, because libproc has no answer for a zombie), as Windows waits on the process object, which the system signals last, after it has closed every handle the process held, and which Microsoft documents as the way to be sure a process has ended (`TerminateProcess` returns before it has); a test that read the exit code instead was refused a folder an ended process had used (with-hide/hide-private#327). A process that refuses to be waited on is read by its exit code, and a wait or an exit-code read that fails confirms nothing, so the process still counts and the failure is logged (`process.alive_unconfirmed`). On Linux a process whose first thread has ended reads `Z` while its other threads are still exiting, so it has ended only once that thread is the last one `/proc/<pid>/task` lists; and a process reaped between the signal and the state read has ended on both systems.
`start_time` reads that same end, so it answers for every process `is_alive` still counts and a process it no longer answers for has let go of what it held: on Windows every query of a live process (`start_time`, `name_of`, `argv_of`, the memory read, the hold `kill_tree` takes) answers `NotFound` only once the object is signalled, and an end asked of a process whose exit code is already set is what was asked; on macOS the start comes from the `KERN_PROC_PID` sysctl `is_alive` reads, since libproc stops answering while a process is still on its way out, and it is the same kernel value; a Unix zombie keeps its start until it is reaped (with-hide/hide-private#585).
Before that, a helper `run_to_end` had ended still counted as alive on Linux until init reaped it (#595).
Windows has no polite `SIGTERM` and no readable working directory, so `terminate` ends the process at once and `cwd_of` says `Unsupported` there.
`argv_of` reads the native process command-line query on Windows with query-only access, through a held process handle, and uses the system's argument parser for quotes and backslashes.
The read is bounded to the Windows command-line limit, retries a changing size at most twice, and rejects an invalid descriptor or failed query; it needs no process-memory read or subprocess.
The native query resolver is shared with listener-owner observation in `hide-platform/src/windows_process.rs`; macOS and Linux keep their existing argument readers.
It has no process group either, and `terminate_group` ends a terminal's foreground job by what stands in for one: a Windows pane's foreground job is named by its first process, the program its shell runs now (`console_foreground`, below), so `terminate_group` ends that process and every process under it at once.
The process table keeps the pid a parent had when its child started and holds no handle, so a row alone can name a later process that took an ended one's pid: every process of the tree is opened and held before the leader ends, and a row counts as a child only when the process its pid opens started no earlier than its held parent and a second look at the table, read while it is held, still lists it under that parent; one opened but not matched so is left alone and named in the answer, and a process that refuses to end once the leader is down is named there too (`GroupEnd::Ended { left }`), since the job no longer holds the terminal.
A leader that is gone is `GroupEnd::Gone`, as a gone group is on Unix, and a table that cannot be read ends nothing; `kill_tree` ends a Windows tree the same way, and `descendants` leaves out a row whose start, or whose parent's, cannot be read.
A job object would hold the tree only from its start, and a pane's program is started by its holder inside no job of this crate's, so the tree is read at the end instead; a helper whose parent had already exited is out of reach, as for `kill_tree` (`ending_a_job_ends_its_leader_and_what_it_started_and_nothing_else`).
The same stand-in names a Windows console's foreground for the pane holder, which on Unix reads the terminal's foreground group (`tcgetpgrp`): `console_foreground(shell)` is the oldest process the pane's shell started that still runs, the program a typed line started and the shell waits on, or the shell itself while it runs none, and `group_members(leader)` on Windows is that process and every process under it.
A console host (`conhost.exe`, `OpenConsole.exe`) is never a member or the foreground, since a console process that made a new console gets one as its child and it runs nothing of the console's own.
So the core's own engine reads a Windows pane as it reads a Unix one: an idle shell is the group's only member, which is when a start is typed, and an agent the shell runs is the foreground its screen rules follow (`a_consoles_foreground_is_the_program_its_shell_runs_or_the_shell`, `processes_name_the_shell_and_the_program_that_holds_the_terminal`).
The holder names no agent: it keeps no agent table, and the engine already reads any program in the foreground after a start as the agent it started.
`image_of(pid)` names the program file a process runs: where that file is now, and the identity (`FileId`) of the file the process was started from, which stays its answer when the app around it is renamed aside or a new file is put at its path.
macOS reads the identity from the process's own mapping (the lowest file-backed region whose file the kernel names at the program's path, `PROC_PIDREGIONPATHINFO`, whose structures libc does not declare and `process.rs` states with their SDK sizes), because the path alone still names the old program after a new file took its place; Linux follows `/proc/<pid>/exe`, which reaches the running file even once it is deleted.
Windows names a process's image by the path it started from and keeps no identity of the file that follows a rename, so `image_of` says `Unsupported` there.
`running(file)` lists the processes that run a program file, by the file's identity: on macOS and Linux the one `image_of` reads, on Windows the identity of the file now at the path a process started from, so there a process whose program was renamed aside may be left out, and a process of another file is never counted.
`boot_id()` names this boot of the machine (`/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, `kern.bootsessionuuid`), because a Linux start time counts from the boot and a pid and start time recorded in an earlier boot can name a process of this one; Windows answers `Unsupported`, where the job a dead holder held ended its pane, so no record of an earlier boot names anything that runs.
The one start helper, the pane bootstrap's process identity (`hide-host/src/pane_peer.rs`, the single copy `hided` now reuses) and the AI process cap's measurement (`hide-ai/src/process.rs`, which only maps the answer) are the callers of record; a raw `Command::spawn` that outlives its call is a review rejection (practice `process.md`, rule 1), except the ones that are deliberate: `hided`'s detached daemon (`spawn_owned`), the default-app handoff and, on Unix, the opener helper's own CLI (`hide-node/src/opener.rs`, the node's, which hided's node role runs), whose owner is a socket the supervisor watches (on Windows that helper is an `OwnedChild`), and the Tailscale probe that tokio kills on drop; no grep gate enforces it yet.
Dropping an `OwnedChild` after the child was waited for names nothing on Unix, because the child's pid may be another process's by then, so a caller that wants a finished child's leftovers ended calls `kill_tree` at the moment it exits (the kit and the codex shutdown do); a Windows job ends them when it closes.
A Windows job has no breakaway, so a helper an owned child daemonizes dies with the job; the daemons the app starts on purpose (`hided`) start through `detach`, which on Windows also makes this process's standard handles uninheritable first, since Windows hands a child every inheritable handle and a daemon holding the CLI's output pipe would keep `hide connect`'s caller waiting for the end of that output as long as the daemon lives, and a start that must outlive its owner goes through `start_resident` instead.
`start_resident` starts a child that outlives its starter and keeps nothing of it, which is how a node starts a pane's holder ([The pane holder](#the-pane-holder)); it is not `detach`, which leaves the daemon in its starter's session and job.
On Unix the child is a grandchild that leads a session of its own: the intermediate child calls `setsid`, forks again and exits, so the resident is no child of the starter's and can never take a controlling terminal.
It starts with every signal at its default and none blocked, its standard streams on `/dev/null`, and no descriptor of the starter's but the ones the caller lends (at most four), which arrive in order from descriptor 3 and are named in `HIDE_RESIDENT_LENT` for the child's `take_lent`; `start_resident` answers only once the program runs, as `Command::spawn` does.
A program this process has just written (a holder copied into its version folder) is busy on Linux while a child another thread forked still holds the writer's descriptor, until that child runs its own program, so a start refused with `ETXTBSY` is tried again, up to 20 times 10 ms apart (`a_start_waits_out_a_program_another_process_holds_open_for_writing`, Linux only, since macOS runs a program file open for writing).
What it runs is a `ResidentCommand`: a program named by an absolute path, its arguments, changes to the starter's environment and a working folder, and nothing else a `Command` carries, since the start decides the rest the same way on every system.
On Windows it starts with `CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB`, `DETACHED_PROCESS` and a process group of its own, inheriting only the lent handles (named on a `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST`, so no handle another thread makes inheritable meanwhile reaches it); it starts suspended and runs only once it is found outside the starter's own job, the one the starter's owner ends it with (Electron ends `hided`'s with the app).
A starter whose own job does not let it break away, or keeps it anyway, is refused with that job's limits (`PermissionDenied`); a job above the starter's that keeps the child (a CI runner's or a test harness's, which does not let a process leave it) is allowed, since the starter's owner does not end it, and `start_resident` answers it as `Resident::outer_job` for the caller to record, while the child reads that job's limits with `own_job`.
The starter's own job keeps the child, answered the same way, when it neither lets a process leave nor ends its processes when it closes, as a CI runner's job is when the daemon lands in it by leaving Node's and Electron's libuv jobs silently: closing it ends nothing, as Herdr v0.9.5 keeps its server in such a job (`launch_server_daemon_command`); a kill-on-close job that lets no process leave is still refused (`a_job_that_ends_nothing_on_close_keeps_the_resident`, `a_start_inside_a_job_that_keeps_its_processes_is_refused`).
`a_resident_child_keeps_nothing_of_its_starter`, `a_resident_child_outlives_what_ends_its_starter` and `a_start_inside_a_job_that_keeps_its_processes_is_refused` hold it; on CI the first prints the jobs the run had.
`Session` ends what a resident started as a whole: a terminal session on Unix, and on Windows a kill-on-close job only its owner holds, which also ends the tree when the owner dies without a destructor.
`adopt` names the session's leader before it is waited for; on Unix every process whose session id is the leader's is a member, with its descendants, and a session id is not reused while a member lives, so what outlives the leader is still found.
`left_by(leader, started)` (Unix) names the session of a leader recorded earlier by its pid and start time, for what is left of it once the process that held it ended without ending it; once a process with another start time holds that pid the session is over and nothing is found (`a_session_left_by_its_holder_is_found_again_by_its_recorded_leader`, `a_recorded_leader_whose_pid_another_process_holds_names_no_member`).
`end` sends `SIGHUP`, then `SIGTERM`, each with 250 ms to take, then `SIGKILL` until two looks 10 ms apart find no member, within the caller's limit, and answers `SessionEnd::Ended` only then; otherwise it answers `Unconfirmed { left }` with the pids still running, never success (`ending_a_session_ends_every_member_and_what_they_start_meanwhile`, `a_session_whose_leader_exited_still_ends_what_it_left`).
`set_output_aside` is the one place a process redirects its own standard streams: a login agent's output is a file launchd opened once, at the job's start, so renaming it there leaves the process writing on under the new name, and a core that runs for weeks grew it without bound.
Asked at the start of `hided core-login` and then every minute (`hided/src/login_item.rs`), it renames the file to `core.log.1` once it passes 1 MiB, replacing the one before, and moves standard error, and standard output when it went to the same file, onto a new private file at the old name with `dup2`; output that is not that file is left alone, and Windows, which starts no login agent with a file for its output, answers `Unsupported` (`output_appended_to_a_file_is_set_aside_past_its_limit_and_goes_on_in_a_new_one`).
A child started before a set-aside and given the core's standard error keeps writing to the file set aside.
`fs` is the third module and the one place a file is made private, locked, replaced, linked or identified.
It takes a path where a caller holds a name and `Handle` (`AsFd` on Unix, `AsHandle` on Windows) where it holds an open folder or file, so `hide-host` passes its `cap-std` handles straight through and nothing in the crate depends on `cap-std`.
`private` makes a folder or file only the current account can use (0700 and 0600 on Unix; a protected access list naming the current account alone on Windows, set at creation so there is no wider moment) and answers `is_private`, `others_can_modify` and `owned_by_current_user` for the checks that decide whether a folder may hold code the account runs; `Access` names the three cases a writer needs (private, private and runnable, keep what the replaced file had).
Every folder Hide makes under `~/.hide` and in its state folder is made private (`private::create_dir`, `create_dir_all` or `own_dir`), never with `std::fs::create_dir_all`, whose folders take the umask's mode: a device helper's bridge folder once made `~/.hide/state` 0755 that way, and a core moved onto that machine later refused its delivery ledger, whose parent must be private.
`private::own_dir` makes a folder this account's private one whatever an earlier program left there: it makes a missing one and every missing folder above it private, restricts one the account owns that others can reach, and refuses a link, a file or another account's folder without changing it; it opens the entry itself (`O_NOFOLLOW | O_DIRECTORY`, or a reparse point opened as itself on Windows) and judges its owner and access and sets its mode or access list through that handle (`fchmod`, `SetSecurityInfo`), so a link swapped in after the look cannot redirect the change; the daemon's state folder is opened through it ([hided and the WebSocket boundary](#hided-and-the-websocket-boundary)).
It judges the last name only: a link among the folders above, such as a `~/.hide` that leads elsewhere, is accepted and followed, as the delivery ledger's start follows it when `establish_dir_durability` resolves the chain from the filesystem root, because the folders above are the caller's to trust and an operator may keep `~/.hide` on another volume.
`lock` is an advisory lock on a file or a folder that ends with the process: `flock` on Unix and `LockFileEx` on Windows through the standard library, with a wait that gives up after a time or when the caller cancels.
The wait tries again after 1 ms and then twice as long each time, up to 20 ms: the locks taken this way are held for a read and a replace, and a flat 20 ms sleep made each of a restore's eight concurrent pane starts pay 20 ms for every record write it met.
Dropping a lock releases it before closing its descriptor: under `flock` the lock belongs to the open file, and a child another thread starts in that moment keeps a copy of the descriptor until it starts its program, so a lock left to the close stayed held and a one-try lock elsewhere read it as busy (#820); `fs::a_dropped_lock_is_free_while_a_child_started_meanwhile_still_holds_its_descriptor` holds such a child in that moment.
`cap-std` opens its folders with `O_PATH` on Linux and the kernel answers `EBADF` to `flock` and `fsync` on such a descriptor, which refused every save on Linux once (#285), so a folder is always locked and flushed through a fresh readable descriptor of the same folder; `hide-host/tests/it/save.rs` and the contract test that locks through an `O_PATH` handle are the proof.
Windows refuses a byte-range lock on a folder (`ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`) and a lock file inside a checkout would put a file in someone's work, so a folder is locked through one of 65536 empty files in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hide\locks`, picked by the folder's identity: two folders that pick the same file only wait for each other, the count cannot grow, and the folder is trusted only when the account owns it and nobody else can change it.
That lock is one account's, so two accounts working in one folder do not exclude each other on Windows as they do under `flock`.
`atomic` replaces a file whole or not at all (`write_file`, `replace_file`), exchanges two names (`exchange`: `RENAME_SWAP` on macOS, `RENAME_EXCHANGE` on Linux; on Windows a `ReplaceFileW` that parks the old file under a `.hide-swap-` name and a rename, so the replaced name never shows a partial file, but it names nothing for the moment `ReplaceFileW` moves the old file aside and the other name is empty until the rename, which `EXCHANGE_IS_ATOMIC` says) and renames without replacing (`rename_no_replace`: `RENAME_EXCL`, `RENAME_NOREPLACE`, `MoveFileExW`).
The legacy writers provide whole-file visibility with best-effort parent sync, which on Windows never reaches a folder flush, since they open the folder without the backup semantics a folder handle needs.
Their file flush remains `sync_all`, which on macOS is `F_FULLFSYNC` and also empties the device's cache.
Only holder records and their incarnation counter choose `write_file`'s explicit `WriteOptions::UntilReboot`: `fsync` on Unix, without macOS's extra device-cache barrier, and the same `sync_all` on Windows.
Those records name processes that cannot survive a reboot, and their owner recovers missing, damaged or older records after power loss; every other caller keeps its existing file barrier by passing `Access`.
The macOS file barrier cost about 5 ms a write against 0.2 ms for `fsync` in the diagnostic, and a pane holder's start paid it three times under one lock (a restore of 66 panes queued about a second of it).
The opt-in `write_file_durable` shares the bounded temporary pipeline and checks file sync, a same-folder rename (`MoveFileExW(REPLACE_EXISTING | WRITE_THROUGH)` on Windows, the form the `atomicwrites` crate uses) and a fallible open and flush of the parent folder on every system.
Its file is always the account's alone (`DurableAccess`: private, or a private program): it never keeps the access of the file it replaces, because Windows keeps an access list only through `ReplaceFileW`, which has no write-through form.
Its errors distinguish `BeforeReplace`, `ReplacementUncertain` and `ReplacedNotDurable`; the last retains the installed `FileId`, all retain the original I/O cause, and failed owned-temp cleanup reports its own path and cause separately.
Neither uncertain outcome restores old bytes or deletes the destination: the caller must suspend assumptions about the old version and validate recovery before using it again.
The parent and its ancestry must already have an established durability boundary; this writer does not create or sync ancestors, `private::create_dir_all` still provides no parent-chain barrier, and OS acknowledgement promises neither universal power-loss protection nor a kernel-call cancellation deadline.
A folder's barrier is `atomic::sync_dir`: `fsync` on Unix, and on Windows `FlushFileBuffers` on the same folder opened again with the right to add an entry (`NtCreateFile` of an empty name relative to the folder's handle, since `ReOpenFile` refuses every folder, and with no backup intent, so a privilege never grants what the access list does not), since `NtFlushBuffersFileEx` refuses a handle with neither write nor append access and its normal flush, unlike the data-only ones, takes a folder and writes its data and metadata through the storage cache; etcd's `fileutil.OpenDir` flushes a Windows folder the same way.
PostgreSQL and SQLite skip a folder's sync on Windows instead, which this layer does not do: a folder that cannot be flushed is an error, never a quiet success.
The opt-in `private::create_dir_all_durable` establishes a descendant chain from an explicitly supplied already-durable trusted ancestor, preflighting at most 64 normal components and syncing each existing or newly created child and its containing parent; every one of them is the account's own, so a refused flush there fails on Windows too.
The opt-in `private::establish_dir_durability` first establishes an existing account-owned trusted directory's canonical ancestor chain from the filesystem root, with at most 64 components, checking its identity and each fallible directory barrier without creating or removing entries; its returned canonical path can anchor sibling state and home directories without treating existence as durability.
That operation requires a caller-trusted stable ancestor namespace, permits shared system ancestors and resolves their existing aliases, and does not infer privacy or protection from another account for those ancestors.
It refuses links and directories another account can modify, leaves existing permissions intact, and reports the last completed and uncertain component with the original I/O cause while retaining the partial chain for explicit recovery.
On Windows an ancestor is flushed only to keep the chain's next folder in it, and only when that folder's owner is the account (its user, or the owner its token gives what it makes; an owner that cannot be read counts as the account's) and the account owns the ancestor or may add a file or a folder to it, which `AccessCheck` answers for the process's token before any flush; the leaf is always flushed, and a failure is an error.
An ancestor whose next folder the system made is passed over (`C:\` for its `Users`), because nothing this account did can have left that entry unwritten and a drive root's flush writes out everything the drive holds unwritten: right after an install it took 3 to 5 s of a first start on the Windows runner, and 0.2 to 2.4 s of a later one, while every other folder took milliseconds (#1515); one the account may not flush is passed over too (`C:\Users` for a standard account) (`hide-platform/tests/it/fs.rs`, `an_ancestor_is_passed_over_only_when_the_account_neither_owns_nor_may_add_to_it` and `an_ancestor_is_flushed_only_to_keep_a_folder_the_account_made`).
The document save in `hide-host/src/save.rs` is exchange-and-verify on top of these and keeps its contract on every system; its checks (a regular file, one name, owned by this account, writable) are answered by `identity::link_count`, `private::handle_owned_by_current_user` and `permissions::Permissions`, so they mean the same on Windows.
`link` makes a link a caller can replace in one step (`replace_link`, the kit's `current` on macOS and Linux) and ask about (`is_link_to`); the name is never missing while it is replaced, and a path opened through it at that moment finds the old target or the new one on macOS and Windows but can answer "not found" on Linux, where the path walk that follows the link can meet the swap.
A link is a symbolic link on Unix; on Windows a junction for a folder, which needs no privilege and leads only to an absolute path on this machine, and a symbolic link for a file, which needs the privilege or Developer Mode and otherwise fails with `NeedsPrivilege`, a typed answer (`needs_privilege(&error)`) that a caller with an alternative takes.
`identity` says which file a name leads to (`FileId`: a device and an inode, or a volume serial and a 128-bit file id), whether two names are one file (`/tmp` and `/private/tmp`, a link and its target), the id of one entry of an open folder (`entry_id`, which the Explorer's "replaced while the prompt was open" check compares on every system), a canonical spelling with the `\\?\` prefix removed where the short form means the same, the path an open file or folder is at now (`path_of`: `F_GETPATH`, `/proc/self/fd`, `GetFinalPathNameByHandleW` with its `\\?\` prefix kept, so hided's root boundary compares a file and its root by prefix at any length), a `Stamp` (length, write time, change time) that tells whether a file changed between two looks, and whether a folder tells `Name` from `name` (asked of the folder at run time, because a Mac or Windows volume may be either).
`private::open_own_file` opens a file only when the name itself is the account's own regular file with no other name (a symbolic link at the name is not followed, a hard link is refused, a pipe does not block), which the label generator's lock, the daemon's locks and the pane credential reads stand on; `fs::open_regular` is the same refusal of links, pipes and devices without the ownership, for a file the operator picked to attach; `private::create_dir_all` makes a chain of private folders.
`private::handle_others_can_modify` checks the permissions of an already-open descriptor, so retirement decides from the same ledger, progress or run-state file it reads; the kit also refuses links at each owned directory before reads and removal.
`private::inspect_directory_entry` authenticates a real directory or returns an inspected system-owned alias target without following it.
It follows the sticky rule: a system folder others may add entries of their own to is still safe to rely on, since only their right to delete, rename or re-permission it or what is in it (on Windows `DELETE`, `FILE_DELETE_CHILD`, `WRITE_DAC`, `WRITE_OWNER`, or rewriting it) takes away a name a caller depends on; Unix states it as a root-owned sticky folder such as `/tmp`, and Windows as a folder owned by SYSTEM, Administrators or TrustedInstaller whose access list gives others no more than `FILE_ADD_FILE` and `FILE_ADD_SUBDIRECTORY`, which a drive's root gives every signed-in account (`inspection_lets_others_add_to_a_system_folder_but_not_delete_from_it`).
A drive's root also hands that group the right to change any folder made in it, so such a folder is refused, while Hide's private folders cut inheritance (a protected access list) and pass; retirement validates every component of an external state override and each alias target namespace before treating a missing ledger as empty.
`space` answers what an entry takes on its volume (allocated bytes, links and identity, from one `lstat` on Unix and by opening the entry on Windows, which has no call that answers from a name) and how much the volume has left, for the disk usage walk and the cleanup's free-space line.

`watch` is the fourth module: a `Watcher` watches folders, each with everything under it, and puts what changed on one `Changes` queue, which the caller drains on its own schedule.
A change is the path that was created, written, renamed or removed, once however many times the system said so while it waited, under the spelling the caller watched (FSEvents answers with the real path); reading a file is never a change (inotify's access events are dropped, and Windows is not asked for them).
On Linux a folder made under a watched one is watched only once its creation is read, so what is made in it before then is reported as that folder alone; a caller that waits for one exact path makes it in a folder that existed when the watch began.
The queue holds at most 4096 paths; past that, or when the system's own queue overflowed or it stopped watching, the waiting paths give way to one `Change::Overflow` that says anything under a watched folder may have changed, so what waits is bounded however long a burst lasts and a lost change is never silence; once the reader takes the overflow, what changes after it queues again.
`Watcher::keeping` takes a filter on the path relative to the watched folder, applied where the system reports it, so a burst no caller asked about neither fills the queue nor overflows it.
macOS and Linux are watched through `notify`; Windows is watched with `ReadDirectoryChangesW` directly, one thread per folder, because `notify` drops the answer Windows gives when its buffer overflows (no entries, or `ERROR_NOTIFY_ENUM_DIR`, on which it also stops watching); `watch` returns once that thread has started its first read, because a folder is watched only from then and a change made just before would be lost.
The Git watch is the caller, on the node that holds the repositories (`git_watch`, `hide-host/src/git_watch.rs`): one call holds one watcher over the projects' common directories, keeps only Git's facts (`HEAD`, `index`, `packed-refs`, `FETCH_HEAD`, `refs/`, `worktrees/`), and reports the repositories that changed, an overflow, or that nothing did, at least once a second so the caller can end it; the node ends the watcher when its caller stops answering or the node closes.
The core's side in `hide-core/src/worktrees.rs` starts that call on a thread of its own and drains its reports on the coordinator's tick outside the runtime lock.
The thread keeps at most 256 reports for the tick and never a heartbeat; a report past that is dropped and kept as one re-read of every project (`git_watch.mailbox_full`), so a tick that falls behind costs reads, not memory.
With no renderer attached the coordinator ends the watch (`git_watch.rested`) rather than leave its reports unread, and the first read after a renderer attaches starts it again and reads every project once it is watching, as after any gap.
A stopped watch's thread ends on the node's next report and the reader joins it; the reader's end waits up to 3 s for those threads and names any still running (`git_watch.stop_unconfirmed`).
When the watched set changes it starts a new watch and keeps the old one, read after the new one in each pass, until one pass after the new one reports that it is watching, so a repository in both is never unwatched and a change the old one reports as the new one starts is still read.
An overflow becomes a `git_watch.overflow` diagnostic and a re-read of every watched project, where an inotify overflow used to be dropped without a word.
A watch that ended (`git_watch.ended`) or could not start is tried again after 30 s, and once it is watching every project is read again, because anything may have changed in the gap; a set change before then passes that re-read on to the watch that replaces it.
No watch event wakes the core: the coordinator's tick reads the queue, as it read the callback's map before, so the notifier's fan-out is unchanged.

`host` is the fifth module and answers where the account's things live and what the machine is called: `home_dir` (`HOME`, `USERPROFILE` on Windows), `state_dir` (`~/Library/Application Support`, `$XDG_STATE_HOME` or `~/.local/state`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%`) and `state_dir_under` for a caller whose state follows a home it was handed, `herdr_config_dir_from` (the folder the read-only Herdr import reads Herdr's `session.json` and `herdr.sock` from, in the order Herdr uses: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/herdr` when set, then `%APPDATA%\herdr` on Windows, then `~/.config/herdr`; a relative variable is `InvalidInput`, no home is `NotFound`, and `hide-platform/tests/it/host.rs` checks each case), `login_path` (this process's `PATH`, which starts no shell) and `find_program` (an execute bit on Unix, `PATHEXT` on Windows), `login_shell` (the `PATH` and the environment the account's login shell sets up: `$SHELL -ilc` prints the `PATH` between two marks and then `command env -0` between two others, past whatever the startup files print, under a deadline and a stop flag; the shell gets the login variables only, so its environment is the account's and never the daemon's or a terminal's; the shell's own `PWD`, `OLDPWD`, `SHLVL` and `_` and any value that is not UTF-8 are left out, and an `env` that cannot list with NUL ends leaves the environment unread while the `PATH` still holds; `Unsupported` on Windows, whose processes already get the account's `Path`), `account_environment` (Windows only: the environment the system builds for the account's sign-in, `CreateEnvironmentBlock` without this process's own, which is what Explorer gives a terminal; `Unsupported` on macOS and Linux), `default_shell`, `trash` (`NSFileManager` on macOS, the Recycle Bin, the freedesktop trash), `primary_language` (the first of `defaults read -g AppleLanguages` on macOS, the account's `LocaleName` on Windows, `LC_ALL`, `LC_MESSAGES` or `LANG` on Linux, as a BCP 47 tag; `NotFound` for the `C` locale), `tailscale_cli` (the app's CLI on macOS and Windows; `Unsupported` on Linux, which has no fixed place), `name` and `machine_id` (`IOPlatformUUID`, `/etc/machine-id`, the `MachineGuid` the Windows registry keeps).
`programs` is the one search for an agent's CLI: the login shell's `PATH`, this process's own `PATH` and the usual install folders, as `search_path`, `account_path`, `find_cli` and `cli_path_with`.
The same ask keeps the environment the shell exports (`login_shell_environment`), and `account_environment` answers the environment a new terminal of the account starts with on every system (that one on macOS and Linux, `host::account_environment` on Windows), for a caller that starts an agent the way the operator's terminal would (Desk's process); no caller starts the shell a second time for it, and an environment the shell did not list is logged as `platform.login_shell_environment_unread`.
The install kit's "installed" and Hide AI's backends both read it, so there is no second program search (`hide-platform/tests/it/programs.rs`).
The login shell's answer is the one thing the crate remembers between calls, and it stays here on purpose: it is a fact about the account (what `$SHELL -ilc` prints), not about a caller, so a cache per owner (the kit's target, Hide AI) would start the operator's shell once for each and could disagree about the same program.
It is keyed by the shell and home it was read for and capped at eight pairs, kept until one of the shell's startup files changes, and asked again after sixty seconds when the shell did not answer, which is logged as `platform.login_shell_unread`.
Each shell and home pair has its own lock, held across the ask, so callers for the same pair that arrive cold together wait for one shell and read its answer (`callers_that_arrive_cold_together_start_one_shell`) while a caller for another home never waits behind it (`a_slow_ask_for_one_home_does_not_hold_another_home_behind_it`), and a stop raised by the caller that is asking ends the shell and remembers nothing.
A CLI found by this search is run with it too, never with the daemon's `PATH` alone: the Memory version probe and every Hide AI child take `cli_path_with` or `account_path` (`hide-ai/src/program.rs`).
Every program a node starts by name uses `programs::command` (found on the account's search and run with it), including `git` and `gh` (`hide-host/src/{git,git_command,worktrees,clone,gh}.rs`).
Only a process's first `command` waits for the login shell: until a first read of the search (`account_path_now`) has finished, the caller waits for it, at most the shell's deadline and a second (`FIRST_READ_WITHIN`), so a fresh process such as the `hide` CLI finds on its first command a `gh` that only `.zshrc` puts on the `PATH` (`a_fresh_process_runs_what_only_the_login_shell_finds_on_its_first_command`); after that a caller takes the search as last read while a thread of its own reads it again once it is ten seconds old, so a caller's own deadline (`GIT_DEADLINE` for a git read) bounds its run, and the per-command cost is one lock and a clock read, the startup files' stats moving to that thread.
A daemon starts that first read as it comes up (`warm_account_path`), so its own first command seldom waits, while a device's node role starts none until a command asks, since a link that runs no command needs no shell; a read that panics is finished all the same, so it holds off neither its waiter nor the next read.
The caller that must have the shell's current answer, a move's `gh` check, asks `account_path` and runs `command_on` with it.
A daemon an SSH exec or a login item started has the system's folders alone on its own `PATH` (`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`), so a core a move put on a Mac mini found no Homebrew `gh`, and Git there ran its hooks, filters such as `git-lfs` and credential helpers without the account's folders; run with the account's search, a child finds what it starts by name where the operator's terminal would (`a_command_runs_what_the_login_shell_finds_with_the_path_it_was_found_on`).
The search is asked again only when a startup file changes, so a tool the operator installs into a folder those files name is found by the next command without a restart.
A test that shims one of these programs on a child's `PATH` therefore also controls the login shell, by naming a stand-in shell or removing `SHELL`, since macOS's `path_helper` puts the system's folders, and its Git, ahead of the folders a shell was handed.
Each refuses with `NotFound`, `InvalidInput` or `Unsupported` rather than guessing; hided's environment registry hands its own values to the `_from` forms, so the variables it depends on stay listed in `hided/src/env.rs`.
The Windows check builds the whole workspace, tests included.
`listeners` observes Windows TCP owners through the native IPv4 and IPv6 listener tables and reads each owner's cwd from bounded process-parameter memory, while the node's Unix reader (`hide-host/src/ports.rs`, the `listening_ports` call the core's `ports.rs` makes) retains `lsof`.
Its `ObservedWorkingDirectory` is attribution data, never the kernel proof `process::cwd_of` promises, and cannot authenticate a pane or checkout caller; that API and its Windows `Unsupported` answer are unchanged.
Each observed cwd is resolved with `fs::identity::canonical` before checkout ancestry is compared, so alternate case, junction and safely shortened verbatim spellings name the same directory.
A resolution error other than `PermissionDenied`, or a retained verbatim form whose prefix cannot compare reliably with a shortened checkout path, makes the sample unavailable instead of making the checkout idle.
The reader requests only query, memory-read and exit-observation rights, checks process birth identity around the read and after a final table sample, and refuses unknown architectures, unnormalized or changed records, invalid UTF-16, unreadable live owners other than permission-denied cwd observations, and exceeded limits.
At most 4096 rows, 512 owners and two 1 MiB tables are considered, with three allocation attempts per table and a ten-second work budget checked between native calls; each owner costs six bounded memory reads, including at most two 65534-byte cwd strings, and one filesystem path resolution, aggregate cwd text in either the observations or the returned sample is capped at 1 MiB, and every handle closes within its call.
An owner whose cwd observation returns `PermissionDenied` is excluded because protected owners are outside the current user's cleanup targets; an owner absent from the final listener tables is also excluded after an unreadable cwd.
Other incomplete observations and any owner or identity change become `unavailable_reason`, so destructive checkout cleanup remains refused.
The ports reader reads on its own `BackgroundRead` thread, outside `Mutex<Runtime>`, at the existing five-second refresh, and the coordinator picks the answer up on its next wake and publishes only changed state through the existing notifier.
One read is in flight at a time and the refresh interval starts after that completed sample, so a slow read cannot trigger immediate repeated work and never delays a session publish.
The work budget is checked between bounded local kernel calls and does not claim to preempt one; there is no retained read job to cancel after return.
Cleanup reads a fresh sample on its existing worker before removal; discovery starts or stops no server.
