What has not moved yet: the `O_NONBLOCK` open that keeps a FIFO from stalling a reader (`hide-host` document, bytes, index and save, `hide-session`), the `readlinkat` in `hide-host/src/list.rs`, hided's root opens in `boundary.rs` (`openat` beneath the pinned root on Unix, a final-path check on Windows) and its Windows `ShellExecuteW` opener, and the stop signals in `hided/src/lib.rs` (tokio's per-system handlers).
What stays Unix by design until a later slice: the one-time move of a Mac's old state folder (`hided/src/state_move.rs`; no Windows build ever wrote that folder, so `Env` names none there).
hided starts on Windows, and `hided/tests/it/handshake.rs` runs there except the tests that reach a checkout through a folder link, which on Windows is a junction judged by the boundary's final-path check, and the FIFO test.
On Windows a pane bootstrap caller is bound to its pane when it descends from the pane's shell; the checkout binding needs the caller's working directory, which `cwd_of` cannot read there, so a caller outside a pane is refused `caller_unavailable`.

`path` is the sixth module and decides how a path is spelled between machines: UTF-8 with `/` between names, the spelling Git's index, LSP and VS Code's remote URIs use.
A path below a root (a checkout, a History scope) is a `RelPath`: no leading `/` and no empty, `.` or `..` name, so it can only name something under the root it is joined to; the host protocol's paths, the file index's rows, Git's changed files and every relative path in a frame are this.
An absolute path keeps its root as the owning system writes it and only its separators change: `/repo/src` on macOS and Linux, `C:/repo/src` and `//server/share/src` on Windows, with the `\\?\` prefix gone where the short spelling means the same path and the drive letter upper case, so one folder has one spelling.
On macOS and Linux both spellings are the native ones, so the wire there is what it always was; `hide-platform/tests/it/path.rs` holds it to that and states the rest on all three systems (one relative spelling for a file below a checkout, a `\\?\` root relating to its short spelling, `..`, absolute input and another drive refused with a typed `PathError`, case following the root's volume, which `relative` asks of the folder only when two spellings differ).
Only the machine that owns a path converts it, once per direction: `to_wire` and `relative` on the way out (the catalog, hided's boundary answers, the CLI's caller path, and the file index), `from_wire` and `RelPath::to_native` on the way in (`relative_path` in `hide-host/src/root.rs`, what Hide sends the engine; hided's boundary still opens the wire text as given, which is the native spelling on macOS and Linux and one Windows reads with `/` too), and `to_native` refuses a name the system cannot hold as written (a `\\` or `:` on Windows, a device name, a trailing dot) rather than reading it as something else.
Everything else relates wire spellings by their names alone (`wire_relative`, `wire_join`, `RelPath::parent`), which is correct whatever system owns them, so the core, hided and the web shell join and compare a device's paths with `/` and never ask their own filesystem or their own system's rules about another machine's path.
This differs from treating an absolute path as an opaque value only the web displays: the shell, the core's persisted state (`expanded_paths`, editor tabs, drafts, `workspace-views.json`) and the snapshot already key and join absolute paths with `/`, and one spelling keeps all of that and the Unix wire unchanged.
`to_wire_lossy` is for a path that was always sent and is shown or compared rather than read back; one with no wire spelling keeps the system's own text, which on macOS and Linux is the same.
The desktop host is the other place this computer's paths meet the page: `desktop/src/main/wirePath.ts` states the same rules in TypeScript, letter for letter, answers the folder picker and the terminal-link probe in the wire spelling and reads every path the page names (a reveal, an open, a probe) back with `from_wire`'s rules, so a native `C:\repo`, a rooted `\repo` or a drive-relative `C:repo` from the page is refused on Windows; `wirePath.test.ts` holds it to the Rust tests' expected spellings, the Windows ones on every system.
A device's node spells every absolute path it answers on the wire and reads every one it is handed with `from_wire` (`hide_host::root::wire` and `native_absolute`, which also takes a native absolute path from a core on its own machine), so a Windows device's `C:/work/app` reaches a Mac core as an absolute path: Project facts and catalog comparisons (`Call::Project`, `Call::PathFacts`), the worktree list, a registration's root, real paths, a repository's Git folders, a clone's folder, the Git watch's folders and the account's home in `Hello`.
The core relates those by names only (`is_wire_absolute`, `wire_relative`, `wire_join`, and `comparison_by_names`, which keeps a root's `/`, `C:/` as well as `/`), and the core's own engine binds a device's worktree by the names its node answered (`engine/own/worktrees.rs`), so a Windows device's files, Git and pane folders work from a Mac with no rule of the core's own system applied to them.
Letter case is the owning node's to settle: it answers the spelling its filesystem resolves (`identity::canonical`), so two spellings of one folder on a volume that ignores case reach the core as one, and the core compares names exactly.
A Project's id hashes its root's wire spelling (`hide_project::project_id`), so the device's own session reading and a core on another system derive one id; on macOS and Linux that is the text it always hashed, and a Windows Memory store keyed by an earlier build's spelling (`\\?\C:\...`) moves to the new id once, when it is opened for writing (`rekey_root_spellings` in `hide-memory/src/store.rs`).
Not spelled yet: the daemon frame's state folders, which the shell only shows.

`user_agents` answers what a core move needs from the machine taking the core, named for what the caller asks rather than for launchd: whether the system keeps login agents (`supported`), what an agent needs of the account's login (`login`: not needed, logged in or logged out), how long the machine waits on power before it sleeps on its own (`sleeps_on_power`), and the install, one-shot start, start, last exit, loaded, installed, unload, remove and forget of one agent named by its label.
launchd is the one implementation (`user_agents/launchd.rs`, with `/bin/launchctl`, the `gui/<uid>` domain, the property list under `~/Library/LaunchAgents` and `pmset`); every other system answers `Unsupported` with the reason and holds no agent, which is what makes a move to it fail its session and power checks, and a Linux or Windows implementation is added beside it without reshaping its callers.
`UserAgents::fixture` runs the stand-ins of a folder in the programs' place (`HIDE_PREFLIGHT_PROGRAMS` names one), and a fixture HOME's kit gets `UserAgents::none`, so no test reaches the account's real login agents.

`stdio` ends a command-line program quietly when the reader of its standard output leaves, as `hide agent list | head` does.
Rust turns a failed `print!` into a panic whose message ends in the operating system's error code, so `hide` installs one panic hook first thing in `main` (`exit_quietly_when_stdout_closes`) instead of every print site handling the failure: when the code is `BrokenPipe` by the standard library's own classification (`EPIPE` on Unix, a closed pipe on Windows, so no table of codes is kept) the process exits with status 141, 128 plus `SIGPIPE`, which is what a shell reports for a command a closed pipe killed, and prints nothing; any other panic, including a print that fails on a full disk, goes to the hook that was installed before.
`hide-platform/tests/it/stdio.rs` writes to a pipe whose reader is already gone on every system, and `hided/tests/it/closed_stdout.rs` shows `hide version` doing the same.

`wsl` answers which WSL distributions this Windows account has, and which of them run, without starting one (PRD wsl-device D-01, D-13).
`distributions` reads the account's own `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Lxss` registry entries: each distribution's name, id, WSL version (the VM-mode bit of `Flags`), whether it is installed (`State`), whether its first-run setup is still pending (`RunOOBE`) and which one is the default; an account with more than 64 entries is a failure rather than a shorter list.
Reading the registry starts no WSL process at all, so opening Add device never wakes WSL, and it needs no parsing of `wsl.exe --list --verbose`, whose answer is localized text; a key with no id or no valid name is not a distribution and is left out, not guessed.
`running_from` asks `wsl.exe --list --running --quiet` under a deadline, which answers from the WSL service without starting a distribution, and `decode` reads its UTF-16 or UTF-8 answer.
With `--quiet` WSL answers a list with nothing running by exiting 0 with no output (only the form without `--quiet` prints a sentence and exits -1, in WSL's `WslClient.cpp`), so a listing that times out or exits nonzero, whatever it wrote, is a failure that says nothing about which distributions run: the attempt fails and is tried again as Hide's own, which may not start the distribution, and a failing service never reads as a stopped one.
Off Windows `distributions` and `program` answer `Unsupported`, while `running_from` asks whatever program it is given, so the connector's tests run on every Unix runner with a stand-in `wsl.exe`.

`hide-platform/tests/it/ipc.rs` (both ends, a duplicate that reads while the original writes, an endpoint's kind) and `hide-holder/tests/it` (a node's connection to a pane's holder, its release and takeover) are where a change to the local stream is proved; a pane's output is the high-frequency path, and on Unix it is the same blocking `read` as before.
The daemon's start is proved by `hided/tests/it/connect_stop.rs` (`hide connect` starts hided beside the CLI in a private home and state folder, `hide status` names it and `hide stop` ends it) and `handshake.rs` (its state file and the WebSocket handshake); with `engine::contract` in `hide-core`, where the core's own engine over holders started from the built `hide-holder` opens a workspace, runs a line typed into its pane and reads it back, the Windows check runs all three on Windows, in Windows PowerShell on the pinned ConPTY runtime, and they are the proof that hided and its panes start there.

## Resident process ownership

The process that starts a resource and the lifetime owner are not always the same: the desktop host deliberately starts session services that outlive its window.
That product lifetime is the local exception to treating host quit as the end of every child; it does not exempt the service's own workers from engineering principle #14's cleanup rule or #15's caps.
The following table describes Hide's current macOS startup path, not an operator's separate service configuration or a promise of restored live processes.

| Process | Starter and lifetime owner | Stop condition | App quit | Reboot and login |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| hided | `hide connect` serializes discovery in its state folder, returns a matching healthy daemon or starts the sibling `hided`; the daemon owns the core and its background work. | `hide stop`, a stop signal or idle expiry; default idle expiry is 600 s with no clients and no pane of this machine's holders that may still run, unless daemon keep-alive or paired-phone Mobile keep-alive holds it. A bundled connect also replaces a healthy daemon of another build in that same state folder, except a core its login item runs, which it updates or refuses (Updating the core); an unbundled CLI refuses it. | Continues; no-window screen readers pause, while label work and the daemon's own lifetime policy remain active. | The old process is gone; `hide connect` starts another on demand. These discovery paths install no hided login service. |
| Device node (`hided node serve`) | The core starts one `ssh <alias>` for a consented device, whose start script execs the node; the node serves that child's stdin/stdout and, for the link's life only, its panes' bootstrap socket (`hide-host/src/panes.rs`). | EOF, unusable request framing or output failure ends admission and closes the pane socket, its streams and its folder; scoped workers finish before node exit. Core close/revoke ends the `ssh` child, which ends the node; consent revocation drains admitted work up to its bound. | A helper may continue while the surviving daemon retains its connection; window closure alone is not helper shutdown. | The process/channel is gone. A later consented connection starts another helper; this helper path installs no login service. |
| Node-role hided (M) | `hide connect` on a machine whose state folder has a placement record starts the sibling `hided`, which runs the node role; it owns its one SSH connection to C, the attach channel, the relays, the local forward and the watch thread, all ended with it. | `hide stop`, a stop signal, or idle: no screen open and no holder pane that may still run, by the same rule as the core role (`server::watch_idle`). | Continues; the host does not signal it. | Gone; the next `hide connect` starts it. Nothing is installed to start it. |
| Desk process (the chosen agent's ACP adapter) | The core's Desk worker (`hide-core/src/runtime/desk/worker.rs`) starts it tied to hided (`OwnedChild::spawn_tied`) on the operator's first message while Desk is switched on, and is its one owner; see [Desk](#desk). | `새 대화`, `다시 시작`, Desk switched off, a switch to another agent, the stream's end, the tree crossing 48 processes or 4 GiB after a turn, the session leaving its ask mode, or the worker's end; each ends the whole tree and revokes its capability. | Continues with hided; ends with it, however hided ends. | Gone; the next message starts another and loads the last session. Nothing is installed to start it. |
| Attach role (`hided attach`, C) | C's sshd starts it on the exec channel M opens; it starts no core and pipes the channel to C's running core. | Its channel ends, C's core socket closes, or 30 s pass without a byte from M. | Not the app's. | Gone with sshd; M dials again. |

The local executable authorities are `desktop/src/main/{host,spawn}.ts`, `hided/src/{cli,env,lib,server}.rs`, `hide-node/src/ssh/host.rs` and `hide-host/src/serve.rs` with `hided/src/node_cli.rs`.
Which of these a `hided` process is comes from its arguments, read once before anything else runs (`hided/src/role.rs`): no argument at all is the daemon, `core-login` alone is the daemon as a moved core's login item starts it, each other role in the table takes its own words and refuses the ones it does not know, `--version` and `--help` print and end without reading the environment, and any other argument is refused with exit 2 before an owner watch, a state folder, a lock or a log is touched, so a stray argument on a device can never start a second core there (`hided/tests/it/arguments.rs`).
The one-release kit retirement stage is `hide-kit/src/coordination_retirement.rs`; it does not start a resident service.
It reads legacy v1 and current Hide-only v2 Sasu registries without importing them, checks their retained run states, and refuses if the authoritative revision disappears after selection.
After reboot, hided and its watches start with the app; no login automatic start is added.
An app exit preserves service ownership, but a reboot ends the prior daemon, pane holders and helper processes; persisted layout/session references are not continued execution or proof that an agent completed its task.
hided's replacement checks the named daemon's health and process identity before signalling it, and leaves pane processes alone (`cli.rs::connect`, `cli.rs::stop_daemon`).
The device helper admits 4 running requests and 32 queued requests on the core connection; revocation's drain bound is 250 s, while each call has its own deadline (`hide-node/src/ssh/host.rs`, `hide-host/src/serve.rs`).
A device has one connection, the `ssh` child whose standard streams are the node's link, and the device's engine, files, Git, terminals and pages are that link's calls and streams; its pane service holds at most sixteen callers and eight streams, and at most four devices dial at once (`MAX_DIALING`, `hide-node/src/ssh/device.rs`).
Desktop CLI children, attach streams, provider children and bridge helpers have narrower owners than these session services; their cleanup and budget belong to their existing feature sections and the [resident work ledger](PERFORMANCE_TESTING.md#resident-ticks-timers-and-watchers).

## The pane holder

A pane's holder (`hide-holder`) is one small program per pane that keeps the pane's terminal: its PTY, the program in it, and the terminal parser (`hide-vt`) that reads everything the program writes whether or not anyone is connected.
It outlives the node that started it, so a node that ends and starts again finds its panes still running (PRD engine-bundle-2-pane-holder).
Every pane runs in one: this machine's node starts and adopts holders from its start, a device's node when the core that dialed it asks ([The node's holder panes](#the-nodes-holder-panes)), and the core's own engine's panes are holder panes ([The core's own engine](#the-cores-own-engine)); every package carries the holder (`hide-holder` beside `hided`, and on Windows its pinned ConPTY runtime in `holder-conpty`).

A node starts it with `start_resident` ([The platform layer](#the-platform-layer)) from a version folder, lending it one pipe on which the holder says `ready holder=<pid> program=<pid> job=<limits|none>` once its program runs and its socket listens, or `failed <reason>` before it exits; `job` is the Windows job above the node's that keeps the holder, if any, for the node to log.
A log file it cannot open, or a pipe it was lent and cannot take, fails the start rather than running a holder that cannot say what happens to it.
The holder works in its own version folder, never the folder it was started from (on Windows a working folder cannot be removed or replaced, and the app's would be held for as long as the pane lives), and runs its program in the folder the start names (`--cwd`, which is required).
A panic on any of its threads writes `holder.panicked` (after a line another thread is writing; only a thread that panicked inside its own log line writes none) and aborts the holder at once (and says `failed` if it had not said `ready`), so the pane ends as with a holder killed outright rather than running on with part of the holder gone.
It holds the program in a `Session`: on Unix the PTY child leads a session of its own, and on Windows the child starts suspended inside the holder's kill-on-close job and only then runs (`spawn_command_in_job` in `vendor/portable-pty`), so nothing the program starts escapes the job.
Terminating the pane and the program's own exit both end the whole session the same way, and the holder ends after it; on Unix the whole session is the program's session, every session a process found in it leads, and every process under one of them, so a helper the program started with `setsid` (Codex's plugin sync) ends with the pane, and so does what it starts after the program ended, found by its session's id once init took it (`hide-platform/src/process/session.rs`); an end it cannot confirm closes the connection with `tree_end_unconfirmed` and the pids left, writes `holder.tree_end_unconfirmed` to its log and exits with a failure, and is never read as a clean end.
The PTY is closed on a thread of its own while its last output is still read, since a console that closes with output nobody reads can wait for ever; a holder killed outright takes its pane with it on Windows through the job, and on Unix the kernel hangs up its session and the next reconcile ends what ignored the hangup ([Pane records and reconcile](#pane-records-and-reconcile)).
A Windows holder has no console of its own and runs the pane only on the pinned ConPTY runtime in its folder's `conpty/`, checked against its sha256 before it is loaded; a missing or changed runtime refuses the start, and there is no fallback to the system's ConPTY (`vendor/portable-pty/PATCHES.md`).

`hide-holder-protocol` is what a node and a holder say to each other over the local stream, and the only holder crate a node links.
Every message is a length-prefixed frame of at most 4 MiB and 1 KiB, the largest fragment and its header; a connection's first message, at most 4 KiB within 2 s, is either the node's hello (the versions it speaks and the capabilities it accepts), which the holder answers with the one version both speak, a generation number and the pane's program and size, an ask, or a watch (both below); a first message the holder cannot take closes that connection alone with a reason code.
One connection holds a pane at a time: an accepted hello takes it over, the connection it replaces is closed with `taken_over`, and nothing that connection sent afterwards applies; a wrong, slow or oversized opening never disturbs the connection that holds the pane.
Version 1 carries, from the node, input bytes, a paste, a pointer event, a wheel, named keys (to a holder whose welcome names the `keys` capability, `ClientMessage::Key`, D-21), one submission (to a holder whose welcome names the `submit` capability, `ClientMessage::Submit`: text parts, a gap of at most 2 s, and a submit, neither empty; it counts at least 4 KiB against the holder's 1 MiB input queue, so at most 256 wait, and the holder logs one `holder.submitted` line for each), a size, the theme, a redraw, a release (let go and leave the pane running) and a terminate (end the pane, then the holder); from the holder, screen fragments, notices and the reason for a close.
A connection's reader encodes every message that becomes the program's input (bytes, a paste, a pointer event, a wheel, named keys) under the pane's lock and queues it for the one PTY writer itself, in the order the connection sent it (a submission's gap runs on that writer, which writes the holder's answers to the program meanwhile and the connection's later input after the submit), so a key wakes no other thread on its way and nothing on the run thread holds it up (PRD engine-bundle-3-core-owns D-12a); a size, the theme, a redraw, a release and a terminate go to the run thread.
The reader holds the connection's generation from its check until the bytes are queued, and a takeover changes it only between two messages, so what a replaced connection sent before the takeover is written and what it sent after is not.
A notice says what the holder refused while the pane runs on, with a reason code, a count and bytes, and goes only to a node whose hello accepts the `notices` capability, so a node built before notices is sent none and the protocol version stays 1; a reason code a node does not know reads as unknown, never as a broken frame.
What the program writes to the clipboard (OSC 52, text of at most 192 KiB) goes as one `HolderMessage::Clipboard` to the connection that holds the pane, only the latest write while one waits, and only to a node whose hello accepts the `clipboard` capability; with no such connection the write is dropped and logged `holder.clipboard_dropped`, so a connection that takes the pane later, a redraw or a reattach never gets an older copy (with-hide/hide-private#659).
The node hands it to its output sink as `OutputSink::clipboard`, never as the pane's output: a device sends it up its link as `TerminalUp::Clipboard` (node protocol 79) ahead of its panes' output and only while the core draws them, the core takes it only for a pane it attached there, the core's relay passes it to a linked node's screens for a pane that node draws, and the hub hands it to the windows connected at that moment as a `clipboard` frame kept in no ring, which only the window in front writes to its clipboard, and only for a pane it shows (`terminalShown`).
Each of those steps keeps, while it cannot send yet, the latest copy of each pane in the order written (`hide_node::terminal::copies::WaitingCopies`, at most 8 panes, the oldest dropped and logged), so a hidden pane's copy never pushes out the one the operator made on screen.
Input waits for the PTY behind a 1 MiB queue; past it the connection is closed (`input_queue_full`) and the pane runs on, and at most eight openings read their first message at once, a ninth being closed with `opening_full`.
Input or a size the PTY refuses, or a size the parser refuses, closes the connection that sent it (`input_failed`, `resize_failed`, with the error) and the pane runs on; the rest of that connection's input is dropped, and the next connection's is tried again.
Every connection the holder does not take is closed with a reason, including one that opens while the pane ends, which is told the reason the pane ended.

The screen goes out as display-only fragments (`screen`, the one capability a holder sends), drawn from the parsed terminal, never the program's own bytes (PRD engine-bundle-2-pane-holder D-7).
A full fragment starts an epoch, numbered across the holder's life, at sequence 0, and the deltas after it count up in the same epoch; each carries the size it was drawn at.
A full one first puts the receiver back to a known display (the normal screen, a soft reset, autowrap and reverse video off, a clear), so whatever the receiver drew before is gone, and no fragment turns on an input mode or asks the receiver anything, so a terminal that draws one answers nothing; the encoder is Herdr v0.9.5's `render_ansi.rs`, changed for this (`hide-holder/src/encode.rs`).
Hidden text is sent as hidden (SGR 8), not drawn in the background color, which shows it on the receiver's default background.
Since every cell is placed with autowrap off, a receiver cannot tell a row the program's text ran past from one that filled it and ended with a line break, so a full fragment, and a delta whose rows wrap differently from the last sent, also says which rows soft-wrap, as the parser marks them, in a private OSC (`ESC ] 7719 ; <cols> ; <rows> ; <hex> ESC \`, `WRAP_OSC` in `hide-holder/src/encode.rs`); the web shell reads it for terminal links (`web/src/terminalWrap.ts`).
A Windows holder writes none (`Capture::without_wraps`): ConPTY draws the console's screen again and places a wrapped line's rows itself, so it does not reliably give the parser a soft wrap (CI's Windows holder saw none for a 100-character line at 80 columns), and saying none keeps the receiver's last-column rule rather than reading every row as ended.
The same fragments say, on every system and in the same form, which rows end with a hyperlink the next row does not carry on (`ESC ] 7720 ; <cols> ; <rows> ; <hex> ESC \`, `LINK_END_OSC`, `Frame::link_ends` in `hide-holder/src/screen.rs`): a row whose last written cell carries a link and whose next row's first non-blank cell carries another or none.
An agent's TUI breaks its long lines with line breaks, so no row of its soft-wraps and a soft wrap cannot tell a URL it broke from one that filled its row; an agent that marks its links puts the whole address on every piece, so the link end tells them apart, and the shell reads it in an agent's pane, where it ignores the line breaks (hide-private issue 591).
A pane says it shows links (`FORCE_HYPERLINK=1`, below), so Claude Code marks its URLs; Codex marks them always.
They travel inside the screen bytes, so neither the protocol nor the snapshot wire changes: a receiver that does not know them drops them, a shell drawing an older holder's fragments hears none and keeps its last-column rule, and a program cannot write them to the receiver, since fragments are drawn from the parsed cells, never the program's bytes.
The screen is pulled, not pushed: the PTY reader only marks it changed, and the connection's own writer draws it as it is when the connection can take a write, at most once per 16 ms, so a slow node gets fewer, larger fragments and never a queue, and with no connection nothing is drawn.
The first change after input reaches the program is the one exception: it is drawn at once rather than after the 16 ms, so a key's echo never waits on the fragment before it, at the cost of at most one fragment more per input message; output the program makes on its own stays paced.
A stream paced 16 ms after its last render whatever the change made the next key's echo wait whenever the round trip from one echo to the next key took less than 16 ms, which the node's shorter path made common.
The writer is woken for that change even while it waits out the interval.
The reader wakes the writer only when the writer waits for a change, not while it waits out the 16 ms: a wake per read cost a 100 MB flood about 100,000 wakes and put the holder's CPU above the Herdr server's.
An allocator keeps what a flood's work freed, about 5 MB more than an idle holder on macOS, so once a connection's screen has been still for a second after a fragment its writer gives those pages back (`hide_platform::memory::return_freed`), once, and then waits with no bound until the next change; an idle holder therefore wakes once after its last fragment and never periodically.
The writer that sent a flood's fragments is the one whose return gives most back: on macOS a debug holder released right after a flood read 7.0 MiB after the next connection's return against 5.5 MiB after the flooding connection's own; a holder flooded with no connection keeps less to give (5.2 MiB after 300 MB, release).
A connection's first return is logged (`holder.memory_returned`), and so is one after 1 MiB of the program's output, which is what the tests wait on; the others are not, so a pane that redraws a line every second or two does not fill its log.
A connection is sent a full fragment when it takes the pane over, after a resize and when it asks for a redraw, which is how a receiver that lost fragments, or fell behind, is put right.
While the program holds its output (synchronized output, mode 2026) the writer waits, up to one second from the latest start of the hold, which each `?2026h` restarts as in Ghostty and kitty, so a half-drawn screen is not sent.
A full screen larger than one fragment is split between rows into several, the first full and the rest deltas of its epoch; a row is bounded well below a fragment (64 bytes of text and a 2 KiB link per cell, 1024 columns), so a screen is never refused: closing a connection for its size would recur on every reattach to the same screen.

Input bytes go to the program as they came, already encoded by the node.
A paste, a pointer event and a wheel are sent as what they mean and encoded at the moment they reach the holder, for the modes the program has on then: a paste in bracketed paste mode or with its line breaks made carriage returns, a pointer event in the program's mouse protocol or dropped when it tracks none, and a wheel as the program's mouse report, as arrow keys on the alternate screen with mode 1007, or as a scroll of the holder's own view; the holder never guesses a paste from bytes.
Input moves a scrolled view back to the bottom.
Input and the answers to the program's questions reach the PTY through one writer, in the order they came.

The holder answers the program's questions whether or not a node is connected, each once, in the order asked; who answers what is fixed in a table in `hide-holder/src/answers.rs`, split between libghostty and the holder so nothing is answered twice.
Color questions are answered from the theme the node gives at the holder's start (`--theme`, part of the pane start a node adapter makes, so the program's first question is answered before any node connects), then from each change a connection sends; a color the program set itself wins over the theme until it resets it, and a reset returns to the theme.
A color no theme names, as in a start without one, is answered with libghostty's default, so a program never waits out its own timeout for an answer.
The kitty keyboard query (`CSI ? u`) is not answered: this path sends no kitty-encoded keys, so the program keeps to legacy keys (D-9).
The holder never knows the pixel size of the screen that draws the pane, so it gives every cell a stand-in of 10 by 20 pixels (`CELL_PIXELS` in `hide-holder/src/pane.rs`): the text area and cell pixel questions (XTWINOPS 14t, 16t) are answered with it, and pointer events in pixels (mode 1016) are told in it, so a program converting one to the other lands on the right cell; size reports (mode 2048) stay unsent.
The device attributes and XTGETTCAP advertise only what this path carries.
Answers wait for the PTY behind a 64 KiB queue; past it the answers of one parse (one read of the PTY, a resize or a theme) are refused whole, as are those of every parse after it until the program has taken what waits, and the program's output goes on being read: the first refusal of such a run is logged with its reason (`holder.answers_refused`, `answer_queue_full`) and sent as a notice, and its end with how many answers and bytes were refused (`holder.answers_resumed`).
A node logs each notice it is sent with the pane's id (`pane_holder.answers_refused`, `pane_holder.answers_resumed`) and its session goes on; nothing reaches the screen, since the operator cannot act on it.

An ask is a connection's first message in place of a hello, answered on that connection and closed, without taking the pane over or moving the screen's scroll position (D-11, D-18), except a scroll to.
A read gives the last 1 to 2000 rows as text, soft wraps joined, cut from the oldest side to 1 MiB and marked truncated when rows were left out.
A process list gives the shell's pid and the foreground process group with up to 256 members and their names; on Windows `hide_platform::process::console_foreground` proves shell readiness from the shell's live children, excluding console hosts and validating process birth times, and otherwise names the oldest child, following only a single-child cmd or PowerShell wrapper chain.
A process table or child identity that cannot be read is unknown with the reason, never proof of an idle shell.
A styled read gives the rows the screen shows now, wherever a connection scrolled it, or the last 1 to 2000 rows a read reads, as the terminal drew them with soft wraps kept, each with its styling as escape sequences, cut from the oldest side to 1 MiB at a row's start so no sequence is cut in two.
A holder built before styled reads closes such an ask as a first message it does not know (`hello_invalid`), which the node answers `unsupported_holder`.
A visible read gives the rows the screen shows now, wherever a connection scrolled it, as text with soft wraps joined.
A scroll ask gives where the screen is in its scrollback, in rows above the bottom and the most it can be; a scroll to moves the screen to a number of rows above the bottom, past the top clamped to it, answers the same, and sends the connection that holds the pane the moved screen, as any client may move a pane's viewport.
A holder built before visible reads or scroll asks closes them `hello_invalid` too, which the node answers `unsupported_holder`; the own engine then reports no scroll for the pane, so ⌘F there opens the agent's own search.
An ask out of its bounds is closed with `ask_invalid`, and one the holder could not answer with `ask_failed`.
The holder keeps a JSON-lines log beside its socket (`holder.started`, `holder.connected`, `holder.taken_over`, `holder.connection_refused`, `holder.ending`, `holder.ended`, which says whether the holder exits with a failure, and the failures), naming the pane and the holder's pid and never what the program wrote, and sets it aside past 1 MiB; a line it cannot write is counted and the next line it writes is preceded by `holder.log_lines_dropped`.

A watch is a connection's first message in place of a hello that follows the pane's facts and takes nothing over (PRD engine-bundle-3-core-owns D-18, D-21); its messages are kinds of their own behind that opening, so the protocol version stays 1.
A watch that accepts the `facts` capability is answered with the version both speak and the version of the holder's screen rule evaluator (`hide_screen_rules::ENGINE_VERSION`), and is then sent the pane's facts, whole each time any of them changed: the folder the shell last reported (OSC 7, or OSC 9;9 from PowerShell; a whole path only, at most 4 KiB), the terminal title (OSC 0 or 2, at most 256 characters), the bells and the prompt marks (OSC 133;A) since the holder started, whether bracketed paste is on, the program in the terminal's foreground other than the pane's own (its pid, its name, and up to 64 arguments in 8 KiB), and what the pane's screen rules read on its screen.
A watch that also accepts `line_editing` is told in every facts frame whether the terminal edits lines, reads keys, or cannot say, its canonical mode as the program set it, read from the master the holder keeps by the platform layer, which reads a process's terminal the same way (`hide_platform::process::master_line_input`, `line_input`); the byte sits after the screen and before the package, in a frame of a watch that agreed it and in no other, so a node built before it is sent the frame it reads and a node reading a holder built before it hears nothing of it (`read_watch_holder`).
Windows' pseudoconsole keeps its program's console input mode (`ENABLE_LINE_INPUT`) inside the console host, which answers only a process attached to that console, and a process attached to a console is ended by the console's close whatever its handler answers, so the holder never attaches itself: it starts itself again as a helper (`hide-holder --console-input <shell pid>`, an `OwnedChild` in a kill-on-close job) that attaches to the console the pane's shell runs in, ignores interrupts and answers one byte per ask over its standard streams (`hide_platform::process::console_input`, `hide-holder/src/console_input.rs`).
The helper is started the first time the writer reads a program at least 100 ms after the program took the pane's foreground, on a recheck or, for a program that keeps writing and so is never rechecked, on the facts, so a short command never starts one; after that first ask it is asked on rechecks only, one byte each way every 100 ms, the facts between them carry the last answer, and before the first ask a program reads as editing lines, the mode a console starts every program in (`ENABLE_LINE_INPUT`), so an agent that took the foreground past its start's settle is not typed into before the console was asked.
It lives until the console first reads keys under the program, for at most `LINE_EDITING_RECHECK_FOR`, one per pane; the recheck that starts it waits up to 2 s for it to say it attached, and each ask waits up to 500 ms, which the facts the writer sends wait on too.
A program's wait starts at most two helpers; past that, or when one cannot start, the holder says it cannot for that program from then on and logs `holder.console_input_unread` with the reason; a program still editing lines when the wait passes its bound, on any read, is said not known from then on too, without a log line, since every long command (a build) edits lines that long.
A program that once read keys is read so until another takes the foreground.
A holder built before watches closes the opening as a first message it does not know (`hello_invalid`).
The node gives a watch one rule set at a time, the JSON of a `hide_screen_rules::Manifest` of at most 1 MiB, or none; the watch's reader compiles it, and a set that cannot be read or compiled reads `unknown` with the first line of why.
The screen is read as its last rows, as many as it has, as text, with the title and the progress (OSC 9) the program last sent; the highest-priority rule that matches gives the state and the rule's id, a rule that says the screen proves nothing keeps the state before it, and no match reads `unknown`.
A new rule set starts afresh, and a change from one set to another or to none drops the title and progress the rules read.
There is no pending-idle hold (a short wait before an idle read is believed): a working agent's title spinner keeps its state between redraws, which `hide-holder/src/watch.rs`'s claude-code test reads chunk by chunk across every spinner frame.
The foreground program is the leader of the terminal's foreground group, or its first member once the leader has ended, when the group is not the pane's own program's; it is named by its first argument's file name without `.exe`, or for node, bun, deno and python by the script it runs without its folder or extension (`hide-holder/src/foreground.rs`, derived from Herdr v0.9.5's `src/detect/mod.rs`).
Its arguments are read once per process (`hide_platform::process::argv_of`), which is known again by its pid and the system's name for it, a name an `exec` changes; Windows uses the same console-child proof as the process list and reads arguments through the bounded native process query.
A failed argument read logs `holder.foreground_arguments_unreadable` with the pid and error kind, never the arguments, and retains the native process name and busy state.
For a runtime's script on every system, `hide_platform::process::package_of_script` extracts the nearest npm package from its path without reading files, so a program started as `node …/node_modules/<package>/dist/cli.js` is known by its package as one an npm launcher starts on Windows is; the holder preserves the executable or script name and reports the package separately.
The core matches the name first, then the definition’s exact `packages` entries.
A watch negotiates `program_package` before the holder appends this optional facts field, so older watchers receive the original frame and new watchers still read older holders; the node link carries it as an optional field.
Packages that are not declared remain unknown, including nested dependencies; the holder carries no agent table.
The facts are pulled as the screen is: the PTY reader, a resize and a rule set mark them changed, the watch's writer reads them at most once per 16 ms and sends them only when they differ from the last it sent, and nothing else wakes it but one bounded case, so an idle pane's watch sends nothing and the holder still never wakes on its own.
A foreground the system could not say (the terminal's group, the members of a group whose leader has ended, or its first member's name unread; on Windows a process table it could not read) is never sent as the pane's own program holding the terminal: a watch that accepts `foreground_unread` is told so in every facts frame, after the line editing byte, and the holder logs `holder.foreground_unread` with the reason once per spell; a node built before it is sent no foreground, as before.
A program turns line editing off without writing anything, so while a program other than the pane's own holds the terminal with line editing on, the writer asks the terminal again every 100 ms (`LINE_EDITING_RECHECK`) for at most 120 s from when that program took it (`LINE_EDITING_RECHECK_FOR`, the deadline of an agent's start), and reads the facts again only when the answer moved; a shell at its prompt and a program that reads keys are never asked on a timer.
The first facts on a watch, and the facts after each rule set it is given, are sent whatever they are, so a node that knows nothing yet, or that changed which set fits, hears the pane at once.
A holder keeps one watch: a newer one replaces it and the older is closed `taken_over`, a late rule set from the older changes nothing, and the rules stay with the pane until the newer watch gives its own.
The OSC reader is Herdr v0.9.5's `OscStreamCollector` and the folder report's parser its `parse_reported_cwd` (`hide-holder/src/osc.rs`); the parser's own reports of the folder, the bells and the clipboard writes are taken after each read, so none of them grows with the program's output.

A holder never runs from the app, which an update replaces while panes run: each build's holder, and on Windows the ConPTY runtime beside it, is copied once into a folder of its own under `~/.hide/holders`, named `v<protocol version>-<content hash>` (`hide_kit::holders`, paths in `hide_kit::layout`), apart from the runtime copies under `~/.hide/runtime`.
A folder is made in a staging folder and renamed into place whole with a marker naming it, so a folder by that name is complete or absent.
Preparing a folder, using it and cleaning up never overlap, by one lock file in the root: `prepare` holds it shared until the caller's holder runs from the folder, and `prune` holds it exclusively.
`prune` removes only what it has claimed by renaming it and then found unused: on Windows no file in it may be held by a process (a holder, an OpenConsole its ConPTY runtime started, or a holder too old for this build to speak to), and a folder a running program keeps from being renamed is in use; on macOS and Linux no process may run its holder.
A claimed folder found in use gets its name back, one that cannot be judged is kept, and more than eight folders left after a prune is reported.
A node prunes once each time it starts, after `Holders::recover` (`Holders::prune_folders`), keeping its own build's folder: the reconcile first settles the holders that died, so their folders go in the same start; it logs `pane_holder.folders_pruned` naming the folders it removed and the ones kept in use, with how many failed, `pane_holder.folder_remove_failed` for each folder it could not judge or remove, `pane_holder.folders_over_cap` past eight, and `pane_holder.folders_busy` when starts held the lock for the whole wait.

A pane keeps the folder it started from until it ends, so after an update the panes that ran on keep the earlier build's holder, and the fixes in it never reach them; this Mac and every device alike (with-hide/hide-private#646).
An agent that sleeps in its pane (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) leaves only its shell there, so its wake ([Agent sleep](#agent-sleep)) is when the holder is renewed: the wake first asks the pane's node to renew it (`Engine::renew_holder`, `holders::PaneCall::Renew`, protocol 83), and the node of the pane's machine decides, so a device's node compares with its own build.
A restore's resume renews nothing: a pane it resumes keeps its holder until its agent next sleeps and wakes.
While the pane's agent is asleep the pane takes only the sleep's own input, the keys that end the agent and the wake's start line (`Typist::Sleeper`, `PaneCall::SleeperInput`): the operator's keys are dropped, the core's other input is refused with `pane_asleep`, and the core's input still waiting for the writer when the pane went to sleep is cancelled to its caller, so nothing but the wake reaches a shell the renewal may end.
The node renews a pane whose record names a version folder other than its own build's (`Panes::folder_of`; the name is a content hash, so the test is "another build", never "older").
Whether the earlier holder may be ended is judged once, in `Holders::endable`, in this order: the record names a running holder and the shell it started, this build's folder is ready and held, the pane is asleep, every write the node handed the holder before is written (`terminal::Service::writes_settled`, within 5 s), those of a session released or replaced before included, whose writer writes what it was handed until it ends.
What the pane's input to its holder has come to is one value the node keeps per pane apart from its sessions (`terminal::HolderInput`): the writers still writing, eight at most, and whether a write to this holder ever failed, which a release, an attach of the pane or another, or a forget does not clear; only a new holder clears it (`Service::holder_replaced`, which in the same step attaches the pane again under a new generation, so nothing of the earlier holder is counted against the new one; a pane no screen holds is released instead, and its next input attaches it to the new holder for that input alone), or the holder's confirmed end (`Service::holder_gone`); a writer still running at the bound, or a failure, keeps the pane, and the shell runs alone (`hide_platform::process::runs_alone`).
Running alone is judged by exactly what the holder's end ends, against the holder and shell the record names by pid and start time: on Unix every process of the terminal session the shell leads, a background job and one left there by a parent that exited included; on Windows every member of the kill-on-close job the holder holds, found by duplicating the holder's job handle (`NtQueryInformationProcess` with `ProcessHandleInformation`), with the console host the job starts not counted.
Only then does the node end the earlier holder as a close does and start the pane again under the same id, its reservation naming the earlier incarnation (`Holders::renew`), so the pane's letters, parent and children, watch, tab and launch choice stay with the id and the record never reads the pane as closed or started twice; its screen attaches again at the size the core named, and its facts watch starts again under a generation no earlier watch had, so the earlier watch's late end changes nothing.
A renewal and a close of the same pane take the pane's turn (`holder/turns.rs`) and keep it until their last effect is done, in the order they asked, eight waiting at most, a renewal waiting 45 s and a close 60 s; so a close during a renewal ends the holder the renewal left, and a renewal after a close finds the pane closed.
What the renewal did is one value the core reads whole.
`current`, `renewed`, or `kept` with why are panes the holder the record names runs: `kept` means that holder was not touched (`shell_unknown`, `pane_awake`, `holder_folder_unread`, `holder_folder_unprepared`, `pane_input_unsettled`, `pane_busy`, `start_unprepared`, `holder_not_ended` for a close that never took the pane, `pane_runs_program`, or `holder_renewal_unsupported` from a node that cannot renew), and the wake goes on in it.
A refusal resumes nothing: `holder_renewal_pane_closed` when the pane's record is gone or ended, `holder_renewal_busy` when the turn did not come, `holder_renewal_lost` when the earlier holder ended and the new one did not start, `holder_renewal_unsettled` when the record could not be read, the earlier holder's close did not finish or the new start may have left something (the record stays for the next reconcile), and a device's answer that never came; the wake fails with `agent_wake.not_resumed`, and only a lost or unsettled pane is marked as one a restore could not start, which offers to close it.
The engine logs `engine.holder_renewed`, `engine.holder_current`, `engine.holder_kept` or `engine.holder_renewal_refused`, and the node `pane_holder.renewed`, `pane_holder.renewal_current`, `pane_holder.renewal_kept` or `pane_holder.renewal_refused` with its outcome.
A renewed shell has just started, so the wake waits for its first prompt as a start into a new tab does.
A sleep is not begun while a reopen of the pane runs, and a reopen refuses an asleep pane, so the two never change one pane's holder together.
A shell pane, an agent still at work, and an agent whose operator turned sleep off are never renewed: their holder takes the new build when the pane closes or the machine restarts, since ending it would end what runs there; an agent that closes its pane to sleep (Grok, OpenCode, Pi, omp) wakes in a new pane, which starts from the current folder already.

What the renewal does not cover, accepted for with-hide/hide-private#646:

- A daemon killed between the earlier holder's end and the new reservation finds the pane ended `terminated` and closes it, as a pane closed at that moment would be; no holder is left behind and the agent's session files stay, and no time bound is claimed for that window.
- A shell timer (a `TMOUT`, a prompt hook started by a timer) that starts a process after the shell was judged alone is ended with the earlier holder.
- Bytes the node handed the holder before the writes settled may still sit in the holder's own queue, a submit's delayed Enter or the shell's unread input when the holder ends; telling the node what the holder has written through is with-hide/hide-private#700.

### Pane records and reconcile

A holder outlives its node, so what owns it is its record, not the node (PRD engine-bundle-2-pane-holder D-13, D-14, D-17).
Each pane of a state folder has one, `<state>/holders/records/<pane>.json` (`hide_kit::layout::pane_record`), in a versioned format (`hide_holder_protocol::record`, format 2, at most 64 KiB): the pane id, the state folder it belongs to (the folder's own file identity, which a rename keeps and a copy does not), the start's incarnation, the holder's and the program's pid with the start time each had, the protocol and version folder it runs, the digest of its command, the boot it started in, its phase (`reserved`, `preparing`, `running`, `closing`, `ended`) and, once ended, why, with the exit code and any pids left.
Format 1 running records remain readable and retain their format when updated.
Format 2 can also carry the reservation's connection owner, logical request number, original request digest and recovery folder, without persisting its command or environment; `reserved` requires this metadata and names no process.
The node exposes reserve, exact-incarnation start and cancel as typed pane calls, with the original request digest computed before shell integration changes its command.
Only the worker changing that reservation from `reserved` to `preparing` expands the shell and starts its holder; an old incarnation or a cancelled request is refused before expansion.
Cancel can precede reserve and writes a terminal record for that same intent, so a delayed reserve cannot recreate it.
Each connection issues increasing logical creation numbers, distinct from transport call IDs, and uses the same number for reserve, start and cancel.
Holder renewal carries a number from that same issuer (`PaneCall::Renew`, protocol 93), admitted before any close or replacement and used through the replacement's reserve and start; the node never issues an independent number behind the core's counter.
The core retires a renewal after a definite answer, including `current` and `kept`; an unknown answer or unsettled replacement retains its pending number until owner turnover, as a node-issued replacement did.
Its owner keeps the highest observed number and at most 128 unresolved entries, including gaps for issued calls not yet received; a jump that would exceed the bound or overflow is refused before advancing the window.
A completed number is absence below that high-water mark, so a late reserve, start or cancel cannot return even after its ended record is pruned.
Retirement closes admission under the same owner mutex as worker admission and completes only after every admitted worker has finished its mutation and cleanup; no I/O holds that mutex.
Unresolved ended reservations remain pinned in the record cap, while confirmed retirement releases them on the same owner, allowing more than 128 cumulative creations without growing a history.
A definitely unsent creation also retires its issued number; losing the retirement answer retains its core slot until the same retirement is confirmed.
The core admits eight active and eight waiting creation intents before placement or durable reservation, and retains the original placement and request through unknown reserve/start/cancel outcomes.
Only confirmed durable reservation permits publication; authority and parent existence are checked again after that answer, and failed publication cancels the exact intent.
One intent state serializes the cancellation claim with topology publication, so a cancellation selected before publication cannot leave a visible cancelled pane.
Placement starts, completion and withdrawal belong to that same intent; callbacks run outside all engine locks, and cancellation waits for an in-flight callback before withdrawing exactly the successful placements and retiring the request.
A placement still in flight at the existing start bound leaves cancellation unanswered and retains its admission until a later resolution observes actual cleanup.
Closing selects and marks its panes in one topology hold before node I/O; a late split into a closing pane or a new tab in a wholly closing workspace is refused, while a pane published before selection is included in a tab or workspace close.
The in-memory closing mark remains after an unresolved close, so another close resolves the original scope instead of admitting new children behind it.
Cancellation and a late successful start both finish terminal-service cleanup before their request guards leave.
A later close of a started pane uses record ownership and incarnation checks, without reopening its retired creation request.
A new owner reports interrupted reservations with their original pane ID, incarnation and recovery folder; legacy ended records report the incarnation but need a saved layout for the folder.
`hide_kit::panes::Panes` is the node's side of it, a library hide-node calls; its diagnostics (`pane_holder.*`, naming the pane, the incarnation and the holder's pid, never the pane's output) go to the sink the caller gives.

A connection acquires the state folder's exclusive `records/.owner-lock` through the platform file-lock implementation before crash repair or fresh reconciliation.
Its `PaneSlot` and each admitted node request share the bound holder adapter, which retains that lock through the request's last mutation and cleanup, even when its caller times out or disconnects.
Closing the connection permanently closes admission and releases only its own reference; queued requests cannot reactivate it, and an acquisition finishing after close cannot install a new owner.
A new connection cannot reconcile or allocate pane IDs until every previous worker has finished and it acquires this same lock; failure to acquire is an unresolved outcome, never evidence that the old work ended.
The stable lock file is never removed or replaced, and node start, close, forget and reconcile require the acquired ownership context.
Holder processes retain their separate exact-incarnation record claim and do not inherit connection ownership.
The pure liveness query counts records without pruning them.
A failed or incomplete record scan refuses connection ownership; a completed scan with individual unreadable records retains the bound owner and usable panes.
Those unreadable IDs remain present, count against the record cap and refuse their own starts without changing their bytes.

Every change of a record, a start's reservation, the count against the cap and a removal happen under one lock file, `records/.lock`, and nothing that waits on another process runs under it: a holder starts, a tree ends and a connection opens outside it, and what they found is written under it after a fresh read that shows the record has not moved.
A start is keyed by its pane id and original request digest: concurrent claims create one holder, a running match answers that holder, and a still-preparing match reports an unresolved start.
An ended reservation refuses the original start; a deliberate replacement names its previous incarnation and starts only once the earlier processes are confirmed gone.
Legacy records retain their prior adoption and restart path until replaced by a format 2 reservation.
Cancellation writes its intent under the same record lock that matches the request, before any process cleanup.
The holder's final write and the node's lost-holder settlement both preserve that decision; confirmed cleanup ends as terminated, while unconfirmed leftovers remain closing and cancellation reports an unresolved outcome.
A cancelled holder's final write still leaves its record closing, because it cannot prove its own exit while writing; only the node's cleanup followed by an exact-record compare and replace completes it.
A holder that already wrote ended but still runs follows this same closing path, including when cleanup refuses or the connection disappears before it runs.
While something of the earlier start runs on, its holder by pid and start time or on Unix a member of its program's session (elsewhere a pid its end says was left), the start is refused with those pids.
A record of another state folder or one that cannot be read refuses the start.
A state folder keeps at most 128 holders: every record not ended counts, and so does one that cannot be read, since it may name a holder; the 129th start is refused `holder_cap` with a `pane_holder.start_refused` line, however many ask at once.
Closing a pane whose start has not written its holder in yet writes it `closing`, which stops that start, and answers that the pane is still starting.
Ended records stay so the next node can say why a pane ended, at most 128 of them, the oldest removed first with its log, except one whose holder still runs or whose pane left processes running (its program's session on Unix, and every live pid its end names even when that session was read), which is kept and logged (`pane_holder.ended_kept`); a forget refuses such a record the same way.
A restart that names the incarnation it replaces and finds that record gone therefore starts the pane under a new incarnation and logs it (`pane_holder.replaced_record_missing`): closing a restore's finished panes writes them newer ends, so the cap can drop an interrupted record before its restart reaches it, and nothing of the dropped one runs.
The incarnation comes from a counter of its own (`records/next`), so a pane started again never reuses an earlier start's number; a process moves the counter on 64 at a time and gives those numbers out itself, so the counter is written once in 64 starts.
A record and the counter are replaced whole with `write_file`'s `WriteOptions::UntilReboot` (see the platform layer): on macOS they flush to the device but not past its cache, since their holders cannot outlive a reboot, and a full device flush per write cost a restore of 66 panes about a second.
What a power loss may leave instead, an empty, cut-off or older file, never stops the panes starting again: a node that opens the folder removes every record that cannot be parsed and was last written before this boot began (`process::boot_time`; `pane_holder.record_removed`), the reconcile ends an older readable one as of an earlier boot, and a counter that cannot be read or is behind an incarnation a record holds is moved past all of them (`pane_holder.incarnations_mended`); a record damaged in this boot, or of a format this build does not know, is left and reported as before, since its holder may run (`Panes::mend_after_a_crash`, `records_a_power_loss_left_empty_cut_off_or_old_do_not_stop_the_panes_starting`).
A start's version folder name is the hash of the holder's bytes, taken again only when one of its files changed (identity, length or time), so a start does not read and hash the holder each time; a folder is still made only under the name its bytes give.
Each start's `pane_holder.started` line gives when it found its folder, reserved its record, started the holder and read its `ready` (`prepared_ms`, `reserved_ms`, `spawned_ms`, `ready_ms`, `took_ms`), and the holder's `holder.started` line when it wrote itself in, listened, started the program and wrote `running` (`claimed_ms`, `listening_ms`, `spawned_ms`, `running_ms`), so a slow start says where its time went.

The start writes the record `preparing` and starts the holder with the record's path, the lock's and the incarnation (`--record`, `--record-lock`, `--incarnation`); the holder writes itself in before it starts the program, opens its parser and listens at its socket, then starts the program and writes the program and `running` in one write, and only while the record still reserves its start, so a holder whose start was given up on, or one of an earlier start of the pane, never writes over it.
A holder whose own start fails after it wrote itself in records `start_failed` with the reason.
A start whose holder said `failed`, ended without a word (its report pipe closed with no line, logged as that rather than as silence), or said nothing within 10 s reads the record again under the lock: a holder that wrote itself `running` meanwhile (a late `ready`) is taken as started; a reservation whose holder is gone is removed; one whose holder still runs is ended `start_unconfirmed` and that holder ended whole outside the lock.
When the pane ends, by a terminate or by its program's exit with no node connected, the holder writes why (`terminated`, `program_exited` with the exit code, `tree_end_unconfirmed` with the pids left, `holder_failed`) before it exits.
It waits at most 5 s for the lock; an end it cannot write is logged for a person reading the log (`holder.record_unwritten`, with the reason, the incarnation, exit code and pids left), and the next reconcile settles the pane as one whose holder was lost.

A node reconciles when it starts, judging up to eight panes at once (a worker that cannot be started is logged and its share left to the others) and taking up none after 30 s (`RECONCILE_BUDGET`): a judgment under way runs to its own bound, the longest a close's at about 42 s, and what was not taken up is answered pending for the next reconcile, which the node asks for until `Reconciled::is_complete`.
On this Mac (load average 8 to 14) 128 panes whose holders were killed, with trees that ignore the hangup, were settled in 8.8 s.
A holder killed while the daemon runs is settled by that same start, which the daemon asks for rather than settling the pane a second way: an attach that cannot connect asks `Panes::holder_gone`, which reads and changes nothing and answers `true` only for a `running` record of this folder whose holder is confirmed gone (`Identity::gone`: no process under its pid, or one that started at another time; a process table that cannot be read, or a holder that is merely slow or busy, answers `false` and the attach is tried again).
The daemon then starts `hide restart --daemon <pid> --started <start>` as a resident child (`holder_restart`, logged as `daemon.restart_for_lost_holder`), naming itself by pid and start time, so the forced end `hide restart` makes of a daemon that does not stop in time never reaches it; the command ends that daemon and starts the next beside itself while the holders keep running, all under `connect.lock`, and does nothing when that daemon was stopped or replaced since the request, so a successor another `hide connect` started meanwhile is never ended.
A request is admitted at most once in ten minutes across restarts, the check and the record of it, written before the helper starts and withdrawn if the start fails, under one lock of the state folder (`holder-restart.lock`, `holder-restart`), so the panes one loss takes at once ask once; a pane lost while a request is suppressed stays unreachable until the next restart or start.
The desktop host follows the new daemon as it follows any other (`daemon.lost`, then `daemon.found`).

- A record whose holder runs, pid and start time both, is adopted; a `closing` one is asked to end again, ended by its pids when nothing answers for it at its socket (on Unix its own session and the session each of its children leads, found before the holder ends so they are not lost to reparenting, and on Windows its tree, whose job ends the rest), and stays `closing` for the next reconcile while it refuses or runs on past its bound.
- A record whose holder is gone is ended `holder_lost`; on Unix what the program's session left, found by the program's recorded pid and start time (`Session::left_by`), is ended first, and its socket and lock file are removed (the lock waited out for up to 2 s, for Windows). Leftovers it cannot end keep the record `closing` with their pids for the next reconcile.
- A `preparing` record with no holder written in is a start under way for 10 s, then ended `start_interrupted`.
- A record ended `start_unconfirmed` whose holder still runs in this boot, by pid and start time, has that holder ended whole.
- A record from another boot is ended `machine_restarted` and nothing it names is touched, whichever state folder it names as its owner: the owner is the folder's volume and number, and macOS may number a volume anew at each boot, so the record is taken as this folder's (an ended one keeps its end and takes the new owner).
- A record that cannot be read, of a format this build does not know, of another state folder in this boot, or of a protocol older than this build speaks to is left as it is and reported, never taken for no record.

The records are the only way to a holder: a node starts one only with its record's path, the holder writes itself into that record under the lock before it starts its program, and a record is removed only once nothing it names runs, so every holder a node started is named by a record.
The reconcile therefore reads the records and nothing else; a holder whose record a person deleted by hand runs on until its program ends, as a tmux session does once its socket is deleted, and the next start of its pane binds over its socket.
A terminate whose connection ends with no `Closed` (a holder closes a connection whose output it could not hand over, and a terminate it had not read goes with it) is sent again on a new connection while the holder runs, until the close's 20 s bound (`pane_holder.terminate_again`).

A pid reused within one boot is told apart by the start time recorded with it, and a session id is not reused while a member of the session lives.
What remains is a process whose pid and start time both repeat, which the clocks make negligible within one boot (`start_time` in [The platform layer](#the-platform-layer)), and on Unix a program the holder had started but not yet written in when it was killed, which the kernel's hangup ends unless it ignores it.

### The node's holder panes

`hide-node/src/terminal/holder.rs` is the node's side of its holders (PRD engine-bundle-2-pane-holder D-10, D-11, D-15, D-17).
This machine's node runs it from its start; a device's node runs holders when the core that dialed it asks (`Call::HoldersStart`, [A device on the core's own engine](#a-device-on-the-cores-own-engine)), which every link's start does.
A Windows device's node runs inside the job Windows OpenSSH makes for its session, which allows breakaway, so its holders leave it through `start_resident` as this machine's do and outlive the link ([A device's ssh](#a-devices-ssh)).

The daemon builds its terminal service and holders in one place, `Holders::start_local`, which the restart lane's and the measurements' node (`hide-node/examples/holder_node`) call too, so what they prove is the daemon's own assembly ([The holder restart lane](TESTING.md#the-holder-restart-lane)).
It opens the holders of the state folder, builds the service with `Holders::attacher`, which opens a pane by its holder record over the holder's socket (`holder::open_holder`), and starts `Holders::recover` and then `Holders::prune_folders` on a thread of its own; the holder program is the one beside the daemon's own (on Windows with the pinned ConPTY runtime in `holder-conpty` beside it, from `contracts/conpty.json`'s NuGet package, so no Herdr is asked for the holder's files).
On Windows a holder leaves the node's job (`start_resident`), so a node whose innermost job forbids breakaway refuses every holder start: a GitHub runner's step runs in such a job (no limit flags at all), while Node and Electron start their children in a libuv job that allows it (kill on close, breakaway and silent breakaway), which is how the app starts its daemon; the restart lane therefore starts its node through Node's `child_process.spawn` (`scripts/holder-restart-spawn.mjs`), not from the runner's shell.
The service holds every pane over a holder and keeps the rules of [The terminal path](#the-terminal-path): the attach cap of 64, held keys, the frame guard and the reports.
A holder pane says four things through its transport rather than through the service: it keeps its own size, so it attaches with none and at the size its holder's welcome names unless the core or a view already named one, and a size it already has is never sent again (a holder resizes its PTY, and signals its program, on every resize it is sent), so where the service asks for the whole screen with a same-size resize line (a redraw, a view at the grid the session runs at, a frame lost) it asks through `SessionWriter::redraw`, which a holder writes as `ClientMessage::Redraw`; its fragments are delivered as frames, untranslated, and a fragment out of its epoch's order ends the session `protocol_error`; its input goes out as the bytes, pastes, named keys, resizes and wheels the service writes, which the holder encodes for its program's settings, named keys only to a holder that reads them (another refuses them `terminal.unsupported_holder`, sends nothing and keeps its session); and its close names a reason (`hide_holder_protocol::CloseReason`) rather than words.
A close that says the pane ended (`program_exited`, `terminated`), that another node took it over (`taken_over`), or that its holder speaks a version older than this build speaks to (`unsupported_holder_version`) leaves the pane in `ended`, `taken_over` or `unsupported` with no retry; only a manual attach tries again, and a pane taken over gets no notice drawn over its screen, since whoever took it shows it.
Keys typed into a pane taken over are refused, so nothing this node typed after the takeover reaches the program, and the holder drops what the earlier connection had sent ([The pane holder](#the-pane-holder)).

`Holders::start` starts a pane through `hide_kit::panes` with the node's theme (the holder's `--theme`), which is not part of the start's key, and asks the service to attach it with no size, so a size the core already named for the pane is kept (the start's is the holder's own, not a decision); asked again for a pane that lives it answers that pane and starts no second holder.
Its node attaches a pane it started or found running whether or not a screen draws it, so two orders meet after a daemon starts again over a restore (PRD engine-bundle-3-core-owns D-7, B44): the core may ask for a pane from the saved layout before its shell's holder is started, and that attempt is refused; the attach the holder's start then asks for is recorded at once, at the core's size, and opens once the earlier attempt and any transport it opened have ended (its late answer is dropped by its generation), without waiting for that attempt's retry clock, while a pane that never gets a holder, or whose holder refused its attach, stays on that clock.
And a pane attached at its holder's own size before any size was named takes the first view's grid as its size, as an attach after that view would have, whether the view arrives while the holder is being opened or after, since the core reads that grid as the size it saved for the pane and sends no resize for it (`a_holder_pane_its_node_attached_before_a_view_drew_it_takes_the_view_s_grid` and the holder-pane tests after it in `hide-node/src/terminal/tests.rs`).
`Holders::terminate` marks the pane closing in the service, ends it through `Panes::close`, and forgets it once it ended.
`Holders::read`, `Holders::read_styled` and `Holders::processes` ask on a connection of their own, which takes nothing over, in the version the pane's record names (`hide_holder_protocol::ask` takes it), since a holder answers an ask only in its own version; `LocalPanes::read_styled` answers a holder that refuses a styled read `unsupported_holder`, judged where a watch's is (`holder::too_old`, the one place a node judges a holder built before what it opened).

Each pane the node starts or finds running is followed on a watch of its own (`hide-node/src/terminal/holder/watch.rs`), one per pane and read on a thread of its own, beside the service's screen connection and never counted against the attach cap, so a pane past the cap is followed as an attached one is.
The node tells the sink the engine gives it (`PaneHolders::watch_facts`) each facts the holder sends, the folder in the wire spelling (`hide_platform::path`), and tells a sink set later the last facts of every pane at once.
One lock is held across each call of the sink, so a pane's facts arrive in the order they were read; giving rules never takes it.
The node keeps each pane's last `ScreenRules` and gives its holder the first set whose `min_engine_version` the holder's evaluator reaches, again on each watch it opens; when no set fits, the pane's screen reads `no_rules_for_holder`, and since a holder answers each rule set with its facts, the sink hears it from the watch's own thread, in order with the rest.
A holder that refuses the watch is told to the sink once as `unsupported_holder`, as is a holder too old to speak to at all; the node judges a holder too old for facts in one place (`too_old`, `hide-node/src/terminal/holder/watch.rs`).
A watch that ends any other way than with its pane (another watch took it, the connection broke, the holder sent what a watch never carries) tells the sink once that the pane's screen reads `watch_lost`, its other facts as last told, until a later start of the pane follows it again.
A watch that ends with its pane (`program_exited`, `terminated`), or a terminate, forgets the pane; one another node took over, or one that failed, leaves the pane known, and the pane's next start opens it again.

When the daemon starts, `Holders::recover` runs on a thread of its own: it reconciles until everything found is taken up and every record it settled was written (at most eight rounds of `RECONCILE_BUDGET`, then it logs what the next start takes up): a record that could not be written, its lock held past its 5 s wait as a loaded machine holds it after a reboot, is judged again by the next round rather than counted as running, since a pane counted running is adopted and never starts again, and the panes left unjudged after the rounds are logged by name with why (`pane_holder.recovery_unjudged`); asks the service to attach every holder that runs, by pane id, so the first 64 attach and the rest are reported `unavailable` with `attach_limit`, as a start past the cap is, and run on with their screens held by their holders; it reports each pane once, by what the last round that took it up found, logs the panes still pending after its rounds by name (`pane_holder.reconcile_unfinished`), and reports each pane that ended while no node was there as `ended` with the reason its record names, and each holder too old to speak to as `unsupported`, through the same reports a session's state takes.
On this Mac a node killed outright with 66 panes found 65 running again and drew 64 first screens in about 0.14 s.

### The core's own engine

`hide-core/src/engine/own/` is the one implementation of `Engine` (PRD engine-bundle-3-core-owns D-2, D-3, D-5): it keeps a machine's session itself and runs each pane in a pane holder, with no Herdr server.
