It makes workspaces, tabs and panes and lays them out (split, split at a ratio, close, zoom, resize, swap, move to a new tab or beside another, a saved layout given back), binds workspaces to checkouts and makes worktrees, saves its session and lays it out again when the daemon starts, keeps focus, names and Hide's tokens, and reads (plain, or styled as escape sequences), types and pastes into, presses named keys in and lists the processes of a pane.
It starts agents and follows their state ([Agents on the core's own engine](#agents-on-the-cores-own-engine)).
It reads and moves a pane's scroll position through its holder's scroll asks, so ⌘F opens the find bar over a pane with history and a find scrolls its match into view.
A pane's folders, which the disk cleanup and a worktree removal guard (`Engine::pane_folders`, `Engine::pane_places`), are its own and, while a program other than its shell holds its terminal, each folder that program works in: the pane's node reads them from its system for the foreground members the holder lists (`HolderForeground::folders`, `hide_platform::process::observed_cwd_of`: the kernel's answer on macOS and Linux, the process's own parameters on Windows), so a checkout a program moved into is not removed as unused. A closing pane is asked like any other until its holder has ended, since a close still under way or one whose end failed leaves its program running, and one read of every pane shares its caller's bound: each holder ask is given what is left of it and none starts once it has passed, the panes left unasked being unknown.
A folder its machine could not read is unknown, never none: `pane_folders` lists the pane with no folder, which the cleanup refuses as unknown, and `pane_places` refuses its answer, so no removal's close is confirmed past it; a pane still starting or whose terminal could not start runs no such program, and each read asks every pane's holder at most once, outside the topology lock.

Every daemon runs it (PRD engine-bundle-4-herdr-removal D-2): hided reads no Herdr socket, binary or default socket, the core is created with no socket and so with the own engine, and its live state is scoped to the engine folder (`hide_kit::layout::engine_dir`, `<state>/engine`).
The login item starts no Herdr, the desktop host runs no Herdr check (`desktop/src/main/host.ts`), and the idle probe asks no Herdr.

The topology (`own/topology.rs`) sits behind a mutex of the engine's own, never `Mutex<Runtime>`: workspaces, the checkout each is bound to, their tabs, each tab's split tree, focus, zoom, names and tokens.
The tree rules live once in `own/layout.rs` (D-4), and the drawn-ahead predictions (`runtime/pane_prediction.rs`) call the same functions, so a layout drawn before an answer is the one the engine then has: a split halves the pane it splits, or keeps the ratio asked within 0.1 to 0.9; a resize moves the split on the pane's edge toward its direction, or on its opposite edge when the pane touches the tab's side there, and stops at those limits; a swap trades two leaves; a close gives the sibling the parent's place; a zoom ends on a split, a move out or in and a close of the zoomed pane, and a tab of one pane never zooms.
A layout given back (`apply_layout`) is checked against its limits first, 24 panes and 16 levels, and refused `invalid_layout` with its reason past them; applied over a tab it keeps every pane of that tab the layout names running in its new place and starts only the rest.
A pane keeps its id wherever it moves, across workspaces too, so a letter, a mission or a parent that names it still finds it.
Its ids take the shape `<workspace>:t<n>`, `<workspace>:p<n>` (numbered in a 32-letter public alphabet, `own/ids.rs`, derived from Herdr v0.9.5's `src/workspace.rs` under Apache-2.0) and are never reused while the engine lives, so every caller and the snapshot wire read them as they always have.
A workspace it makes is `h<n>`, a letter Herdr never starts a workspace with (Herdr makes only `w<n>`), so a Herdr that runs on beside Hide and makes workspaces of its own never makes an id this engine made, and a workspace moved from Herdr keeps its `w<n>` (PRD engine-bundle-4-herdr-removal D-26); tab and pane numbers count within their workspace, so workspaces that do not meet share no id.
One reader in `own/ids.rs` (`workspace_of`) reads both letters for the saved session's check, the counters and the gathering of running panes, and the engine's workspace count moves only with its own `h` numbers; outside the engine the hooks' first-run read of their pane records (`hide_agent_hooks::counters::every_pane`) takes file names of both letters, reading their shape and never the engine's ids.
The engine asks a machine's holders through `PaneHolders` (`hide-node-link/src/holders.rs`: start, terminate, read, processes, input); this machine's answer is `LocalPanes` (`hide-node/src/terminal/engine_panes.rs`) over `Holders` and the terminal service, which attaches each started pane as it attaches any holder pane ([The node's holder panes](#the-nodes-holder-panes)).
A pane's holder record is named by its id with `:` written as `_` (`hide_kit::panes::holder_pane`), since a record's name is a file name on every system.
A new pane reserves its id and starts its holder outside the topology lock.
A new tab or split enters the topology `starting` before its holder starts, and the call is answered then, with the shell starting after the answer: the holder's start (three flushed writes of its record and two programs started, about 50 ms) had stood between the chord and the screen, which shows a created tab once the answer names it (perf-gate rows 22 and 23); its terminal attaches once the holder runs, and keys typed meanwhile wait in the pane's hold.
Its holder starts on a thread of its own that ends with the start and holds the machine's holders, not the engine, so an engine let go meanwhile ends and saves at once while that holder runs on for the next restore to gather (`start_after_answer`); one that does not start leaves its pane where it was drawn, marked with the holder's reason, which the session gives as the pane's `restore_error`, so the screen shows that its terminal could not start and offers to close it, as for a pane a restore could not start; it also logs `pane.start_failed` with that reason.
All starts, including restores and synchronous creations, share one admission gate (`own/starts.rs`): eight holders start at once and at most eight additional starts wait, admitted before a background thread is made.
A full queue refuses `holder_start_queue_full`; an asynchronous pane keeps that refusal in its visible failure state, and a synchronous creation returns it to its caller.
Waiting for admission uses the existing holder `START_LIMIT`; completion, timeout and thread-start failure release admission.
The pane's in-memory `Starting` holds its actual start result and wakes its readers on completion, so `pane_processes`, foreground and identity lookup and plain or styled reads immediately after creation wait outside the topology lock, up to `START_LIMIT`, and return the original start failure if it failed.
This adds one bounded wait to an early read, no work per input byte, no success snapshot publication, and no change to the node's existing input buffer or attach ownership.
The view can attach before a holder's start is registered, for a new pane or a saved pane while recovery judges the records: constructing `LocalPanes` first tells the shared attach owner (`Known` in `hide-node/src/terminal/holder.rs`) that every pane on this node belongs to its holders.
An unseen pane then waits in the same bounded start lookup as a registered starting pane, without adding a map entry, until the holder is ready; a deadline reports a holder failure and never falls through to another path.
A start lists the record paths under that same lock: when their count is below the live-holder cap and no higher than the ended-record retention cap, neither cap can be crossed and no record needs parsing for admission; at either boundary it reads and counts the records, including unreadable records as live, and prunes ended records as before.
Once a holder says ready, its node reads the atomically replaced record and checks the reserved incarnation without taking the records' writer lock: that read mutates nothing, and waiting behind unrelated starts had held completed starts' workers before they could take another pane.
A call whose outcome hangs on the start waits for it and is refused with the holder's code and reason (`holder_start_failed`, `holder_cap`, `invalid_cwd`, ...), its drawn pane taken out, so nothing of it is left: a spawn's pane, which a placement records (below), and a tab that replaces another; a new workspace's first pane, a worktree's and a layout given back enter the topology once their holders run and are refused the same way.
A close ends the holder first and then removes the pane; a pane still `starting` is removed at once and its holder left to the start, which ends it once it finds the pane gone (`OwnEngine::end_and_remove`, `start_drawn`).
A pane whose program exits on its own while the node holds its screen closes: the node tells the engine (`PaneHolders::watch_ends`), and the engine removes it as a close would.
A read answers `recent` and `recent_unwrapped` with the last rows of the holder's screen and scrollback and `visible` with the rows its screen shows now, wherever it is scrolled to, each with soft wraps joined, and refuses any other source (`unknown_read_source`).
A pane given no program runs the account's shell with Hide's shell integration, prepared for each pane as the node prepares it for a tab Hide opens (`engine_panes::PaneShell::Account`, `hide_host::shell_integration::prepare`), so it says its folder and marks its prompt on its screen; a shell the integration does not reach runs plain, and an account with no usable shell refuses the start (`shell_unavailable`); `PaneHolders::shell_launch` says which, for the starts that wait on the mark.
The holder starts every pane program with `TERM=xterm-256color`, `COLORTERM=truecolor`, `TERM_PROGRAM=hide` and `FORCE_HYPERLINK=1` (it shows OSC 8 links, the `supports-hyperlinks` convention, which Claude Code reads since it knows no `TERM_PROGRAM=hide`), the terminal it emulates, whatever its starter's environment held (an app opened from the Dock has no `TERM`), and without every `HERDR_*` variable, the outer terminal's handles, a parent agent's (`hide-holder/src/pane_env.rs`, D-9) and the holder's own launch metadata (`hide_platform::process::OWNER_LAUNCH_KEYS`), which Hide's hook helper in the pane would otherwise take for its own owner and do nothing; the node adds `HIDE_PANE_ID`, the pane's id, after every other variable, so a process in the pane names this pane alone.
Every other variable is the holder's starter's, on every system: on Windows the account's registry environment, made first as Windows makes a sign-in's (the system's variables, then the user's, a user variable replacing the system's except `PATH`, which joins them), only adds a variable the starter lacks, and `PATH` keeps the starter's folders first and gains each registry folder it lacks, so a CLI installed since the daemon started is still found while a daemon started with its own `PATH` or temporary folder hands them to its panes, as on macOS and Linux (`vendor/portable-pty/PATCHES.md`; upstream and Herdr replace them with the registry's).
A process that names such a pane is proved by the pane's record alone: `PaneHolders::proof` reads the record's program and its start (a record still `reserved` or `preparing` is refused `pane_starting`, one whose program ended `pane_not_running`), `OwnEngine::pane_identity` answers the pane as its own terminal (ids are never reused) with that shell and start (`PaneProof::shell_started`), and `hided/src/pane_auth.rs` (`proved_shell`) accepts a caller that descends from that shell and refuses `pane_changed` when the shell's start the kernel reads is not the recorded one.
The `hide` CLI, the hooks, the OpenCode plugin and the Pi extension read the pane from `HIDE_PANE_ID` (`hide_agent_hooks::pane`, `hided/src/env.rs`), and letters, spawns and missions act on the credential the proof gave, never on the shape of the id.
A spawn's pane is on its record before its holder starts (D-11): the coordination executor gates the engine with a placement (`engine::Placement`, `coordination/executor.rs` `SpawnPlacement`), and a new pane's id, reserved under the topology lock, is recorded on the spawn (`Mutation::Place`) under `Mutex<Runtime>` once the topology lock is let go, and the holder starts once both are; the two locks are never held together.
A start that fails withdraws the placement in the same call (`Mutation::Withdraw`), so no spawn names a pane that never ran, and the spawn is refused with the holder's reason.
An agent start or saved-agent resume provisionally records its name and session before typing, so an early hook can bind to that identity; a definite input refusal withdraws only the same unconfirmed attempt and restores the preceding agent and pending hook.
While that rollback is possible, the same claim reserves the preceding listed name too, so another pane cannot take it before restoration; delivery completion, confirmation or expiry releases that backup reservation.
A matching session report, including the same value, or foreground observation invalidates that rollback claim; an unanswered write keeps the provisional identity because it may have reached the program and is never resent automatically.
One start may await its foreground in a pane within the existing 120-second deadline; after expiry a new attempt may start, without restoring the expired attempt if either input later fails.
The attempt claim and its backup are memory only, and screen-rule publication rechecks the current agent kind and definition catalog under the topology lock before updating its cache and enqueueing the decision; rule serialization and the holder's actual rule call stay outside that lock.
The engine types through `PaneHolders::input` as bytes, a paste or named keys (`PaneInput`, D-21), which the node writes behind every key typed into the pane and the holder encodes for the program's modes when it writes them; a caller's keys (`Engine::send_keys`) go as named keys where they are one, and a single character or a Ctrl chord of a letter (an agent's own search opens with `ctrl+o` then `/`) as its bytes, in their order; this typing is the engine's, never reported to the core as the operator's, and a pane no screen holds, released or known to its node only from a control such as `Asleep` that came before any attach (a device just linked), is attached for it and released again once the input ends unless the core attached it meanwhile (`Inner::attach_for_input`), the input waiting in the pane's hold (64 KiB, 3 s) as a new pane's keys do.
A prompt, which a forced letter's bell and a spawn's brief are typed by, goes through `PaneHolders::letter` as one submission the holder keeps whole (`ClientMessage::Submit`, to a holder whose welcome names the `submit` capability; one built before it refuses the letter with nothing typed): the text (a paste when the agent takes bracketed paste), then Enter 300 ms after the text was written (`engine::own::prompt_text`): a Copilot prompt starts with a focus report (`CSI I`), since Copilot ignores a typed Enter after it lost focus until told focus came back, and a Codex prompt on a Windows machine ends its text with a Right arrow before the gap, which flushes Codex's paste burst so the Enter submits; the operator's keys are never given either; while the operator's keys typed into the pane from the text until the Enter was handed over are held, 64 KiB and 3 s at most, and written after it in the order typed (`hide-node/src/terminal/mod.rs`, `type_letter`, D-13); a letter begun while another is typed into the same pane shares that hold, and the keys follow the last submit.
Both calls answer only after the session writer has written and flushed each input, never merely after the node queued it; this proves transport delivery, not that the agent took or executed it.
A command's queued-to-writing admission and cancellation share one receipt lock: a queued expiry, close or refusal returns `HolderError::Refused` and cannot write later; a write error or a timeout after writing began returns `Unreachable`, since some bytes may have been sent, and is never automatically resent.
Each input keeps the existing 64 KiB and three-second bound, the writer's 256 KiB backlog still applies, and receipts and whole letters, including zero-byte commands and the configured submit gap, share the node's existing 64 outstanding-input slots with side-channel permits.
A released view reports `released` and draws nothing immediately, while the same service retains a command's connection until its write or reported failure, and a letter's through body, gap and submit; a newer visible attach cancels that deferred release and asks for a full frame.
Closing a pane or the node cancels queued commands; a letter whose submission reached the holder is submitted whole even when the pane begins closing in its gap.
The local and remote `PaneCall::Input` and `PaneCall::Letter` replies keep their existing wire shapes and carry these outcomes; the real-holder fixtures in `hide-holder/tests/it/node/transport_ownership.rs` gate the Local/LocalPanes handshake, writer and shutdown boundaries.
A pane the core holds asleep at its node (`TerminalControl::Asleep`, while a sleep record names it) takes none of the operator's keys or a screen's answers, but the engine's own typing goes through, since the sleep's quit key and the wake's resume line are typed there while the record holds it.
Whether the letter was taken is the agent's own record of it ([delivery.md](delivery.md#input-an-agent-did-not-take)).

The engine keeps the coordinator's wake given to `Engine::changes`; every topology change calls it, and the coordinator reads `Engine::session` whole and publishes that `ProjectionState` as it is (`session_sync/pulled.rs`); a read the engine's wake brought that equals the last one published is not published again, while a wake the core asks for through `RepublishWaker` (a drawing ahead, a hook report, a path answer) and a start's settle always publish (`coordinator.rs`, `publishes`).
Each session read is also handed to the lineage writer, so a fork's owed registration settles once its session shows and its pane carries the fork's provenance tokens (`coordinator::observe_pulled`).
Each session carries the moves of the tab the keyboard's workspace shows, one each time it changed and none for a focus of the tab already shown, recorded as each hold of the topology lock ends (`Topology::note_shown`), in `SessionTabMoves`; the core answers the tab moves it asked for from them (`runtime/tab_focus.rs`, the list of tab moves sent and not yet answered), so a tab focus or a creation on this engine waits on no confirmation and never times out.
Nothing is replayed: there is no subscription, replica or event application, and the coordinator publishes the session as it reads it.
The session is saved to one file, `<state>/engine/session.json` (`hide_kit::layout::engine_session`, `own/store.rs`, D-6): format 1, every field named and an unknown field or format refused, replaced atomically and durably by one save thread that writes at most once per burst of changes, 200 ms after the last, and at once when the engine `open` returned is dropped: that engine alone holds the save thread, so its drop has written the last change before it returns, even while a holder start finishing or a fact arriving holds the engine's shared state a moment longer on another thread.
It holds the workspaces with their checkouts, tabs, trees, focus and zoom, each pane's folder, name, tokens (all but Hide's server mark, which vouches for agent state sequences the engine does not save; status-model.md, Across an engine restart) and agent session, and every id counter; a pane's command and environment stay in memory, since an environment can carry what is not the session's to save.
A file that cannot be read, names a format this build does not read, or does not hold together is moved, never deleted, to `<state>/engine/backups` under a name of its own, the newest three kept, and `engine.session_unreadable` logs why.

A daemon's engine opens with the saved layout, so a screen draws its tabs at once, and lays it out again when the node says what it found of its holders (`PaneHolders::recovered`, `own/restore.rs`, D-7): the node's records say which panes exist, the save says where they go.
A pane whose holder runs is taken as it is, the same id and the same process; a saved pane whose program exited, or that a node ended, while no daemon ran closes, its tab and workspace with it when it was their last, as a pane whose program exits closes (`HolderRecovery::closed`); a saved pane whose holder ended under it, as every one has after a reboot, gets a new shell under its own id in its saved folder, eight at a time, or in the home folder with one line saying why when the machine's node says no folder is there (`Call::Directory`, `HolderStart::notice`), and in its folder when the node cannot say, so a start that fails there marks the pane; a shell that cannot start marks its pane with the reason (`restore_error`) and keeps the pane's agent, which the next restore resumes there.
A running holder the save does not place, because the daemon died before it saved or the save could not be read, is gathered into a new tab named `restored` of the workspace its id names, made again under that id when it is gone, so no running shell is lost or ended.
Every id counter is then taken past every id the node's records hold, and no pane is made until the restore has finished, so a new pane never takes the id of a record a holder still runs or ran under.
A pane's record, not the save, holds that it exists until the coalesced save catches up, and holds its end and its close (a close writes the pane's intent `cancelled`), so records keep their flush to the device (`WriteOptions::UntilReboot`): a record replaced without it could come back after a power loss without a new pane, or as running for a pane that ended, and the restore would lose the one or open the other again.
`engine::contract::a_restart_after_the_machine_went_down_brings_each_pane_back_under_its_id_and_no_ended_one` holds the restore to this over a real node and real holders: with a save older than the last pane, a record gone, one left empty before the boot and, on Unix, one of an earlier boot, every pane comes back under its id, and the pane whose program exited and the one the operator closed stay closed.
The node names a pane by the core's id (`hide_kit::panes::core_pane` reads a record's name back), so the service attaches a found holder under the id the session gives it.

A worktree this engine makes goes under Hide's own folder, `~/.hide/worktrees/<repo>/<branch as a folder name>` (`hide_kit::layout::engine_worktree`, `own/worktrees.rs`, D-28), with `git worktree add` run by the node of the machine the panes run on (`GitCommand::WorktreeAdd`), and opens in a new workspace bound to it; a checkout anywhere else, one under `~/.herdr/worktrees` included, is opened where it is and never moved, since the agents in it, their resume records and the folder trust entries name that path.
A workspace's binding (the repository's shared `.git`, its main checkout, the checkout and whether it is linked) is projected and saved with the session; removing a worktree ends its workspace's panes, closes it and has the node remove the checkout without force (`Call::WorktreeRemoveClean`), which Git refuses while it holds changes.
The core touches no machine here either (PRD core-host-node D-21): the engine holds that node's `NodeLink` and reads a checkout's repository (`Call::Repository`), a repository's worktrees (`Call::WorktreesRegistered`) and a branch (`GitCommand::HasLocalBranch`) through it; only the saved session is the core's own store.

A daemon of this engine lives while one of its panes may still run (D-10): the idle clock (`hided/src/server.rs`, `watch_idle`) counts the node's live pane records (`Holders::live_panes`, a record that cannot be read counted as live) every five seconds, and ends the daemon ten minutes after the last screen closed only once none is left, since the holders outlive the daemon and the daemon is what keeps their letters and states going.
A holder whose record went with a deleted state folder is not ended by the next node, which knows nothing of it; it ends when its shell does (D-8).
`engine/contract.rs`'s `the_own_engine_meets_the_engine_contract` runs the engine contract over holders started from the built holder ([TESTING.md](TESTING.md#choose-what-to-test-and-where)).

#### A device on the core's own engine

Every device, one the core dials over SSH or as a WSL distribution and one whose node dials the core, runs its panes on an engine of the core's own and no Herdr (PRD engine-bundle-3-core-owns D-22, B35; engine-bundle-4-herdr-removal D-2).
A dialed device's connector asks for the payload with the holder (`HelperPackages::payload_for` in `hide-node/src/ssh/host.rs`): no Herdr and no pin go up, the holder goes beside the helper, and a build that carries no holder for the device's system connects nothing and says why on the row.
Once the helper says hello, the connector asks its node to start its holders (`Call::HoldersStart`), as the core does for a node that dials it.
The node opens them over its own state folder, `~/.hide/device-node` (`hide_kit::layout::device_node_state`), apart from the records of a Hide that runs on the same account, with a terminal service that attaches each pane over its holder, and its pane socket proves a caller by the pane's holder record (`PaneSource::Holders` in `hide-host/src/panes.rs`): the pane id is its terminal, the record's program its shell, bound by that program's start time, so `hide` in a device's pane is proved as in any pane of this machine (D-9).

The core asks every machine's holders one way.
An engine holds a `LinkPanes` (`hide-node-link/src/link_panes.rs`) over that machine's node link, sends `Call::Pane` for a start, an end, a read, an input, a letter, the recovered panes or new screen rules, and holds one `Call::PaneWatch` open for the panes' facts and ends; this machine's node answers in the daemon's process (`hide_node::Local::with_panes`), a device's at the far end of its link, so no caller branches on the machine.
A node answers pane requests on a lane of their own, nine at once (`PANE_LANE`), so a start that waits for its holder never holds up files, Git or terminals; the watch keeps the latest facts per pane and at most 512 reports, drops the oldest facts past that and logs `pane_watch.facts_dropped`.
The operator's keys and a pane's screen output never take these requests: they ride the terminal service's attach as before, on this machine in process and on a device over its terminal line, so a key costs what it did, and the requests carry only the engine's own work, a few per action.

The core opens a device's engine once its node is ready (`Runtime::open_own_device_engine`, `hide-core/src/runtime/own_devices.rs`), off the runtime lock, with its session in `<state>/engine/devices/<id>` (`hide_kit::layout::device_engine_dir`, which takes only a plain id), and lets it go with the link, which saves it.
Every new link starts a new node, which finds the holders that ran on, and the new engine lays the saved session out around them as this machine's does, so a pane keeps its id and its process across a node's restart (`hided/tests/it/device_own_engine.rs`, in the remote mailbox lane).
A device of another system or processor than the core's, such as a Linux device dialed from a Mac or a WSL distribution from a Windows PC, gets its holder from the release's device kit, which carries it beside the helper ([BUILD.md](BUILD.md#device-helper-release-bundles)); a local build has no published kit and a developer folder supplies `hide-holder-<os>-<arch>` instead.
`hided/tests/it/wsl_device.rs`'s own-engine walk runs a pane in a holder inside a real WSL 2 distribution with no Herdr there.

#### Agents on the core's own engine

The own engine starts, recognizes, reads and resumes agents by their definition files ([Agent definition files](#agent-definition-files), PRD engine-bundle-3-core-owns D-16 to D-21): so an agent with a definition file and no other code in Hide (gemini and the other definition-only ones) starts, shows its state and resumes on this engine.
The definitions are the core's read of the operator's folder: hided reads them once before it opens the engine, so the restore that starts with it has them, and after every read the core settles (`settle_agent_definitions`) it hands the engine the new set off the runtime lock (`Engine::set_agent_definitions`).

A start (`own/mod.rs`, `start_agent`) refuses `agent_pane_busy` unless the pane's shell holds its terminal alone, and `agent_name_taken` for a name another pane's agent runs under; it then records the agent as starting and types one line into the shell: the definition's first executable, its `[start] args`, then the caller's, quoted for the shell the pane runs (a pane a caller made run cmd.exe takes no start, `agent_start_refused`; POSIX quoting, or for PowerShell a script test that runs a `.ps1` shim directly and anything else through `Start-Process`, `own/shell_line.rs`, derived from Herdr v0.9.5's `src/platform/`, `src/agent_resume.rs` and `src/terminal/title.rs` under Apache-2.0).
The agent is listed while it starts, for at most the start's deadline, and from then on while its program is the pane's foreground.
`hide_prompt`, which a start waits for before it types, is answered from the holder's count of the shell's prompt marks (OSC 133;A, which Hide's shell integration writes once its startup files are done), never from a token a program reports.

What each pane runs and shows reaches the engine as pane facts (`PaneHolders::watch_facts`, `hide-node-link/src/holders.rs`): the folder the shell last reported (OSC 7, or OSC 9;9 from PowerShell), the terminal title, the bells, the prompt marks, whether bracketed paste is on, whether the terminal edits lines, the foreground program with its arguments, and what the pane's screen rules read.
The holder sends them whole on a connection of its own that takes nothing over and is not one of the node's attached screens, so a pane no screen shows is followed as one that is shown and costs no attach.
The engine lays them on the pane under its topology lock (`own/agents.rs`, `apply`): a foreground program a definition's `executables` names, by the name its holder gives it, is that agent, started from the shell or by a start, and while a pane runs an agent, whichever way it started, any other program in its foreground is still that agent, run by a wrapper or a runtime under another name (`node …/cli.js`), until the shell holds the terminal again, and a terminal whose foreground the holder could not say (`foreground_unread`) is no such evidence: the agent keeps its kind, name and session until the holder reads the terminal again; the pane's folder and title follow the facts, the title without the one activity glyph an agent turns in front of it (Claude Code's spinner, Braille or `◐◑◒◓`, and `·✢✳✶✻✽`), compared and projected without it, so a turning spinner, which the holder's facts carry every frame, changes nothing the session shows, while the holder's screen rules still read the whole title; and the state is the screen rules' read, under the status names the agent list uses (`idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, `unknown`), with a stop after work read as `done` and its `completion_seq` until the agent works again, and a read with no matching rule is idle.
A start the engine typed takes input once its program shows, its screen rests and at least 3 s have passed since the start (`START_SETTLE`), and only while the terminal does not edit lines (`Live::line_editing`): a program reads keys only after it turns the terminal's line editing (canonical mode) off, and until then what is typed waits in the terminal's line, where the Enter that submits it reaches the program as a line break.
Pi 1.0.4 started on a Linux CI runner had not done so 3 s after its start line, and the brief typed at that mark sat in its editor unsubmitted (nightly 41789009557); typed into Pi 1.0.4 before it does on macOS, a brief stays in its editor the same way.
Where the holder cannot say (a holder or a node built before the fact, or a Windows console its helper could not read, [The pane holder](#the-pane-holder)) the start is judged by the settle alone, as before, never taken as reading keys, and logged once as `agent.start_settled_unread` with its pane when it settles; a device pane reads the same signal from its own node's holder.
When the program turns line editing off, its start begins its settle again from then, as an answered question does: OpenCode 2.0.29 takes the keys about 0.3 s after its start and drops what is typed until its input box draws about a second later, so a brief typed as it took the keys was lost whole and its first turn, which reports its session, never came (the Linux journey's `native_identity_unavailable`).
The settle and the 120 s deadline are two clocks (`Live::settles_from`, `Live::started`): only the settle starts again, and the deadline runs from the start and nothing moves it, so a program that takes and gives back the keys every second, which once held its start pending for good, ends its start at the deadline.
An agent whose definition names a ready screen (`[start] ready`, an idle rule of its `[screen]`) is typed into only once its screen has matched that rule since the start, and stays so whatever its screen reads next (`Live::ready`), except that a match before the screen read anything else since the program showed, which can be the last run's screen in a woken agent's pane, counts only while it lasts: OpenCode 2.0.29 reads keys and draws its composer before its model loads, 2.0 to 4.7 s after its start on macOS, and refuses the Enter of a line typed before then, which a brief typed at the settle on Windows met (journey-win); its rule is the model line under its composer (`model_line_idle`).
A pending start ends at its settle or its deadline with nothing the holder reports changing when the screen already rests, as a woken agent's pane does, still showing the last run's screen: each read of the session names, from the same instant that decides each start's `launch_pending`, the next such moment (`ProjectionState::settles_at`, `PaneAgent::start_changes_at`), and the coordinator that publishes that read reads the session again then (`coordinator_wait`, `settle_due`), so the core reads the start settled and its row stops saying `starting` (`a_start_whose_screen_already_rests_is_read_settled_once_its_settle_passes`); any other read only reads, so a lookup between the two cannot take that moment away.
While the start is pending the row says `starting` whatever the screen or the last hook report reads, unless the agent works or the engine saw a turn of it end since the start (`completion_seq`, which a quick first turn within the settle sets; `agent_state::agent_starting`): read at rest at once, a woken Codex, Claude Code or agy took the operator's prompt typed half a second after its wake into a program still starting, which dropped it (Windows journey 41929631031), and Claude Code's and agy's rows still read their last run's finished turn from its hook (41937427750).
Whether a program takes input is one answer, `PaneAgent::takes_input`, which `delivery_agent` (through `PaneAgent::readiness`), `pane_agent_status` and `prompt_agent` all ask, and it is apart from whether the start is pending: a start ends at its 120 s deadline, but a program that still leaves the terminal editing lines, or whose foreground the holder could not say, or whose settle since it last took the keys or had its question answered has not passed, takes no letter however long ago it started (`delivery_agent` reads it not ready and `prompt_agent` refuses `agent_not_ready`), so a letter retried past the deadline is typed neither into its line nor into a screen it is still drawing.
A start the engine types records the session its resume names, so a woken agent names the conversation it resumed at once, except when an agent whose integration reports its session as a file's path (Pi, omp; `SessionFormat::reports_session_path`) resumes by id, whose session then waits for its own report (`agents::started_session`): an id taken as a woken omp's session read as another conversation than the path its registration held, so the registration was refused (`identity_changed`); resumed by the file's path (Pi's `--session <path>`), the path is the session it reports and is recorded. A wake tells the engine it wakes (`AgentLaunch::wakes`), and a woken OpenCode then waits for its plugin's report too (`SessionFormat::reports_session_once_loaded`): the plugin reports once OpenCode has loaded the session, and a prompt typed into a woken OpenCode before then never reached it; a spawn that resumes OpenCode is still known by its resume at once.
An agent whose definition declares no screen rules (omp) never reads at rest, so its start settles on its program shown and reading keys and the settle (`Live::rest_unread`), where waiting for a rest held every omp start pending to its deadline, and such an agent reads idle once its program takes input, its integration's turns outranking that, where read unknown a woken or forked omp stayed a starting row with no state change to publish its settle; and the engine's `pane_agent_status`, which agy's fork waits on before it types `/fork`, reads `unknown` while the agent takes no input, since a screen no rule matches reads idle as soon as the program shows; the fork types it once that status reads at rest, `idle` or `done`, because agy redrawing the resumed conversation can read working for a moment as it starts, which leaves its rest `done`.
A holder that sends no facts (`unsupported_holder`), one whose evaluator is too old for every rule set (`no_rules_for_holder`) or a pane whose watch was lost (`watch_lost`) reads `unknown`, and so does an agent with no screen rules until its program takes input (above).
The rules worker keeps the latest decision per pane, including removing its rules, while the node recovers; only the successful `recovered` answer, after the link has checked its owner, opens delivery before adoption starts.
Facts and ends continue to arrive during that wait, but no rule mutation bypasses the node's owner admission.
The worker holds at most 128 pending panes and one batch of at most 128, reports a new pane beyond the pending cap, and lets an already pending pane replace its decision at the cap.
Recovery failure or worker shutdown discards pending decisions and permanently closes admission; an admitted call may finish within its existing timeout, but the rest of its batch starts no more calls, and no pending decision transfers to a new link.
Both the core's rule-decision cache and the node's watch distinguish an undecided value from explicit removal.
A new node sends no default removal to a surviving holder: its first facts retain the existing rule set and title/progress, and giving the same rules again preserves them.
The core sends its first decision even when the pane is now a shell and that decision removes the old agent's rules; later identical decisions coalesce, and an explicit removal or incompatible rule set keeps its existing meaning.
The watch reserves its initial write before publishing its writer, so a newer decision follows the initial one rather than being overwritten by it; the pane map lock is released before any write.
Facts for a pane that has not entered the topology yet wait, the latest per pane and 128 panes at most, and are laid on once it enters.

Each holder reads its own screen with its agent's rules, on its own grid and title, so a pane's state is read the same whether or not it is attached ([The pane holder](#the-pane-holder)).
The engine hands a pane its rules when its agent changes (`ScreenRules`, the operator's set first and the built-in one behind it, each as its manifest's JSON), from a thread of its own (`own/rules.rs`, one pending set per pane, the newest winning), never under the topology lock or from the facts' sink; a daemon that starts again hands every agent pane its rules at its first facts, and a definitions change hands new rules only to the panes whose agent's rules changed.

A letter reads its agent from the same record (`delivery_agent`, `observed_agent`): its name, or the pane id for an agent the operator typed into a shell, its kind in Herdr's name, its session's digest, its status and sequence, and its readiness (`Launching` while it starts, `Ready` once shown).
A prompt (`prompt_agent`) refuses `agent_blocked` while the agent asks, and `agent_not_ready` while it starts or has not shown; otherwise it types the text, as one bracketed paste when the agent has turned that mode on, and Enter 300 ms later.
A session an agent's hooks report reaches the engine with the hook's status report (`Core::hook_status`, `Engine::hook_session`) and is recorded on the pane, and saved with it, when the pane runs an agent of the hook's kind; a session a start or a resume names is known from its arguments (`resumed_session` reads the foreground program's, by its definition's `[resume] session` selector, a fork's left out).
With no agent known in the pane, the report is the record of the program that holds its terminal when that is a program other than the shell, or when the holder could not say what holds it (`agents::program_may_run`), as a start's is of the agent it types: an agent typed into the shell is otherwise known only by its program's name, and a wrapper, an argument list the system would not give (a native Claude Code's process is named by its version, `2.1.318`) or an unread terminal left it unknown, its hook's session dropped, so it was missing from the core's session and nothing resumed it after a restart (with-hide/hide-private#696).
Such a record is the one a recognized agent has: it is listed, saved and resumed the same way, it ends when the shell holds the terminal again, and a program a definition names as another agent replaces it.
While the shell holds the terminal, the pane keeps only the latest hook session report in memory and takes it when a program shows: as the session of a detected agent of the same kind, or as the record of a program no definition names; a detected agent of a different kind discards it.
A new explicit start, an authoritative session assignment, or closing the pane also discards that pending report, which has no timer and is never saved or replayed for a later agent.
Nothing but Hide's own integration names a pane's session on this engine, so every supported agent's integration reports it when the session starts or the pane switches to another, before the first turn ([agent-hooks.md](agent-hooks.md#which-session-is-the-panes)).

After a reboot, a pane that ran an agent opens its new shell and resumes the agent's conversation in it (`own/restore.rs`, D-7): by `[resume] session` with the saved session, else by `[resume] last`.
The resume names its program as a start, a wake, a fork and a reopen do: by the file the pane's node starts it from (`start_prompt::start_program_file`, asked once per resume on the restore's own thread, off every lock), which on Windows is the program npm's launcher runs, since PowerShell finds npm's `.ps1` by the name and Windows PowerShell 5.1 drops the quotes inside an argument it hands on; a node that starts the program by its name (macOS, Linux, a launcher that is not npm's), does not find it, or cannot be asked leaves the name, and `shell_line::check_resume` holds the definition's words, the name first, before the file takes its place (`agent.resumed` records `by_file` and, beside it, `by_name_cause`: `starts_by_name`, `not_found` or `node_unanswered`, with the pane's id).
Every one of those asks the node about the definition's first executable, never the agent's kind, since the node looks the name up on its `PATH` and Cursor's kind (`cursor`) is not its program (`cursor-agent`), nor Kiro's (`kiro`) its first (`kiro-cli`): a restart's resume has it as its first word, and a wake, a fork, a reopen, a spawn's start, a pane's start from a task and the check before a start on a device read it from the engine (`Engine::start_program_name`, `start_prompt::program_of`, the definition as the engine reads it now, an operator's override included; the device's own engine for the device's check, `Runtime::spawn_target`).
The resume carries the model and effort Hide started the agent with (PRD engine-bundle-4-herdr-removal D-24): the engine opens with the core's launch records (`ui_state.pane_launches`, read from `core-state.json` by `EngineHandle::own` for this machine and handed by `Runtime::open_own_device_engine` for a device, keyed by the engine's pane ids), and a record is read only when it describes the saved agent by the rule a pane's row reads it by (`agent_choice::launch_describes`: the same kind, and its start name or, without one, its conversation), so the saved session format stays format 1; an agent with no such record resumes on its CLI's defaults, and a saved choice the agent does not take leaves the pane a shell with why.
The resumes are typed one pane after another once the restore has let other calls through, each once its shell is ready as every start into a shell waits for it (`agent_start::wait_for_shell`, within 30 s): a restarted pane runs the shell a pane with no program runs, so the resume waits for its first prompt's mark when that shell is the integration's (`ShellStart::of_tab` with `PaneHolders::shell_launch`), as a start into a tab the core just opened with it does, and otherwise for the shell to hold the terminal alone and take the line whole.
Until its resume is typed the agent stays the pane's saved agent (`Pane::restored`, `Restored::Resume`, in memory only and saved as the pane's agent as a resting agent is), so a daemon that ends while a dozen resumes still wait their turn leaves each to the next restore; the pass ends when the engine's owner lets it go (a device's, with its link) and nothing is lost.
A resume that could not be typed (the shell did not answer in its wait, as a machine under the load of a mass restart leaves it, or the input was refused) is tried once more after every other resume has had its turn (`RESUME_ATTEMPTS`, two tries in all, each logging `agent.resume_not_typed` with its `attempt`).
No conversation opens in two panes: a pane whose session (or, for `last`, whose agent in the same folder) another pane resumes or an adopted pane still runs stays a shell.
An adopted pane whose saved agent is not running, its shell the terminal's foreground group (`own/restore.rs`, `at_its_prompt`), is resumed as a restarted pane is: the daemon that typed its resume ended before the line reached the shell (the line then waited in the node and was dropped with the node, `service_closed`), or the agent ended while no daemon ran; a system that cannot prove the shell holds the terminal, or a holder that does not answer, leaves the pane as it is.
An agent that is not resumed for good, in a pane the restore restarted or adopted at its prompt, is no longer the pane's: the resume could not be typed in either of its two tries (the cap, whether its shell would not take it or the load had not settled yet), or the resume was typed and its program did not become the agent (it exits at once or its session is gone: the start's deadline, the one every typed start has, passed with no program shown, or the program showed and left the foreground before the start settled; a program that failed before the holder saw it is a shell the whole wait, so it is named at the deadline, and one that ran past its settle and then ended is an ordinary agent ending in its pane), or its definition is gone or says no resume, or the resume could not be typed safely, or its conversation is open elsewhere, or its folder is gone, or its new shell could not start (that pane keeps its agent for the next restore, as before).
The engine names it in the session (`ProjectionState::not_resumed`, `Restored::NotResumed`, with its pane, definition, session and why, until an agent shows in the pane) and logs `agent.not_resumed`; the core ends its registration with the watches on it and the answer waits of its letters, as a closed pane's registration ends (`Runtime::end_unresumed`, `coordination::not_resumed_registrations`, [delivery.md](delivery.md)), so `hide agent show` reads it ended instead of running with activity unknown while the pane is a shell.
A pane that is not resumed (its definition is gone or says no resume, the resume could not be typed safely, its conversation is open elsewhere, its folder is gone) opens with one line saying why, and a resume is typed so that an agent ending with a failure says so and leaves the shell (`hide: <agent> ended with a failure after its resume; this pane is a shell now.`), a line that is true both of a resume that could not open the conversation and of an agent that ran and then failed; it names no exit code, which zsh and bash spell `$?` and fish refuses, so one line runs in zsh, bash and fish (`own/shell_line.rs`, its `real_shell_tests` run in the rust lane's shell step).

Hooks reach the core from a pane on this engine through the credential its record proves: a hook's report lays its cells on the pane's state (`agent_hooks/facts.rs`, [status-model.md](status-model.md)), and the session it names is saved on the pane off the lock by the engine of the machine the pane runs on, a dialed device's own included, which knows the pane by its bare id (`Runtime::hook_session_target`, `Engine::hook_session`), so a Claude Code pane resumes its conversation by its id after a reboot and an agent spawned on a device binds its identity by it.

#### Importing a Herdr session into the core's own engine

A Herdr session already on this machine becomes the engine's in one place (PRD engine-bundle-4-herdr-removal D-3 to D-9, D-24 to D-27): `own/herdr_session.rs` reads Herdr's `session.json` (version 3 and the versions before it, read only, never written or moved) into the engine's saved session, keeping Herdr's workspace, tab and pane ids, so every Hide state keyed by them needs no new key.
A workspace whose save does not hold together is left out with its reason and the rest are imported.
Which workspaces were imported and which conversations wait are kept in the import record, `<state>/engine/herdr-import.json` (`hide_core::herdr_import`, `hide_kit::layout::herdr_import_in`); every change of a record is made under that module's one lock.
An earlier build's record may still hold a commit mark and a `not_stopped` result: both are read and ignored, so the record reads.

The import reads any Herdr's save and leaves that Herdr running beside Hide: it never stops a server, and a server on the socket only makes its conversations wait (D-8).
The save is offered from the sidebar's line, Settings, the first run and `hide import herdr [--yes]`, and the operator's answer is one event (`herdr_import {action}`: `import`, `look`, `continue`), handled on a worker off the runtime lock through the machine hided installs (`Core::set_herdr_import`, `herdr_import::Machine`).
The import is asked in the record, and hided starts the core role again (`Event::ImportRestart`); before the engine opens, `before_core` imports the asked workspaces and gives their panes' Hide state to the engine the core move's way (D-4), so the engine opens with them and restores them as a reboot does.
A core role that does not start again ends the daemon with that failure (`Halt::Failed`, as any core start that fails), and the import stays asked in the record, so the next start makes it.
A Herdr running on the socket again by then keeps its conversations: the start imports them waiting rather than resuming them (D-8).

An import while the Herdr it reads runs does not resume its conversations, since one conversation open in two places goes wrong: each such pane opens as a shell with a line saying so, and its resume waits in the record (D-8).
Once that Herdr no longer runs, the sidebar offers to resume them, and the next import gives each back to its pane: a pane whose shell holds its terminal resumes it there, and one whose pane runs something else, or whose system cannot say what runs there, resumes in a new tab of the same workspace once the restore has finished; a tab that cannot open leaves it waiting for the next import.
Until a workspace has been imported, `hide` from one of its Herdr panes is refused `pane_not_moved` with the import as the next action (`pane_auth.rs`), and its hook reports reach only the log.

An import or a reboot can end a turn an agent was in.
The restore reads each resumed pane's hook file (`hide_agent_hooks::counters::records`, by the same pane id) and marks a resume whose agent's last turn was running or waiting on the operator; when the resumed agent's hook names its session, `Engine::hook_session` answers true once, and the core sends that agent one letter from `hide:transition` saying its work was cut off (`runtime/transition_letters.rs`, D-22), once it is the agent seen in its pane and within 10 minutes; an agent that was resting gets none.
Only a resume so marked is typed on this machine: an agent whose turn had ended is left resting, since a machine that ran dozens of agents started them all at once after a reboot (2026-11-06, 42 resumes on a machine at load 324), and none was waited on.
Its pane opens as a shell, the engine keeps the agent on the pane (`Restored::Resting`), saved as the pane's agent so a daemon that ends before the core's record is on disk, or the next reboot, finds it again, and names it in the session (`ProjectionState::resting`) until an agent shows in the pane, by a start, its hook or its foreground (a start whose input is refused gives it back).
The core's local coordinator turns each into a sleeping agent before it ingests that session (`Runtime::adopt_resting`), once per pane with no record: the record is made from the row the agent would have had, labels laid on, with the conversation the restore would have resumed even where no label proves it, and with no sequence, so any agent the pane lists later wakes it; nothing is ended.
A start the engine typed whose program has not shown (`start_unshown`, which ends when it shows or at the start's deadline) wakes no sleep record, this one or any other, since a wake's own start is listed before its input is delivered and a refused or failed wake must still find its record to say why; a program that shows wakes it even while its start waits on a question it asks, so the operator's keys reach it.
A visit or a letter wakes it into its conversation as it wakes any sleeper ([agent sleep](#agent-sleep) above).
A device's resumes, whose hook files the core does not read, a given-back conversation that opens a tab of its own, one with no session to wake into, and an agent whose sleep closes its pane or that cannot sleep are typed as before.
A device's engine reads no hook files (`Place::hooks_home`), since they are on the device.

A dialed device of that engine imports the same way, by its node (D-10, B18; `hide_core::herdr_import::device`).
Before the device's engine opens on a link, the core asks the node for the device's save and whether a server runs on its default socket (`Call::HerdrSave`); the node reads them with `hide-host/src/herdr_save.rs`, the code this machine's daemon reads with, so every system a node runs on reads the save alike.
Each device's offer shows under its id while that link lasts (`status.herdr_import_devices`, `herdr_import {action, device}`).
An import is recorded in the device's `<state>/engine/devices/<device>/herdr-import.json`, the save the node read is kept beside it with the device's machine id (`herdr-save.json`, `hide_kit::layout::herdr_save_kept_in`), and the core role starts again; `before_core` imports each kept save before any link is up and gives the imported panes' registrations their pane ids, keeping the device id as their scope.
A device whose machine id the core could not read is not looked at, since its registrations could not be told apart.

## Desk

Desk (PRD Desk 1차) is a room where the operator talks to an agent they choose, one of the agents switched on in Settings › Agents, over ACP, and that agent starts and follows real sessions through the `hide` CLI.
Three parts hold it, each with one job.

- `hide-desk` is the ACP boundary and keeps no state: the ndjson JSON-RPC connection (`rpc.rs`, a line capped at 8 MiB and 16 calls waiting), the session in each adapter's ask mode (`session.rs`), each catalog agent's ACP route, ask mode and pin (`adapter.rs`, which lists the agents of `hide-agent-adapter`'s catalog that start in a pane, and `contracts/desk-adapters/` for the npm adapters), the npm adapters' install (`install.rs`), the process (`host.rs`), the permission rule (`permission.rs`) and Desk's own Codex home with its link to the operator's sign-in (`codex.rs`).
- The core owns the room: the conversation, the choices, the approval cards and the one Desk process (`hide-core/src/runtime/desk.rs`, its worker in `desk/worker.rs`), its store `~/.hide/state/desk/desk.json` written off the lock (`hide-core/src/desk.rs`), and the `desk`, `desk_live`, `desk_jobs` and `desk_mentions` snapshot sections.
  Settings › Labs › Desk's switch (`settings.enabled`, off by default and in a store written before it existed, D-76) is kept there too: while it is off the worker looks at no agent, every `desk_*` event but `desk_settings_set` is refused as `desk_off`, and so no process starts; turning it off ends the process as `다시 시작` does, and turning it on looks at every agent again and downloads every npm adapter not in place at once (D-80), so choosing an agent never waits on a download.
  Each download is an `npm ci` on a thread of its own, started tied to hided (`run_to_end_tied`), so it ends with hided however hided ends; turning Desk off stops every download under way (`Order::Off`), and a stopped or failed one removes its staging folder before it reports, so nothing writes into `~/.hide/desk-adapters` once Desk is off.
  The agent list is the catalog's agents the kit has switched on for this machine (D-79), plus a chosen one since switched off, shown `off` and not sent to; each carries the sign-in Hide AI's provider row for it reads (D-81): `needs_login` is signed out, `ready` or `usage_limited` with its login checked is signed in, anything else unread, the same rows Settings › Agents words, and an adapter in place never reads as signed in.
  The list is composed again when the kit's agents or those rows change (`desk_catalog_moved`), and Desk asks Hide AI to read the catalog when it is turned on.
  Desk's queue keeps its waiting spawns while it is off and starts none (`desk_start_next`), and turning it on starts them in order; the shell tells the desktop host the switch (`hide:desk`), whose app menu carries `desk_terminal` only while it is on, and the shell's own `openDesk` and `deskTerminal` refuse while it is off, whichever menu or chord asks.
- hided gives the process its identity (`hided/src/desk_host.rs`): a capability bound to the process's pid and start time (`Binding::Desk` in `pane_auth.rs`), whose reference file is all the process's `HIDE_CAP_REF` names.

The worker is the process's one owner (engineering practice: resident processes).
Every ACP call, install and file check runs on it, never under `Mutex<Runtime>`; what it learns reaches the runtime as a report under a short lock.
The agent's own messages queue to the worker; past 4096 waiting, reply text is dropped and logged once, while requests and answers still queue, since the agent waits on them.
After each turn the tree is measured, and past 48 processes or 4 GiB it ends, which the room shows as stopped with `다시 시작`.
The process starts tied to hided, so it and everything it started end with hided however hided ends.
A program a tool opens as an application through LaunchServices on macOS is launchd's child and never in the tree: open-computer-use's app agent, which every client of the account shares on one socket under `TMPDIR`, is one, and it stays when Desk's agent ends, as it does when an agent in a pane ends.

A failed turn reads `답을 끝내지 못했어요` with the agent's own one-line reason when the agent answered with an error (a provider's refusal, a model it cannot reach), and with none when nothing the operator can act on is known (no answer, the stream's end); every failed turn is logged as `desk.turn_failed` with the error and the last line the adapter wrote to its error output.
A turn the agent refuses for its sign-in (ACP's `auth_required`, as OpenCode answers for a provider with no key) is the open's refusal: the message goes back to the operator's input with the agent's sign-in command, and the process ends, so the next message starts one that reads the sign-in and the environment again.

The process starts with the environment an agent the operator starts in a terminal has (`hide-desk/src/host.rs`): what it keeps of hided's own (the login variables, the shell, the language and the network route a Dock launch may set), then the account's environment as a new terminal gets it (`programs::account_environment`: every variable the login shell exports on macOS and Linux, read by the same ask that gives the account's `PATH` and kept until a startup file changes, so a start asks no shell of its own; the sign-in's environment on Windows), then Desk's own (`PATH` with `hide` first, its capability, each agent's settings), which win.
So a provider key or setting an agent's own configuration reads from the environment (OpenCode's `{env:BAI_API_KEY}`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`) reaches Desk's agent as it reaches one in a pane, whether hided started from the Dock, which lacks what the startup files export, or from a terminal; the rest of hided's own environment stays out, since a terminal's carries that terminal's session.
No `HERDR_*` and no `HIDE_*` reaches it from either side but its capability, so no pane hook reads it as a pane's session and it is no pane, row or Memory session.
Its working folder is `~/.hide/state/desk/work`, which no checkout holds, so no project's settings or instructions load into it.

Each adapter is held in its ask mode, which ignores the operator's global auto-allow (D-53):

- Claude's session starts with no setting source of the operator's (`settingSources: []`, so no `~/.claude` allow rule, default mode, hook, `CLAUDE.md` or skill), `Bash`, `Read`, `Glob` and `Grep` always asked (`CLAUDE_ASKS` in `hide-desk/src/adapter.rs`) and edits asked by default, its own `EnterPlanMode` denied (entering plan mode asks nothing and leaves the ask mode, which would end the session as one that cannot ask), and `session/set_mode default`; its sign-in is the CLI's own.
- Codex starts in `read-only` (`INITIAL_AGENT_MODE`), whose sandbox refuses writes and the network, including the loopback hided listens on; a command that stays inside that sandbox changes nothing and runs without asking, so it never reaches Hide and the `파일 읽기·검색` and `그 밖의 셸 명령` rows cannot ask for it.
  It runs with Desk's own `CODEX_HOME`, `~/.hide/state/desk/codex` (`hide_kit::layout::desk_codex_home`, `hide-desk/src/codex.rs`), so it reads none of the operator's `~/.codex`: no global `AGENTS.md`, skill, MCP server, hook or rule.
  Before every start Desk writes that home's `config.toml` (commands run with the process's own `PATH`, not a login shell's or a snapshot of one, so the `hide` beside hided is the one that runs; no skill catalog or project instruction file reaches the model) and `rules/hide-desk.rules`, which holds no rule, so an `allow` rule an older Hide wrote there is gone.
  A rule cannot follow the 권한 table: Codex reads its rules once per session, matches a line with a redirection whole, and runs a command a rule lets through still inside the sandbox, where hided's loopback is refused.
  So Desk's instructions ask the agent to run every `hide` command with escalated permissions; Codex asks Hide, the table answers, and an allowed escalation runs outside the sandbox.
  Its command shell is not a login shell but still reads the shell's always-read startup file (`~/.zshenv`), so one that sets `PATH` outright, rather than adding to it, hides the `hide` Desk put first.
  The core refuses a Desk spawn that carries words for the agent's own CLI (`desk_spawn_args`) for every Desk agent, since those words can lift the new session's permissions.
  Codex keeps its sign-in in that home (`auth.json`), so Desk makes that file a link to the operator's own (`$CODEX_HOME/auth.json`, or `~/.codex/auth.json`: Codex's default account as `CODEX_HOME` moves it, [Agent profiles and accounts](#agent-profiles-and-accounts); a relative `CODEX_HOME` refuses the start with that reason) before every start, as Hide AI's Codex homes do (D-81): Codex follows a linked `auth.json` and refreshes through it, and refuses a hard link, while a copy would leave Desk signed in apart from the operator.
  A Windows account that cannot make a file link cannot start Desk's Codex ([INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md#what-each-system-supports)); an operator not signed in gets `login_needed` with `codex login`.
- Pi has no mode, so Desk loads an extension of its own (`hide-desk/src/pi_desk.js`, through a launcher `PI_ACP_PI_COMMAND` names) that asks through `ctx.ui.confirm` before every tool call, reads included, so the table decides them; its marker, naming a pid under the Desk process, proves it loaded, and without it the session is not used.
- OpenCode runs `opencode acp` with Hide's permission configuration in `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`, every tool asking but reading, listing and searching files, which OpenCode merges over the operator's own configuration, so an allow-everything setting there does not apply.
- omp runs `omp --mode acp --approval-mode always-ask --no-extensions --no-skills --no-rules`; its own file tool fails over ACP without asking, so it edits only through a shell command, which asks.
- Antigravity runs `agy acp`, which asks before a command or an edit as it starts; its command request carries the command as `CommandLine` and the folder as `Cwd`, which the permission rule reads with the other agents' `command` and `cwd`.
- Grok has no ask mode Hide can hold (`AskMode` is none): over ACP it starts in an automatic mode taken from the operator's own settings, which nothing on its command line or over ACP changes, and only a Grok home of Desk's own would, whose sign-in could not stay the operator's since Grok replaces `auth.json` by rename.
  Desk lists it as `no_ask_mode` and never starts it ([INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md#what-each-system-supports)).

What an agent runs without asking, whatever a row says, is declared with it (`AdapterId::always_runs` in `hide-desk/src/adapter.rs`, sent as each agent's `always_runs` in the `desk` section), and Settings › Labs › Desk › 권한 shows it dimmed on that row: reads and searches for Codex, OpenCode, omp and Antigravity.

A session whose mode cannot be set, or that leaves its mode, is ended and the agent shown as `no_ask_mode`.
What the agent asks to run is decided in two steps (D-82, D-83).
The Desk worker reads the request into a row of Settings › Labs › Desk › 권한 and the irreversible facts its words carry (`hide_desk::permission::classify`); a request Hide cannot read, or answer with a one-time allowance, does not run (D-60).
`classify` reads text only: it follows each shell line's commands with how each follows the last (`&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`) and the subshells it runs in (`hide_shell::ShellLine::joins`, `scopes`, `bodies`), keeps every folder the shell may be in for each command, and keeps `..` in the paths it names; what it cannot read is the irreversible kind `Unreadable`: a program outside its table of known programs (`KNOWN`, the `git` subcommands of `GIT_SUBS`, the wrappers it reads through), an option of a known one that runs a command (`Known::runs`, `GitSub::runs`), code for a shell it does not get, a program named by its path, a function, `time`, `coproc` or `exec` before a command, and a line that changes the environment (D-89, so the set of what runs unasked is the table, not what Hide failed to recognize), and a path deleted or overwritten after a command that may make a link is one it cannot name; the paths a line overwrites or moves away (its write redirections, `hide_shell::ShellLine::writes`, and the files `KNOWN`'s `Written` and output flags name) are read the same way as its deletions (D-90).
The worker then follows the links on the way to each deleted or overwritten path, an overwritten one to the end, since writing a link writes where it leads (`permission::follow_links`, through `hide_platform::fs::identity::canonical`), which reads the disk, so it runs there and never under `Mutex<Runtime>`; a project registered through a link of its own reads as outside, which asks rather than allows.
The runtime then decides with `permission::decide`, from the table (`DeskSettings::permissions`, kept in `desk.json`), what only it knows (whether an archived session's tree is working, whether a path is inside a project of this machine) and the kinds allowed in this conversation: a request nothing asks about is answered with its one-time allowance at once, and otherwise a card waits with its asks, irreversible kinds first.
The irreversible set is data in `hide-desk/src/permission.rs` (principle 13), and a row's change applies from the next request.
`이 대화에서 계속 허용` adds the card's asks to the conversation's allowed set, which the Desk process's end clears (`새 대화`, `다시 시작`, the process stopping).
`한 번 허용` on a card that archives a working session leaves a grant the archive takes, so `hide agent archive` from Desk is confirmed; the turn's end drops an unused grant.
`거절…` with a line refuses, cancels the turn, and at the turn's end sends the line to the agent framed as the operator's refusal (`hide_desk::refusal_message`), at most 2048 bytes.
`allow_always` is never chosen.
A new conversation, a restart, a stop or the process's end closes every waiting card as a refusal (D-52).

The instructions the agent gets are code-owned (`hide-desk/src/instructions.md`): its role, the `hide` commands it acts with, and to answer in the operator's language.
They go before the first message of a session that starts new, with the conversation so far when the operator switched agents (at most 64 KiB, the oldest left out).
The ACP session id is kept, so the next start loads it (`session/load`) when the adapter can; one that cannot be loaded starts new with the conversation carried, and says so.

The conversation keeps 500 items and 2 MiB of text, dropping the oldest; a message is at most 64 KiB and a reply 256 KiB.
The reply being written is its own section, `desk_live`, so a streamed chunk resends that text alone and never the conversation; the cards (`desk_jobs`) and the `@` menu (`desk_mentions`) are sections of their own for the same reason, so a session's change moves only them.
A publish whose rows moved builds the cards once, from one index of the archive, rows, devices, plans, missions and open Views, and sends a section only when it differs.

## Herdr an earlier Hide left on a machine

No package carries Herdr, and nothing Hide runs starts, adopts or hands over a Herdr server: every pane runs in its holder on the core's own engine ([The pane holder](#the-pane-holder)).
What an earlier Hide left is handled in two places, each a read path for an operator who skipped versions: the import of the Herdr session's saved work into the engine ([Importing a Herdr session into the core's own engine](#importing-a-herdr-session-into-the-cores-own-engine)), and the records and files an earlier build wrote that this build still reads ([agent-hooks.md](agent-hooks.md#herdrs-integration-an-earlier-hide-installed)).
This build takes nothing of Herdr's off a machine: an earlier build's Herdr copies under `<helper root>/herdr` on a device and its Herdr integration entries in agent hook files stay where they are, and the removal of a device or of Hide does not touch them (`hide-host/src/kit.rs`, `hide_kit::record`).
A device helper of an earlier build kept its pinned Herdr in `<helper root>/herdr/<id>/herdr`; the folder is left for the operator to delete once no Herdr server runs from it.

## hided and the WebSocket boundary

`hided` is the product daemon that owns one `hide-core::Core` on its creating thread.
Axum workers send dispatch and snapshot commands over a channel; they never call `Core::create`, `dispatch_bytes`, `snapshot_delta`, `on_change` or drop the handle from another thread.
It binds `127.0.0.1` only.
The WebSocket handshake is the client's first JSON frame `{token, schema_version, snapshot_format?, have_revision?, have_terminal_sequence?, have_terminal_epoch?}`.
Schema 2 clients that request `snapshot_format: "semantic-rest-v1"` receive `rest_format: "semantic-rest-v1"` on snapshot payloads: a delta replaces only fields it carries, merging navigator, terminal and status by their direct fields, while arrays replace as complete ordered lists.
Omission retains a value, `null` clears an optional value and an empty array or map clears a collection; `workspace_view` is explicitly null when absent in this format.
Without the capability, schema 2 keeps the supported complete-rest delta, including the omitted absent `workspace_view`; an unknown format is refused with `schema_mismatch` before snapshot delivery.
A mismatched token, Origin, or schema version, or a ninth concurrent client, is closed with a reason code (`invalid_token`, `origin_not_allowed`, `schema_mismatch`, `client_limit`) and a diagnostic log line.
The web shell follows a new token in its address by retiring the previous socket's pending file reads with `socket_closed` and clearing its browser-comment state before opening the successor; the previous socket's late close cannot reject the successor's reads.
After a valid handshake the daemon reads from the revision the client sent (`have_revision`, the cursor `Core::snapshot_delta_payload` takes), and then one delta frame per core notification burst.
A client with cursor 0 gets a self-contained `snapshot`; a reconnecting client resumes with a `delta` that carries only what changed while it was away.
When the core cannot serve the cursor, because the client's revision is ahead of the core's after a daemon restart, the daemon re-reads from zero and sends a `snapshot` (`server::classify_frame` owns that rule).
Terminal output comes beside those frames from the hub (see The terminal path): a client given a delta resumes every pane from `have_terminal_sequence` when `have_terminal_epoch` names this hub, or, naming none or another hub's, has every pane drawn again; a client given a whole snapshot resets its terminals and is told its new cursor in a `terminal` frame with no chunks.
A frame the daemon cannot produce at all (the core owner thread gone or a transport encoding failure) ends that client's loop, which the browser sees as a bare close and answers by reconnecting; the daemon logs it as `ws.snapshot_failed` with the stage, the only trace of why.
The web shell counts snapshots (`viewGeneration`) and re-requests its terminal view on each one, so a resync redraws the pane instead of trusting what it had drawn.
The token comparison is constant in the token's length (`subtle`), so a refusal does not leak how much of the token a caller guessed.
The Workspace CLI uses the same `/ws` for checkout-scoped commands and results, without giving an agent the shell's unrestricted token or snapshot stream.
Its local bootstrap socket lives in a random private short directory under `/tmp` (the account's temporary folder on Windows, where the path names a pipe and its marker file) so a long state path cannot exceed the Unix socket limit or let another user reserve a predictable path.
A Windows pipe name is global rather than inside that folder, so every client connect checks that the pipe it reached belongs to its own account and refuses one another account holds (`hide_platform::ipc`).
An owner-only record in `pane-capabilities` publishes the socket path atomically; daemon shutdown removes both.
It attests the kernel peer PID and issues a protected file reference, or answers one of the three typed hook reads described below; it accepts no control command, and nothing in the request chooses a Workspace.
Attestation binds a local caller one of two ways, tried in this order (`hided/src/pane_auth.rs`, which issues the credential from the kernel facts the node reads in `hide-node/src/pane_proof.rs`: the pane's shell, descent, the caller's folder, a process's start and the bootstrap socket).
A peer that descends from the shell of the pane named in `HIDE_PANE_ID` (the program the pane's record names, [The core's own engine](#the-cores-own-engine)) gets a pane-bound credential: it records the device, Workspace, checkout, pane terminal identity, and shell process birth, all checked again for each command, so closing or recreating the pane invalidates it (`pane_changed`).
A local peer whose pane attestation does not succeed, because it is not such a descendant, names no pane at all, or names one that the engine cannot confirm, is bound by its working directory instead: hided reads the peer's cwd from the kernel (`proc_pidinfo` with `PROC_PIDVNODEPATHINFO` on macOS, `/proc/<pid>/cwd` on Linux), canonicalizes it, and the core resolves the longest registered, connected checkout path that contains it.
That checkout-bound credential records the device, Workspace, and checkout, and each command rechecks only that the checkout is still registered and its device connected (`checkout_not_registered` otherwise); an unreadable cwd is refused `caller_unavailable`, and a cwd outside every registered checkout is refused `checkout_not_registered`.
This is what lets a Codex tool shell run by the shared `codex app-server` daemon, whose parent is launchd rather than any pane, drive the Workspace of the checkout it runs in; a caller on a device, through its node, is still attested by pane only, except on the screen machine of a core on another machine, whose node proves a caller in no pane by its working directory as well (`NodeEvent::CheckoutProof`) and the core binds it to that node's own checkout only on the link that node dialed (PRD core-host-node-remote-core D-10).
The checkout-bound credential covers the Workspace commands (file, diff, browser, view, workspace info); delivery and agent commands (`hide request`, `inbox`, `watch`, `agent`) act as one agent and refuse it `agent_pane_required`, because only a pane-bound credential names that agent, and a pane hint never stands in for it; `workspace info` lists their capabilities for a pane-bound caller only ([delivery.md](delivery.md#commands-and-caller-identity)).
A pane on an SSH device reaches the same `/ws` through that device's node link, with no other connection to the daemon (PRD core-host-node B18, B19).
