Right after the link's hello, the core asks the node to start its pane service (`Call::PanesStart`, `hide-host/src/panes.rs`), which binds the device's bootstrap endpoint (a Unix socket, a named pipe and its marker file on Windows) in a fresh `bridge-*` folder under `workspace-bridges` in the device's state folder (`~/.hide/state` unless `HIDE_STATE_DIR` or `XDG_STATE_HOME` names another, resolved by `hide_kit::layout` on both the node and the device's `hide`); several daemons may have one device open, so each node keeps its own folder, and a starting service removes the folders of services that ended without removing theirs (a killed node, or the workspace bridge an older Hide ran) once their socket no longer answers.
The device's panes run the `hide` installed beside its helper (see Device file hosts), which bootstraps through each such endpoint when no daemon answers on its own machine.
The node proves each caller with its own kernel, the peer pid descended from the shell that runs the named pane, and sends the proof up as an event (`hide_node_link::panes::NodeEvent::PaneProof`); a pane's program can ask before its holder wrote that it runs, so the node waits for a start under way to settle (`PaneHolders::proof_once_started`, at most `hide_node_link::holders::PROOF_START_WAIT`, 500 ms, well under the shortest hook budget, since every hook asks through this proof, and logs `pane.proof.start_wait` with the pane when it does) and answers a pane still starting then `pane_starting` with "run the same command again in a moment", never `pane_not_found` (with-hide/hide-private#719); hided resolves the pane within that node's own device, whatever the proof names, issues the credential bound to that node and that link (`hided/src/node_panes.rs`), and answers down (`Call::PaneProofAnswer`); the node writes the reference file, which names the node's socket rather than a port (`pane_auth::Route::Node`).
A command's bytes travel the same link as a stream: the device's `hide` opens the node's socket with a `{"stream":true,"token":"…"}` line, the node relays its bytes up as `StreamOpen`/`StreamData`/`StreamClosed` events and writes what comes down (`Call::StreamWrite`, `Call::StreamClose`), and hided serves each stream as a `/ws` connection that accepts only a credential the same node vouched for over the same link.
For that stream's single command the node selects the reference it issued for the prelude's token, reads its pane's record, checks the kernel peer still descends from the pane's shell, and sends the current identity with `StreamOpen` (`hide_node_link::panes::StreamCaller`).
A persistent reference uses the same proof as a one-shot reference; a one-shot additionally requires its holder's pid and start to match the peer, and an older prelude without a token can select only that peer's one-shot reference.
The token only selects the reference, never substitutes for the peer proof; hided takes the identity only for a credential that same node vouched for over that same link and for the pane it names (`pane_auth::remote_identity`).
The proof belongs to one command, never to the reference's eight-hour life: an identity change between stream open and that command remains the same observation window as a one-shot call, and after the core's normal ten-second inspection budget from receipt it asks `PaneInspect` again, including time spent waiting for the handshake or executor.
Ten seconds is the existing scoped first-request and pane-inspection budget, not a new credential lifetime; the scoped connection admits one command and cannot spend that proof on a second one.
The clock starts when the core receives the proof, so an identity change can remain unseen for the node-to-core delivery delay plus less than that budget before validation; this is not a ten-second bound measured on the node's clock.
The node's five-second reference sweep can revoke an ended shell earlier, but it checks file and process survival rather than every terminal identity field, so it is not a substitute for the fresh proof or inspection.
A browser relay uses the proof for its one admission only; after admission its existing claimed connection and display lease govern its lifetime, and retaining a persistent reference does not retain this proof for its next connection.
A stream that carries none, from a peer the node cannot match, is checked against the pane as the node reads it when the command arrives (`Call::PaneInspect`), and a pane whose identity changed is refused `pane_changed` before the core's context is read.
Because the node a credential belongs to is the link it arrived on, never a field of a message, one device's node cannot vouch for another device's pane, and closing or losing the link revokes everything it vouched for at once.
The pane service and that `hide` run on Windows too, and the node reads the account's home there from `USERPROFILE`, on a Windows device as on this machine ([A device's ssh](#a-devices-ssh)).
The node's paths cross the link in the wire spelling (`hide_platform::path`): the endpoint and each reference it answers with, which the device's `hide` reads back with `from_wire`, as it does the reference hided's own bootstrap answers.
A link carries at most eight streams and holds at most 64 chunks of 48 KiB for one; a node serves sixteen callers at once and hided works on 32 proofs across every device, refusing the rest `bridge_busy`; a starting or failing pane service is a `remote_host` record (`host.panes_started`, `host.panes_unstarted`) and a stream that overflows a `node_panes` record in `Logs/core.jsonl`, since a detached daemon's stderr goes nowhere.
Proofs run on hided's blocking executor with a permit held through queued and running work; every callback returns without waiting on its SSH reader's own link.
Reader-callback refusal and stream-close replies have a separate allowance of 32 queued plus running jobs across the daemon, held until the reply finishes on that executor.
If that allowance is full, hided records `pane.refused` with `control_full` and closes only the offending link through its nonblocking close path, marking its credentials dead immediately and waking normal reader cleanup and reconnect.
A reply that fails records `control_unanswered` and closes its link too; dropping a job releases its permit on every exit path.
Every caller turned away is a `pane.refused` record there with the node, the pane it named and the reason it read (B30): one hided refuses itself (`by: core`), and one the device's node refuses on its own, at its caller or stream cap included, which the node reports up the link (`NodeEvent::Refused`, `by: node`) with its fields cut to a bounded prefix, because a device's stderr reaches no log.
Inside the core both credentials are one caller id in the pane slot (`workspace_control::Caller`): a pane id, or `checkout:<nonce>:<canonical path>`, so action retry records are per capability and no core query or action depends on which binding issued it.
A desktop window's browser gateway acts as `gateway:<key>:<canonical path>`, one key per window, which resolves like a checkout caller; only whether its open comes forward reads the difference (`caller_stays_behind`).
Each checkout-bound issuance and refusal is one `pane_auth` record in the diagnostics log with the device, checkout, reason, whether the credential was persistent, and at bootstrap the peer pid (a command's WebSocket carries none), never the caller's path or the reference bytes.
Direct CLI calls own one-shot credentials and release them after their request, while repeated agent session starts in the same attested pane, or from the same checkout, reuse one reference until its pane ends or the eight-hour limit expires.
Only that persistent reference is claimed (`workspace_claim`, then the `.claimed` marker), which lets it outlive its unclaimed 30 seconds; a one-shot command sends no claim and closes after its answer, since the daemon revokes a one-shot token when its connection ends, and a `hide browser` relay, which the daemon starts only for a claimed credential, claims whatever its credential (`workspace_cli::AfterAnswer`).
A command whose `HIDE_CAP_REF` names a reference the daemon no longer holds bootstraps a one-shot credential once, exactly as a bare command does, and runs on it (`workspace_cli::Credential`): the reference's file is gone because it expired or was revoked, nothing listens on its port because the daemon that issued it crashed, the daemon closes the handshake `invalid_token` because it never issued that token, or it refuses the token `credential_expired` before running the command; a reference file left empty, as a power loss leaves one written without a flush, reads as gone too.
The fallback passes the same attestation, so it carries no authority a bare `hide` would not get, and a bootstrap refusal is the command's answer with the bootstrap's next step.
Once a Workspace action result has reached the CLI, a lost acknowledgement of a persistent reference's claim cannot turn that result into a claim that the action was not applied; the claim failure is logged and a later command rechecks its capability.
Hook reads (`hide inbox --hook`, `hide workspace memory` and SessionStart's `hide workspace info --hook`) and the status report use one proof-and-answer exchange through the bootstrap socket on both the core and a node, without a WebSocket upgrade; the hook helper sends them itself through the same client those commands use (`hide_agent_hooks::hook_request`), never by starting `hide` ([agent-hooks.md](agent-hooks.md#what-the-hook-returns-and-reports-back)).
`hide_node_link::panes::HookCommand` (defined in `hide_agent_hooks::hook_request`, under the node link) admits `LetterPull`, `Memory`, `Status` and read-only `WorkspaceInfo`; a Workspace action, a letter send or confirmation, and a browser command cannot be represented on this route.
The caller selects one live route before sending, refuses ambiguous node bridges before sending to any, and never retries a sent request through another transport.
A node sends the typed command with its fresh kernel proof over its own link (NodeLink protocol 31); the core reuses the same credential issuance, validation, delivery executor and Memory lookup as the Workspace route.
Letter and Memory requests own fresh one-shot tokens, held internally and revoked on every return and unwind before their answers are sent; a local reference file is removed with them and a node creates no reference file.
Workspace guidance returns its read-only info and the same persistent reference previously obtained by bootstrap followed by info, with unchanged capabilities and lifetime.
The core claims that reference after the local answer is written or the node accepts its proof answer; a late node answer cannot claim it, and a failed delivery removes only newly issued authority.
The node owns the private file and its claimed marker, removes newly created files on failure, and revokes their token over its own link.
A named reference, when still live, must match the freshly proved pane identity and checkout, and on a node must have been vouched for by that same node and link; it is a constraint on the proof, never a replacement for it.
Letter and Memory reads do not extend a named reference's unclaimed lifetime; an expired reference takes the fresh proof in this same exchange, as a bare caller does.
The same ten-second receipt-age bound applies to a pane proof queued at the core, with a fresh `PaneInspect` after it, and link closure revokes its credentials.
The request and answer are bounded at 16 KiB and 64 KiB, with one answer per local connection, the existing eight local bootstrap workers, sixteen node callers and thirty-two core proof workers.
The two prompt children remain independent and parallel, with their own caller deadlines; the Memory Project is still read from its owning node on every lookup because no existing watcher invalidates all identity facts.
The old scoped Workspace wire still accepts these reads for already-running local clients; the current hook CLI uses only the proof exchange.
The registry has a 64-reference cap, the bootstrap path has an eight-worker cap, and daemon shutdown revokes every reference.
The five-second sweep also drops a checkout-bound reference whose checkout no longer resolves on its device, with a `sweep`-stage `pane_auth` record, so an unregistered project stops counting against the cap before its eight hours end.
A command whose answer no longer matches its credential is refused by the credential's own binding: `pane_changed` for a pane, `checkout_not_registered` for a checkout, each with the next step that binding can take.
The shell handshake marks actual web and desktop renderer connections with `client_kind`; Workspace commands refuse when only the daemon or another CLI client is connected.
Checkout-scoped `hide view select`, `split`, `move`, and `close` resolve the live device and checkout in the core, then apply one existing View layout transition without using the front Workspace as an authorization shortcut.
They leave keyboard pane focus alone; a last View holding an unsaved document refuses close, while a second View of the same document may close by itself.
One request ID carries an action result for up to ten minutes, and the 128-result cap refuses new commands instead of evicting an answer that a retry may need; a second intent uses a new ID.
The CLI returns the request ID on uncertain transport outcomes so the caller can retry that same action or inspect `hide view list`.
File and working-diff opens resolve a caller-cwd path on the calling machine, then use the checkout's existing host channel to read a document or Git status off the core lock.
The core rechecks the caller's checkout membership when it places the result into that checkout's View tree; a missing file, unavailable host, unchanged diff, or layout refusal has a request-scoped CLI outcome.
No open moves the front Workspace, the visible tab or the keyboard pane; an open or select from the operator's own pane, the selected pane of the front Workspace, brings its View forward and opens that Workspace's lane on Files (`AreaIntent::Files`), raising `lane_called` so the page puts it up, and from any other caller the lane keeps its state.
`hide browser open` requires a connected desktop renderer and places a Browser View in the caller's checkout with the same bounded retry result as other actions.
The core checks HTML paths against the caller device's checkout and reads them outside its lock through the consented host channel.
The native host reports page load, completion, failure, and eviction with a load stamp; `hide view status` and `--wait` distinguish page state from View placement.
The desktop host creates pages only when a View has a visible slot, so waiting on a hidden View expires without taking focus.
For a remote Browser View, the desktop host asks hided for the current core-owned address and a route bound to its own process, View, and load stamp.
A remote loopback URL gets a forward through the device's node link with bounded connections (`hided/src/page_forward.rs`), while a remote HTML file gets an owner-only loopback server whose assets are read through the device host's pinned checkout root.
Neither route falls back to this Mac's same path or port; close, device loss, or desktop process exit releases the route.
Client frames are core events (`schema_version`, `kind`, `payload`).
HTTP serves static assets, `GET /health` (`pid`, `version`, `build`, `schema_version`, `clients`), and token-authenticated Browser route resolution and release for the desktop host.
The same desktop authentication registers and releases its process-bound private CDP gateway at `/browser-control`; the pane's scoped `browser_connect` query discovers a checkout capability without receiving either private token (`hided/src/browser_control.rs`).
`/browser-control/action` accepts only browser open, close and select from that registered desktop process and routes them through Workspace prepare/read/commit, not the shell's unrestricted event dispatcher.
`hide browser` page commands reach a display through the same `/ws`: the CLI's scoped request `browser_relay` names a display, hided runs `browser_connect`'s checkout and display checks, connects to the desktop gateway itself, and answers with the display id and whether it is its area's selected View, so the capability URL never reaches the CLI (`hided/src/browser_relay.rs`).
After the CLI claims its credential, the socket carries CDP text frames both ways until either side closes; the gateway's close code and reason reach the CLI unchanged.
A display shown only in the window of a node that dialed its core is relayed by that node's daemon instead: a caller on that node is answered a one-shot relay URL on its own daemon and dials it after the claim, and the core relays any other caller through the node's link ([A core on another machine](#a-core-on-another-machine)); every relay logs `relay.ended` with where its CDP ran and the bytes it carried.
The relay runs in the connection's own task, outside `Mutex<Runtime>`, and changes no core state or snapshot wire.
At most four relays run at once (`browser_relay_limit` past that), because each holds one of hided's eight client connections and half stay free for the shell and other clients.
A message is at most 4 MiB and a binary frame is refused, both closing with 4009; a relay closes with 4008 after 60 seconds without a CDP text frame in either direction (pings do not count) or after five minutes whatever it carries, and a peer that does not take a frame within five seconds ends it.
A close other than a normal one is logged as a `browser_relay` record with the display and the code.
A device pane reaches the same `/ws` through its node-link stream, so its commands take the same path and refusals as a local pane's.
The CDP client, the frame routing and the command flow live in `hided/src/browser_page/`, and the page-side code it evaluates in `hided/assets/browser/` ([BROWSER_DISPLAYS.md](BROWSER_DISPLAYS.md#agent-page-commands)).
New CDP targets name their existing View area and create a distinct display there; default CLI opens retain URL deduplication and active-area placement.
The native inventory carries each browser's area ID from the core-owned layout, including background Workspaces.
Positive browser area scopes ride the same revisioned projection, including empty areas, and require a currently connected catalog checkout.
The core preserves each area's incarnation only while its authority remains present; a revoke/regrant changes it even if snapshot coalescing hides the intervening absence.
The shell only forwards them; the native gateway permanently retires capabilities whose scope disappears or changes incarnation, distinct from closing a page in a still-authorized area.
No HTTP request dispatches a core event.
The first frame after a valid handshake is `daemon` (`version`, `pid`, `schema_version`, `host_name`, the state paths, the idle policy); Settings > About reads it, and it never carries the token.
The daemon owns the core's four observation flags, the Settings one (`ai_settings.observing`, which runs the provider probe and the hook diagnosis), a start surface's (`ai_settings.start_observing`, which runs the provider probe alone), the Sessions tool's (`request_view.observing`, which re-reads running checks, below) and a window's focus (`window_focus.focused`, sent by a window that holds the keyboard on the Workspace screen, so the View in front of any such window is seen; [status-model.md](status-model.md#a-view-to-look-at)): a client's hint is only that connection's demand (`hided/src/demand.rs`, one `ObservationDemand` per flag), each flag follows its first observer in and its last one out, and a connection that closes releases every demand, so a closed tab never leaves a probe or a re-read running.
While Sessions is observed, the local coordinator's GitHub step asks the runtime once a minute (`Runtime::reread_pending_checks`) to raise the generation of each project a row's live pull request has running checks in, so the existing reader reads only those again and a finished run moves its row without a new turn (PRD overview-request-view D-32); a node's project whose listed pull request has running checks is asked for the same way, through the node's read (`reread_node_github`); with no observer or no running checks nothing is asked.
The same step also hands the runtime's request to the advisory poll (`github_poll_reader`, a `BackgroundRead` of its own) and takes back only the paths it saw change (`Runtime::note_polled_changes`), which the runtime asks the existing reader for by the look rule without its thirty seconds; the poll holds no runtime, runs its conditional `gh api` reads one at a time off the lock (`hide_node_link::gh::conditional_read_arguments` is the only form the node runs for it), and its failures stay in the diagnostic log; the projects it is not watching come back as `held`, which marks their GitHub status stale until their next read (`Runtime::note_poll_held`, PRD git-freshness B23).
`hide` owns lifecycle: instance lock, `~/.hide/state/hided.json` mode 0600, default-browser open with `#token=` (the system's handler on each system, `hand_to_system`), idle exit ten minutes after the last client once no pane holder of its machine may run (see The daemon lives with its panes), and `hide serve --keep-alive`.
A stop ends the core before it releases the instance lock: dropping `RunningDaemon` joins the core's owner thread, whose `Core` drop joins the layout and state savers, so the last save is on disk before another daemon can start and before whoever owns the state folder can remove it.
The instance uses the platform's explicit-unlock guard, so an inherited file description from a concurrent fork cannot retain the role after its owner ends; another live instance is still refused immediately.
`hide connect`'s connect lock, the instance lock every role and the core a move starts take, and the state record all open the state folder through one opener (`hided/src/state_file.rs`), which makes it private before any store reads it (`private::own_dir`): a folder of this account that an earlier build left open is restricted and `state.made_private` is logged beside it, and one that is a link or another account's is refused with `state.not_private`, so no daemon starts on it and `hide connect` answers `start_failed` naming the folder; each record is written to the folder's `Logs/core.jsonl` at once (`diagnostics::record_now`), since the daemon's log is not open yet and a refused one never opens it, except that a refused link or another account's folder gets nothing written into it and its record goes to stderr only.
A folder of this account that it cannot open (mode 0000 or 0300, or an access list that shuts the account out) is refused with the fix (`chmod 700`, or full control on Windows), since its mode is changed only through an open descriptor; another account's folder that cannot be opened is still named as another account's.
Both the default and legacy connect locks use that same guard, preserving their existing blocking serialization while releasing ownership explicitly.
`hide <path>` (`hided/src/project_open.rs`; [UI_BEHAVIOR.md](UI_BEHAVIOR.md#opening-a-folder-from-a-terminal)) is one request, `project_open` {request_id, path}, answered as a `workspace_result`: on the core's own machine the command finds or starts the daemon as `hide open` does and sends it on a `/ws` connection whose handshake proves the state file's token with `client_kind: "cli"`, which runs that one request and closes, never a screen; the token is the authority bare `hide` already opens the shell with, and the state file is the account's own (mode 0600).
In a pane, a device's included, it is a scoped request on the pane credential, and the folder's machine is the credential's, never a field of the request; a plain SSH shell on a device, which proves no pane, asks the device's node on its bridge socket with `{project_open: {path, request_id}}` instead (`hide_host::panes`), the CLI choosing that route when it has neither `HIDE_CAP_REF` nor a pane id (`HIDE_PANE_ID`).
The node takes it only when `LocalStream::peer_is_this_account` says the other end runs as the node's own account, the bridge folder being owner-only as well, issues no credential and opens no stream for it, and sends one `NodeEvent::ProjectOpen` up its link; the core answers `ProofAnswer::ProjectOpenAccepted` at once and then `ProofAnswer::ProjectOpen` with the `workspace_result` of `project_open::run` for the link's own device (`hided/src/node_panes.rs`), so the shell gains this one effect and nothing else.
The node bounds the wait for the acceptance (`PROJECT_OPEN_ACCEPT`, 5 s), so a link that ended unnoticed answers `bridge_unavailable` rather than hanging, runs one open at a time and six a minute (`project_open_busy`, `project_open_rate_limited`), and the CLI refuses when several bridges answer (`bridge_ambiguous`: several cores have the device open).
The CLI reads that it runs on a device from what runs, not from where its binary lives: with no core daemon here, a live bridge of this account makes the machine a device, and with no live bridge only a helper's own binary is one, refused `device_not_linked` (connect it in Hide first), while any other binary starts Hide here as bare `hide` does; NodeLink protocol 58 carries the event.
A folder of this machine passes `Boundary::resolve_registration` first with no confirmation; one that line would ask about, outside home, is admitted only when `Boundary::resolve_target` finds it inside a registered checkout, after bringing the roots current once as a refused client event does (they follow the core only while a window is open), and the core is then told to bring that checkout forward and never register (`project_open::Unheld::Refuse`, answered `needs_confirmation` when no registered checkout holds the path by then); anything else outside home is refused `needs_confirmation`; the core then brings forward the deepest registered checkout holding the path, or dispatches the same `create_workspace` Add a project sends and keeps a receipt by request id (`Runtime::project_open`, at most 32, a new request refused `project_open_busy` while all 32 wait) that each outcome of that registration settles, local or device (`settle_project_open`), so the command reads its own answer rather than the `last_error` the next event clears.
hided reads the receipt every 100 ms off the owner thread for up to 30 s (`PROJECT_OPEN_WAIT`, `project_open_unconfirmed` past it, which a retry joins by bringing the now-registered project forward); a settled open sends every renderer of this machine a `window_call` frame naming the checkout that came forward (`{device_id, path, checkout_id}`), which the desktop host answers by showing and focusing its window (`hide:come-forward`) and every page answers as an open of that checkout (`web/src/opening.ts`), leaving All projects or an Overview for it once the core has it in front, and with no renderer the command opens the shell in the default browser.
Bare `hide` and that fallback hand the address to the system (`hide_node::opener::hand_to_system`: `open`, `xdg-open`, `ShellExecuteW`).
`hide connect` is `hide open` for a host that loads the shell itself: the same discovery (the live daemon the state file names when it is this build, else one started and waited for), answered as one JSON line (`ok`, `url`, `port`, `pid`, or `reason` `start_failed`/`no_response`/`other_build` with `detail`, `state_refused` with the `file`, `core_newer` and `update_failed` with the `machine`, `core` and `app` builds) instead of a browser; `hide status --json` is the attach-only probe and never starts a daemon.
Until its first role mounts, a daemon's seat holds `/health` and answers `/starting` at once with the step its start has reached (`seat`, `resume`, `core.state`, `core.herdr_import`, `core.engine`, `core.owner`, `core.services`, `core.mobile`, `core.roots`, then `mounted`; `node` for the node role) and how long it has stood there, and each step's length goes to the Logs file as `start.step` (`hided/src/seat.rs`).
`hide connect` waits for the daemon it started while that daemon makes progress: a `/health` answer, or a later step on `/starting`, gives it ten seconds more, and ten seconds with neither is `no_response` naming the step it stood in; a start passes a fixed number of steps, so the wait stays bounded however slowly each runs (`hided/src/cli.rs`, `wait_started`).
The desktop host allows up to 25 seconds for the whole discovery command before showing a retryable failure, so `hide connect`'s own refusal, which names the step, reaches it for any start that stood still before 15 s of progress; a first start right after a Windows install measured 1.4 to 1.9 s on the runner (#1515).
The daemon leads its own process group, so an interrupt to the terminal job or host that ran the CLI never reaches it.
`hided` takes `OwnerWatch` before anything else, so a starter that passes an owner channel (only the web e2e fixture does) ends the daemon by ending itself; `hide connect` starts it through `spawn_owned`, which removes the channel's key, so the daemon an app started outlives the app.
A release `hided` carries `web/dist` inside the binary (`hided/build.rs`); a debug build reads the directory from disk, so `pnpm build` shows up without a cargo rebuild.
The web shell holds no UI authority: it draws the snapshot, writes the hub's terminal frames straight into xterm.js, and sends one event per operator action.
Each terminal instance owns its one WebGL addon and context-loss subscription through `web/src/terminalRenderer.ts`, including while parked.
The pinned addon's own transient-restoration window runs first; persistent loss or failed activation disposes the addon and leaves the same Terminal, buffer, selection and grid on xterm's normal renderer.
Disposal removes the subscription before the addon and precedes terminal destruction; fallback starts no retry, attach, resize or additional work per key or output chunk.
The addon is bundled with one fix of its own code (`web/src/webglAtlasSlots.ts`, applied by `web/vite.config.ts`): each GPU texture slot uploads again when a different atlas page sits at its index, not only when the version number moves, because after the atlas merges pages a page that moved into a slot can carry the version of the one the slot last uploaded, and every glyph on it was then drawn from the wrong picture.
The build refuses an addon in which the two rewritten statements are not found exactly once, so an update of the addon is read against the fix rather than shipping without it; the check is one more pointer comparison per atlas page per drawn frame.
With `probe=1` in the page URL it also installs `window.__hideProbe`, the only way to read the WebGL-drawn terminal from Playwright or a CDP driver; without the query the writer path is the plain `term.write`.

### The daemon lives with its panes

`hided` stays up while a pane holder of its machine may still run, with or without a window or phone, so letters, agent states and labels keep going when the app is closed (PRD labels-in-hided D-18): the holders outlive the daemon by design, and the daemon is what keeps their letters and states moving.
The idle exit still counts ten minutes (`idle_secs`), but only while no client is connected and no holder pane may run; the daemon counts its machine's holder records every five seconds off the async thread (`hide_kit::panes::Panes::live`, `watch_idle` in `hided/src/server.rs`), a record it cannot read counts as running, and a count that fails keeps the daemon, since ending it would leave panes with no core.
`--keep-alive` and the paired-phone rule behave as before.
`SIGTERM` still ends the daemon gracefully, which cancels the running label analysis and its provider process before it exits.

A build is the SHA-256 of the `hided` executable's bytes (`hided/src/build_id.rs`), hashed once when the daemon starts and reported as `build` on `/health`.
`hide connect` hashes the `hided` shipped beside it and compares: the same build is attached to as it is, and a live daemon of another build is stopped (`SIGTERM`, five seconds, then `SIGKILL`) and replaced by a new one, so the window and its daemon are always one build after an app update (D-19).
The state file records the daemon's process start beside its pid (`pid_started`, from `hide_platform::process::start_time`), and `hide connect` and `hide stop` act on the pid only while that start still matches: a pid another process has reused, another account's included, reads as gone and is never signalled, and its stale state is cleared; a state written by an earlier build has no start and is judged by liveness alone.
Each `hide` command checks the environment keys it reads, and the sets live in code (`hided/src/env.rs`), not in the command's body.
The daemon and every command that acts on its whole configuration check every registered key and report all the invalid ones at once.
`hide stop` and `hide status --json` read only the state folder keys (`STATE_FOLDER_KEYS`: `HOME`, `HIDE_STATE_DIR`, `XDG_STATE_HOME`), and `hide status` also `HIDE_IDLE_SECS` (`STATUS_KEYS`), the idle time it prints when `/health` gives none.
An invalid key outside a command's set, such as an opener or a port, therefore never keeps a running daemon from being asked about or stopped.
An invalid key inside the set refuses with that key's name and exit status 2; it is never replaced by a default, since a default state folder would name another daemon.
`hided/tests/it/connect_stop.rs` holds each of these from the command's exit status and output.
A daemon that will not stop is a `start_failed` answer, never a silent attach to the old one, and the replacement is logged as `daemon.replacing` or `daemon.replace_failed`.
Only a desktop package's own `hide`, in macOS `Contents/Resources` or Windows/Linux `resources` (`hide_kit::bundled_kit_dir`), replaces a daemon: any other `hide`, a development build or a copy, answers `other_build` with both builds named and attaches to nothing, because the installed app's daemon is the operator's (`daemon.other_build_refused`).
Only the daemon of the state folder the CLI was given is looked at, so a development or e2e daemon elsewhere is never replaced, and stopping a daemon leaves its panes' holders and their agents running.
Each connect holds `connect.lock` in the state folder from looking at the daemon until the one it attaches to answers, so two connects never both replace it; a stop removes `hided.json` only while it still names the stopped pid and never unlinks `hided.lock`, so a daemon started since keeps its state and its instance lock.
A daemon that has ended counts as stopped before its starter reaps it, although Linux still lists an unreaped process's start time.
Before any of that, a connect whose state folder is the default `~/.hide/state` moves the legacy default `~/.local/state/hide` into place once (PRD hide-home-layout D-05; `hided/src/state_move.rs`): under the legacy folder's own `connect.lock`, which an older `hide connect` takes too, it stops the daemon the legacy `hided.json` names, then renames the whole folder in one `rename(2)`, so there is never a copy in two places.
That pid is signalled only once it is proven to be the daemon: a state that recorded its daemon's process start is proven by the kernel's answer for that pid, as `hide stop` judges it, so a daemon too busy to answer `/health` within its one-second request is still stopped and the folder still moves (issue 863); a state an earlier build wrote without a start (before v0.3.0) is proven only by `/health` answering as that pid, because liveness alone also passes a reused pid.
The folder moves only while its `hided.lock` is held across the rename: after stopping a proven daemon, the connect waits at most two seconds for that lock, because macOS can stop reporting a dying process's identity before its descriptors close.
The platform lock helper owns this bounded wait and the acquired lock; an unproven holder is still refused immediately and never signalled, and a lock that stays held answers `start_failed` without moving anything.
A legacy folder that is a link or not this account's is not moved, one other accounts can write to is refused with the `chmod go-w` that fixes it (only when it would move; beside an existing new folder it is just left), the moved folder is made 0700, `~/.hide` must be a private folder of this account, and a daemon that will not stop leaves both folders as they were and answers `start_failed`.
`HIDE_STATE_DIR` naming `~/.hide/state` itself counts as the default, since that is the value `hide connect` hands the daemon it starts.
When `~/.hide/state` already exists nothing is merged: the new folder is used, and each daemon start logs `state.legacy_left` with both paths while the legacy folder remains.
A folder `HIDE_STATE_DIR` or `XDG_STATE_HOME` chose is never moved (D-04).

With no window attached the daemon does only the work that keeps labels current (D-20, B29).
`hided` counts web and desktop renderers, tells the core `ui_attached` when the first arrives and when the last leaves (under one lock, so two windows arriving together cannot leave the core told the opposite of the final count), and refuses `ui_attached` from a client, because a window that sent it would pause the readers every other window draws.
While none is attached the session-sync coordinator rests the readers that only feed what a window draws: foreground processes, provider usage, ports, worktrees, GitHub and disk, and the Background AI probe.
Label work, which runs on the coordinator's own wakes, goes on, and the root follower skips its snapshot reads while no client is connected and catches up with one read when the next client arrives (`RootFollower::resume`).
The readers resume on the coordinator's next wake after a window attaches.
Local hook diagnosis belongs to the existing kit pump, not the session coordinator: one startup read, another after a successful apply, and a refresh due one second after completion while a window observes Settings.
A device's hook diagnosis is read the other way round, by that device's own coordinator (`kit::DeviceDiagnosisReader`, one `BackgroundRead` worker per device, due a minute after its last answer, window or none), because the doorbell reads a pane's composer only for an agent version Hide knows and a device's panes have no other way to say theirs ([delivery.md](delivery.md#catching-an-agents-screen-change)); the core keeps the last answer per registered device (`Runtime::ingest_device_hook_diagnosis`), drops it with the device, announces nothing, and a link that is down or a call that fails leaves the last answer in place.
The pump serializes diagnosis and installation on its existing worker, keeps one next-read deadline instead of a tick queue, and publishes only changed answers after releasing Runtime.
Core shutdown stops pump admission before closing its fixed node, rejects replies from that retiring owner and joins the pump outside Runtime.
`hided/tests/it/connect_build.rs` and `hided/tests/it/handshake.rs` (`the_daemon_outlives_the_idle_window_while_its_herdr_answers`, `the_daemon_exits_after_the_idle_window_when_its_herdr_is_gone`, `a_window_cannot_say_whether_windows_are_attached`) own these rules.

### The core's node id

The core names its own machine by a node id, never by the literal `local` (PRD core-host-node D-21; `hide-core/src/node.rs`).
The id is the machine's own id, `hide_platform::host::machine_id`, lowercased and checked to `[0-9a-z-]{1,64}`, read once when `hided` starts (`NodeId::of_this_machine`) and handed to the core in `CoreOptions::node_id`.
It is the id of the navigator's own device row, whose `kind: "local"` stays as its role, and the `device_id` of this machine's registrations, Workspaces, letters, labels and Workspace views, the device half of every project id (`hide_project::project_id`), and the device half of a folder project's owner mark.
An event or a `hide` command that names no device still means the core's own node, so the wire keeps its shape and only the value of this machine's `device_id` changed; a `device_id` of `local` now names an unknown device, and no device is ever registered as `local` or as the node's own id ([A device's id](#a-devices-id)).
The web shell reads the id from the navigator's own device row (`localDeviceId` in `web/src/snapshot.ts`); before the first snapshot names it the id is empty, which an event carries as no `device_id`.
A device's ids are scoped to it as `remote:<device>:<kind>:<id>`, while the core's own node keeps the engine's bare ids, and one module builds and reads that form: `hide_node_link::address`, re-exported as `hide_core::address`, which `hide-node`'s router, `hided` and the core all call and nothing else formats or splits.
It lives in `hide-node-link` because the router cannot depend on the core.
A pane is a `PaneAddress`, either a pane of the core's own node or a device's pane by the device's own id; a typed `remote:<device>:pane:<id>` from a `hide` command parses into the same type, and a `remote:` id that names no pane is refused rather than read as a local pane.
Two pane ids are the same pane only on the same device (`address::same_pane`), so one raw pane id on two machines is two panes.
Each agent and pane row publishes its machine as `device_id` and the pane's id on that machine as `device_pane_id`, and each editor tab its machine as `device_id`; a raised ask names the device its pane is on as `open_device_id`, because a disconnected device publishes no rows to find it by.
These are derived fields, written by `Runtime::stamp_row_addresses` as a snapshot is taken and never compared (`model::Derived`), so a stamp is never a change and a projection that has not stamped yet is equal to one that has.
The web reads them and never reconstructs a machine from an id; every reader that names a row's session (a pane head's record button, a 태스크 row, `revealTask`) finds the device on the row, because the session's ledger row is kept under the device id and a session named with the core's own node id for a device's pane finds no record.
The desktop host learns it from the shell's browser sync (`node`) and keys the shared loopback partition and the pages it loads directly on it.
A workspace whose `hide_owner` mark was written for `local` is still read as this node's folder (`OwnerOpen::on_node`), so a folder project opened before the change keeps its Workspace.

A state folder written under `local` is converted before the core starts (`hide_core::node_migration::convert`, called from `hided`'s `start_daemon` after it holds the instance lock).
`core-state.json`, `workspace-views.json`, `labels.json` and `delivery-ledger.json` are rewritten whole through a temporary file and a rename; Project Memory and the link record (`links.sqlite3`) re-key their project ids, and the link record its device names and records each replaced project id for the old session search file's retention (`retention_aliases`), in one SQLite transaction each; the old session search file is never written.
The originals are copied under `node-migration-backup/<unix ms>/` first; a start that resumes an unfinished conversion keeps them in that same folder and copies each store once, so retries add no copies, and recording the same replaced ids again changes nothing.
`node.json` is written last, so a start interrupted before it converts again, and a start of an already converted folder writes nothing.
A store that cannot be converted stops the daemon with the file and the reason, written to the Logs file at once with the daemon's pid; `hide connect`, which sees its daemon exit before answering, reads that record and answers `state_refused` with the file, which the desktop host's failure page shows under the reason. A JSON file its own loader cannot read is left to that loader, which already reports it.
A store whose loader has a size limit (the delivery ledger's 16 MiB) is checked before anything is written: one the longer node id would push past that limit stops the start with every file as it was, and one already past it is left to its loader.
The project pairs the session search index is re-keyed with come from the node's Projects in Project Memory and the folders registered under either name, so a start retried after a later store failed still finds them; a row whose new key is already taken is a stale copy and is dropped and counted.
`node.json` records the node that owns every unqualified key in the folder (a pane id, a tab id, a checkout path), whichever machine runs the core.
A folder that names another node is refused today only because nothing yet reads another node's state; a core that does extends this rule without changing the file.
`KEYS` in `node_migration.rs` lists every machine-bound key a store written before this change can hold, with how it is covered, rewritten or owned through `node.json`; that set is closed, since a store written since names the node id or holds unqualified keys `node.json` covers.
Its contract test holds a value at every key the table names and fails when a rewritten key still names `local`, when an owned key changes, or when a converted file still carries `"local"` anywhere.
`UNBOUND` beside it names the rest of a state folder, which holds no machine key, and a test fails on any file in a converted folder that neither list names.
Project ids hash the node id with the root, so a Memory receipt a transcript carries from before the conversion no longer matches a project id and is not honoured.

### A device's id

A machine has one id wherever it is seen: its machine id, which is its node id when it runs a core and its device id when a core dials it (with-hide/hide-private#671; `hide-core/src/runtime/device_names.rs`).
Every key that names a device is derived from that id (its projects' digests, its panes' and tabs' `remote:<device>:` addresses, its letters, its Memory Projects, its engine folder), so the same machine's records keep one name when it changes role.
`register_device` takes no id: an SSH device is registered under an id its alias makes (`device_command::device_id_for`, the one fold of an alias) and marked `naming: "pending"` (`model::DeviceNaming`).
Two readings name the machine on every connection: the start script's probe, read on the device before anything is installed and bound into the consent (`HostIdentity::machine_id`), and the node's Hello (`MachineIdentity`), both from `hide_platform::host::machine_id`.
A Pending device's first connection checks that both readings agree, that the id is a node id, that it is not the core's own machine and that no other registration has it or reaches it, then closes the link and renames the registration and every choice the core state saves of it to that id (`naming: "named"`); one already under its machine id is named in place.
The new id connects only after a save of the core state that holds it has succeeded (`acknowledge_device_naming`, in both save paths), so a core that stops before the save finds the Pending registration and names it again, and nothing is ever written under an id the file does not hold; Retry asks for the save again.
A Named device opens only when this connection's probe reads its id and its node reports the same, or reports none because it could not read it; anything else closes the link with `EstablishError::MachineName`, which is not retried, since the alias now reaches another machine and only removing it and adding the new one changes that.
`--machine`, `hide device remove` and `hide device retry` take a device's id or the SSH alias it was added with (`Runtime::machine_named`): the alias stays the name people use, and an alias two registrations share is refused with their ids.
WSL distributions keep `wsl-<distribution>-<digest>`: a distribution runs no core, distributions imported from one tarball share `/etc/machine-id`, and the consent names a distribution by its install id rather than a machine id ([What each system supports](INSTALL.md#what-each-system-supports)).
A node that dials the core is already registered by its node id.

A device an earlier build registered under its alias is renamed once, at the start, after the node conversion and before the core is created (`node_migration::name_devices`, called from `start_core_role`).
Its machine id is the one its consent bound; a registration whose consent bound none connects once, binds it (`host.consent_machine_bound`), is held with "Restart Hide to finish naming this device", and is renamed by the next start.
Each device is checked against every store before anything is written: its machine id is an id, not the core's and not another registration's, no other registration reached the same machine, Project Memory holds no Project of its roots under the new id (Memory is re-keyed strictly, so card numbers stay), the link record holds no rows under it, its engine folder does not exist under both ids, every registered project's root is known to some store, and every JSON store renames to one its loader reads with nothing left naming the old id.
A device a check refuses keeps everything under its old id and is held unconnected, with the reason in the start's diagnostic record (`node_migration.devices_held`), so nothing new is ever written under the old id.
The plan is written to `device-ids.json` first, then Project Memory, the link record (with the retention the old session search file keeps under each old Project id), the delivery ledger, labels, Workspace views, missions, Local issues, composer marks and hook facts, the engine folders under `engine/devices/`, and `core-state.json` last; then the plan is removed.
Each store's original is copied once to `node-migration-backup/device-ids-<unix ms>/`, every step leaves what it already renamed as it is, and a start that finds the plan resumes it to the same result; a write that fails stops the start and names the file, as the node conversion does.
`name_devices` and the core move map a store through the same `KEYS` rows (`node_migration::reown`'s `map_id`, `apply_pattern`, `map_views`, `map_project_settings`), so a key added to the table is renamed by both.

### The core and its nodes

The core decides and keeps state; it never touches a machine (PRD core-host-node D-21).
Every file, process, socket and session-file read is a node's, asked through one contract, `NodeLink` (`hide-node-link`), addressed by node id (`Runtime::node_link`): the core's own node answers today, and a device's helper answers for its machine.
The contract crate sits below both sides, so the core holds only the trait and the wire types, and the machine side (`hide-node`, over `hide-host`) never depends on the core.
The core's own node is `hide_node::Local`, which answers in hided's process through `hide_host::serve`; the core gets it in `Core::create`.
The node answers `PaneInspect` from the pane's holder record; local and linked nodes read the same `hide_host::pane_peer` terminal id, shell pid and kernel start proof on the machine that owns the pane, without accepting a caller-selected socket.
Closing it refuses new calls and wakes pending callers with `Unknown` through their existing one-answer channels; it neither polls nor starts a cancellation thread.
There are at most 64 admitted machine calls, and a timed-out or closed caller does not free its slot until the actual work ends.
The weak answer-sender list is pruned on admission and bounded by those same slots; closing one node affects its clones, never another node.

| The core's | The node's |
| --- | --- |
| Every decision, the runtime and its snapshot | Files and folders: lists, bytes, saves, stamps, path facts (`Call::PathFacts`), new projects (`Call::ProjectCreate`), the project guardrails' policy file (`Call::GuardrailPolicy`) |
| Its own stores: UI state, saved Views, the delivery ledger, labels, the link record, local issues, saved GitHub answers, its log, and their one-time node-id conversion | Processes: git, `gh`, the AI CLIs, ports, agent sleep's process groups, the file opener (`hide-node/src/opener.rs`) |
| Which node a call goes to | Session files, the install kit, pane credential proofs and the bootstrap socket (`hide-node/src/pane_proof.rs` here, `hide-host/src/panes.rs` on a device) |

`scripts/check-core-touches-no-machine.py` holds the line: production code under `hide-core/src`, that opens a file, starts a process, opens a socket or reads a session file fails it, unless the file is one of the core's stores, listed with its reason, or something a later layer of the PRD moves out, listed with that layer; each listed file carries how many machine touches it keeps, so a new one in a listed file fails too.
The SSH transport is the node's (`hide-node/src/ssh/`): the system `ssh`, which a node starts and owns.
The core reaches a device only through `hide_node_link::device::{DeviceConnector, DialedTransport}` for a device it dials and `DeviceTransport` with an `Arrived` node for a node that dials it (`hided` builds the connector and hands over each arrival, `Core::create` takes the connector) and keeps the decoding of what a device's engine sends (`remote.rs`).
No later layer is listed any more: layer 3 moved the terminal attach child and the clipboard image's removal to the node, and layer 4 moved the label generator's lock (`Call::LabelLock`); an entry that no longer reaches a machine fails the check, so none outlives its layer.

Every `git` a node runs starts at `hide_host::git_run` (PRD git-freshness D-11), because nothing Hide runs has a person at a terminal: `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, empty `GIT_ASKPASS` and `SSH_ASKPASS` with `SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=never`, `GCM_INTERACTIVE=never` with `-c credential.interactive=never`, `--no-optional-locks` and a closed stdin, the same on macOS, Linux and Windows.
A run that reaches a remote (a fetch, a clone) starts through `git_run::remote`, which keeps the operator's own ssh in Git's order (`GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, then `core.sshCommand` as `git config` reads it in that repository, then `GIT_SSH`, then `ssh`) and, when that command is `ssh`, adds `BatchMode=yes`, a connect timeout and keepalives after the operator's own options, so their key and options stand and an option they set wins; a wrapper or `plink` runs as configured, with nothing to answer a prompt.
`git_run::output` ends the whole process tree at its deadline (15 s for a read, 10 minutes for a change such as a checkout, a fetch's own bound) and refuses an answer past its output cap (256 MiB unless the caller names less); a clone keeps its own streaming run and stall clock but starts from the same command.
A credential helper still answers from what it already holds, which is how a background fetch uses the operator's login without asking.
`git_run`'s own test fails when product code in `hide-host` spells a Git process any other way.

### A device's ssh

An SSH device is reached with the system `ssh`, one child per device that Hide starts and owns, exactly as `ssh <alias>` in the operator's terminal (PRD system-ssh-device-link D-01, D-02): OpenSSH reads the alias, its keys, the agent, ProxyJump, certificates and Tailscale SSH, and the core never sees any of it (`hide-node/src/ssh/device.rs`).
The command line is `ssh -T -o … -- <alias> <wrapper>`, and `ssh -G` decides the options: Hide adds a connect timeout and keepalives only where the configuration left OpenSSH's default, because a command-line `-o` wins over it, and what makes the connection one owned process (no forwards, no shared master, no configured remote command); `LogLevel` is never lowered, so a sign-in banner still reaches the row (D-12, `hide-node/src/ssh/openssh.rs`).
An attempt has one clock for everything ssh does before the start script answers: `ssh -V`, `ssh -G` and the sign-in together get `SIGN_IN_TIMEOUT` (90 s, not counting the time a question waits for the operator), and the attempt's cancel ends a question still running, because the first start of a program on a busy or newly booted Windows PC can take seconds, which is the device still connecting, not ssh failing (with-hide/hide-private#584); the row reads connecting until then, as it does while a dial waits its turn.
The wrapper reads one line of start script from the child's input, which then runs in lock step over the same input and output: a probe (user, uid, home, system, processor, `sha256sum`, machine id, whether it unpacks gzip), the helper root, the install of what the version folder lacks, each file a counted run of bytes checked against its digest and renamed into place, and the exec of `<helper> node serve`, whose standard streams are then the node's link (`hide-node/src/ssh/bootstrap.rs`); a WSL distribution runs the same script through `wsl.exe`.
A device that unpacks gzip (`gzip` on a POSIX device, .NET's `GZipStream` on every Windows one) is sent each file packed at the fast level (`zput`), since the link, not the device's disk, is what a first connection after an update waits on (with-hide/hide-private#582); the digest is the file's own, so a stream that did not unpack whole fails as a file that did not arrive, and the script reads the whole stream even then, so the next step stays in step. A POSIX device without `gzip` is sent the bytes as they are (`put`), and so is a WSL distribution, whose `wsl.exe` pipe on the same PC is no link packing pays for (its install took 1.0-1.1 s raw against 4.2-4.7 s packed); a core update over the same script packs as a device does.
A connection to a core's machine ([A core on another machine](#a-core-on-another-machine)) runs the same script with four more steps: `run` (a command by its words, no shell between, answering its status and both outputs, each capped), `fput` and `fget` (one file, whole, checked against its SHA-256), and `attach`, the exec of `hided attach` in the script's place.
So a connection signs in once, and its engine, files, Git, terminals and pages are that link's calls and streams; the link's end ends the child, and the child's exit ends the link.

A Windows device answers the same steps from a PowerShell form of the script (`hide-node/src/ssh/bootstrap.ps1`), in the Windows PowerShell 5.1 every Windows 10 and 11 carries, with no setting changed on the device.
ssh runs one remote command whatever the account's login shell is (`bootstrap::remote_command`): every POSIX shell (sh, bash, zsh, fish, csh, tcsh) runs only its first statement, the wrapper; `cmd.exe`, Windows OpenSSH's default shell, reaches a short PowerShell wrapper through the `&` its lack of single quotes leaves bare; a PowerShell login shell (5.1 or 7) finds no `exec` and runs the same wrapper as its next statement; and an MSYS or Cygwin `sh` (Git Bash) hands over to it from the script's first statement.
The wrapper is readable PowerShell that holds no character any of those shells reads inside its quotes (`the_powershell_wrapper_holds_nothing_a_login_shell_reads_inside_quotes`), because Windows' malware scan refuses an encoded PowerShell command beside the `sh` words when a PowerShell login shell reads the line; it answers `script powershell`, and the node sends the PowerShell script as its byte count and text, which the wrapper takes past the `sh` line the node sent first.
The wrapper turns PowerShell's module auto-loading off and imports `Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility`, the one module the wrapper and the script use, by name: auto-loading finds a cmdlet by reading every module on the module path when the account's module analysis cache is unusable, which took a fresh CI runner's first `Write-Output` 12 to 38 s with nothing said meanwhile, and the import by name costs under a second (with-hide/hide-private#580); a cmdlet outside the import fails at once by name.
Windows PowerShell 5.1 runs it even under PowerShell 7, whose .NET has no access lists to read.
The install folder and every folder above it are checked by owner and access list with `hide_platform::fs::private`'s rule, files and folders are made with an access list only the account can use, links are refused anywhere on the path, and files are renamed into place with `File.Replace`; `hide-node/src/ssh/bootstrap_windows_tests.rs` runs every step against a real `powershell.exe` through each of those login shells in the Windows lane.
Below the install folder, on both systems, every folder on the way to a file is checked again before the file is written, reused as held or started (`below` in the POSIX script, `Below` in the PowerShell one): a link there, or a folder another account owns or can change, is refused by name, so nothing under the install folder leads a write or a start out of it or lets another account swap what runs, and a missing folder is made private.
A `run` command starts suspended in a job of its own that allows a resident to break away and ends what it holds when it closes (`HideRunTree`), so everything it starts is in that job before it runs; when the command ends, past its output cap, or on a failure part way, the job is ended and its end confirmed, so only a resident that left the job outlives the command, and an end Windows does not confirm ends the script and with it the link, so the node never reuses a connection with a command of its still running.
A Windows device runs no Herdr: it connects on the core's own engine, as every device does.
Its helper reads the account's home only through `hide_platform::host::home_dir` (`USERPROFILE`), never from the `HOME` Windows OpenSSH sets beside it, so its kit, state and panes follow the one variable the start step replaces for a development home of the node's own (`HIDE_DEV_DEVICE_HOME`, which also moves `HOME`, `APPDATA`, `LOCALAPPDATA`, `TEMP` and `TMP` inside it; [docs/VERIFICATION.md](VERIFICATION.md)).
With such a home both start scripts clear every variable that would move a folder Hide or an agent keeps below the home somewhere else, one list for both (`hide_host::serve::HOME_FOLDER_VARIABLES`: `HIDE_STATE_DIR`, the `XDG_*` base folders, `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `CURSOR_CONFIG_DIR`, `ZDOTDIR`), and set each agent account variable a definition marks `isolated_home` to its default folder inside that home, made private (`agent_home_variables`: today `CODEX_HOME`, because Codex on Windows reads the account's profile folder from Windows rather than `USERPROFILE`), so nothing the account's environment or profile names takes the helper's state, kit or a pane's agent out of that home.
The first Hello after a connection's install wrote the helper waits up to 60 s (`FIRST_HELLO_TIMEOUT`) instead of 15 s, since Windows scans a new `.exe` on its first start and a real PC's first Hello once took longer than 15 s; a helper the device already held keeps the 15 s bound, on every system.
Its node is the `hided.exe` the script starts with the link's pipes, inside the job Windows OpenSSH makes for the session, which ends what it holds when the link ends and lets a process break away; the node's pane holders leave it through `start_resident` ([The platform layer](#the-platform-layer)), so a pane and its program outlive the link and the next connection's node adopts them.

A Windows core dials the same way, with the `ssh.exe` its `PATH` finds (Windows' own OpenSSH on a person's PC) and the `hide.exe` beside its programs as the askpass.
What it puts on a device comes from one rule in `HelperPackages` (`hide-node/src/ssh/kit/select.rs`), the same on every core: a developer's `<name>-<os>-<arch>` file first; for a device of the core's own system and processor, the core's own programs, found under their system's names (`hided.exe`, `hide.exe`, `hide-agent-hooks.exe` and `hide-holder.exe` on Windows, as the package and its runtime copy hold them), and the holder's ConPTY folder under its one name, `holder-conpty`, on every system; for any other platform `contracts/device-kits.json` carries, the kit of the core's own release, fetched and checked against that release's manifest ([BUILD.md](BUILD.md#which-programs-a-device-gets)).
A platform the contract does not carry, such as a Windows ARM PC or an Intel Mac, is refused when the probe reads the device's system, before anything is sent, with the reason the contract gives.
The `windows wsl` lane proves both directions a Windows runner can reach: its own OpenSSH Server as a Windows device and an sshd in its WSL 2 distribution as a Linux device, each over `ssh.exe` with terminal, files and Git (`hided/tests/it/windows_ssh_device.rs`).

What ssh asks is the operator's to answer on the device's row, never on a terminal: the child runs with `SSH_ASKPASS` set to the `hide` beside the helpers, `SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force` and a one-time token, and that `hide` hands each question over a private local stream (`hide-node/src/ssh/askpass.rs`, `Desk`) to the attempt's `SignIn`, the core's `RowSignIn` (`hide-core/src/runtime/device_sign_in.rs`).
The desk takes a question only from a process of this account (`peer_is_this_account`) that carries the token: another process of the same account is inside Hide's trust boundary, as it is for the bridge socket, which checks its peer the same way.
A desk's folder carries its process id, and the next desk removes the folder of a process that is gone.
The row shows it as `DeviceSnapshot.sign_in` (`contracts/snapshot-wire-enums.json`: `device_sign_in_kind`): a masked question with ssh's sentence, with the `ssh-add` line for a key's passphrase (`ssh-add --apple-use-keychain <file>` on macOS), whose file is the whole path: ssh prints at most 100 bytes of it, so a longer one is the one key file of the alias (`ssh -G`, expanded as ssh expands it) that it begins, and with none or two the row offers no line (B9); a server not in known_hosts with its fingerprint, to trust or not, which OpenSSH then records; a yes or no; a security key's touch; a sign-in page in the browser, which waits up to five minutes; an attempt waiting for its turn behind the four that dial at once shows nothing, since the operator has nothing to do about it (design principle 13), and reads as connecting.
The `device_sign_in` event answers the question it names, so an answer to a question ssh no longer asks reaches nothing; a question waits at most five minutes, and an answer passes from the event to the askpass child and nowhere else, never into the snapshot, a file or a diagnostic (B10).
An attempt nobody pressed for (`Wake::NotAllowed`, the core's own reconnect) asks nothing: its first question ends it as `sign_in_needed`; the app opening and the row's Sign in or Retry may ask (D-06).
The device row's `RowSignIn` refuses such a question itself; a connection to a core's machine (`Session::open`) hands an unallowed dial's questions to `NoSignIn`, so its screen never shows one.
The first question an attempt gets no answer to (Cancel, five minutes unanswered, or an attempt nobody pressed for) ends the whole attempt (B8): the desk holds that question and any later one unanswered, because an askpass that answers nothing has ssh send an empty secret, which the server counts as a failed sign-in, or try its next key, and the attempt ends ssh, its askpass with it, within a second.
Once a device's last attempt stopped on what only the operator can change (a sign-in needed or refused, a changed server key, an unsupported device, a missing or old `ssh`), nothing Hide does by itself starts its `ssh` again: not the core starting, a read or a kit job that needs the link, a due retry, nor its session answering again (`start_device_host` with `HostAttempt::Background`, B14); only the row's Sign in or Retry, `hide device retry` and, for a sign-in, the app opening start the next one, so a server never sees a sign-in nobody typed.

Each attempt is the core's to end (B26): it carries a `Cancel` (`hide-node-link/src/device.rs`) the core keeps in the device's slot (`device_attempts`, `runtime/hosts.rs`), which removing the device, withdrawing its consent, a newer attempt and the core's shutdown set, and its turn in the queue, each question, the install and the start look at it.
The attempt has ended only when no share of it is held: its worker holds one until the attempt returns, and the reaper of its `ssh` (`ChildLink` in `hide-node/src/ssh/host.rs`) holds another until that `ssh` is reaped, so a working link's attempt ends only once the core closes it and its `ssh` is gone.
Until the link is handed to the core, a cancel kills that `ssh` at once, which also ends an upload blocked writing to it; from the hand-off on the link is the core's to close and a cancel leaves it running.
Its `ssh` is an `OwnedChild::spawn_tied` (The platform layer), so it ends with the core's process too.
The slot keeps every attempt until it has ended, and an attempt reaches `ssh` only once every earlier one in the slot has ended, waiting up to four minutes; one cancelled while it waits gives up without dialing and stays in the slot until its worker returns, so two never run for one device, across a removal and adding the device again included; a run leaves the slot as it ends, and the slot with its last run, so a removed device keeps nothing there; shutdown waits up to five seconds for them.
The install's three-minute deadline starts after the sign-in, so the time the operator takes to answer a question is not taken from it.
The probe must report a machine id (`/etc/machine-id`, a Mac's hardware id) of up to 128 letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`: a device without one installs nothing and the row says how to give it one, so no consent is ever bound to a user, host and port alone.
An OpenSSH older than 8.4, which has no `SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE` to send a question to Hide, runs with `BatchMode=yes`; Microsoft's Windows port asks the askpass whenever it is set, so keys and the agent still sign in and a question ends it as `openssh_old` (B21).

A run that did not connect is classified in one place, from ssh's exit and its last error lines (`openssh::classify`, `SshProblem`): the sign-in was needed, refused, or its browser check timed out; an access policy such as a Tailscale ACL refused it; the server key no longer matches known_hosts, which Hide refuses without asking; the name was not found, the device did not answer, or the proxy command failed; the device's system is unsupported; there is no `ssh`; OpenSSH is older than 8.4; or none of these (D-13).
That class decides the retry policy and goes to the diagnostic log; what the operator does about it is one grouping, `SshProblem::action` (`hide-node-link/src/device.rs`), which the row and `hide device` both read: sign in (needed, refused, a browser check that timed out), check the changed server key in a terminal, open Hide again once an update replaced it (`reopen_hide`), or retry everything else.
`DeviceSnapshot.problem` (`DeviceProblem` in `hide-core/src/model.rs`; `contracts/snapshot-wire-enums.json`: `device_problem`) is that grouping as the row draws it: `sign_in_needed` or `sign_in_refused`, `host_key_changed`, `hide_updated` for a Hide an update replaced on disk, which only opening Hide again mends and which offers no Retry, and `cannot_connect` over ssh's last line in `message`, with `ssh_missing`, `openssh_old` and `unsupported` as retries ssh has no useful line for, which the row words in the operator's language (the operator's 2026-10-30 decision, superseding the per-class row of B18-B21).
ssh's lines go to the diagnostic log with each link cut to its host (`openssh::kept_line`), since the rest of a sign-in link carries the code or token that signs in, and the row alone is shown the whole link while its check waits; a refused sign-in, a changed server key, a missing `ssh`, an old OpenSSH and a replaced Hide are retried only by the operator, since a retry of Hide's own would be refused again.
The row keeps the last attempt's class and words while the next attempt runs (`DeviceHost::problem` and `failure` in `runtime/hosts.rs`), so neither a retry nor what the device's session says about a link that already ended replaces the reason and its action; only an attempt that ends otherwise does (B13, B18).
Because the device's engine rides the helper's link, an SSH device needs the helper's consent to connect at all, and its row's message is the link's.
For the same reason the device's session reads its engine again the moment the link is ready, rather than at the next reconnect its attempts before the link backed off to.
Its checkouts' pull requests are read on this machine with this machine's `gh` login, by the repository each checkout's `origin` names, as a node's are ([A core on another machine](#a-core-on-another-machine)); the device runs no `gh`.

### WSL distributions as devices

On Windows, each WSL 2 distribution of this PC is a device of its own, reached through `wsl.exe` instead of SSH (PRD wsl-device).
A registration stores the distribution's name (`wsl_distro`, `LinkOrigin::Wsl`) instead of an SSH alias; its id is `wsl-<name>-<digest>`: the name lowercased with any letter but an ASCII letter, a digit or `-` written as `-`, and the first eight hex digits of the SHA-256 of the exact name, so the digest, not the readable part, tells two names apart; its name is `WSL <name>`; both are the core's, so the Add device dialog shows the name and has nothing to type.
A build before this field reads a WSL record as a registration with neither an alias nor a distribution and drops that record alone; its SSH devices stay (`persistence.rs`'s downgrade test).
The core reaches it through the same `DeviceConnector` (`wsl_transport`, `wsl_distributions`) and `DialedTransport::establish` as an SSH device, and `hide-node/src/ssh/wsl.rs` is the transport.
Its order refuses before it writes anything: a WSL 1 distribution or one whose first-run setup is pending is `Unsupported`, saying what fixes it (`wsl --set-version <name> 2`, or finishing the setup); a stopped distribution on an attempt that may not start it is `Stopped`, after one running check and no other call; then one `wsl.exe -d <name> --cd ~ -e sh -c …` runs the same start script as an SSH device ([A device's ssh](#a-devices-ssh)), whose probe reads the user, uid, home, `uname` and `sha256sum`, and the identity (the user, the distribution as host name, port 0, and `wsl:<distribution id>` as machine id) must match the consent, or it is `IdentityChanged` and asked again; a consent from before the machine id, which named `wsl:<distribution id>` as its host key, still matches.
The install sends only what the version folder lacks or holds damaged, each file a counted run of bytes the script checks against its digest and renames into place, so a cut connection leaves no half file and the next one resumes.
The script then execs `<helper> node serve` on the same child, its stdin and stdout the one link (`hide-node/src/ssh/bootstrap.rs`); the distribution's panes run in holders the node starts there, and the kit runs once on connection.
The link owns the child: its end closes the child's stdin, waits five seconds, then ends its process tree, and the child's exit ends the link; the pane holders outlive both.
The five seconds start when the link ends, not when its input is free: a write blocked on a child that stopped reading holds the input, the input is closed once no write holds it, and ending the tree is what frees that write.
The core ends every device's link as it stops (`Core`'s drop, after the coordinators that could dial one again), so quitting Hide ends each distribution's helper; on Windows the job object also ends `wsl.exe` when hided exits without a destructor, and the helper then reads the end of its input, which the WSL lane proves by killing a process that holds a link.
At most four `wsl.exe` calls run at once across every distribution; each has its own deadline (10 s for the running check, 60 s for the probe, 180 s for an install or kit pass).

Starting a stopped distribution is a decision the core makes once per attempt (`HostAttempt` in `runtime/hosts.rs`): the app opening (`app_open`) and the operator's own reconnect (`device_host_retry`) may start it (`Wake::Allowed`), and every background retry, a link that ended and an automatic kit or project pass may not (`Wake::NotAllowed`).
A `Stopped` answer leaves the device unavailable with no retry scheduled, the row's "not connected", until one of those two asks again; the app opening while such an attempt is still running is kept in `device_wake_pending` and taken by the next attempt.
An SSH device takes the same argument and ignores it.
Add device's listing reads `wsl_distributions` beside the SSH hosts on the same worker; a WSL 1 distribution or one whose setup is pending is listed with why it cannot be chosen, and an unreadable registry is `wsl_problem`, never an empty list.
A WSL device's ports and disk are read through its node, as a node that dialed in reports its own (`reports_own_facts`), and its pull requests with this PC's GitHub login (D-18); its agent hooks and settings are written in the distribution's home only.

### A core on another machine

Layer 4 of the core-host-node PRD lets the machine with the screen run its daemon without a core, attached to the core on another machine (PRD core-host-node-remote-core).
Nothing the operator does writes the record that turns it on yet: the move of layer 5 and the test fixtures write it, so a machine without it runs exactly as before.
Below, M is the screen's machine and C the core's.

One program takes three roles.

| Role | Runs | Started by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core and node | The core, its own node, the screens on loopback: every machine without a placement record | `hide connect` (`start_daemon`) |
| Node | No core: the node's link to C, M's screens on loopback, M's terminals and file reads (`hided/src/node_role.rs`, `node_daemon.rs`) | `hide connect`, when `<state>/core-placement.json` names C (`start_node_daemon`) |
| Attach | No core: pipes the standard input and output of the node's `ssh` to C's running core, byte for byte (`hided/src/attach.rs`) | C's sshd, as `hided attach`, which the start script of M's `ssh` runs in its own place |

The placement record (`hided/src/placement.rs`) names C's SSH alias in M's `~/.ssh/config`, C's node id, the `hided` C runs as its attach role, and C's state folder when it is not the default.
It is the account's private file, at most 4 KiB, and one that is anything else, names M's own node id, holds a control character or a value over 1 KiB, or names a program or state folder that is not absolute in the spelling between machines, is refused at start with a diagnostic rather than read; `start_daemon` refuses a state folder that has one, so the core role never starts beside it.

M dials, C never does (D-04).
M's node reaches C as a device is reached, with one system `ssh` it starts and owns ([A device's ssh](#a-devices-ssh); PRD system-ssh-device-link B33): OpenSSH reads the alias, its keys, the agent, ProxyJump and Tailscale SSH, and `ssh -G` reads it again at every dial, so a fix the operator makes reaches the next one.
Its start script probes the machine and then execs `hided attach` in its own place, so the `ssh`'s standard input and output are the attach role's (`hide-node/src/ssh/session.rs`, `upstream.rs`).
What ssh asks goes to the screen whose press started the dial, by the device row's rules (PRD system-ssh-device-link B33): the same question, field, fingerprint, browser link and key touch, five minutes per question, check or touch, Cancel or no answer ending the attempt, and nothing kept.
