Only the operator's prompts, the agent's text and an interruption leave hided, each cut at 20,000 characters and marked; tool calls, tool output and injected context stay on the Mac.
The terminal reads the pane's rows through the engine (`read_rows`), 200 lines at first and 200 more per pull up to 1000; it sends rows only when their text or the asked count changed, and offers older rows only when the engine reports it cut some (`truncated`).
A reply is the text submitted through the engine (`Engine::submit_text`); the quick keys are `enter`, `esc`, `up`, `down` and `ctrl+c`.
Before that write the phone asks the pane's node for `input_permit`: the same creation request holds its byte reservation, so a fork's 64 KiB and 30-second caps include phone input and desktop keys together, with no second fork lookup in the core.
A permission waits behind earlier desktop input in the pane hold and controller writer before the phone can write.
A pane without a control attach is allowed: the permit changes neither attachment, grid nor focus, and the existing engine write still decides whether that pane exists and can take the input.
Permission is not delivery acknowledgment: `input_result.ok` becomes true only after the engine has taken the write; a discarded holder, a refused permit or a permission wait past 35 seconds returns `input_refused` before any write, keeps the phone's text and releases its request-id claim for a deliberate retry.
A failed engine write retains the existing uncertain-outcome rule, so a repeated id never sends it twice.
At most 64 permission callbacks wait per node or device link; the existing holder timer expires reservations in every creation or pane holder at 35 seconds (`INPUT_PERMIT_MAX_WAIT` in `hide-node-link`, which the core's and the phone's waits share), shutdown drops waiters, and the device writer wakes at that deadline to forget unanswered callbacks even without further input.
Creation requests currently belong only to the core machine, so a remote device node does not hold phone input for a fork; its permission still preserves the controller write order and answers pane closure or sleep.
The callback only hands its answer to the waiting phone worker or device uplink; it never calls back into the node, takes the Runtime mutex or performs I/O, and adds no resident worker or timer.

After permission, a phone writes to the engine directly, so the rule that a pane whose agent ends, sleeps or wakes takes no input is the core's input gate (`hide-core/src/input_gate.rs`), which the runtime keeps equal to its sleep records (an `Ending`, `Sleeping`, `Waking` or `Failed` record closes the pane; a refused end, a woken agent or a closed pane opens it).
A writer that bypasses a node's terminal (a phone's `input`, the agent's find keys) takes an admission from the gate immediately before its write and holds it until the write returns; a closed pane refuses it (`asleep`), never judged from a list read earlier, and the worker that ends the agent closes the pane first and waits for the admissions already held before it signals the agent, so a write admitted before the end lands in the agent and none lands behind it.
A write still held when the worker's six seconds pass is not waited out and not ended under: the worker signals nothing, logs `agent_sleep.drain_stalled`, and the sleep fails like an end the agent refused (the agent stays awake, the pane reopens, the pane backs off for an hour), so that write lands in the agent.
The gate is a flag and a counter behind its own small lock, taken by the runtime without waiting and by the end worker off the runtime's lock; nothing holds `Mutex<Runtime>` across a write.
A node's terminal drops a key, a paste and the bytes a screen answers its terminal with for the same panes (`TerminalControl::Asleep`, which the core sends from the same records); a paste already held for a pane that sleeps waits with the keys typed behind it.
That path is not behind the gate, because the node can be another machine, so a key or paste the node accepted before it heard `Asleep` can still land in the shell once the end has begun.
The window is bounded: automatic sleep never takes a pane on screen (`SleepStore::due` skips every pane of `agent_sleep_on_screen`, the core's shown tabs and a node's `shown_node_tabs`), and a key reaches only the keyboard's pane, which is always shown; so only an operator who picks Sleep agent on a pane they are typing into, or a paste stalled at that moment, can meet it, and only for the time the node's `Asleep` takes to arrive.
What would close it is a node acknowledgement bound to the sleep's generation, which the end worker would wait for beside the gate's drain; it is not built because that window needs the operator's own action to open.
The phone's list still carries the core's `sleep` (`PhoneSleep`: state `sleeping`, `waking` or `failed`, the failure's plain reason, the age and the last progress line), but only to draw the detail.
An `input` is answered from its request id's claim first, so a repeat of a reply that landed, or whose landing is in doubt, keeps its `ok` or `uncertain` after the agent sleeps; only a new write meets the gate, and a refused one claims nothing.
`wake_agent` names a pane the list holds and an optional `fresh`; for a `sleeping` or `failed` row hided dispatches the desktop's own `agent_wake` event for that pane, a `waking` row is acknowledged without a second dispatch, and any other pane is `unavailable`; the answer is the `sleep_result` frame with the pane's `<device>|<pane>` key as `sleep_id`, and the row's next list carries the progress.
A reply is at most 2,000 characters with no control characters, and a request id the phone repeats after a lost answer is written once: a repeat answers `ok` after a confirmed write, `in_flight` while the first is still running, and `uncertain` when the first write may have reached the pane, so the phone asks the operator to check rather than typing it again.
Neither path goes through the attach set or a core key event, so a phone never moves the desktop's visible tab, focus, terminal size or attach window; a device pane uses the core's existing API connection to that device, and a device that is not connected reads as `device_unreachable`.

The phone's missions are a second frame beside `agents`, `{type: "missions", items, failed, omitted}`, built from the same `rest` the agent list is built from, on its own `watch` channel in `Mobile`, so a mission change never rebuilds or resends the list and the list never carries missions.
`agent_state/tally/phone/missions.rs` reads each mission item through a private `Deserialize`-only copy (`MissionIn`, `NodeIn`), which is the whitelist: the frame holds ids, titles, statuses, the decision, its question and answer state, each step's pull request, stage and attention, and the Conductor's name and kind, and never a path, a branch, a session, a review, a report or a criterion.
A step and the Conductor carry an `agent` key only for a row the phone's list holds, so a step opens its worker's detail (`openDetail`, the same navigation the list uses) and never a pane the phone could not open, and a step's `escalation` is the cause and blocked line the core already put on that worker's agent row.
The frame is capped as the rest are: at most 24 open and 24 finished missions, newest first, and within the list budget above, which leaves out first the steps of finished missions, the oldest first (the row stays with `nodes_omitted`, and its page says how many steps stayed on the Mac instead of counting progress), then finished missions and then open ones, the oldest first; a step of an open mission is never left out alone, because its progress cells and its decision read every step; the missions left out are counted in `omitted`, which the phone shows as one dimmed line under the list, and recorded as `missions.capped` when the record first goes over a cap, not again while it stays over; a record the core could not read is `failed` and an item that does not parse is skipped with `mission.projection_invalid`, never drawn half.
Which mission waits on the operator, the four groups, a row's one line and a step's mark are not decided here: `web/src/missions.ts`, `missionList.ts` and `missionAnswer.ts` hold one rule for each over the narrow `MissionBrief` type, the desktop's mission screen calls them with its full `Mission` and the phone with `PhoneMission`, so the two screens cannot group, count or word the same record differently, and the desktop's decision banner and the phone's mission page draw one `answerView`.
`answer_mission` carries a request id, the mission, the question's key and exactly one of an `option` counted from 1, a written `text` (non-empty, one line and at most 500 characters once the spaces around it go, `missions::ANSWER_LIMIT`; `missions::answer_text` is that one judgement, which the core's `mission_answer` makes too, so the phone never refuses an answer the core would take) or `resend`; it is refused before anything is dispatched, as `gone` for a mission the frame does not list and `invalid_request` for any other shape, and a refusal claims nothing.
Otherwise hided takes the request id's claim (`reserve_input`), dispatches the desktop's own `mission_answer` event and settles the claim `Written` on one blocking thread, so a repeat of the same press, on this socket or another, answers `ok` from the claim and `in_flight` while the first is still running, and the core's answer per question key is the second layer: the Conductor gets one answer to one question however many presses arrive.
A dispatch that failed releases the claim, so the phone may send the id again.
`ask_mission_material` carries a request id, the mission and the question's key, is refused `gone` for a mission the frame does not list, and is claimed and dispatched the same way as the desktop's own `mission_material` event; that the Conductor was asked comes back on the question as `material_asked`, and a decision's Views ride the mission as `decision_views`, each with the pane of the agent that opened it while that agent is open, so a row opens that agent's 볼 것 and never a View by a path.
`reopen_mission_view` carries a request id, the mission, the question's key and a row's `view`, is refused `gone` for a row the frame does not list, and is claimed and dispatched as the desktop row's own `mission_view_reopen` under that request id; what the core did comes back on the row's `reopens`, and the phone opens the agent's 볼 것 once the row is open again, says why when its own press is refused, the question moved on or the device stopped answering, gives up on a press the core never answered for after 30 s (the core's wait and a margin), and sends one such press at a time.
The reasons the operator can act on (a changed question, a Conductor that is gone, a device that stopped answering) are not in the reply: the core records them on the mission as `answer_failed` and they arrive in the next `missions` frame, where the phone words them with the desktop's own `mission.banner.*` and `mission.noConductor` messages; the reply `mission_result` only says whether the event reached the core.
The phone keeps the written text in its store until a reply says the answer went, and a lost connection turns an unanswered press into the offline line while keeping both the text and the request id, so pressing it again after the reconnect is the same request.

The phone's pull requests are a third frame beside `agents` and `missions`, `{type: "prs", projects, items, feedback, omitted}`, built from the same `rest` and republished on its own `watch` channel in `Mobile`, so a pull request change never rebuilds the agent list.
`agent_state/tally/phone/prs.rs` reads the workspaces' pull requests, the board's rows (`agent_scope.prs`) and the cards `pr_card_read` filled through `Deserialize`-only copies, which are the whitelist: an item is the list's own `PullRequestSnapshot`, its project id, the board's group and reason, the agents the phone's list holds for it, whether a checkout of its branch exists, and a card trimmed to its head, files (at most 50, with `files_total`), merge options, failed parts and write; the body, the review threads and every path stay on the Mac.
Items follow the board's order, the rows the desktop folds are not listed, and the frame is capped at 48 open and 8 lately merged pull requests, the rest counted in `omitted`, which the phone shows as a line under the list.
The frame carries the one feedback read the core holds, which the phone matches to the request id it asked with, never a card or a thread of another pull request.
Which of the phone's four groups a row stands in, its line, what the Merge button says and why it is off are not decided here: `web/src/mobile/prModel.ts` sorts the board's reason into the groups and calls the desktop card's own `mergeWhy`, `defaultMethod`, `primaryAction`, `confirmHolds` and `checkSummary` (`prCardModel.ts`), the desktop's `prReview` and `readingOfStatuses` judge the rest, its `ReasonLine` and `ApprovalCount` draw a row's line with the approvals where the desktop list puts them, and `delegatePrompt` (`prDelegate.ts`) writes the hand-over's first instruction, so the two screens cannot group, count or word one pull request differently; the phone imports `i18n/translator` and not the shell's `i18n/client` (the same hook), which is why those two parts read it from there.
`read_pr` (with an optional `look_again`), `read_pr_feedback`, `merge_pr` and `delegate_pr` each become the one core event the desktop card sends (`pr_card_read`, `pr_feedback_read`, `pr_merge`, `pr_delegate`, `mobile/prs.rs`), and only for a pull request the phone's own `prs` frame lists, named by the frame's key and never by a project, a path or a repository; a key the frame does not list is `gone`, a settled pull request `settled`, and any other shape `invalid_request`, each refused before anything is dispatched.
`merge_pr` carries the head commit the card showed and a method the card offered (none for a repository with a merge queue, which takes none); it is refused as `unread` before the card was read, as `head_moved` when the card the core holds now shows another head, and otherwise reaches `pr_merge`, whose own rules then apply as they do for the desktop: the core refuses a head the list moved past and a second write while one is working, and the write is `gh pr merge --match-head-commit`, so GitHub refuses a head it moved past.
A merge is an effect, so hided takes the request id's claim (`reserve_input`) and settles it on one blocking thread: a repeat of the same press, on this socket or another, answers from the claim and reaches GitHub once, `in_flight` while the first is still being sent; a read is no effect and is sent each time.
What GitHub then did comes back as the card's `write` in the next `prs` frame, and `pr_result {request_id, action, pr, ok, reason}` says only whether hided sent the request.
The phone keeps one request id for the same intent (the pull request, the head and the method) until an outcome is known, a lost connection keeps it and the text, and a refusal that sent nothing gives the next press a new one.
`delegate_pr` carries the prompt (at most the start sheet's 4,000 characters), a kind and an optional model, and reaches `pr_delegate` with `stay_behind`: the agent starts where the desktop's hand-over would start it, in the checkout that holds the branch or in a new worktree of it, and the core moves nothing on the desktop, because `stay_behind` reaches both starts (`AgentStartInCheckoutPayload` and `CreateWorktreePayload`, whose `focus` is `!stay_behind`).
It is answered by the `start_result` frame under its request id like a start from the sheet, and a refusal the core says before any start holds the slot carries that request id (`Runtime::delegate_pr`), so the phone is told rather than left to wait out the 90 seconds.
`web/src/mobile/PrsScreen.tsx` draws the tab, `PrDetail.tsx` the page with its merge confirmation, and `PrDelegateSheet.tsx` the hand-over; the phone's store keeps the open page, the confirmation (which closes without sending when the page no longer shows the head, queue and method it named), the sheet's prompt and choice and the last result, and sends no event of its own.

Push is Web Push that hided signs and encrypts itself with `ring`: a VAPID ES256 key made once and kept in `mobile.json`, RFC 8291 `aes128gcm` bodies, and a POST through `ureq` over rustls on a blocking thread, never under the core lock.
Only the push services' own hosts are accepted as endpoints (Apple, FCM, Mozilla, Windows), parsed as an `https` URL with no userinfo and no port but 443 and posted without following redirects, plus a loopback endpoint in a debug build for the e2e.
`agent_state::push::Transitions` (`agent_state/turn.rs`) owns notification state and the ten-minute disappearance ledger; hided owns subscriptions, mode policy and delivery.
The first list only seeds the transitions; after it, a root agent entering Needs You or Done sends one notice per subscribed phone, a descendant's question, approval or error raises its root, and the notice's tag (`device|root pane`) replaces the one before it.
A stopped turn with agent summaries on waits to announce Done until its final analysis lands, including the existing one timeout retry; its row keeps following the activity and demand facts meanwhile.
The label worker carries one pending lifecycle sequence per pane through the snapshot to the shared notification judge, so an asynchronous Question judgment cannot be preceded by a premature Done notice.
Success, terminal failure, an unreadable session, cancellation by a newer lifecycle state, or turning summaries off ends that wait; no notification timer or polling is added.
Every fallback that ends the wait finalizes this turn's notice as Done at one point: a terminal analysis failure, an unreadable session, turning summaries off, or entering provider recovery (for example a login or usage limit, recorded as `notification.provider_recovery`).
A later recovered judgment or turning summaries back on still updates the row but does not announce the same lifecycle sequence again.
A new turn, a native unanswered question, a separate core ask, and a raised descendant remain new notification causes; the same root tag still replaces a previous notice.
A relay push also carries `room`, the same derived base64url device room as the QR, so the phone's per-room worker opens the correct Hide; each Hide retains its own VAPID key.
A push payload carries the root's row title as `title`, `state` (`needs_you` or `done`), its published `status_code` and exact chosen second-line `detail`, the project as `place`, the `tag`, `device_id`, `pane_id` and `clear`.
The sentence is untranslated and never logged; terminal content is still excluded (operator-approved change 2026-10-13, [status-model.md: With and without Hide AI](status-model.md#with-and-without-hide-ai)).
The phone page gives its worker the translated group and row-status words, kept in `hide-phone-words` so a closed app still notifies: with a sentence the body is the row word, sentence and project joined by ` · `; without one the old group word and project remain.
An older worker ignores the new fields; a new worker with an older page's words uses the group word, and with no stored words it draws only the sentence and project.
Encryption accepts at most 3,993 plaintext bytes, so the aes128gcm HTTP body is at most 4,096 bytes including its 103-byte overhead; a payload beyond that returns the fixed size-limit failure through the existing push delivery diagnostic before a POST.
An agent that leaves the list is remembered for ten minutes, so one that comes back in the same state is not announced again; the cost is that the notification of a root that left for good is cleared up to ten minutes later.
The mode decides whether it is sent: never for 끔, only while no desktop renderer is connected for 앱이 닫혀 있을 때만, and always for 항상; a phone viewing that agent's detail is skipped in every mode.
A root that turned Seen rides the next notice's `clear` list, and the app closes those notifications when it opens, because iOS drops a subscription that receives a push it does not show.
A 404 or 410 answer drops that subscription, and the phone registers again on its next connection.
The iOS app has no Web Push: it registers an APNs device token and a per-computer push key inside its encrypted session (`apns_registration`), kept in its phone record instead of a Web Push subscription, and its notices are encrypted the same way and handed to the relay over the running device socket, which signs them for Apple and forwards them storing nothing (`docs/RELAY_PROTOCOL.md`, Push relay).
That send runs on the same blocking thread as a Web Push send, waits for the relay's answer at most 30 seconds through a bounded queue of 8 and at most 32 unanswered requests, and takes no lock while it waits; a `token_gone` answer drops the registration, a `token_rejected` answer (Apple refuses the token for its environment or topic) keeps it and is a configuration diagnostic, and every other failure is a diagnostic without retry.
It needs the relay method and a relay that said it forwards pushes; without them the notice is dropped with a diagnostic.

The desktop app's agent notifications (PRD first-run-onboarding D-09, D-10) run the same `Transitions` a second time in `hided/src/desktop_notices.rs`, on the projection the follower already read, so a burst still serializes one snapshot however many consumers it has, and independent of Mobile: the phones' ledger and the desktop's never share a seed.
A desktop window asks for them with the `desktop_notices` event (`{wanted}`), which hided accepts only from a desktop client and never sends to the core; the demand is per connection (`demand.rs`), so a closed window takes its own with it, and the first projection after the demand turns on only seeds, so nothing already waiting is announced.
A judgment that announces or clears something is one `agent_notice` frame (`{notices, clear}`, including the root's `status_code` and `detail`) broadcast to the desktop windows with a backlog of 16 (a browser tab holds no receiver); one function, `judge_pass` in `hided/src/mobile/mod.rs`, decides each pass for both sides, so the phones' and the desktop's switches never change what the other announces; a window that falls behind misses those notifications, which is logged (`agent_notice.lagged`), and the next change is announced as usual.
The core stores separate desktop Needs You (`desktop_notifications`) and Done (`desktop_notifications_done`) choices.
A missing Done choice in an older store inherits the former shared choice; new installs default both off and the wizard enables Needs You only.
Each toggle is one event; Not now disables both in one event, repeated choices publish nothing, and both use the existing coalesced off-lock UI-state writer.
A window asks for notices while either is on, filters each notice by its own group, words it in the interface language and hands it to the host, which drops it while a Hide window has the keyboard and closes the ones `clear` names.
The app icon count sums the device scopes' raised Needs You and unread Done groups, including folded rows, while each group's own switch is on; reading Done removes it from the count, and phone push settings stay independent.
While Mobile is on with a phone paired, hided skips the ten-minute idle exit.
The records are `mobile_transport`, `mobile_pairing`, `mobile_phone`, `mobile_push` and `mobile_store` in `Logs/core.jsonl`, and none carries a code, a credential, a subscription key or an APNs device token.
The operator notice for a held letter or an unanswered inactivity warning uses the same delivery: `push::notice_route` judges, from values only and under the Mobile mutex rather than `Mutex<Runtime>`, whether a phone can be reached at all (mode against the connected renderers, the Mobile switch, a Web Push subscription or an app registration), and a phone that cannot be reached is not sent to; the core's own engine shows no notification, so the phone is the one channel that reaches the operator.
The phone's reason is a code, and when it was not reached the one `human.channels_failed` record names it (`docs/delivery.md`).

### Panes, tabs and the attach window in the web shell

The center draws the visible tab's `pane_layouts` entry as nested CSS grids (`web/src/PaneGrid.tsx`): a split is a two-track grid sized by the layout's ratio and every leaf is a pane with its own xterm instance (`web/src/terminals.ts`, keyed by pane id).
An instance lives as long as the core streams its pane (PRD S2 D-05, amendment 1): leaving a tab parks its terminals in a hidden lot in the document, still fed by the chunks the hub keeps sending for every attached pane, and coming back re-parents them into the pane hosts and fits them, so the last frame is on screen in the same tick and only a size change goes out (`terminal_viewport` with `new_view: false`, `terminal_resize`).
A chunk for a pane that has never been shown is dropped; its first show requests a full frame with `new_view`, as does a parked pane's next show after a self-contained snapshot, which reaches the pane's node directly.
The core passes a `terminal_resize` on to the node only when the size changed, so a new view at the grid its session already runs at gets its full frame from the node, which asks the engine for the whole screen as a redraw does.
`retainTerminals` disposes an instance only when the core reports the pane `released` or stops listing it; the core attaches all shown Agent tabs on its own tick, fills the bounded retention window with recent tabs, and reports `released` for the rest, which the pane header draws as a caption whose click sends `reconnect_pane`.
The store keeps the `rest` section structurally shared across frames (`web/src/share.ts`): the core resends the whole section whenever any part changes, so an untouched workspace, tab or pane row keeps its object reference and its memoized row does not re-render.
A divider drag moves a guide line and sends one `resize_pane` on release, computed from the travel over the split's span; it names the pane just before the divider for a drag right or down and the pane just after it for a drag left or up, the panes whose edge on that side is the divider, so the divider the operator grabbed is the split that moves however the tab is nested; a change outside the core's `0.001..=0.5` sends nothing.
A zoomed tab draws only the zoomed pane, over the whole canvas, so its fit and `terminal_resize` follow the full geometry the engine gave the PTY; the other panes' terminals stay parked and fed.
The wheel is the engine's (PRD S2 B19): the instance has no local scrollback, a wheel event over a pane becomes whole rows in `web/src/wheel.ts` (trackpad pixels accumulate with their remainder, a wheel notch moves at least one row), the rows of one animation frame go out as one `terminal_scroll` with the cell under the pointer and the crossterm modifier bitset, and the core answers with the viewport frame; ⌥ + wheel is left to the browser.
The core routes that event by the pane's session (`scroll_pane` in `runtime/terminal.rs`): a controlled pane's session writes `terminal.scroll`, which the pane holder routes to the program's mouse handling or the history; and a pane with no session yet (no size reported, or its attach still starting after a tab switch) keeps the lines for its first frame.
The wheel has one owner: the capture listener stops the event before xterm sees it, because xterm turns a wheel over a buffer without scrollback (ours, and any alternate-screen program) into cursor-key bytes on the PTY and answers a mouse-tracking program with its own wheel report, both of which the holder already decides from `terminal_scroll`.
The holder redraws the viewport in place, so the screen alone cannot say which history row a screen row is: every full frame, and a delta whose view moved, says it in the holder's private OSC 7721 (`VIEW_OSC` in `hide-holder/src/encode.rs`, read by `web/src/terminalView.ts`), the history row of the screen's top row and the most it can be, counted from the oldest row kept, with whether the program takes pointer events and whether the alternate screen shows.
A drag selection is kept in those history rows (`Selection` in `web/src/terminals.ts`), so it stays on its text while the wheel or new output moves the history under it, and the part on screen is drawn with xterm's `select`; each row it covers is read into it whenever a frame shows that row, so a copy holds the rows scrolled away too, and a selection none of which is on screen keeps its copy text selected in xterm's input textarea so the browser fires a copy event for ⌘C and the Edit menu, until the next click, drag, select all or key.
Held past the screen's top or bottom edge, a drag scrolls the history toward the pointer as a native terminal does: one `terminal_scroll` at a time every 30 ms, the next only once the frame answering the last arrived or 500 ms passed, by one row and one more for every row of distance but never a whole screen, so every row the drag passes is shown and read; a wheel turned during the drag follows the same rule; the selection ends at 20,000 rows (`MAX_SELECTION_ROWS`, `terminal.selection_capped` in the log).
A frame that shows another screen (the alternate one, a history that shrank, another width) ends the selection, since its history rows now name other text; a holder built before OSC 7721 says nothing, and a wheel then ends the selection rather than leave it on other text.
The history row of a kept row moves when a full history drops its oldest rows while the screen is scrolled up; a selection made across that moment can cover rows that slid by the dropped count, which this does not correct.
Keyboard focus has one reporter: a pane's textarea gaining focus under the pointer is the operator moving focus and goes out as `focus_pane`, while the focus the shell itself moves to follow the snapshot's focused pane (`focusTerminal`) is never reported back, because that echo, arriving at the core while the engine's confirmation of the previous move was still in flight, kept two panes trading focus on a slow runner.
A snapshot older than the operator's last click must not pull the keys back, and the page tells such a snapshot from a real move by state, not by time: `web/src/ws.ts` numbers each operator `focus_pane` it sends (`client_id` for the page load, `sequence` per page, counted only once the frame has left the socket), the core records the last number it applied for each page in `focused.operator_focus` of the snapshot, in the same event that moves or refuses the focus, and `PaneView` follows the snapshot's focused pane only while the number applied has caught up with the number sent (`operatorFocusSent` and `operatorFocusApplied` in the store, `web/src/operatorFocus.ts`).
Once caught up, a snapshot whose focus moves onto another pane is a real move (the core followed the engine, or refused the click after an earlier answer had moved it) and is followed as before.
What the page follows is the focus moving onto a pane, never the catching up itself: the answer to a click on the pane that was already focused moves nothing, so the keyboard stays wherever the operator took it while the answer was on its way (the sidebar, Overview), where following the catching up pulled it back into the terminal (#608).
For the same reason a refused click whose answer leaves the focus on the pane it was already on moves no keys, as before the numbering: the keys stay on the clicked pane and the focus ring shows the core's.
A move that arrives before the snapshot has caught up waits for it once, and is dropped when the focus leaves that pane first or when the keyboard is no longer where it was when the move arrived, because the operator has taken it elsewhere since.
The record is capped at 16 pages, oldest evicted with a `pane.focus.sequence_evicted` diagnostic (a page whose entry was seen and is gone takes everything it sent as applied, because the core reads it as having nothing in flight), and a new connection starts with nothing awaited, because a number lost on a closed socket will never be answered.
A remote pane's focus goes to its host as `remote_control` and is not numbered: the local core never applies it, so it has nothing to acknowledge, and the same guard does not cover a stale device session.
A pointer gesture follows one routing state in `web/src/terminals.ts` (PRD S2 B20), as Ghostty routes it: a primary press over a program that takes pointer events (OSC 7721's flag) goes to it as `terminal_mouse` press, motion while the button is held (one per animation frame, at the cell reached, and past the pane's edge at the cell it would be as `outside`, beside the grid's nearest cell) and release, unless ⇧ is held, which selects instead; otherwise a single press starts the drag selection above, and one that never left its cell is sent on release as a `terminal_mouse` press and release at the pressed cell, which the holder reports only to a program that tracks the mouse; ⌥ + press, a double or triple click (xterm's word and line) and a press on a link stay local and send nothing.
The press sends `focus_pane` first, through the textarea taking focus.
The cell is read against xterm's own screen element, which is exactly `cols` by `rows` cells; the pane host around it is larger by the fit's remainder, and a cell derived from the host drifts by up to one row and one column toward the far edge, which is where a full-screen program's one-row hint sits (the first real-session clicks on Claude Code's "Jump to bottom" missed for that reason).
The core passes `terminal_mouse` to a controlled pane's node as `TerminalControl::Mouse` and the node to the holder as `ClientMessage::Mouse`, which the holder encodes in the program's mouse mode and format at that moment or drops (`Pane::mouse`), for every program alike: in cells at the grid's nearest cell, a motion that stays in it reported once, and in pixels (mode 1016) at the cell's middle, past the edge too, negative above the pane, as Ghostty tells a drag out of its surface, which is how Claude Code hears a selection dragged past the top and scrolls (on Windows at the nearest cell, since ConPTY drops a report below zero, a release too; [INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md#what-each-system-supports)); a node sends `outside` only to a holder whose welcome names the `mouse_outside` capability, and an older holder is told the nearest cell; xterm's own mouse reports never fire because the holder's frames carry no mouse mode: a `terminal.frame` is a `CSI row;1H` redraw of every row with only synchronized-output and cursor-visibility modes, so xterm's mouse tracking is never switched on.
The same frames pad every row to the full width with written spaces and never soft-wrap, so a copy of the selection is assembled in `web/src/selection.ts` rather than by xterm: trailing whitespace is trimmed from every row, a row whose last cell is non-blank continues onto the next row with no break, and a real line end stays `\n`, and the leading whitespace every non-blank line shares is removed as the program's margin while the indentation between lines is kept (a single line loses its leading spaces entirely, and a drag that starts past column 0 leaves its cut first line out of the margin); a full row is kept apart where the holder said it does not run on (`paneRowWraps` in `web/src/terminalWrap.ts`, the same answer a link's join reads: a line break in a pane with no agent, or a link that ends at the row's edge in any pane), and joined where nothing was said, as for an agent's own line break.
An Escape the shell answers (a cycle, a close confirmation, the sheet, the find bar) is stopped at the window capture listener, because the pane's textarea keeps keyboard focus under the sheet and xterm would send the same press to the program as an ESC byte.
Closing follows one flow in `web/src/close.ts`: an unknown activity status asks for `refresh_status` first, a working pane asks once, an idle pane closes with `confirmed: false`.

### Settings and workspace management in the web shell

Project choices live in the additive, versioned `ui_state.project_settings` map, keyed by `hide_project::project_id` of the owning device and its canonical main-worktree root.
The catalog supplies that root; neither the visible workspace id nor the stored primary checkout identifies the settings, and a remote root is never resolved on this machine.
An unset issue or base field retains the legacy path-based choice, an explicit automatic choice shadows it, and a partial patch leaves omitted fields unchanged.
`project_settings_set` admits the exact catalog device/root pair and validates the repository and existing branch before the existing coalesced state writer saves it outside the runtime mutex.
The confirmed record and its consumers move only when that exact save acknowledges the pending record; a failure retains the prior record with a request-scoped failed receipt, and closing a client does not cancel the write.
A core move gives the records of a machine whose id changes the new id and the key made from it (Moving the core), so the choices follow the project to the new core and back.
Records are bounded to 256 projects, and transient receipts to 512 entries so a busy refusal can settle its caller without replacing an active write; receipts are not persisted, and unrelated `ui_state_update` echoes preserve both maps.
Completed receipts displaced by a later caller remain request-scoped within that bound, so a coalesced snapshot still exposes each saved outcome; clients retain an observed terminal outcome when another writer replaces the project's latest receipt.
An explicit repository is a private provider target, not a git remote or credential change.
The existing GitHub reader separates its cached checks by repository as well as root and generation; changing the confirmed connection removes the previous screen data, moves the generation and rejects late remote answers for the old repository.
Before a connection changes, the record retains up to 200 existing checkout issue references by checkout path, branch and bare number, with their original repository.
Bare issue numbers on those unchanged branches keep that identity after restart, while an explicit owner/repository reference names its own target; prior issue creation and PR replies cannot attach to a different repository's same-number resource.
This adds bounded map lookups to link projection and uses the existing readers and save queue, with no polling, subprocess or machine I/O under the runtime mutex.
Remote worktree requests carry the confirmed device/root base choice, and a base change discards the one old in-flight answer before the coalesced reread.
The search slot likewise refuses joins to an invalidated worker and resolves every fresh target from the confirmed connection before a provider read answers.
`project_memory_navigate` scopes focus and the right lane's Hide AI tool to one checkout and calls that lane forward; a remote lane changes only when the existing pending choice reaches its exact front, and a refused focus drops the choice.
An accepted newer checkout, pane, tab, device, file or local Memory navigation supersedes that pending Memory choice before its late acknowledgment or checkout arrival can move the screen.
Memory projects expose their own hook-preparation and failed-action state, preserving confirmed values and cards for Retry.
Settings retries only its enable or disable action; card deletion, forgetting and promotion retain the Hide AI tool's confirmation and card identity.
Tests in `hide-core/src/runtime/tests/project_settings.rs` cover the save acknowledgment, failed save, fallback, identity and late-answer boundary.

#### Project guardrails

A project's protections are a field of its settings record (`guardrails`, record version 2; a version 1 record reads as every protection off), saved by the same `project_settings_set` and validated in the core (`hide_agent_hooks::guardrails::Rules::validate`: at most 32 paths of at most 200 bytes, no duplicate, each a pattern the gitignore reader takes); a Git protection on a plain folder is refused `project_settings_not_git`.
The hooks never ask the daemon: each machine holds one policy file its agents' hooks read (`~/.hide/agent-hooks/guardrails.json`), and the core has that machine's node write it (`Call::GuardrailPolicy`, `hide-core/src/runtime/guardrails.rs`), so the decision stays on the agent's machine and a tool call costs no round trip ([agent-hooks.md](agent-hooks.md#project-guardrails)).
The file names every project of that machine with a protection on, whether or not it is registered, since a project shown from an engine workspace is guarded too; removing a project clears its protections, a save still on its way included (`Runtime::forget_project_guardrails`).
A settings record keeps the fields a newer build wrote (`ProjectSettings::unknown`, `Rules::unknown`), so saving a newer record again here loses none of them; a change keeps the record's copy of them rather than its own, since the shell sends back what it was shown, so nothing a change names beyond this build's protections reaches the policy every hook reads.
A save that moves a machine's policy is delivered first and saved after: the record waits outside the frame the state writer saves until its machine answers, so Saved means the machine has the new file, and a refused or timed-out write (10 s) fails the save `project_settings_policy_failed`, keeps the confirmed record and writes the confirmed policy once more.
One worker thread per machine (`hide-core-guardrails`) writes one call at a time and computes the policy when it takes the job, so a burst of changes is one write of the newest state; each write carries a rising sequence and the node keeps the last it applied, so a write that outlived its 10 s wait never lands over a newer one and is answered with the sequence the node holds, and a core whose sequence fell behind it (another core's write, a clock set back) moves past it and writes again, up to three times in a row before the saves fail; nothing is added under `Mutex<Runtime>` but the map reads that build the policy, and a device that is not connected is written when it is, not on every save.
Only a core on the folder the account's hide picks with no `HIDE_STATE_DIR` (`~/.hide/state`, or `$XDG_STATE_HOME/hide` where that is set: `Env::account_state_folder`, passed as `CoreOptions::account_state_folder`) writes this machine's file: one on a relocated folder, a test's or a verification run's on the operator's account, writes nothing under `~/.hide` (`hided/tests/it/connect_build.rs`), and its saves settle as delivered, since this machine's hooks follow the account's own core.
The core writes its own machine's file after `Core::create` and each device's when it is Ready, so a file changed outside Hide is put right at the next start or connection; a device that goes away is forgotten.
Tests in `hide-core/src/runtime/tests/guardrails.rs` cover the ordering, the failed delivery, a base branch change, the folder and path refusals, the removal and the start, and `hided/tests/it/node_contract.rs` the node's write.

Interface language is a core-owned UI preference: `interface_language_set` alone changes `ui_state.interface_language`, and unrelated UI saves preserve it.
The existing coalesced persistence queue stores the raw choice; snapshot serialization publishes English for an invalid stored value while keeping that value and logging a diagnostic.
Clients resolve an unset choice from their own primary system language and apply only confirmed snapshot choices.
[LOCALIZATION.md](LOCALIZATION.md) owns the supported languages, translation boundary and current integration coverage.

The color theme is owned the same way: `color_theme_set` alone changes `ui_state.color_theme` (`hide` or `neutral`, Hide by default), `ui_state_update` carries it through, and the current value again saves nothing.
The store keeps it as text beside the mode (`theme`), so a value this build does not know loads as Hide with the `ui_state.color_theme_unknown` diagnostic instead of making the store unreadable.
The shell puts `palette-hide` on the document root beside the mode class, and the phone projection carries the value so a paired phone draws it; the desktop host cannot read the store before it attaches, so its window color before the page paints is Hide Dark, read from `web/src/tokens.css` by `desktop/scripts/build.mjs`.

The agent logo view mode is a core-owned UI preference the same way: `agent_logo_mode_set` alone changes `ui_state.agent_logo_mode`, an unknown stored value reads as `hidden` with a `ui_state.agent_logo_mode_unknown` diagnostic, and unrelated UI saves preserve it.
The pane turn row mode follows it: `pane_turn_row_mode_set` alone changes `ui_state.pane_turn_row_mode`, an unknown stored value reads as `one_line` with a `ui_state.pane_turn_row_mode_unknown` diagnostic, and unrelated UI saves preserve it.

Settings (`web/src/SettingsSheet.tsx` for the sheet and one module per page under `web/src/settings/`, rules and the list's order in `web/src/settings.ts`) lists its pages in two groups, App (General, Notifications, Devices, Shortcuts) and This Mac (Agents, Hide AI, Mobile, GitHub), with About apart, and opens from the sidebar's gear or ⌥; which page is open is page-local UI state (`web/src/ui.ts`): General (`GeneralTab`, `AppearanceGroup`) writes `accent_hex` and `font_size` through `ui_state_update` (the sidebar's right edge writes `sidebar_width` the same way, 220 to 440, a value outside refused into the diagnostic log), Notifications (`NotificationsTab`) writes the desktop switch the first-run wizard shares and the `mobile` frame's push mode, GitHub (`GithubTab`) sends `github_request` with `refresh` for its Check again, and About (`AboutTab`) reads the `daemon` frame and `status.{herdr,environment,diagnostics}`; its Terminal engine row reads `status.herdr` (the field keeps its old name), the state and message the session sync reports for the engine. Agents reads each device row's `kit` (its seven `agents` with their pieces, `partial` and `features`, and `sessions`, how many of the agent's sessions run there now), shows one machine at a time, and sends `kit_check` (the core reads this Mac and every connected device, so Check again is one event for all), and `kit_agent_set`, `kit_reinstall` and `agent_permission_set` (an agent's 권한) for the machine on screen, Devices (`DevicesTab`, one `DeviceRow` per machine, `DeviceDetails` for what a healthy row does not show) reads each row's `kit`, mentions only a part that needs the operator and sends `ssh_hosts_list` when its Add dialog opens and `register_device` (the alias of the Host chosen from `status.ssh_hosts`, the name, always the kit consent the dialog states; the dialog is opened by the Add device button, or `ui.openAddDevice()` from the rail and the Add project host list), `kit_check`, `kit_reinstall`, `device_host_consent`, `device_host_retry`, `test_device`, `retry_connect`, `focus_device` and `remove_device` (the sidebar's device switcher sends `focus_device` too), Agents also sends `agent_sleep_set` (`after_hours`: null for Never, 12, 24, 48 or 72; 24 until one is chosen) and counts this machine's sleeping agents from the navigator, Hide AI reads `status.background_ai` and sends `ai_settings` and the worktree-name switch of `issue_settings_set`, and Shortcuts writes the running host's own set (`browser_shortcut_bindings` in a browser, `shortcut_bindings` in the desktop app).
Every row shows what the snapshot says; an edit is pending until the snapshot carries it, and a refusal is matched to the edit by the core's `last_error` kind and time.
The core clears `last_error` at its next event of any kind, so every refusal it records is also written to the diagnostic log as `error.reported` with its `error_kind` and message; a client that never reads the snapshot in between (a fixture, a headless driver) still finds the reason there.
While a device is selected the sheet shows a device chip saying that selecting it changes where files, Git and panes run and not where Settings live; with This Mac selected no page speaks of ownership (PRD settings-cleanup D-02, replacing S5.5 B35); the Agents page lists one machine's agents from its install kit at a time, This Mac first and then each device in the Devices order, with Reinstall only on an agent whose piece needs it (PRD settings-cleanup B13, B67).
A device row shows only what that device reported (its helper's platform and the staged connection test's results), and a connection that did not come up names its class (`problem`, `contracts/snapshot-wire-enums.json`: `device_problem`) with the action it needs, while what ssh asks waits on the row (`sign_in`) ([A device's ssh](#a-devices-ssh)); Hide never edits known_hosts and keeps no answer.
Add device lists the account's Host entries from `status.ssh_hosts`, which the `ssh_hosts_list` event fills (`runtime/ssh_hosts.rs` asks `DeviceConnector::ssh_hosts`, answered by `hide-node/src/ssh/hosts.rs`): one worker off the lock reads `<home>/.ssh/config` and the files it `Include`s (at most 16 files of 256 KiB, four levels deep; `~` and a relative path resolve like `ssh` does, `*` and `?` match in the last component), keeps each concrete alias in file order (a `Host` line with several aliases yields each; a pattern with `*`, `?` or `!`, and a name starting with `-`, names none), and resolves up to 32 of them with `ssh -F <home>/.ssh/config -G -- <alias>`, four children at a time, each an owned child under a three-second deadline with a login environment plus `HOME`.
`-G` prints the resolved configuration without connecting, so `address` reads `user@host:port` and nothing is opened or written; `-F` names the account's own config because `ssh` would otherwise read the passwd entry's home.
Each registered device's alias is resolved too (at most 16 more), so `added_as` carries the device's name for an alias a device already uses and for any alias that reaches the same `user@host:port`, the host name compared in any case (`SshAddress::endpoint_key`), on the default server and never through a custom socket; `ssh_registration` in `runtime/ssh_hosts.rs` is that decision, and the first-run rows and their Connect ask it too, so one config shows one added state on both screens.
An alias with no address carries `problem` (`ssh_missing`, `ssh_failed`, `timed_out`); a missing or unreadable config is `ready` with no host.
A request while one runs joins it, a dropped runtime stops the children, and the list is read again on each request, never stored: a device is still an alias and a name.
The first-run step's machines are one cancelable worker's read (`machine_profiles_list`, `runtime/machine_profiles.rs`): the account's Host entries through `DeviceConnector::ssh_hosts`, Add device's listing with its bounds and filter, and this PC's WSL distributions through `DeviceConnector::wsl_distributions`.
It reads no Herdr configuration, so a computer with nothing to list settles as an empty, ready list and the step is skipped.
Rows are grouped by the resolved `user@host:port`: a second alias of the same key adds no row (`ssh:<alias>` names the first), a different user or port stays apart, and an unresolved Host is keyed by its own name.
A row's added state and its connect's device come from Add device's `ssh_registration`, so a press after a Connect that registered it converges on that device; otherwise it goes through `register_device` as Add device's does, with the press's consent, and the core gives the device its id ([A device's id](#a-devices-id)).
The listing tells an incomplete read (`truncated`: a size, depth or file bound) from one that could not be read (`unreadable`: a config that exists but is not a readable text file); a wildcard Include whose folder could not be listed is unreadable too, while a bound that cut an Include is incomplete; an unreadable config fails the whole read with Retry, an incomplete one keeps the step, and only a missing config is an empty list.
An attempt such a Connect starts is recorded by device and generation (`first_run_attempts`); `first_run_sign_in_withdraw`, which the step sends as it goes away, raises that attempt's `RowSignIn` withdrawal and answers its waiting question Cancelled, so it ends as `sign_in_needed`, and an attempt of a later generation, which the device row or another screen started, is left alone.
A row's id, target, address and connect state remain together in `status.machine_profiles`; discovery runs no SSH command, status probe, authentication or reconnect, and an unreadable list is a failed read rather than an empty list.
Configuration-only target resolution reads the account's SSH configuration once with the same 16-file, 256 KiB-per-file and four-level include bounds, compares up to 64 existing registrations, and compares the resulting user, hostname and port together, never the label.
Each configuration file opens through the platform's nonblocking regular-file helper, which refuses a pipe, device, directory or symbolic link at the opened name even if it changes during the open; bounded chunks and include processing check one three-second read budget.
Include expansion shares that absolute deadline across every file and pattern, visits at most 1,024 directory entries, spends at most 1,048,576 units on names and iterative wildcard comparisons, accepts patterns up to 4,096 bytes, and keeps at most sixteen matching paths before sorting.
Crossing an Include bound refuses the whole saved-target configuration; Add device reports a truncated listing and resolves no registered extras from that partial read.
Literal hostnames, `user@host`, SSH URIs and IPv6 destinations need no Host entry; a configuration requiring Match or a proxy route the connector cannot apply remains unavailable instead of silently selecting another route.
`machine_profile_connect` carries only a discovered profile id and explicit helper-installation consent; the core registers the row's Host or WSL distribution through the existing device registry and reuses a device already registered for the same endpoint.
A refusal (`no_consent`, `invalid_target`, `discovery_pending`, `device_limit`) and a connection attempt stay on the selected row.
The existing first-run kit owner supplies the recorded agent choices when that device reports its onboarding hold.
Copy diagnostics carries versions, paths, states and the core's recent diagnostics, applies the shared diagnostic privacy policy below, and has no terminal output or pane input among its inputs.
`retry_connect` is a new connection attempt: it retires the device's coordinator and transports and connects again from its registration, keeping the device focus, and a connected device refuses it.
`remove_device` removes Hide's own record of a device and nothing on it (PRD S5.5 B26): its registration, its project registrations and pins, its expanded folders, its open file tabs and its closed items go, while its host, panes, agents and folders are left as they are; a dirty tab closed this way leaves its draft in the browser, where a draft no tab stands for is offered to export or discard, and the confirmation counts the projects, tabs and drafts before anything is removed.
Before `remove_device` is sent the page writes every draft of that device's tabs it still has queued, and a draft that could not be stored (B44) holds the removal: the confirmation names it until it is saved or exported (Export releases exactly the text it downloaded, so a later edit holds the removal again, and the confirmation then says that draft leaves only as the exported file, because the page cannot confirm the download was kept), since closing its tab would lose it; once the drafts are being stored the removal can no longer be kept from the dialog.
The web's `ui_state_update` echo omits `workspace_registrations` and `device_registrations`, which their own events own, so a stale echo can never undo a registration.
The folds are owned the same way: `project_checkouts_fold` (a flip, or a set when it carries `expanded`), `checkout_agents_toggle` and `agent_tree_toggle` apply against the core's own sets, and `ui_state_update` neither reads nor writes `collapsed_workspace_ids`, `expanded_checkout_ids` or `expanded_agent_pane_ids`; a fold computed from the shell's last snapshot and sent as a set loses a toggle the core has not echoed yet.
It also omits `sidebar_width` unless the action explicitly changes that width, so an unrelated UI save cannot undo a drag before its snapshot arrives.
The accent swatches read the `--color-accent-choice-*` tokens; the chosen value replaces `--color-accent`, and `font_size` scales the interface text tokens, the sidebar's included, through `--interface-scale`; `terminal_font_size` is every terminal's base size in `web/src/terminals.ts`, which a pane's `pane_text_scales` entry multiplies, and the editor keeps `editor_text_scale`, so no two of the three apply to the same text.
`terminal_font_family` is the installed font every terminal draws in ahead of the `--font-mono` token; `web/src/terminalFonts.ts` appends one fallback after that token's generic family, the bundled Symbols Nerd Font Mono as a `FontFace` of its own whose `unicode-range` limits it to the Private Use Areas and whose `size-adjust` fits it to one cell as xterm's WebGL renderer lays a cell out from the primary font, capped by the room above and below the baseline, since xterm draws a fallback glyph at its own size from the left of its cells and cannot scale it; CJK text is left to the system's fallback at the terminal's size.
A fit depends on the primary family, its pixel size and the device pixel ratio, so one fitted set (a plan) serves every terminal drawn at the same three: a terminal holds its plan while it lives and takes a new one only when its size, the Terminal font or the pixel ratio changes, never on attach, a tab switch or a resize; it draws in the primary family until its plan's faces have loaded, then sets the full family, which makes xterm measure its cell again with every font loaded, and only a grid that changed goes out; an unheld plan stays for reuse until eight newer ones push it out, and a face leaves `document.fonts` when no plan lists it.
`@xterm/addon-unicode11` gives the terminals Unicode 11 widths, closer to the widths the pane holder lays its frames out with than xterm's default Unicode 6.

The sidebar's project, checkout and agent rows open a menu on a right-click, or the menu key or ⇧F10 on the focused row (`EntryContextMenu` in `web/src/components/entry-menu.tsx`, rules in `web/src/workspaceManage.ts`, the items in docs/UI_BEHAVIOR.md); an action a row cannot use is drawn disabled with its reason, and one the host cannot perform (Finder in a browser tab) is not listed.
Each item is one existing event: `focus_checkout`, `create_tab` (a device's `remote_control create_tab`), `set_primary_checkout`, `workspace_pin_set`, `remove_workspace`, and the tab close flow's `close_tab` for the tab that holds an agent's pane.
Pin and Remove are offered on a row the engine shows without a registration too (PRD sidebar-context-menus D-14): `workspace_pin_set` with `pinned: true` on such a row registers it with the id, label, root and device the row already carries and pins it in that event, with no filesystem read under the lock, and the next catalog rebuild adopts it as the same row; a device's row qualifies only once its helper grouped it under its root. `remove_workspace` on such a row closes its panes through the same close worker and retires nothing, so the row leaves with the engine's workspace, and every row carries the removal gate's counts.
An agent row carries the session id the engine recorded (`session_id`, absent when none), which Copy session id reads.
The dialogs (`web/src/WorkspaceDialogs.tsx`) send `create_worktree`, `set_checkout_purpose` and `remove_worktree` and read only the receipt for their own request (`task_operation` by kind, id and target; `worktree_removal` by checkout and id), so another page's or an older request's answer is never shown as theirs.
Add a project's Clone from URL is one core job in one slot, `repository_clone` (`hide-core/src/runtime/clone.rs`): the core parses the URL again (`hide_node_link::clone::CloneSource`, which the node parses once more when it reads one off the link: https, ssh, the scp form and `file://`; the name has to be the one the URL gives), refuses a second clone while one runs (`repository.clone_busy`), and lets the same URL and folder sent again join the running one, so a double submit is one clone and one registration.
A worker thread owns the run and takes the lock only to write progress or the result; it asks the node of the machine the clone names, the core's own or a device's (`core.node_link`; `device_id` on the event, judged first by that node's `Call::NewFolderTarget`, `repository.clone_unavailable` when it cannot be reached), for the clone (`repository_clone`), which reports each new stage and, at least once a second, that it still runs, and the worker answers every report with the cancel flag, so a cancel reaches Git within a second; on the node `hide_host::clone::clone_repository` opens the parent under its home by handle and runs `git clone --progress` from the non-interactive launcher (`hide_host::git_run`) with `GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL=https:ssh:file` in its own process group, into the target folder it makes itself through the parent's handle (a create that fails when anything holds the name, refused as `TargetExists`), opens as itself and empty, holds open (`hide_platform::fs::held`) and runs Git in, cloning into `.`, so the folder holds a partial repository while Git runs and nothing renames it afterwards; no step after the hold goes by the target's name, so a parent or target name swapped for a link out of home writes nothing there.
A cancel (`cancel_repository_clone`), the runtime going away, or `STALL_LIMIT` (120 s) without a line from Git stops the whole group, empties the clone's folder through its held handle and then removes the name with a remove that refuses a non-empty folder (never recursively by name), so a cancelled, stalled or failed clone leaves nothing under the target's name, and a non-empty folder put in its place keeps its contents while an empty one can be removed. A finished clone is answered only while its full target path, resolved from the root so a moved or replaced folder above it counts, still names the held folder; otherwise the node answers `moved`, keeps the clone wherever it went and the folder in its place untouched, and the core registers nothing. That check is not an atomic handoff to the registration: a rename between it and `create_workspace` is the same as a rename right after the folder is registered; a daemon killed mid-clone can leave its partial folder under the target's name, since nothing runs to remove it.
Failures are read from Git's C-locale stderr into one `CloneFailure`, which the snapshot carries as its code (`failure`: `authentication`, `unknown_host_key`, `not_found`, `unreachable_host`, `stalled`, `target_exists`, `moved`, `git` or `io`) for the shell to word, with Git's last `fatal:` line, credentials removed, as `git_line` only for `git`; the failure's sentence goes to the `repository_clone` diagnostic, and the URL is kept only in the job, never in the snapshot or a log line, which carry the host.
The stage is Git's own name for it (`Receiving objects` and the like), which the shell words for the six Git prints and shows as cloning otherwise.
A finished clone goes through the same local `create_workspace` event Browse folder sends, so it is registered, refused or deduplicated exactly like a picked folder.
A created worktree's pane is focused with one `focus_pane` once the snapshot lists it, through the same follow a start holds, because only a focus request is tracked until the engine confirms it; focused before the catalog placed it, the worktree's checkout never came forward (with-hide/hide-private#311), and a late focus event for the pane left behind cannot undo the move.
A dialog or sheet returns keyboard focus to a terminal through `focusTerminal` on the core's focused pane (`restoreFocus`), never by re-focusing the textarea that held it, which would be reported as the operator moving there.

The device rail, the sidebar's full-height left column (`web/src/components/device-rail.tsx`), always shown unless the operator hid it, sends `focus_device` for a device tile; each tile's Needs You and unseen Done counts are read from the snapshot's agents in the web, and whether the rail shows is the core's `ui_state.device_rail_visible`, persisted and sent with every `ui_state_update` beside `left_sidebar_visible`.
Selecting an SSH device makes it the context (`web/src/remote.ts`, the remote Agent area in `web/src/WorkspaceScreen.tsx`): the sidebar lists that host's workspaces and agents and the canvas draws its visible tab from `status.remote[].session`, the projection the core already builds over SSH with every id scoped to the target (`remote:<target>:pane:…`).
The web follows the host's own focus rather than keeping a selection, because the core attaches exactly the panes of that host's focused tab and, on a node that dialed in, of the tab each other Agent area shows (`node_shown_agent_tabs`); a pane is placed by the rectangle the engine reports for it, and there is no divider because a remote pane's size is its host's.
Keystrokes and viewport go out with the scoped pane id to the router, which sends them down that device's node link, and scroll to the core, which sends the wheel the same way; focus, split, zoom, close pane, new tab, tab focus and close tab go out as `remote_control` with the device as `target_id` and a fresh `request_id`, and the core checks every id against that host's session before anything is sent, so a stale or local id is refused rather than retargeted.
The pane's own id decides where a click-to-focus goes, and a close confirmation carries the device it was asked about.
A device that is not connected takes no command: the web says so and sends nothing; its sidebar is only the device's name, `연결 안 됨` and `다시 연결`, never its last tree, while the center keeps the last session on screen under a Retry banner while it is `stale`, and draws the connection's own state when there is no session.
The Explorer, file tabs and History run on the device's own helper; worktree creation and deletion, registration, pin and project removal run through the device's engine and helper (see Device catalogs); a tab drag and reopen closed act on the device (see Tab reorder ownership and Reopening locally closed work); find in pane reads the device pane through that device's engine, and a device that is not connected answers the reason in the find bar; a remote checkout's purpose is written through the core.
The core also refuses `create_pane`, whose target is implicit, while a remote device is focused (`pane.device_mismatch`), so a split never falls back to this machine.
Typing into a remote pane makes it the core's terminal pane, so `focus_device` back to this machine, or removing the selected device, hands the keyboard back to `ui_state.selected_pane_id` or the drawn tab's focused pane (`return_keyboard_to_local_pane`).
Registering or removing a device refreshes only the device rows (`rebuild_device_rows`); rebuilding the whole catalog there dropped every checkout's tabs until the next session publish.

### Workspaces in the web shell

The shared Overview (`web/src/Overview.tsx`) keeps its selected device, optional canonical project scope, open panel and tab in window-local `ui.ts` state, and persists none of them.
Work, Projects, Backlog and History use that device and project scope; Usage is independent and keeps the core's own native-node account boundary.
It overlays a mounted Workspace or renders as its central fallback page; its modal is not a Recent Panels visit and Agent cycling uses the existing pane order without a Workspace origin.
Project activation uses `projects.ts` to choose this device's recent usable checkout, then primary, then first usable checkout.
The existing `focus_checkout` payload accepts `project_expanded` alongside checkout disclosure, so admission validates the target before either fold or focus changes and persistence keeps the existing collapsed-project state.


The web shell has a Workspace and one shared Overview page, with Overview also available as a modal over the Workspace (`web/src/{Overview,MainScreen,WorkspaceScreen}.tsx`).
The Overview shows `Work · Projects · Backlog · History · Usage`, initially Work, with the chosen tab retained only for the current window.
Work uses the core's canonical agents, explicit lineage and bounded delivery metadata, Backlog the union of source-qualified project issues, Projects the existing catalog and disk sweep, and History retained requests from the link ledger.
The page, modal visibility, device, project chip, tab and panel are window-local state in `web/src/ui.ts`, never core state, so each window keeps its own.
Recent Panels restores the shared page, while the transient modal does not enter recent history.
Which screen is showing is the shell's own location (`ui.ts`), not core state: the page starts on the Workspace the core has in front only when the core marks it `resumed`, the Workspace the operator last chose, in this process or before a restart (D-11): a `focus_checkout`, `focus_pane` or `focus_tab` the core accepted, or a device `remote_control` focus or Workspace open once the device's front lands there while its request lives (`PendingChoice` names what drops it), so a refusal chooses nothing and a front only the engine's own focus moved is not resumed; a first run, a last Workspace that is gone, or any other front starts on Main once the device in front has settled (`startupScreen` in `navigation.ts`), and moving between screens creates or ends nothing.
A device Workspace is known only when that device's session arrives, so the first screen waits for the device in front rather than for this machine's engine.
Main and Overview first draw the accepted catalog, device sessions and agent rows; a device that is connecting or cannot answer leaves its live counts unknown rather than zero, while Usage keeps its own node's readings.
`runtime/overview_graph.rs` projects explicit current-launch model and effort facts and content-free delivery edges into `model/overview_graph.rs`; delivery endpoints join only with exact device, pane and native-session proof.
Graph metadata contains direction, kind, time and count, never a letter's subject or body, and keeps the newest 2,000 letter edges.
The source delivery ledger keeps its existing 5,000-item admission and finished-item expiry, independently of graph retention.
The renderer groups and lays out these facts without AI inference, with a bounded graph worker and a fifty-row list fallback when layout is unavailable.
`OverviewProjectHome.tsx` combines the retained Project controls with that project's real sessions and checkouts and scoped links into Work, Backlog and History; no second project store is introduced.
`OverviewHistory.tsx` sends a bounded `session_work_search` through the existing link worker after one cancellable 180 ms input debounce, never a background polling timer.
`links/ledger_store.rs::ledger_search_page` applies device, immutable original project root, agent, status and time criteria before SQL `LIMIT 51`, returning fifty sessions plus a continuation cursor ordered by activity, device, agent and session id.
The query is at most two hundred characters and SQL wildcard characters are escaped for literal matching; each session returns at most two bounded snippets with saved request offsets.
Original operator requests are the default search input, including unjudged requests saved while summaries were Off or failed; generated titles and task summaries are opt-in and no raw transcript index is consulted.
Search reuses the existing RPC admission, worker queue, retained-request and 64 MiB ledger bounds; request ids and connection generations reject late answers.
The web keeps one fifty-result page and at most two hundred cursor entries, preserving its query, filters, page, scroll and selected row beneath a wide inert record detail.
Opening a matched request carries its exact retained offset and literal query to Requests; a missing retained offset is unavailable rather than another request's text.
A project's issues and memos ride on its catalog row as `tasks` and a checkout names its item as `task_key` (PRD task-agents-views D-14, `hide-core/src/tasks.rs`): each source has an adapter there that projects its own answer into one source-neutral shape, GitHub issues and Local issues today, so the web never reads a GitHub shape and a later source (Linear) is one more adapter.
`ui_state.project_issue_sources` retains the operator's source default by project path for older entry points, with `tasks::source_kind` choosing GitHub for an eligible repository and Local otherwise when no preference exists.
The Overview projection includes Local issues and eligible GitHub issues together, preserving source-qualified keys, independent failures and the failed source's last known rows.
Local issues live in one file, `local-issues.json` in the state directory (`CoreOptions.local_issues_path`, `hide-core/src/local_issues.rs`): the runtime reads it once when it is created, holds the store in memory, applies a change there under the lock, and hands the whole store to a save thread that writes through a temporary file and a rename, the UI state's own pattern, so no file I/O happens under `Mutex<Runtime>`; a file that cannot be parsed is an error the source reports, never replaced by an empty one, and the store is capped per project and in projects.
A core move keeps the projects of the machine that gives up the core in the same file, under `devices` by the id the folder names that machine by (`node_migration::reown`), and the move back makes them its projects again.
While that machine is a node that dials the core, the core reads and writes its projects' Local issues there, by its node id (`LocalIssueStore::project` and the writes take the machine); every other entry is kept unchanged through every save.
A Local key names only a project path, so `local_issue_update` and `issue_set_open` name the project too, and a key whose path is not that project's is refused rather than applied to another machine's project at the same path.
A checkout of a Local project is linked by the same chain as a GitHub one (the manual `issue` token, a pane token, `branch.<b>.issue`, then the branch number), read as `L-N`.
Creating an issue is `backlog_add` (see [Session work records](#session-work-records)): a Local issue lands in the store and a GitHub issue is a title-only `gh issue create` on the existing worker with its durable intent and repository epoch checks.
`issue_detail_request {workspace_id, task_key, comments_after?}` resolves the owning device from the registered project and checks that the task belongs to that project's projection before reading it.
It reads the actual body and metadata off the runtime lock, with GitHub comments paged fifty at a time up to two hundred and each comment bounded to four thousand characters; a Local issue answers from the existing store.
Every `IssueDetailSnapshot` phase carries `workspace_id`, `device_id` and `task_key`, and the shared `web/src/issueDetails.ts` reader exposes its body, metadata and comments to Backlog detail and Start only when all three match the selected project and item; a matching path or task key alone cannot reuse another device's detail.
The core retains this resolved identity in both the running read and the one latest pending read, and checks the project's device and task membership again before starting queued work and before applying an answer (`runtime/issues.rs`).
An initial read joins only the same three-part identity while it is reading; a comment-page request additionally requires the same current cursor, more available comments, room under the retained-comment cap and no page already loading.
Only the current generation can apply its answer to that identity's slot: an initial answer requires `reading`, while a page answer requires `ready`, a page still loading and the same cursor.
Late or mismatched answers are dropped, and a failed later page retains the body, comments and retry cursor already read.
The existing one running worker, one latest pending request and comment bounds remain; the issue-work slot retains loading, failed, cursor and limited facts.
`local_issue_update` and `worktree_name_suggest` keep their existing store and background-AI paths; the Overview adds no issue writer or poller of its own.
`github_search` (`{request_id, query}`, PRD cmdk-navigation B16-B19) is the one on-demand GitHub search read: the shell sends it when the operator asks, never while they type, and the core runs it on no timer, so an idle daemon searches nothing.
It covers the core's registered GitHub projects (a local Git project whose source is GitHub) and those of a node that dials it, searched by the repository name the node read with the core's login and left out while the node has not named one (`github_search_targets`), at most 20 of them with a `message` on the answer and a `github_search.capped` diagnostic when more were left out; a project the GitHub reader has not read yet is resolved by the search's own worker with the same `gh repo view --json nameWithOwner`, so the search never depends on what was read earlier, repositories are taken once per `owner/name` ignoring case, a project with no GitHub remote is skipped, and a project that fails to resolve for any other reason fails the search, which then cannot say it covered every project.
With no GitHub project it answers `ready` and empty, and a query that is empty after trimming or over 200 characters is answered `failed` in the slot, never as nothing found.
A search is two calls however many repositories there are (GitHub allows about 30 search calls a minute): one `gh search prs` and one `gh search issues`, a `--repo owner/name` for each repository, `--limit 20 --json <fixed fields>`, and the query's words as separate arguments after `--`, so it matches like a search box rather than as one quoted phrase and no word can be read as a flag; the shape is one entry of the node's `gh` allowlist (`hide_node_link::gh::is_search_call`: fixed positions, fixed field constants, up to 20 path-safe repositories, words within the query cap), and `gh search prs` has no head branch, so a hit carries none.
Every call runs under the 15-second `COMMAND_TIMEOUT`, on one `spawn_issue_worker` thread off `Mutex<Runtime>` that makes the repository resolutions and then the two calls one after another, and the answer holds at most 20 pull requests and then 20 issues.
A hit from a repository that was not asked for is dropped, because a `repo:` qualifier typed in the query would widen GitHub's search to it, and a hit's link must be on `https://github.com/`.
It answers in `issue_work.search` (`request_id`, `query`, `phase` `working`, `ready` or `failed`, `results` of `{kind, repository, number, title, state, url, is_draft}` with `state` `open`, `closed` or `merged`, and `message`), absent from the wire until the first search and, like the sibling slots, plain strings.
