A machine that dials this core, the one a core moved off, has its kit kept the same way through its link, with no consent and no helper upload: the core asks with the command folder a device gets by default (`~/.local/bin` in that machine's home, which `HIDE_HOST_CLI_DIR` moves) so the node installs into that machine's own home, from the app it runs (`Services.kit`); removing its row takes nothing off it, since it registers again on its next link.
Each link's kit work ends with that link (`Env.stop`), so a node that dials again starts its kit with a stop of its own.
Two registrations of one account can connect at the same time: the helper upload stages each file under a name no other connection uses, keeps a final file that already holds the expected bytes, and takes a helper folder another connection created first, and the account lock orders the two applies.
An answer a worker brings back after its registration went or its removal started changes nothing (`ingest_device_kit_answer`), so a slow install never brings back a device the operator removed.
A device without consent, with an outdated one, or on a platform this build does not carry installs nothing and its row says why (B17, B21).
Removing a device with its helper connected takes Hide's parts and the helper root off it on that device's worker, after any kit call already running there, and closes the helper connection afterwards; a device added again waits to connect until that is done.
Without a connected helper, the registration goes and a `kit` `device.kit_left` record names what stayed (B24).
The hooks, the `hide` link and the helper root belong to the device account rather than to one registration, so while another registration's consent is bound to the same user and machine (by machine id when both consents carry one, else by the host key both carry, so a consent bound to its machine and one from before that still compare, else by host name and port), removing one of them leaves the kit for the other, records the same `device.kit_left`, and the device row's `kit.shares_account_with` names that registration for the confirmation.
Each machine's report reaches the shell as `DeviceSnapshot.kit` (`components` with `kit_component_id` and `kit_component_state` from `contracts/snapshot-wire-enums.json`, `busy`, `unavailable`, `offers_reinstall`), and every apply writes one `kit` `apply.completed` record naming each part's outcome.
A device's agent panes are judged by the same `hide_agent_hooks::diagnosis::instrumentation` as a local pane, from what the pane's hook reported to the core (`RemoteSessionSnapshot.pane_hook_tokens`, laid from `agent_hooks::facts` and not sent to the shell) and that device's kit (`agent_hooks::device_hook_status`), in `Runtime::derive_device_session` (D-21).
The kit part read is the one for the dialect that counts for the pane's agent (`agent_hooks::kit_hook_status`): Claude Code's or Codex's hook part, or, for an OpenCode or Grok pane, the hook piece of that agent's row (`KitSnapshot.agents`), on this machine as on a device; a change of that piece re-judges the local panes (`runtime/kit.rs`, `pane_judgement_inputs`).
`desktop/e2e/device-kit.spec.ts` proves a device's kit over a real SSH connection: the install, each part's row, the installed hook's SessionStart in a device pane, a part the operator took out staying out until Reinstall, and removal leaving another tool's entries and retained records.
The isolated sshd logs in as the account running the suite, so `desktop/e2e/device-home.ts` proves its private HOME before registering the device; otherwise kit writes would reach the operator's own files.

### Device catalogs

A device's projects are grouped by the same rule as this machine's (`device_catalog.rs`): a project is a repository identified by its main worktree on that device, and each checkout a tab sits in is a row under it, so two engine workspaces in one repository are one project, two workspaces with tabs in one folder are one checkout row, and a workspace whose tabs sit in two repositories is split between them.
The facts come from the device's helper (`Call::Project`, answered by `hide_project::facts` there), asked on a worker once per directory; the runtime keeps the device's session as it came (`device_raw_sessions`) and publishes the grouped one.
A new connection asks about every directory again and re-reads every repository's worktrees, whether its helper or its engine session arrives first, and what the last connection answered stays until the new answer replaces it (`reread_device_facts`), through a Retry as well; removing the device forgets it (`forget_device_directories`), and so does a helper whose machine is no longer the one the operator allowed (`IdentityChanged`).
The answers are kept while the device is, so a pane back in a folder it left is grouped at once; past `MAX_KNOWN_PATHS` directories, or repositories, only those the session still shows are kept, and the prune is logged.
A pane's `hide` command is bound to its checkout when it starts and refused as `pane_changed` if that changed before it ran, so forgetting the facts would regroup the device's panes by folder for the moment the helper takes to answer and refuse every command that straddled it.
Regrouping happens whenever a device's facts, worktrees, registrations or kit change, and the raw rows carry no lineage, so a regrouped session is published only after the lineage pass across every machine (`refresh_agent_lineage`) has put back what a subtree close waits on (`close_descendant_pane_ids`).
Ids stay scoped to the device: a project is `remote:<device>:project:<sha256(device, root)>`, so the same path or repository on two devices is two projects, and a checkout is keyed by its folder (`remote:<device>:checkout:<hash of its root>`, `device_catalog::checkout_id`), so it names no engine workspace and keeps its id as workspaces open and close there.
What a command sends to the host is read from the session instead of parsed from an id (`remote_control`): `create_tab` and a purpose go to the checkout's owner (see Checkout owner workspace), opened first when none is; `focus_workspace` brings the checkout's most recently used tab forward: the core remembers the last tab the device's engine had in focus under each checkout (`device_recent_tabs`, as `visible_tab_ids` does here), and with nothing remembered or the tab gone, the owner's active tab, else the first workspace's; it opens the owner only for a checkout with no tab; a tab or pane command goes to the workspace holding that tab.
A directory the helper has not answered for is a row named by its folder (never by an engine workspace label), holding every workspace in that folder, and `status.remote[].catalog` says why (`resolving`, `unavailable` with the reason, or the folders it refused); it is never grouped into a repository by a guess and never read on this machine, and a registration on another device is never inspected here.
A directory the helper answered it cannot read, such as a worktree whose folder was removed while an engine workspace still holds a pane there, is placed as on this machine (`device_catalog::recorded_place`): by the deepest worktree of the device's Git worktree list holding it, else by the repository the engine recorded for the checkout it attached the workspace to (`workspace.worktree.repo_root`, kept on the raw row as `CheckoutSnapshot::engine_repo_root`, core only, and asked of the helper with the session's directories), and it stays a row of that repository with `exists: false`; only a folder none of them places is a row of its own.
Whether such a folder is a Git checkout is unknown, so a request that would open its owner is refused (`remote.control.checkout_unconfirmed`) rather than opened as the wrong kind; an owner already open there still takes its tabs.
View areas are stored by device and path and file tabs are re-found by path, and a fold saved under an old, workspace-keyed id is renamed to the folder-keyed id when the device's session names that workspace (`device_catalog::legacy_checkout_ids`), so the change loses nothing a workspace-keyed id held.
A device's worktrees are read by its helper too (`Call::Worktrees`, the same `hide_host::worktrees::read` this machine runs in process, keeping what it measured in the device's own state folder across its restarts), on a worker after the device's facts answer and again after each task there, and are carried onto its rows by path as the helper reported them (`device_catalog::apply_worktrees`), so a same path on this machine never lends a device its branch, dirt or gate.
Between those reads the device's own Git watch says what moved (PRD git-freshness D-08): `fetch.rs` keeps one `worktrees::DeviceGitWatch` per connected device, a `Call::GitWatch` over that device's link following the common directories its worktree answer named (`Runtime::device_git_watch_sets`), so finding them asks the device nothing; a repository whose refs, HEAD or worktrees changed and stayed quiet for 300 ms is read again (`Runtime::device_git_changed`), measuring again only the worktrees whose HEAD, index or base refs moved (`reuse_unchanged`), a change during a read is read right after it, a read that failed reads every repository again on the next change the watch reports or 30 s later, whichever comes first (`Runtime::retry_device_reads`), and with no window attached the watches rest and read every repository once they watch again. A new link replaces the device's watch, and one that went down drops it until the link is back.
Creating or deleting a device's worktree takes that device's engine and helper together (`WorktreeTarget::device`): the branch is checked (`Call::BranchCheck`) and the new directory resolved (`Call::Directory`) by the helper before the engine's worktree creation runs there, a deletion is gated on the device's facts, closes that device's panes by the engine's own ids and removes on the helper, and the receipts (`task_operation`, `worktree_removal`) carry `device_id`; the branch-description mirror of a purpose is written on this machine only.
A device's registrations live with this machine's in `ui_state.workspace_registrations`, keyed by the device's project id, and are carried onto its grouped session (`device_catalog::apply_registrations`): a registered project the engine has no workspace in keeps its row with its main checkout, keyed by its folder, and no tabs, and only a registered row carries a pin and the panes a removal would close.
Registering on a device asks its helper (`Call::Registrable`, `hide_host::register::check`), which judges the folder against that device's own home, `~` included, by the same rule as this machine's `$HOME` line, the same function: a folder outside that home is judged only with the event's `confirmed_outside_home` naming it, carried to the helper unchanged, a symlink under home that leaves it stays refused, and home, a folder holding it, or a folder of a repository holding it is never a project; it names the project the folder belongs to, and a project outside that home other than the folder confirmed is asked about by its root (`HostError::confirm`, carried to the shell as `last_error.confirm`). hided passes a device's `create_workspace` through instead of applying this machine's home, and nothing is created on the device; a refusal is named by the helper's code (`workspace.create_refused.not_found`, `.not_a_directory`, `.outside_root`, `.needs_confirmation`, `.project_holds_home`), so the shell words it, and asks its question, as it does for this machine's.
A helper reports in `Hello::windows_drives` where it shows the drives of the Windows PC it runs on when its machine is a WSL distribution (`hide_platform::host::windows_drives`: a kernel release naming `microsoft` or `WSL_DISTRO_NAME`, and `/etc/wsl.conf`'s `[automount]` `root`, `/mnt` by default), and the device row carries it as `host.windows_drives`, which Add a project reads to spell a pasted `C:\` path as that device's own path; an ordinary Linux server reports none.
The registration then opens the project's first terminal there itself, as a registration on this machine does (`checkout_owner::open::spawn_workspace_creation`): once the helper's folder facts confirm the checkout (`request_device_facts`), the core sends the device the same tab request New tab sends, so the shell sends no second event (`open_registration_terminals` in `hide-core/src/runtime/device_catalog.rs`).
At most 16 such terminals are kept waiting or sent at once (`REGISTRATION_TERMINAL_LIMIT`), and each leaves with its device's answer, the helper's failure to confirm the folder, or the device's removal; a checkout that already has a tab there opens none, and its request carries a failure report (`FailureReport::Log` in `hide-core/src/runtime/agents.rs`), so each failure point, a refusal before the send, a worker that did not start or the device's failed, refused or unknown answer, writes the diagnostic log (`registration.terminal_failed`) instead of the notice and leaves no failed operation to retry, and the project stays registered on its start screen; what opens no terminal by choice is logged as `registration.terminal_skipped`.
Removing a device's project closes its panes through that device's engine by their own ids and then removes only the registration, as on this machine.
Opening a registered device project the engine has no workspace in, from its row or a new tab, opens its owner at the registered folder through that device's remote control, keyed by the folder while in flight.

A device's checkouts are found in the same catalog lookup as this machine's (`catalog_checkout`: the navigator, then each device's engine session), and the checkout in front is the selected device's own focus (`front_checkout`), so a file opened on a device lands in the checkout that asked and showing it moves no focus on this machine.
Each device signs in as its own ssh config says, by the system `ssh` itself ([A device's ssh](#a-devices-ssh)).
A local path is judged inside its checkout after resolving the folder that holds it, so a shell that spells `/var` for `/private/var` still opens it, while the document keeps the path as the shell sent it.

### Retiring Home

Hide keeps no Home: an agent or a tab starts in a registered project's checkout, and a start with no project offers Add a project (PRD retire-hide-home D-01, D-02).
Older releases kept `~/hide` on each device, with one link per registered project, a Hide `AGENTS.md`, a `CLAUDE.md` link to it and the marker `.hide-home.json` naming every link Hide made; this release removes what that marker lists, once per device (`runtime/home_retire.rs`, `hide-host/src/home.rs`).
The store the release before wrote flags one registration per device as Home; `persistence` reads the flag once and records a `HomeRetirement` in `ui_state.home_retire` (not serialized to the shell), leaving the registration, an ordinary pinned project, exactly as stored until the helper has looked at the folder (B8, B13).
For each pending device the core asks its helper once, on a worker with the runtime lock released, for `home_retire` (`Call::HomeRetire { keep_empty, settle }`, helper protocol 87; this machine's runs in process) when the helper is ready and the core has seen its projects; a helper older than 87 is not asked and is asked when its updated helper becomes ready (D-06), because connecting replaces a helper whose digest differs.
`keep_empty` is true when the core recorded a session or an open pane in that registration (`home_kept_open`), which keeps the folder as a project even when nothing else is there (D-04, D-08).
The helper removes only what the marker lists: a link while it is still a symlink to the target the marker recorded, `AGENTS.md` only while it is exactly the guide an earlier build wrote (its head, one of two introductions, one bullet per project in the order of the names, its tail; on Windows the marker lists no link and the bullets stand alone), `CLAUDE.md` while it is still Hide's link or import, and the marker last (D-11, B10).
A folder with no marker, a link the operator changed, a guide or a file they touched in any way stay where they are.
A folder that stays keeps its marker through the first call; its answer (`kept`, `marked`) makes the core rename a registration still named `Home` to `hide` and save it, and only then does the core send the second call (`settle`), which removes the marker; a stop between the two asks the first call again with the same answer, so the name and the marker converge (B10).
A cleanup a helper tried and could not finish (an unreadable marker, a refused permission, a file or folder it cannot read, a session store it cannot read) leaves the project named `hide` as well (B11).
When only the marker is left and nothing keeps the folder, Hide first records, in its own store (`~/.hide/home-retiring.json`, written durably), the name it will set the folder aside under (`~/.hide-home-retiring-<token>`), the folder's identity and the marker's text, and then renames `~/hide` to that name without replacing anything; the marker and that folder are removed there. The record, and the folder still being the recorded one, is the only claim Hide has on a folder of that name: a stop after the rename is finished by the next run, which finds no `~/hide`, while a folder that merely has such a name, or took the name before the rename, is the operator's and stays (the stale record is dropped). A leftover that is empty or holds only the marker goes; one that also holds a file that arrived, even after the marker was removed, goes back to `~/hide` whole with its marker (written whole to Hide's own file beside the record and renamed into the empty slot without replacing; a link or any non-file in that slot is never followed or replaced, and fails the call), so the call still answers marked and kept until the core has saved the new name. A `~/hide` that exists again is never replaced: the folder and the record stay, the call fails and a later run finishes the return.
A `~/hide` with no marker, empty or not, is never removed.
The answer (`HomeRetired`: the folder, whether it is `kept`, whether it was `marked`, and the `removed` and `changed` entries) settles the registration: a folder that is gone takes its registration with it, and a folder with no marker changes nothing (B8).
Each retirement holds an exclusive lock on the account's home folder, waits at most 20 s for another and then answers `busy`; the folder is owner-only.
A failure (an unreadable marker, a refused permission, a file or folder it cannot read, a session store it cannot read, a timeout) keeps the project, reaches only the diagnostic log (`home.retire_failed`, design principle 13) and is asked again at the next launch; a refusal is not asked again in the same launch.
Removing a device, or losing its connection, leaves its `~/hide` and its agents on it; registering it again continues them.
The consent contract does not change: the helper's scope already includes `~/hide`, and the add-device wording no longer names it.

### The iOS app host

`mobile/` is a Capacitor host that carries the phone web app (`web/src/mobile/`, the same build the hosted site serves) inside an iOS app, and owns nothing of the phone's behavior: pairing, the relay, conversations and replies stay in the web app.
It owns four things.
The web folder: the loader at the root, the current protocol's bundle and every older `p/<n>/` bundle that `mobile/retained-bundles.json` pins (path, size and SHA-256 per file, reviewed by a person; the build trusts the pin, not the site), assembled by `mobile/scripts/assemble.mjs` and served from the app's own scheme (`capacitor://localhost`), with `server.url` never set and nothing executable fetched when the app runs.
The one runtime fact the web app reads about it, `appHost()` in `web/src/mobile/appHost.ts` (the page's scheme is `capacitor:`): the current protocol registers no service worker, shows no Home Screen install step, words the version screen for the app when the computer is ahead of every bundle in it, and draws a link that is not `https` as plain text, since the app opens nothing else outside.
Those properties hold for the current protocol only: the retained older bundles (`p/1`, `p/3`, `p/4`) predate `appHost()` and keep the behavior they shipped with, so a service worker registration or an install hint in one of them is not a defect of the app host.
The bridge: Capacitor's script message handler answers every frame of the page without asking which frame or origin called, and the phone draws agent-made HTML in a frame (`look-frame.html`), so `BridgeGate` replaces it and passes on only a call from the main frame of the app's own origin that names a plugin in a fixed list (`BridgeGate.appPlugins`), while `NavigationPolicy` is the one rule for both ways a page can leave: a navigation goes on only inside the app's origin or to an `https` address, and `window.open` or a link with a target makes no new window and opens outside only for `https`; every other scheme is cancelled.
The page routing: `PhoneRouter` answers `/p/<n>/` with that bundle's page, where Capacitor's own router would answer the root page for every address without a file name.
The native code is the local Swift package `mobile/ios/App/HideShell`, whose tests load a real web view and prove a call from a sandboxed frame is refused (and that the same page reaches an ungated handler), and the `AppTests` target hosted in the app, which loads the app's own `ShellViewController` and proves the app installs that gate (the test fails if the install line goes), because a package test over `BridgeGate` alone would pass with the gate unused.
`BridgeGate.appPlugins` names five plugins, and `mobile/scripts/check-versions.mjs` fails when that list and the `jsName` of the plugins in the package differ: `HideKeychain`, `HideScanner`, `HideApp`, `HidePush` and Capacitor's `Console`; the check also allows exactly one local package beside Capacitor's (`HidePushCore`) and no other.
`HidePush` has no call that reads a private key, sends an action or takes a key of the caller's own: it reports whether notifications are allowed, turns them on for one computer (asks iOS only then, registers with Apple, makes that computer's key and answers with the public half and the token), forgets a computer's key, hands the page the agent a tapped notification named (once), hands back the text of a reply that did not arrive (once), posts the demo's sample, and opens this app's page in iOS Settings.
The push keys are one Keychain item per computer in a shared group (`<team prefix>.me.grab.hide.ios.push-keys`, `AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly`, not synchronizable, at most 16), which the notification extension also lists; the pairing credential stays in the app's own group, first in the app's `keychain-access-groups`, which the extension does not list, so the extension cannot read a pairing.
The extension (`me.grab.hide.ios.notification-service`, `mobile/ios/App/HideNotification`) has no network and decrypts with `HidePushCore`, the local package the app, the extension and their tests share (the RFC 8291 decryption, the notice, its words); a `simctl push` of the relay's body was not seen to start the extension in the simulator (its notification pipeline finished without a `HideNotification` process), so the simulator proves the extension's class in a test hosted in the app (`NotificationServiceTests`) and only a real phone proves the delivery.

The app's own `UNUserNotificationCenter` delegate (`PushCenter`) receives a tap and a Reply, and `mobile/capacitor.config.json` sets `ios.handleApplicationNotifications` to `false` for that reason: left on, Capacitor's bridge installs its `NotificationRouter` as the delegate when the web view loads and replaces `PushCenter`, so a tap never opens the agent and a Reply typed while the app is open is never sent. `check-release-app.sh` refuses a build whose configuration leaves it on.
A Reply typed on a notification is sent by the app's process (`PushActions`, `ReplySender`) over `RelayPhoneLink`: sockets by `URLSessionWebSocketTask`, the handshake and frame format by the relay protocol library (`hide-relay-ios`, a static library the mini links without Rust), and only the order of join, sign-in, hello, send and result in Swift ([RELAY_PROTOCOL.md](RELAY_PROTOCOL.md#replying-from-a-notification)).
The pairing credential is kept by `HideKeychain` (`PairingKeychain.swift`): one Keychain item per computer in the app's own access group (`<team prefix>.<bundle id>`, named in code from the `AppIdentifierPrefix` the build writes into the Info.plist, so a shared group added to the entitlements later for an extension can never become the group a pairing secret lands in; `PairingKeychainGroupTests` reads the group off a saved item), readable only while the phone is unlocked (`WhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly`), never synchronized or backed up to another device, and the plugin's API is closed (`save`, `read`, `remove`, `list`, each argument checked for shape and size, at most 16 items), so the web app can neither ask for another app's item nor write a value the pairing code would refuse.
The page's own storage keeps only the computers' names and ids, no secret (`appStore` in `web/src/mobile/hosts.ts`), so `HostStore` has two implementations, the browser's and the app's, behind one async interface; the app's runs every operation on one queue, because a list read between a save's Keychain write and its row write would take the new item for an orphan and delete it; a list entry whose Keychain item is gone is dropped, and an item with no list entry is removed.
A Keychain item survives deleting the app on iOS, so the first start of an install, told apart by a marker in the app's own defaults, clears what an earlier install left.
`HideScanner` reads a QR code with AVFoundation, asks for the camera only when `scan` is pressed, and returns the text of the first code that is a Hide pairing link (`PairLink.accept`), which the web app decodes with the same decoder as a pasted link; there is no third-party scanner plugin to keep current.
The camera is set up before the view is shown and a refusal or a failure only changes what it shows (guidance and a way to iPhone Settings), so the close button exists in every state and every way out of the view answers the page's promise once and frees the next press.
The words it draws come with the call (`ScannerText`), from the page's own catalog.
A pairing link `https://app.withhide.dev/#pair=<code>` opens the app through a universal link (the `applinks:app.withhide.dev` entitlement and the `apple-app-site-association` file the hosted phone site serves, which `scripts/phone-release.mjs` publishes and checks); the app registers no URL scheme of its own.
`SceneDelegate` hands the link to `PairLinkInbox` and does not pass a pairing link on to Capacitor's scene proxy, which would keep it in `lastURL` for the life of the process.
The inbox accepts only that exact form (no query, port or user, at most 1024 bytes), keeps it in memory for one minute and gives it out once, to the page's `takeLink`; the web app then asks the person before it connects, so a link never pairs a phone by itself.
The page tells the host its light or dark choice through `HideApp.appearance`, which sets the window's interface style so the status bar and keyboard follow it, and the shell turns the web view's bounce and zoom off, gives the keyboard the bottom of its frame so the reply field stays visible (measured from the window, since the web view is the controller's own view, and with the web view's own keyboard handling taken off so room is made once), and supports the portrait iPhone only.
The build is in [BUILD.md](BUILD.md#the-ios-app).

### The desktop host

`desktop/` is the Electron app this repository ships: it shows the web shell hided serves in its own window, holds no UI state and embeds no daemon.
It meets the daemon only through the `hide` CLI: `hide connect` (reuse the daemon the state file names, or start one) and the attach-only `hide status --json`, so there is one discovery path and never a second daemon.
The CLI is found in this order, every tried path logged once (`desktop/src/main/cli.ts`): `HIDE_CLI_PATH` (an unusable value ends the search), this worktree's newest `target/{debug,release}/hide` when run unpackaged, the packaged app's own `Contents/Resources/hide` when run packaged, PATH, the CLI that last attached, the login shell's PATH (packaged only), then the install folders (`wellKnownDirs`): `~/.local/bin`, `/opt/homebrew/bin` and `/usr/local/bin` on macOS and Linux.
On Windows the CLI is `hide.exe`, PATH is split on `;` and an entry without a drive (`\tools`) is skipped, as `hide_platform::host::find_program` skips it, and no login shell is asked: Windows has none, and an app started from the Start menu already has the account's PATH.
The Windows install folders are each installer's own, for the programs Hide runs: `~\.local\bin` (`USERPROFILE`; Claude Code's installer puts `claude.exe` there, the kit puts `hide.cmd` there for the operator's shell, while the host uses its packaged `resources/hide.exe` directly), `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\OpenAI\Codex\bin` (the Codex installer), `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Git\cmd` and `%ProgramFiles%\Git\cmd` (Git for Windows for the account or the machine), `%APPDATA%\npm` (npm's global folder, where `npm install -g` puts `claude` and `codex`), `%ProgramFiles%\GitHub CLI` and `%ProgramFiles%\nodejs`; a folder whose variable is unset is left out rather than guessed, and `env.locations_missing` names the keys once at start.
An app opened from Finder or the Dock gets launchd's PATH (`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`), not the operator's, so a packaged app normally stops at its own bundled CLI; the steps after PATH exist for a bundle that is missing it: the login shell (`$SHELL`, or the account's login shell in the user database when SHELL is unset, run `-ilc` through `env` with shell-env's Oh My Zsh guards; with neither the step is skipped and `cli.login_path` says `no_shell`, bounded at ten seconds, VS Code's default for the same question) costs seconds on a real rc file and once timed out at five, so it is asked only when PATH and the remembered CLI both miss, and asked again on the next search when it failed.
A CLI found on PATH, through the login shell or in an install directory is remembered in `cli-path.json` under the profile once it attaches, and read back as a candidate that must still be executable; an override, a worktree build or the app's own bundled CLI is never remembered, and an unreadable file is a diagnostic, not a stop.
Every `hide` child also receives PATH with the install folders appended after the inherited entries, with duplicates removed; a daemon newly started by the app inherits that PATH and can find an installed `git`, `gh` or agent CLI even when Finder launched the app with launchd's bare PATH.
When PATH is absent, the child starts with the system's own folders (`systemDirs`) so setting it for user tools does not lose system commands: `/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`, and on Windows the default system Path under `%SystemRoot%` (`System32`, the Windows folder, `Wbem`, Windows PowerShell, OpenSSH), none when SystemRoot is unset.
Attaching to an already-running daemon does not change that daemon's environment.
The host is a small state machine (`desktop/src/main/host.ts`): `connecting` shows the host's own status page and becomes `attached` or `failed` with one of `cli_missing`, `start_failed`, `no_response`, `other_build`, `state_refused` (with the file the daemon refused) `core_newer` (titled as an app to update) or `update_failed` (titled as a core not updated), each naming the core's machine and both builds, and a Retry; `attached` polls `/health` every two seconds without forking, leaves the shell for the `core_newer` or `update_failed` page when a node's health names that reason with its `builds`, and becomes `lost` after two misses, leaving the shell's own disconnected state on screen; `lost` asks `hide status --json` every three seconds and loads the next daemon's URL when it names a different one.
The window takes one navigation at a time: while its status page load is in flight, a render waits for it once and then shows whatever state is current, because a shell load started during it (a daemon that answers at once, as on a relaunch while `hided` still runs) lands but is reported as a failed load and leaves Playwright waiting on a navigation that never finishes, and a Retry hash set before the page commits is lost.
Only `connecting` may start a daemon; Retry, a second launch and a Dock click run it again from `failed` or `lost`.
Quitting the app never stops hided, and the daemon leads its own process group, so an interrupt to the host that ran the CLI never reaches it.
Every child the host starts goes through one helper with a cap of one in flight, a hard timeout and a kill on quit (`desktop/src/main/spawn.ts`), and every environment key it reads is in one registry (`desktop/src/main/env.ts`).
The renderer is sandboxed with context isolation and no Node integration; the preload exposes only `window.hideHost` (`kind`, `onCommand` for the app menu's commands in, `reportBindings` for the stored macOS pane chords out, which the main process takes only from its window's page on the daemon origin, checks as a short string map and resolves with the shell's own rules, `platform`, the host's `process.platform`, which names the OS file manager in the menus, `revealPath` for a menu's `reveal_external` (Explorer, History and sidebar rows and View tabs), which the main process takes only from the same page and only as an absolute path in the wire spelling that exists, and hands to `shell.showItemInFolder` in the system's own, which selects the file or folder in the OS file manager and opens nothing, `probePaths` and `openPath` for terminal links, which the main process takes only from the same page, answering at most 64 absolute or `~/` paths with their physical path and kind, both directions in the wire spelling, and opening only a path it has itself judged not to run anything, `notify` and `onNotificationOpen` for the agents' notifications, which the main process takes only from the same page as an id, a title of at most 120 characters, a body of at most 400 and an `unlessFocused` flag that drops an agent's notification while a Hide window has the keyboard, shows with Electron's `Notification`, replacing and closing the one shown under the same id, and whose click brings the window forward and hands the id back, keeping the last 16 shown for their click (`desktop/src/main/notify.ts`), `withdrawNotifications`, which closes up to 64 of those by id, `notificationPermission`, an invoke answered by the notification permission helper on macOS (`unsupported` elsewhere, `no_service` where no notification service answers), `openNotificationSettings`, which opens Hide's page of macOS's notification settings, and `reportBadge`, the app icon's count of root agents that need the operator, taken only from the same page as a whole number up to 9999, `comeForward`, which the shell sends on the daemon's `window_call` frame after `hide <path>` brought a project in front and the main process takes only from the same page, restoring a minimized window and showing and focusing it as a second launch does, `pickFolder` for Add a project's Browse folder, an invoke the main process answers only for the same page, with `dialog.showOpenDialog` (`openDirectory`, `createDirectory`) as a sheet on its window and the chosen folder in the wire spelling or null (a folder with no wire spelling is refused with the reason, which the page's diagnostic shows), which hided's `$HOME` line then judges like any other path, `openPractice`, which the main process takes only from the same page with one of the interface languages and, optionally, a chapter id in the core's spelling, and answers by opening the practice window on that chapter or its list, or bringing the open one forward, and `browser`, the browser displays' pages, see [BROWSER_DISPLAYS.md](BROWSER_DISPLAYS.md)); navigation and new windows are held to the daemon origin and anything else goes to the default browser; only the daemon origin gets clipboard permissions.
The practice window ([UI_BEHAVIOR.md](UI_BEHAVIOR.md#practice-window), `desktop/src/main/practice.ts`) is a second window on the daemon origin with no preload and no token: its address names the language, the chapter it opens on when one was asked for, the host and the OS the page stands in for, it takes no navigation and opens no window, not even in the default browser (the page holds its own links first, `web/src/practice/outside.ts`), a menu command while it holds the keyboard is dropped rather than sent to the shell, and it closes with the main window.
A window is shown with `show()`, which activates the app, and a second launch or a Dock click shows and focuses it; launched with `--hide-show-inactive` (`desktop/src/main/launchSwitches.ts`), which only the desktop e2e fixture passes, the host uses `showInactive()` and then `blur()` for both, which on macOS orders the window behind every other window without activating the app, so a test run leaves the operator's screen, frontmost app and keyboard alone, and `host.start` records `show_inactive`.
Under the switch the host can still bring something forward in four places the e2e never reaches without focus: `sendCommand`'s `webContents.focus()`, which runs only after a browser page was given native focus, which only `@needs-focus` specs do; restoring a minimized window on reopen; the folder picker sheet; and `reveal_external`, which brings the OS file manager forward; `desktop/e2e/reveal-external.spec.ts` replaces `shell.showItemInFolder` with a recorder for that reason.
One instance runs per profile, closing the last window keeps the app on macOS and quits it on Windows and Linux (`window-all-closed` in `desktop/src/main/index.ts`), as each system's apps do, window bounds persist in `window-state.json` under the profile and fall back to a centered default when missing, unreadable or off every display, and the profile is `hide-desktop` in Electron's application data folder, `~/Library/Application Support` on macOS, `%APPDATA%` on Windows and `~/.config` on Linux (or `HIDE_DESKTOP_USER_DATA_DIR`).
On macOS the main window hides its title bar and keeps the traffic lights (`titleBarStyle: "hidden"`, `desktop/src/main/windowChrome.ts`), placed in the left end of the shell's own 32-point top row, which reserves `--size-traffic-light-inset` for them and is the window's drag area (PRD sidebar-titlebar-refresh D-15).
Windows and Linux keep the system's frame, and the shell draws the same top row without that room (D-17); browser display popups keep their own frame on every system.
The shell learns what the frame takes of its row through `hideHost.onWindowChrome`: `{trafficLights, fullscreen}`, asked once by invoke and sent again on every `enter-full-screen` and `leave-full-screen`, since fullscreen takes the traffic lights away; only the window's page on the daemon origin is answered or told.
The status page is a plain file beside the archive (`app.asar.unpacked/dist/static`, unpacked by `desktop/scripts/package.mjs`), because with the shipped `GrantFileProtocolExtraPrivileges` fuse off `loadFile` answers ERR_FILE_NOT_FOUND for a file inside `app.asar`, and every packaged launch since the fuse landed showed a blank window when discovery failed.
Whether the page is on screen is the host's own record (`statusScreen`), never `webContents.getURL()`, which keeps the address of a load that failed.
When the page file will not load, the host logs `status_page.unavailable` and draws the same reason, lines and Retry on a blank page (`desktop/src/main/statusPage.ts`), whose Retry link reaches it as an in-page navigation; it has no Copy diagnostics.
`desktop/e2e/status-page.spec.ts` covers the blank page in the dev build and, when `HIDE_E2E_PACKAGED_APP` names a package, that the package's own page loads; the dev build's page is a plain file, so only the packaged run can see the archive.
The status page gets the window's preload, but `fromShell` refuses every privileged message from a status URL (the file and the plain `about:blank` form), so the host passes `titlebar=hidden` in its address on macOS and the page keeps a top drag strip of the row's height, under which nothing is drawn.
`hideHost.editorAvailable` and `openInEditor` are Open in VS Code (D-13, D-14, `desktop/src/main/editor.ts`).
The host looks for VS Code once per launch, on the first ask: on macOS the app in either Applications folder, else its bundle id through Spotlight (`mdfind`, three seconds); on Linux the `code` launcher on the children's search path; on Windows `code.cmd` on that path with `Code.exe` one folder up.
An open is taken only from the window's page on the daemon origin and only as an absolute path in the wire spelling naming a folder that exists; macOS hands it over with `open -b com.microsoft.VSCode` and Linux with `code`, each a child of `spawn.ts` with a ten-second timeout, and Windows starts `Code.exe` detached, since that window is the operator's.
Every outcome is a log line without the path (`editor.probed`, `editor.opened`, `editor.refused` with its reason, `editor.failed`), and nothing is shown on screen (B16).
The host draws its own words (the app menu, its role items, the status page, the folder picker and the browser display dialogs) from the interface catalogs in the operator's language (`desktop/src/main/language.ts`; [LOCALIZATION.md](LOCALIZATION.md)).
The core owns the one explicit choice, so the shell reports the confirmed value over `hideHost.reportLanguage` once per change, the main process refuses anything but one of the four languages or null, and keeps the last one in `interface-language.json` under the profile so the menu and the status page are right before any daemon answers.
With no stored choice the host resolves the system language itself (`HIDE_DESKTOP_SYSTEM_LANGUAGE`, else `app.getPreferredSystemLanguages()`), and an unusable stored file is logged and read as no choice.
The menu is rebuilt when its language changes as well as when its chords do; the status page can ask the host for nothing over IPC, so the host passes it the sentences in its address and reloads it when the language changes, and the shell's own page follows the core and is never reloaded for it.
The main process imports a catalog and the translator only, never the shell's store or its React modules.
The host log is JSON lines in `<profile>/logs/desktop.log`, rotated once at 5 MB; it never carries the daemon URL, because the URL carries the token.
The shared privacy policy in `contracts/diagnostic-redaction.json` masks recognized credentials (named assignments, provider tokens, Bearer credentials, connection URL passwords and private keys), email addresses and token-shaped hex runs; macOS, Linux and Windows home prefixes become `~` while path suffixes stay useful.
Structured identity fields declared by that policy retain complete hex correlation IDs and build hashes, so records still distinguish the nodes and builds they describe; a hex run inside prose is still masked.
This exception applies only to generic hex matching; credentials, email addresses and home paths are still masked in those fields, and unknown fields and unstructured text retain the hex rule.
The shared `contracts/fixtures/diagnostic-fields.json` cases exercise both the core's real stderr/file entrypoints and the desktop host's file/stderr log.
A home component may contain spaces, so ambiguous unquoted prose between a home prefix and the next separator is also removed rather than exposing part of an account name.
`hide-memory` owns its Rust implementation and retains its original credential-only, quote-safe match extents for serialized project knowledge; diagnostic text overrides for quoted secrets and truncated keys live alongside those patterns; `web/src/redact.ts` reads the same policy for the shell and host.
Fields named for credentials or authorization/cookie headers lose their whole value, even when opaque; quoted secrets include escaped quotes and whitespace, and an unfinished private-key block is removed through the end of the text.
The core's diagnostic writer masks every string in nested records before JSON serialization, off the runtime lock on its existing bounded queue; `emit` before installation or after draining and `record_now` use the same boundary.
The host masks every string field before writing the identical JSON line to stderr and disk, including its write-failure detail; shell and host status-page Copy diagnostics mask before clipboard or fallback display.
This is a final guard for recognizable text, not permission to log personal content or arbitrary credentials: producers still select safe fields, and older rotated logs are not rewritten.
The shared cases in `contracts/fixtures/diagnostic-redaction.json` run in Rust and TypeScript; the core subprocess and host filesystem tests cover actual stderr and file outputs.
The records `hide connect` writes on its standard error (one JSON object with a `kind` per line, such as `daemon.replacing`) are written there under their `kind` with their flat fields (`cli.ts::cliRecords`), since they are lost with the child otherwise.
An exception or a rejection nothing in the main process caught is recorded there as `host.uncaught` (its kind, message and stack, with any address cut to its scheme and any secret-shaped run redacted), and the app keeps running, as Electron's default does, without Electron's error dialog (`desktop/src/main/uncaught.ts`).
That dialog is a modal the operator can do nothing with (design principle 13), and while it is open a quit cannot finish: a desktop e2e quit once waited behind it until the test timed out (issue 675).
`pnpm --dir desktop package` (`desktop/scripts/package.mjs`) builds the release binaries, ships `hided` (which a device also runs, as `hided node serve`), `hide`, `hide-agent-hooks` and `hide-holder` (the pane holder every pane runs in) flat in `Contents/Resources` beside `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES`, refuses by name and leaves no app when any of them is missing or not executable, compiles the notification permission helper (`desktop/native/notification-status/main.swift`, which asks `UNUserNotificationCenter` for the app's authorization and prints one JSON line) into `Contents/MacOS/hide-notification-status` with the app's identifier embedded as its Info.plist and signs it under that identifier, because macOS keys notification settings to the identifier of the bundle it finds by walking up from the executable, signs the bundle and archives it to `desktop/out/hide-v<version>-macos-<arch>.zip` beside a `.sha256` checksum.
The signature is ad-hoc (`codesign --force --deep --sign -`, then `--verify --deep --strict`) unless `HIDE_MACOS_SIGNING=developer-id`, which signs every executable, the helper included under the app's identifier, with the Developer ID certificate, then notarizes and staples the app (`docs/BUILD.md`).
On Windows x64 and Linux x64 the same script ships the same files, `.exe` on Windows with the pane holder's pinned `holder-conpty/` beside `hide-holder.exe`, in the packaged folder's `resources/`, which is the `process.resourcesPath` the host reads, and `desktop/scripts/installers.mjs` wraps the finished app, unsigned (PRD auto-update D-07), with electron-builder reading it as prepackaged: a per-user NSIS installer on Windows, a deb and an rpm into `/opt/hide` on Linux, and on macOS a dmg and the zip the updater installs, each with the update file its system's updater reads ([BUILD.md](BUILD.md)); `.github/workflows/package.yml` builds each on its own runner, installs it and starts it without a window (`desktop/scripts/smoke-package.mjs`).
On Windows the daemon never runs from the install folder, because the installer stops every program under it and Windows cannot replace a file a running program holds: before it starts anything, the packaged host runs `hide runtime prepare` (`hide-kit/src/runtime.rs`), which copies the package's `resources` folder but the window's own `app.asar` (`hided`, `hide`, `hide-agent-hooks`, `hide-holder` with `holder-conpty/` and the rest) into `~/.hide/runtime/<build>` (named in `hide_kit::layout`; a home inside the install folder is refused), under a lock and through a staged folder whose `.hide-runtime` marker, naming the build, is written last and is what `bundled_kit_dir` recognizes together with those four programs, and answers its path; the host then takes the CLI from that copy, so a reinstall or an update leaves the daemon running, and the panes' holders, which run from `~/.hide/holders`, keep their agents (D-10).
The same step removes a build's copy no program runs from (a copy is kept while any of its files is held by a process, which an exclusive write open of each file asks through `hide_platform::fs::in_use`, since Windows lets the folder of a running program be renamed and refuses only the program's deletion), keeps at most four, and writes `runtime.copy_in_use`, `runtime.copy_remove_failed` and `runtime.copies_over_cap` to the host log rather than the screen (D-11); a prepare that fails is the host's `start_failed`.
On macOS and Linux the same command answers the package's own resources folder and copies nothing.
The host's updater (`desktop/src/main/updater.ts`, PRD auto-update) drives electron-updater for a packaged release build only (a version shaped `X.Y.Z` or `X.Y.Z-rc.N`; on Linux one installed from the deb or rpm, which writes `resources/package-type`; on macOS one in a folder it can write): it reads with-hide/hide's release list through Electron's network stack, chooses the highest release whose update file and installer for this system are uploaded, points the updater at that release's download folder, and downloads in the background; it never downloads on its own, and installs on quit except from a Linux package, whose install asks for a password.
Besides launch and every six hours, it looks again when a window takes the keyboard an hour or more after its last look (`AppUpdates.returned`), and on macOS the last window's close quits the app when an update is ready (`installOnWindowClose`), since a Mac app otherwise keeps running with no window and the update would wait for an explicit quit.
Its state goes to the shell over `hideHost.updates` (`onStatus`, `check`, `restart`, `setPrerelease`), heard only from the window's page on the daemon origin; the rc choice is `updates.json` in the profile, and `HIDE_UPDATE_FEED_URL`, declared in `desktop/src/main/env.ts`, points a CI update test at a local feed instead.
Every step is an `update.*` line in the host log, and a failure is a state the About row shows (design principle 13).
`hide_kit::bundled_kit_dir` recognizes macOS `*.app/Contents/Resources` and the Windows/Linux `resources` folder only when its `app.asar` and the parent folder's Electron `hide[.exe]` exist.
A packaged daemon installs the CLI and the configured Claude Code/Codex hooks and publishes their kit report to This machine; the one-release retirement row reports its outcome on every platform.
A packaged CLI resolves its actual executable path before this check and may replace another build's daemon; a standalone copy cannot acquire that authority through a link that merely looks packaged.
The package smoke uses an isolated home with state beneath that HOME authority to check installation, new-shell command resolution and hooks, then a complete second package fixture whose daemon has an executable overlay to change its SHA-256, proving replacement and refreshed paths without compiling twice.
The app icon's badge is the number of root agents in the Needs You group of every device the window shows, the sum of each device scope's `raised` `needs_you` entry (`needsYouCount` in `web/src/agentNotices.ts`), because the navigator's own scope carries no such group and the sidebar shows one device at a time; it is zero while the notifications switch is off.
The shell reports it once its page holds a live snapshot and then only when it changes; the host draws it with `app.setBadgeCount` on macOS (shown once macOS lets Hide notify) and Linux (where the desktop takes the LauncherEntry API), and on Windows, which has no app badge, as a taskbar overlay dot in the dark theme's `--warning` with the count in words as its accessible description, and clears it whenever the host leaves `attached` (connecting, failed or the daemon lost), since the shell then has no live snapshot to vouch for it.
That report is also the host's sign that the shell can open a notification click: a click that came while the status page showed or the daemon was lost, or one that started Hide, waits for the next one, the latest click winning (`ClickGate` in `desktop/src/main/notify.ts`).
On Windows the host writes each toast's XML itself, with Electron's title and body lines plus a `launch` that names the notification, because Electron 44's own toast carries none and a click on a toast in Action Center after Hide quit reaches only `Notification.handleActivation`, which then could not tell which notification it was; it builds Electron's notification presenter at launch (`Notification.isSupported()`), which starts the thread-pool task that makes the Start Menu shortcut and registers the toast activator, so the shortcut is normally there before the first toast, though nothing waits for it, and a click while Hide runs reaches this process instead of a second instance.
The shortcut is named and drawn from the executable's version resource, which `@electron/packager` stamps with the product name `hide` and `hide.ico`; Electron rewrites it when the folder moves and leaves it behind when the folder is deleted.
On macOS the presenter is not built at launch, because building it asks for permission, which the wizard's step asks at its button (PRD first-run-onboarding D-02).
A notification Electron reports as `failed` is logged as `notify.failed` with the system's reason and never the words; on Linux, where `Notification.isSupported()` says only that libnotify loaded, a failure makes the permission `no_service`, which the wizard and Settings show, until a later notification shows (a daemon that started late); every notification is still tried, while on Windows and macOS a failure is the system declining that one notification and stays in the log (design principle 13).
A tray item, global shortcuts, a pet, file drops into a pane and the usage display are not part of this host yet (issue 184).

### The shortcut registry

`web/src/shortcuts.ts` is one table, command to chord per host, matched on `KeyboardEvent.code` at the window capture phase ahead of xterm and Chrome's defaults and never during IME composition (`web/src/keyboard.ts`).
The `⌘/` sheet is generated from the table.
The table is written in macOS chords; `modChord` gives Windows and Linux theirs (⌘ is Ctrl+Shift, and ⌘ with a ⇧ or ⌥ is Alt+Shift) and `PC_KEYS` the few exceptions, each with its reason, so every reader resolves `systemRegistry(system)` for the system the operator types on (`keySystem` in `web/src/host.ts`, `keySystemOf(process.platform)` in `desktop/src/main`).
A stored set keeps macOS chords (`macChord`), so one set means the same keys on either system; [UI_BEHAVIOR.md: Keyboard shortcuts per system](UI_BEHAVIOR.md#keyboard-shortcuts-per-system) owns the table on both systems and the terminal copy and interrupt keys (`web/src/keys.ts`).
The close chord uses the page's recorded keyboard owner: the focused View display first, otherwise the owned visible pane, with tools, absent or retired owners producing a diagnostic and no close.
The new tab chord reads the same owner (`newTabPolicy`): a drawn View area gets its New tab, an owned pane's Agent area gets an agent tab, and anything else the Agent active area.
The recorder ignores the focus the shell's last element regains when the host hands the keyboard back from a native page to deliver a menu command (`installKeyboardOwner`), so the command runs with the page's owner; once it has run, `noteCommandDelivered` gives the owner to the shell element that now holds the keyboard.
It never closes a whole tab; tab controls and their menus name that intent explicitly.
The explicit Close pane command still closes the core's focused pane through the same confirmation path.
⌘F follows where the operator works: inside a View area it opens the document's find, anywhere else the focused terminal pane's find bar, even with an editor open beside it; Escape and × end the pane search and give the keyboard back to that pane.
A pane whose agent searches its own conversation (`own_find` on its row, from the one table in `hide-core/src/agent_find.rs`: Claude Code's transcript search and Codex's full-transcript find) sends `pane_find_open` instead, because a full-screen agent keeps its conversation inside itself and the pane's scrollback holds none of it, so the find bar would search only the rows on screen.
The core asks the engine off the lock whether the pane has scrollback: with none it sends the agent's own keys with `Engine::send_keys` and the agent's prompt, steps and count take over, and with some (an agent drawing inline, such as Claude Code's default renderer, which has no search of its own) it answers that the find bar opens; a failure opens the bar with the reason.
The find bar searches up to the pane's last 10,000 lines; a pane holder answers at most 2,000 rows (`hide_holder_protocol::MAX_READ_LINES`), so on the core's own engine the node reads that many (`Holders::read`) and the count says the history was cut.
The scrollback is the only witness the core asks, because it does not ask whether a pane is on the alternate screen: an inline agent whose output has not yet passed one screen has no history either and gets its own keys, which for Claude Code's default renderer opens its transcript without a search while the whole conversation is still on screen.
Claude Code's transcript toggles on the key that opens it, so a screen that already shows its transcript footer gets only the search key; the footer is the one witness the agent offers, and a footer that changed sends the full keys as before.
The answer names the request that asked (`find.opened`), so the shell acts on it once, and only while the page's keyboard owner is the one ⌘F was pressed with: an answer that lands after the operator moved the keyboard (a click into a document or onto another pane) opens no bar and takes no keyboard, where it used to give the keyboard back to the agent's pane and the next keys went there.
Settings > Shortcuts rebinds the editable commands (`EDITABLE_PANE_COMMANDS`: split right and down, directional pane focus, zoom, close pane, larger, smaller and reset text, Overview, the direct sidebar command and the device rail toggle, the next/previous Agent pane or focused View tab and global next/previous Recent Panels cycles, and the eight chordless area focus and resize commands `AREA_COMMANDS`) in the running host's own set.
The core and the desktop menu refuse a stored or reported set past `BINDINGS_CAP` (48, in `hide-core/src/runtime/events.rs` and `desktop/src/main/menu.ts`, changed together); `menu.test.ts` fails when the editable list outgrows it.
Directional pane focus reads the drawn pane rectangles only when its chord or menu command is answered, within the keyboard owner's one canvas, and shares the area's edge-neighbour policy (`areaLayout.ts`), allowing one physical pixel for DOM edge rounding at page zoom.
This is O(visible panes) work per invocation, with no resident task, timer or queue; an actual neighbour dispatches one existing pane-focus action, and an outer edge or a zoomed canvas dispatches none.
The area commands have no default chord on any host, so they appear in Settings and the desktop Pane menu without an accelerator until the operator binds one.
Each host keeps its set in the core apart from the other's, because the hosts reserve different keys: a browser's in `ui_state.browser_shortcut_bindings`, and the desktop app's in `ui_state.shortcut_bindings`, the macOS chord set, in the removed native app's text form (`command+shift+return`) and command names (`increase_text_size`), with `toggle_conversation` kept but never run here; a save that omits `browser_shortcut_bindings` keeps it.
The desktop app honours the operator's existing macOS chord set (user decision 2026-09-26): hided passes the state file the removed native app wrote (`~/Library/Application Support/hide/state.json`) as `shortcut_import_path`, and the core reads only its `shortcut_bindings` field, once, while its own set is empty, then records `shortcut_bindings_imported` so a later reset to defaults stays a reset; a missing file imports nothing and a later launch may still import, and an unreadable one is a diagnostic.
The core owns that import rather than any shell (S10), which is why the mechanism survived the removal of the native app that used to write the file.
The window listener, the sheet and the editor all read one effective registry (`effectiveRegistry`), and a chord is refused in its row before it is saved when it breaks the host's rules or is another command's: in a browser it needs ⌘, ⌥ or ⌃ and may not be one Chrome or macOS keeps; in the desktop app a pane command needs ⌘ and one printable key, Return or an arrow, while a navigation cycle also accepts ⌃ or ⌥ and Tab, and may not be one macOS or the app menu keeps; on Windows and Linux the same rules read ⌘ as Ctrl+Shift, refuse the Windows or Super key, and refuse the chords Chrome and the system keep there; a stored set that fails them is dropped whole and the defaults run with a diagnostic.
While a row records, the listener runs no command, and IME composition never records.
The Electron column is the macOS chord set the desktop app uses, with ⌘/ kept from the browser because the macOS set has none: the desktop app has no browser keeping chords, so the moved ones return to ⌘.
Each surface reads the running host's column (`web/src/host.ts`: `window.hideHost` means the desktop app): the window listener, the ⌘/ sheet, which drops the "moved for Chrome" note there, and every hint that names a chord.
The desktop app menu is built from the same column for the running system with the stored set applied (`desktop/src/main/menu.ts`), and carries macOS's Services and Hide items only there: the shell reports the set over the bridge when it changes and the menu is rebuilt only when its chords do; a click reaches the same `run` path as a chord, and a chord the listener answers calls `preventDefault` in the page.
The Agent pane or View tab cycles use ⌃Tab in Electron and ⌥Backquote in a browser, with ⇧ for backward; global Recent Panels has distinct command IDs and no default chord, and Recent Projects retains ⌥Tab on macOS.
`areaCycle.ts` routes a View keyboard owner to that area's tabs; every other owner, including sidebar, tools and screens without a drawn Agent area, gets the existing bounded recent Agent pane list across devices, projects and checkouts.
Only an actually focused drawn Agent pane supplies the cycle origin and records a pane visit; a focused View with no other tab stays a no-op rather than falling through to Agent panes.
Main and Overview ignore a View owner left recorded when a shortcut unmounted the Workspace, because no file holds the keyboard on those screens.
One frozen cycle is held in `ui.ts`; membership changes prune candidates, a disappeared View scope cancels, and release dispatches one pane-focus action for an Agent or one `view_layout focus` for a View.
`viewFocus.ts` publishes only owner changes to a bounded set of mounted area subscribers; Agent Views and the lane derive their foreground-colored tab underline from that one owner.
Native browser `before-input-event` matches the same effective registry before the page or menu consumes a cycle key and forwards input through the existing trusted browser bridge.
The host retains at most one held page/release modifier with a cycle identifier, clears it on matching shell completion, window blur, page failure or destruction, and rejects starts from hidden or unfocused pages.
Release from another native page keeps the initiating scope, and a late completion cannot clear a newer hold.
Committed View cycles request keyboard follow after the core confirms selection; a native-page focus intent is bounded to one slot and delivered after visible-slot sync, only in an already-focused window.
Cycle menu items carry no accelerator, so native page and renderer input have one owner; a menu click selects immediately through the same command path.
This adds no per-key subprocess, file I/O, second history, notifier fan-out or unbounded queue; the held preview changes page-local state, and only a committed selection reaches the core.
The numbered chords (`select_tab_1..9`, `select_agent_1..9`, `select_device_1..9`) exist only in the Electron column: their target is the screen order the page knows (`web/src/numbering.ts`: the tabs of the Agent area in use, ⌘9 its last, read from the frame the Agent column last drew, the single sidebar's physical pane occurrences, with raised duplicates assigned only at their first occurrence, and the device rail's tiles, the window's machine first, whether or not the rail shows), so the page answers them and the app menu carries no item or accelerator for them (`KEYBOARD_ONLY`); a pane chord rebound onto ⌘n or ⌥⌘n is refused as that command's, and a stored one already there is dropped alone.
The hold hint is a pure state machine (`web/src/hints.ts`, ported from the removed native app's `HideHintState`: one modifier set, one deadline, revealed after 150 ms of the exact hold) fed by the same window listener from keydown, keyup, blur and visibilitychange, and cleared by any key during the hold or by a layer opening in the ui store; the listener publishes only the family the state reveals (`ui.hint`: `tabs`, `agents`, `devices` or null), computed from the registry's chords for the running host, so a browser reveals nothing and an unrevealed hold renders nothing.
The keycap is `web/src/components/ui/keycap.tsx`, an absolutely positioned overlay the Agent tabs, the sidebar agent row and the device rail's tiles draw only while their family is revealed.
The ⌘/ sheet folds each family into one row with its range (`sheetRows`), and Settings > Shortcuts lists all three read-only.
The design relies on Electron handing a key to the page first and to the menu only when the page leaves it unhandled, so one press runs one command; that order is an assumption, not a verified fact here.
The e2e covers each path alone (a Playwright chord, a main-process menu click, one `create_tab` each), neither reaches NSMenu, and a native keystroke against the app has not been checked: if one press runs twice, the listener stops answering the chords the menu owns in Electron.

The table below is written in macOS chords; Windows and Linux press each one through the rule and its exceptions ([UI_BEHAVIOR.md: Keyboard shortcuts per system](UI_BEHAVIOR.md#keyboard-shortcuts-per-system)).
